Colom’s election will oust Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith and add to an explosive series of Democratic victories in midterm elections that have shifted the balance of power in Congress and are likely to derail the final two years of Donald Trump’s administration.

Colom’s victory also is a seismic rebuke against threats to the ballot box and the relics of a bloody history that made Mississippi among the hardest places to vote in the country.

Mississippi was one of two states alongside Alaska where Americans are still eagerly anticipating the results of Senate elections more than one week after Election Day. Democrats are projected to hold at least 55 seats in the Senate and more than 255 seats in the House of Representatives.

open image in gallery Democrat Scott Colom is projected to flip a U.S. Senate seat in Mississippi held by Republican incumbent Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith, notching another historic Democratic victory in midterm elections that have tipped the balance of power in Congress ( AP )

“While this is not the outcome we worked for or hoped for, I respect the decision of Mississippi voters,” Hyde-Smith said in a video statement Wednesday night. “I want to congratulate Scott Colom and wish him well as he takes on the tremendous responsibility of representing our great state.”

This week, all eyes were on Hinds County, Mississippi’s most populous county and a Democratic stronghold that spans the state’s capital of Jackson, where election officials tallied remaining ballots.

Most of the remaining ballots in the state are affidavit ballots, which voters cast if they did not bring identification with them to the polls or were listed as having an inactive voter registration.

Voters cast 2,426 affidavit ballots in Hinds County. Election officials rejected 1,609 of them, and the vast majority of accepted ballots were cast for Colom.

By Wednesday night, Colom’s lead in the state increased to more than 5,000 over Hyde-Smith, with 99 percent of ballots counted, according to unofficial results from the Associated Press. Colom’s campaign and election analysts determined outstanding ballots would not make up the difference.

Mississippi law does not provide for a recount process for Senate races.

open image in gallery Mississippi election officials continued to tally affidavit and mail-in ballots more than a week after Election Day in a contest that put Colom roughly 5,000 votes above Hyde-Smith ( AP )

The state — marked by a lethal history of voter suppression — is also one of only three states that do not allow early in-person voting and among a dozen that do not allow universal mail-in voting. Republicans have also tried to throw out mail-in ballots that were postmarked before Election Day but arrived later, a challenge that the Supreme Court rejected earlier this year.

Mississippi also has retained a Jim Crow-era law that imposes a lifetime ban from the ballot box against anyone convicted of certain felony crimes, a law that currently disenfranchises nearly 70,000 disproportionately-Black residents — or about 3 percent of the state’s eligible voting population.

Roughly 40 percent of Mississippi residents are Black, but the state’s political makeup for decades has largely been made up of white officials at the state and federal level.

According to the Movement Advancement Project’s ranking of voter access by state, Mississippi is dead last.

“Scott Colom’s historic win is the product of years of organizing and community engagement by groups on the ground, who laid the foundation for the change we’re seeing today,” said Amir Badat with voting rights advocacty group Fair Fight.

“Black voters in Mississippi overcame incredible obstacles — long lines, broken voting machines, voting location changes, and more than 230,000 voters recklessly made inactive and essentially forced into a second class ballot — and still turned out in historic numbers,” Baday said. They made it clear that their voices must be heard, and they took action to win the change they deserve.”

open image in gallery A color lithograth J. Hoover from 1881 depicts abolitionist Frederick Douglas between Mississippi Senators Blanche Bruce, left, and Hiram Revels, right, who were the first and only Black senators from the state until Colom’s election ( Getty Images )

In 1870, the Mississippi legislature sent Hiram Revels to fill one of the state’s two Senate seats left vacant after the Civil War. The country’s first Black senator filled the seat previously held by Confederate Albert Brown, a slaveholder who championed what he called the “blessings of slavery” beyond American borders.

Several years later, Blanche Bruce was elected to the seat once held by Confederate President Jefferson Davis.

But in the turbulent aftermath of the Civil War and emancipation, from white militia terror during Reconstruction through the decades-long Civil Rights movement, Mississippi never elected a Black senator again.

The state’s last Democratic senator was aligned with the conservative Dixiecrats before a massive political realignment flipped the party platforms in the wake of civil rights progress and New Deal economic policies.

John C. Stennis — the state’s last Democratic senator — opposed school integration, voted against the Civil Rights Act and the Voting Rights Act, and tried to block the creation of Martin Luther King Jr. Day as a federal holiday. He served for 41 years until his retirement in 1988.

In 1934, as a trial prosecutor before his political career, Stennis was at the center of a murder case that led to a landmark Supreme Court ruling that determined confessions could not be coerced through violence and torture.

Stennis had argued for a jury to convict three Black men accused of murdering a white man. One of the men on trial was non-fatally hanged twice and beaten while in custody. The others were also beaten until they confessed.

They were each found guilty and sentenced to death before their convictions were overturned.

Like Stennis, Colom worked as a prosecutor and a judge before launching his political career.

Colom, a seventh-generation Mississippian, was nominated by then-President Joe Biden to serve as a federal judge for the Northern District of Mississippi in 2022.

But his nomination was blocked by one of the state’s two Republican senators: Cindy Hyde-Smith.

“To see him now elected to the very Senate where his nomination was blocked is especially meaningful and a testament to his perseverance and the trust Mississippians have placed in his leadership,” said Rep. Bennie Thompson, who has been the only Democrat in Mississippi's congressional delegation since 2011.

“Having another Mississippi Democrat alongside me in Congress who understands the needs of Mississippians means a great deal,” Thompson said. “Together, we will fight to improve access to health care, strengthen public education, expand economic opportunities, and ensure our rural and underserved communities are not left behind.”

News.title: Experts give bleak prediction for UK housing market with sales set to drop to lowest level in years
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Housing market experts are bracing for a weaker year ahead for home sales, with transaction expectations dropping to their lowest level in over three years, according to surveyors.

The Royal Institution of Chartered Surveyors (RICS) said a net balance of 17 per cent of professionals expect sales to fall over the next 12 months, marking the most downbeat outlook since July 2023.

RICS reported that higher mortgage rates continue to weigh on buyer demand.

A net balance of 24 per cent of property professionals reported new buyer inquiries falling rather than rising, according to the October survey. This was unchanged from September, with nearly all parts of the UK experiencing either falling or stagnant demand, RICS said.

open image in gallery House sales are expected to fall over the next 12 months (Steve Parsons/PA) ( PA Archive )

Agreed sales also slipped, with a net balance of 24 per cent of respondents reporting a decline, marking the weakest reading in three months. A net balance of 36 per cent of property professionals saw house prices fall, after values had previously shown signs of stabilising over the summer.

London, East Anglia, the West Midlands and the South East recorded weaker price trends than the general average, the report noted.

Prices continued to rise firmly in Northern Ireland, while modest growth was also reported in Scotland and the North West of England.

Property professionals also revised down their price expectations for the year ahead, with a net balance of 17 per cent expecting falls, deteriorating from a flat reading of zero previously.

The pipeline of new listings could also weaken, with fresh instructions to sell falling marginally overall during October after previously increasing.

In the lettings market, pressure on rents strengthened as tenant demand saw modest growth while landlord instructions continued falling.

RICS head of market research and analysis Tarrant Parsons said: "Home buyer demand remains subdued and respondents are bracing for a weaker year ahead for sales given the persistent macroeconomic challenges being faced."

News.title: Ebola could be raging in DRC for another year, expert warns
News.content:
The Ebola epidemic currently raging in the Democratic Republic of Congo could last at least another year, a leading UK epidemiologist has warned.

Experts have struggled to contain the current outbreak since the first cases of the rare Bundibugyo strain of the disease were reported in May.

There have so far been almost 11,000 cases including 5,000 deaths, making it the second largest outbreak in history, after the devastating West Africa epidemic of 2014-16. Cases have also been reported in Nigeria and Kenya, although transmission has not been widespread.

The outbreak is taking place across a vast area of DRC - North Kivu and Ituri - where conflict and widespread mistrust of authorities, including health workers, have hampered the response.

Neil Ferguson, professor of epidemiology at Imperial College, London, told a press briefing that at the current rate of disease spread that the epidemic could still be ongoing at the end of next year.

“Controlling Ebola outbreaks takes a long time so it is highly likely we’ll still be seeing transmission in a year’s time,” he said.

“We’re ticking over at about 70 confirmed cases a day at the moment and that’s almost certainly quite a significant underestimate of the true number of infections,” said Prof Ferguson, who rose to prominence at the beginning of the Covid pandemic when he advised government on the likely trajectory of the outbreak.

News.title: Many more cattle ranch workers infected with H5N1 than reported, says US farming union
News.content:
Far more US farm workers are infected with bird flu than officially reported, with some suffering “very severe” symptoms, according to the country’s largest farming union.

H5N1 is currently spreading rapidly across US cattle farms in dozens of US states.

Officially, just three people have been diagnosed with the virus in the past month, all following close contact with infected cows.

In total, 73 people in the US have been officially been recorded as infected with H5N1 since 2024, mostly dairy farm workers. Three have died.

But United Farm Unions (UFU), which represents thousands of workers across the US, said it was aware of many more farmers experiencing symptoms consistent with H5N1 who had not been tested.

“We have now connected with a number of workers and have confirmed that more workers are sick with avian flu symptoms who have not been tested,” the UFU wrote on X.

Symptoms range from “very mild to very severe”, the post added, including mild upper respiratory infections and conjunctivitis to severe flu-like symptoms, bone pain, persistent coughing and high fever.

The ongoing outbreak is worrying disease experts.

“H5N1 is not a virus to be casual about- or to let spread unchecked, given every mutation is like the virus buying a lottery ticket to acquire human-to-human transmission,” said Dr Devi Sridhar, a public health researcher at the University of Edinburgh.

Referring to the statement by the UFU, Professor Francois Balloux, director of the UCL Genetics Institute, added: “The most puzzling aspect to me is not even the incompetence and paralysis of the authorities but the resignation and fatalism. It feels like reading some chronicle by a mediaeval peasant.”

Of the roughly 1,000 people infected with H5N1 since the virus was first identified in the late 1990s, almost half have died. However, most historical cases have resulted from contact with wild birds, while the strain circulating in cattle, known as genotype B.12, is thought to cause much milder illness.

Concerns have nevertheless grown after an unidentified farm worker in Washington state died in late October from the cattle-derived H5N1 strain, raising questions about whether the virus may have mutated.

The Trump administration has been heavily criticised for allowing bird flu to run rampant through America’s wild and domestic animals, putting people at risk.

Deep cuts to the federal agencies responsible for managing human and animal health, the US Centers for Disease Control (CDC) and the Department of Agriculture (USDA), have resulted in the scaling down of surveillance and testing programmes amongst both livestock and farm workers.

Every infection, animal or human, raises the chance the virus could mutate and eventually gain the ability to spread between people – something which experts have long warned could trigger the next pandemic.

As flu season begins, experts are concerned a dairy worker infected with ordinary seasonal flu could catch H5N1 at the same time, and the two viruses could mix to create a new, more dangerous strain that could spread between people – a phenomenon known as “reassortment.”

“It is clear that workers are not being informed of the risks of handling sick cattle and infected milk. They are being given no information on flu shots or avian flu testing,” the UFU said.

Estimates suggest that over half of the 150,000-strong dairy workforce in the US are immigrant or undocumented workers, driven in part by high demand for intensive year-round labour and a lack of domestic applicants.

Many are reportedly worried about coming forward for testing over fears they will come into contact with US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), the federal agency emboldened under Trump, which has been tasked with deporting one million immigrants every year.

Yakima Valley, the region of Washington State where the three recent H5N1 cases have been reported and where the virus is spreading through dozens of dairy herds, is in the midst of an ICE crackdown.

News.title: Young women must ensure they are vaccinated as measles cases surge, doctors say
News.content:
But the dangers for pregnant women, say experts, are often ignored.

There has been relatively little data on maternal and infant measles deaths related to pregnancy in the West since the late 1960s, after the MMR vaccine was introduced and case numbers fell significantly.

Pregnant women are known, however, to be much more vulnerable to illness from measles than others, as the mother’s body, to stop it from rejecting the pregnancy, shifts its immune response significantly and becomes more susceptible to disease.

Between 2000 and 2025, 36 children and adults died from measles or related infections in England and Wales, according to NHS data, but whether or not any of those people were pregnant has not been made public.

“Given the recurrence of measles outbreaks and the number of cases occurring in adults, there may be value in better understanding the impact of measles infection during pregnancy in the UK,” Kirsty Le Doare, professor of vaccinology and immunology at City St George’s, told The Telegraph.

One study by the US CDC conducted in Namibia looked at 55 unvaccinated women who contracted measles during their pregnancies.

Of them, 53 required hospitalisation for complications arising from the virus, ranging from severe diarrhoea, pneumonia, and encephalitis (swelling of the brain).

Another meta-analysis, published in The Lancet in 2018, analysed data from 19 academic papers from countries including France, Germany, and the UK that had studied pregnancy-related measles between 1941 and 2012.

Of 420 pregnancy-related measles cases, 18 deaths occurred, mostly from pneumonia.

“Measles in pregnancy is serious and can cause stillbirth, premature labour and miscarriage,” the NHS website reads. “There is no medical treatment for measles; MMR vaccination is the best protection against becoming seriously unwell,” it adds.

“We know that if you catch measles during pregnancy, you are very likely to end up in hospital,” Professor Helen Bedford, a professor of children’s health at Great Ormond Street Hospital, told The Telegraph.

“You are much more likely to have pneumonia, and there are higher rates of encephalitis. These are all complications that can happen in adults with measles, but they do seem to occur at much higher rates during pregnancy,” said Prof Bedford.

News.title: Gaza floods are an “immediate humanitarian emergency”, warns Trump’s Board of Peace
News.content:
Donald Trump’s Board of Peace has accused Israel of an “insufficient” response to deadly floods that have hit the Gaza Strip.

In a rare statement, the US-led body, charged with ending war in Gaza and rebuilding the Strip, called on Israel “to act immediately to authorise and facilitate the entry of all necessary winterisation and humanitarian supplies”.

“The situation no longer represents simply a threat posed by the approaching winter, but an immediate humanitarian emergency,” they said on Monday.

The Board has been pushing Israel for at least a month to speed up its “winterisation” policies so that residents in Gaza are better able to withstand the coldest months of the year.

The statement followed a weekend of torrential rain and winds that battered the decimated territory’s displacement camps, causing widespread flooding, landslides and several deaths.

A mother and her three young children were killed when a sand dune collapsed onto their tent in Deir al-Balah, central Gaza. The children, aged four, five and eight died on Sunday. Their mother also suffocated under the sand.

News.title: Fears over Ebola spread in DRC as patients flee attack on treatment centre
News.content:
A statement from the health body said: “Health facilities have been attacked and patients, including hundreds people with confirmed or suspected Ebola infection, have fled in search of safety raise serious public health concerns.



“In an Ebola outbreak, every interruption to patient care, contact tracing and disease surveillance creates additional risks for communities already facing extraordinary hardship.



“People must be able to seek treatment safely, and health workers must be able to deliver essential services without fear of violence.”



The body called for a “corridor of peace, protection of civilians, patients, health workers and health facilities, and for safe, sustained access to affected communities”.



The ADF is one of the most feared of scores of armed militia operating in eastern DRC.



The group was originally formed in Uganda in the 1990s by people accusing the government of persecuting Muslims. The army routed the group and the remnants fled across the border, starting a campaign of terror in DRC, before swearing allegiance to IS in late 2018.



The group has since become notorious for its bloody attacks on civilians, which human rights groups say have amounted to war crimes or crimes against humanity.



Earlier this year, Amnesty International, said that advances by the separate Rwanda-backed March 23 movement (M23) militant group in the same region had left Congolese forces overstretched. The ADF had been able to increase attacks in the resulting security vacuum.



The charity said the great majority of victims were Congolese Christians, but the ADF also kills local Muslims who disagree with their interpretation of Islam.



Officials said the attackers struck the village about 30 miles west of Beni around 11 pm local time ‌on Thursday, officials said.



The medical director of the Kelele hospital, Dr Christian Kakule Vulembera, told Radio Okapi, a UN-backed radio station: “Around midnight, the hospital emptied of its patients. All the patients left, including those who were in isolation for suspected Ebola virus infection.”

Attempts to curb the Ebola outbreak have been undermined by suspicion and poor security, with local people frequently turning on health workers.



Conspiracy theories are rife that the outbreak is a hoax to enrich aid agencies, or alternatively that health workers are spreading the disease for their own ends.



Doctors Without Borders, the medical aid charity, over the weekend condemned an attempted arson attack targeting an Ebola treatment centre in Biautu, Beni, North Kivu, where 36 patients were hospitalised.

Protect yourself and your family by learning more about Global Health Security

News.title: Man Utd are in relegation trouble and Carrick must be sacked
News.content:
Michael Carrick says he has been given no assurances about his future beyond this afternoon’s crucial game against Aston Villa at Old Trafford.



United are searching for only their second Premier League win of the season and first in 70 days after the club’s worst start to a campaign for 40 years piled the pressure on Carrick.



They dropped into the relegation zone last night following Nottingham Forest’s victory over Manchester City and will be bottom by the end of the weekend if they lose to Villa and Crystal Palace and Sunderland both win.



The Old Trafford hierarchy opted to give Carrick more time to try to turn their season around following a 3-0 hammering by Bournemouth and 4-1 drubbing in Como, since when United have been beaten 2-0 by Chelsea and recovered from two goals down to overcome Roma 3-2 in the Champions League on Tuesday night.



Asked if he had been told outright he would still be in charge next week, Carrick said: “No - no. Just carry on as absolute normal.”



Pressed on when he felt his future was uncertain, the head coach added: “No, no. Whatever happens and what’s going to happen is going to happen in terms of the game, we’ve got to prepare right.



“I’m really looking forward to playing at home on the back of the other night. The supporters are hopefully looking forward to coming and energised and feeling good about what they might see and we’ve got to repay that.”



Another defeat would leave the United board with a big decision to make around Carrick’s future at a time when they are under severe attack from the fanbase.



United’s game against Roma was briefly interrupted when tennis balls were thrown on to the pitch in the first half of a game notable for more furious protests against the Glazers and Sir Jim Ratcliffe.



Three people were arrested by Greater Manchester Police for throwing items on to the pitch and are understood to have been hit with automatic three-year football banning orders as a consequence.



More in-stadium demonstrations are expected today with regular match going fans encouraged not to buy alcohol or drinks inside Old Trafford and again release green and gold balloons before kick-off.



Green and gold were the club’s original colours as Newton Heath and have become a symbol of protest against the ownership.



Asked why there had been such a big drop-off from last season, Carrick added: “It’s just inconsistency, that’s within games,” he said.



“It can be a number of things, it’s never just one thing: a bit of decision-making, a bit of concentration, things going against us in certain points, sometimes we haven’t helped ourselves. So there’s no excuses for it, it is what it is. The great thing is we can do something about it.”

News.title: Energised England deliver statement win to take heat off Borthwick
News.content:
England’s players delivered on their self-created ultimatum to “do it for Steve” by annihilating an abysmal Australia. Barring an extraordinary sequence of events, Borthwick will now remain as head coach through to the World Cup.

Even if Rugby Football Union chief executive Bill Sweeney’s vote of confidence in the head coach last week was delivered without caveats, he would still have been forced to play the role of reluctant Caesar if the crowd turned mutinous, as they did four years ago. That resulted in Sweeney delivering the thumbs down on Eddie Jones’s reign.

Yet this did not come to pass, as England showed plenty of fire and fury on behalf of their head coach after his control of the dressing room was questioned last week. With 14 minutes to go the crowd, who had been muted on Remembrance Sunday, broke into a rendition of Swing Low, indicating their own approval.

It was not perfect. Attack coach Lee Blackett will be hugely frustrated that they only scored seven tries from a staggering 22 entries into the Australia 22. They also took their foot off the Wallabies’ throats in the final quarter, although they did surpass their highest points total against the visitors. Probably the biggest disappointment was the injuries suffered by wing Immanuel Feyi-Waboso and centre Seb Atkinson, who had both enjoyed strong games until that point.

Sports.title: WTA Finals: Sabalenka stunned by Andreeva as Svitolina battles back vs Muchova
Sports.content:
World No 3 Mirra Andreeva booked her place ‌in the semi-finals of the WTA Finals with a stunning 6-4 6-0 win over Aryna ‌Sabalenka on Wednesday, while Elina Svitolina battled back to beat Karolina ​Muchova and keep her hopes alive.

Andreeva, the 19-year-old French Open champion, won her second straight ​Group 2 match and advanced as group ‌winner after Svitolina earlier defeated Muchova 3-6 6-2 6-2.

The result eliminated Muchova from ​semi-final contention, while Svitolina will face Sabalenka in Friday's final group match with the remaining place in the last ​four at stake.

Svitolina, who was demolished 6-4 6-0 by Mirra Andreeva in her opening round-robin match, told Sky Sports: "It was not an easy task to do.

"I was pretty angry at myself, to be fair, after the first match and after the first set also. Things didn't go my way, so I tried to direct this anger towards the ball and found my game in the end.

"I played good. I think the level was back in the third set. I just tried to give it all in this match because I know I would be eliminated if I lost.

"So I just tried to really release all this energy and find, you know, these openings against Karolina. She's such a tough opponent.

"It's the last tournament of the season, so you know, I just have to really put my head down and deal with all the small injuries.

"I mean, it's normal that everyone is tired. Everyone is struggling with something here and there. I will just try to do my best, have an ice bath and try to heal as much as possible in like 48 hours."

Britain's Norrie beaten by Fritz at Stockholm Open

Britain's Cameron Norrie was knocked out of the Stockholm Open on Wednesday following a straight-sets defeat to Taylor Fritz in the round of 16.

World No 10 Fritz battled to clinch the first set 7-5 and subsequently wrapped up the win with a 6-3 victory in the second set to book his spot in the quarter-finals.

Image: Britain's Cameron Norrie was knocked out of the Stockholm Open by the USA's Taylor Fritz

Norrie reached Tuesday's last-16 clash with a straight-sets win over James Duckworth in the opening round, while No 1 seed Fritz received a bye into the second round.

Fritz started the match strongly with two aces to hold in the opening game, but had his serve broken by Norrie in the third game.

The Briton strengthened his grip as he held his serve, but Fritz replied with a break of his own to take the contest to 5-5.

He piled on the pressure, serving three aces in the following game and broke Norrie's serve in the 12th game to win the first set.

A tight tussle saw little separate the pair in the second set until Norrie had his serve broken in the eighth game and Fritz subsequently held serve to see out the match.

Sports.title: Porter: PL darts format 'solid' as 'fresh concepts' loom and Smith enters the mix
Sports.content:
The current Premier League Darts format is "solid" but "fresh concepts" are coming soon, says PDC chief executive Matt Porter.

Speaking to Sky Sports on Wednesday, Porter touched on whether changes are coming to the Premier League, and also whether Ross Smith may be included and Michael van Gerwen may miss out on the tournament in 2027.

Premier League Darts, broadcast exclusively live on Sky Sports, has undergone several format changes since its launch in 2005. The most recent revamp, introduced in 2022, saw the competition reduced to eight players, with a nightly winner crowned at each weekly event.

Under the current format, each of the 16 regular league nights features a mini-tournament, consisting of quarter-finals, semi-finals and a final, giving players the chance to collect valuable points and secure a nightly victory.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Speaking on Love The Darts, Michael Bridge and Stuart Pyke discuss whether the Premier League needs a format change for 2027

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Luke Littler won the premiere league by beating Luke Humphries.

Each nightly winner is awarded five points, while the runner-up collects three. The two losing semi-finalists receive two points apiece, with the four players beaten in the quarter-finals earning no points.

The previous format, last used in 2021, featured 10 players competing in a round-robin league. Each player contested one best-of-12-leg match per night, with the bottom two in the standings eliminated following the ninth week of action, famously known as 'Judgement Night'.

The remaining eight players then continued in the round-robin format for a further seven weeks, before the top four progressed to the play-offs - a stage of the competition that remains unchanged under the current format.

"I think the format is solid," Porter said. "I think the fact you see the top players playing each other every week is strong.

"It's great for the live crowds in the arenas. It keeps them engaged. It keeps fans on TV engaged until the end.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights of the Premier League final at The O2 arena between Luke Littler and Luke Humphries.

"Previously, when there'd been just more generic league stage matches, you'd see a fall off in attendance and you'd see people leaving the arenas as the evening went on, and that's not something we want.

"But we're very conscious of the need to keep it fresh. The Premier League format has evolved a number of times over its 20-odd year history, and it will continue to do so.

"So we've got a couple of little concepts that we're looking at and things we'll introduce at the right time.

"We'll never keep everybody happy, but as long as they're talking about it, that's all we can ask for."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Speaking on Love The Darts, Emma Paton, Michael Bridge and Stuart Pyke debate whether the 2026 Premier League final was the best ever.

'Smith now one of the best players in the world'

Speaking recently, Smith said he believes he 'definitely' deserves a Premier League debut on current form, having secured a second TV major title of the season at the Machineseeker European Championship.

Smith joined Van Gerwen, Phil Taylor, Rob Cross and Peter Wright as a multiple winner of the European Championship, following his 2022 success by defeating Martin Schindler 11-8 in the final in Dortmund on Sunday.

'MVG's record speaks for itself'

Van Gerwen, a seven-time Premier League champion (2013, 2016, 2017, 2018, 2019, 2022 and 2023), has endured one of the most challenging seasons of his career.

The 37-year-old has progressed beyond the opening round in just one of his last five tournaments, reaching the quarter-finals of Players Championship 30 before suffering defeat to Scott Williams.

That loss further underlined Van Gerwen's struggles this season, having suffered first-round exits at four European Tour events: the European Darts Trophy, German Darts Grand Prix, Flanders Darts Trophy and Swiss Darts Trophy. "He's had a difficult year, but, you know, he's committed to the tour.

"He's stuck by what he wants to do, and I think he'll come again."

Sports.title: Korda seeks LPGA Hall of Fame place and familiar success at The Annika
Sports.content:
World No 1 Nelly Korda makes her long-awaited return to competition this week at The Annika, live on Sky Sports Golf, seeking a fourth title at the event which would earn her a spot in the LPGA Hall of Fame.

Korda will make her first competitive start on the LPGA Tour since the FM Championship in August, and first appearance since the Solheim Cup in September.

The 28-year-old is already a three-time winner in her six prior starts at The Annika driven by Gainbridge at Pelican Golf Club, and is chasing her fifth win of the season.

"Eight weeks - I don't remember the last time I took that long off," said Korda.

"It was nice but by the middle of it I was ready to get going. There is only so many hours you can go out and practise and beat balls.

"I'm very excited to be back. I think it's more the rejuvenation of being really motivated to come back out, and sometimes when you play a lot and you travel a lot, you start to get a little stagnant.

"I'm not saying you're not driven but you just get a little tired, a little worn out, your body gets a little drained.

"When you do take that time to have a little bit of time for yourself to re-energise your batteries, you're very motivated to come back and play against the best players in the world and test yourself.

"Sometimes I just have to take that break. A lot of people may not agree with it. I have to really listen to myself and know what's best for myself."

Korda recently clinched her second player the year award after another year of excellence.

"Obviously it's not just me but it's my entire team behind me. I'm the one hitting the shots and grinding, but there is so much that goes on behind the scenes.

Sports.title: Meeting of two lost souls: can Pochettino make it work at Manchester United? | Barney Ronay
Sports.content:
Welcome, Mauricio, to the meat grinder. Or rather, welcome back. We’ve been expecting you. There is nothing surprising in the news Manchester United may be on the verge of appointing Mauricio Pochettino. United are always on the verge of appointing Pochettino. This is a club that has spent 13 years hiring and firing the same structurally doomed manager – same shellshocked eyes, same irresolvable macro-problems – and the last eight years almost but not quite doing this to Pochettino.

Well, maybe we’re finally here. Maybe he just needed to be broken enough to make it fit. And who knows, perhaps there is even a kind of accidental synergy here.

By now Pochettino has been thoroughly processed through the soul-extraction machinery of elite club football. He arrives at Old Trafford pre-minced, pre‑haunted, a 54-year-old already bruised by his experiences at Paris Saint-Germain, Chelsea and Levy‑era Spurs. This is a head coach so steeped in the blood of dysfunctional super-clubs that turning back is pretty much the same thing as heading on into its ultimate form in the west end of Manchester.

The problems at Old Trafford are of course unrelated to the appointment of the latest managerial avatar. The constant hiring and firing is a symptom not a cause. This is essentially a distraction, a false flag drawing attention from the avarice and incompetence of the executive tiers.

Still, though, it is necessary on these occasions to set out the reasons why the latest appointment probably won’t work. First up is the obvious sense of diminishing returns.

How do you solve a club that has won two major trophies in 10 years of steady downward progress? Easy. You hire a coach who has also won two major trophies in 13 years of steady downward progress. How do we get back to the dimly remembered recent past? We hire the dimly remembered recent past.

Does this feel like a magic bullet? At this stage hiring Pochettino is like booking the bloke who did Gangnam Style to play the Super Bowl. Yeah, huge fan. Remind me. Weren’t you quite big in 2013?

View image in fullscreen Pochettino at Spurs: ‘The world’s most handsome oil rigger.’ Photograph: Dylan Martinez/Reuters

So much for all that then. It is more interesting to linger on the fact that, as ever with this great belching toxic volcano of a football club, there is always hope, and some kind of logic that says maybe this is the one. We see it every time. Ageing aura-master? Yep, do it. Hot young systems zealot? Get him in. Random ex-player, who will be transformed almost instantly into a damp, doomed figure crumpled on the touchline like a divorced dad at the school railings? We have a vacancy.

This time there are two things in Pochettino’s favour. First, the memory of his best days at Tottenham: the charisma, the barking laugh, the way of striding around looking like the world’s most handsome oil rigger. Plus of course the visceral, hard-running style of that early Spurs team, football as life, pain, exhaustion, delirium. There will be moments. Just give us some of these. In the end everyone here just wants to feel something.

Second, and more seductive, is the sense of some kind of shared redemption arc, a union of lost souls. Broken club, meet broken manager. You two are going to get along. This happens in movies, the Leaving Las Vegas dynamic: rock bottom, healing, redemption. Is this convincing? Do we have, of all things, not hope – obviously not that – but doomed hope?

Pochettino does have an incompleteness to his career. This is a manager who never manifested the full promise of those early years, headhunted by Southampton, then poached again by Spurs, where he offered a compelling injection of energy. That Pochettino was a hugely moreish figure. You wanted to hear him speak, clap his dimpled cheeks, to breathe in his Eau de Gaucho scent as he whispered gruff words in your ear about struggle and suffering, and maybe invited you to a barbecue later.

View image in fullscreen Mauricio Pochettino spent a year and a half working with galácticos at PSG. Photograph: Franck Fife/AFP/Getty Images

A decade on, Pochettino still has the air of someone looking for a home and a final form. It is an interesting exercise just trying to decide what really broke him. Maybe it was PSG, January 2021 to July 2022, still the source of his only major trophies.

In Paris Pochettino seemed to arrive pre-burnt out, required to make sense from a standing start of a bunch of supernova galácticos. This was High Decadence-era PSG, source of the original despot‑general Kylian Mbappé meme, and a time when Neymar seemed to be more or less continually dancing on crutches in an elite underground disco dressed in a solid gold bowler hat and shoes made from moon rock.

Those who know Pochettino reported a disillusionment with superstar egotism, the swagger of unproven young players, training that became a losing battle for intensity. And yes, there is a pre‑United klaxon here. How’s that going to work out? Does it seem like an obvious cultural fit?

Then again, maybe it was Chelsea that broke him, an ill-fitting season before a mutually agreed departure, shot through with frustration at an unbalanced squad and an incoherent hierarchy. Again, does this sound like a man ideally geared to make sense of a squad assembled under six managers and the interventions of pub-chat Big Sir Jim?

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

You could even make a case it was Spurs that broke Pochettino, even if for five seasons this was his peak time in club management. The good times died at Tottenham because Pochettino couldn’t convince Daniel Levy of the need to build from a point of strength. That team was destined to eat itself. Pochettino was high on the Marcelo Bielsa school of football as a game of running, victory as a function of physical and emotional exhaustion.

In the end the thing that made Poch-era Spurs work was also the thing that killed it, a high-energy team that became a zombified entity, a squad of degraded parts, Pochettino himself already a little sad and war-weary.

So, welcome to Manchester then. Do any of those elements sound familiar? Maybe there is something interesting here. Maybe it’s a fit. United might be a ghost ship, trapped in a never-ending doldrums. Pochettino may also be the wrong side of his own prime. Hansi Flick won his first trophy at Bayern Munich in 2019, the same age as Pochettino. But long‑serving 54-year-old managers don’t tend to surge into their best years at this level.

View image in fullscreen Kobbie Mainoo has the press-resistant, quick-passing qualities to thrive under Mauricio Pochettino. Photograph: Simon Stacpoole/Offside/Getty Images

Then again, football is often emotion as much as detail, and Manchester United is definitely this right now, an entity that just needs to feel good, to give off heat, to keep rolling along. Pochettino’s arrival would at least be a story, a meeting of last chances and final saloons. Do we have an arc here?

If so, it needs to start with an extended action sequence. United are third from bottom of the Premier League. The squad is a random bin fire of divergent parts. On the plus side there is something astringent and purging about Pochettino’s best style, the high-intensity 4-2-3-1. There are even some players there that might fit.

Kobbie Mainoo has the necessary press-resistant, quick‑passing qualities. Carlos Baleba and Andrey Santos are much better hard‑running midfielders than they’ve looked so far. Which isn’t saying much. They haven’t looked like this at all. Matheus Cunha and Bryan Mbeumo will be asked to hustle, which they can do. Benjamin Sesko hasn’t really got going. But Pochettino likes a big man.

The defence needs speed and a willingness to play a high line, meaning more than ever that Harry Maguire looks like a horse‑drawn train in a world of Ford Model Ts. Has Bruno Fernandes ever really been asked to play with more discipline and less risk? This will now happen.

And yes, we have been here before so many times. There is no magic bullet, no mega‑vaccine, no masterplan coming together in appointing Pochettino. Nobody is draining the swamp, flame‑throwing the boardroom, or raging at the managed mediocrity installed at every level.

Pochettino himself is like a walking vision of better times and diminished powers. But there are always other chapters, and in this case a sense of something that might just offer its own sense of shared theatre, private and public; a chance, however remote, to unbreak yourself.

Sports.title: Complaint filed to IRS in relation to Fifa head Gianni Infantino’s housekeeper
Sports.content:
A complaint has been filed to the United States Internal Revenue Service calling for an investigation into claims an individual on the Fifa payroll was working privately as a housekeeper for Gianni Infantino.

If the IRS investigates and finds the claims to be proven then Fifa could lose its tax-exempt status in the US. Fifa has 501(c)(4) status in the country, a category for organisations “created to promote community welfare for charitable, educational or recreational purposes”.

The complaint, which has been seen by the Guardian and is supported by a number of documents, claims an individual “performed domestic work exclusively for Fifa president Gianni Infantino and his wife, Leena Infantino, at their Miami residence, while receiving compensation or benefits through a Fifa-affiliated entity”, and argues that “senior leadership, acting in their official capacity and on behalf of Fifa, have abused the entity’s tax-exemption status”.

Quick Guide How do I 

The complaint goes on to argue: “If organisational funds or resources were used to pay for services benefiting a leader’s household, the arrangement raises serious questions about private benefit, financial reporting, compensation, and governance. The materials also raise questions about the accuracy of representations in employment, payroll, tax, and immigration records. We ask the agencies to investigate the underlying records and determine what occurred.” The IRS has been approached for comment.

The news comes as Fifa’s activities, and specifically Infantino’s involvement in the failed Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) scheme and his relationship with the Trump White House, are to come under intensified scrutiny from Democratic politicians in the US after the “blue wave” at the midterm elections. A spokesperson for the ranking member of the House judiciary committee, representative Jamie Raskin, said the committee had not requested documents related to the housekeeper but was “looking closely at those developments”.

A Fifa spokesperson said: “Matters related to the Fifa president’s personal and home life are private; however, for the avoidance of any doubt, the costs of any domestic staff are met by the Fifa president personally.”

The complaint, if taken up, would probably take months to complete and commonly the results of IRS investigations are not published. Any action taken as a result, however, would be in the public domain. The complaint was submitted by the Washington DC lawyer Abed Ayoub, who works in immigration law and has served as the national executive director of the American-Arab Anti-Discrimination Committee (ADC). Last year the ADC was part of the campaign Game Over Israel, which called for Israeli football teams to be banned from international competition.

Fifa said: “We urge the media to act responsibly. As Fifa stated in August, it is evident that there is a concerted and ongoing effort by some to undermine Fifa and its president. Fifa welcomes legitimate scrutiny. But scrutiny is not a licence to amplify false allegations. Where reporting is inaccurate or misleading Fifa will continue to challenge it directly and vigorously.”

Infantino has been described by his predecessor, Sepp Blatter, as a “dictator” who “no longer knows any borders”. Blatter, Fifa’s president for 17 years before resigning amid a corruption scandal at the organisation, made the remarks in an interview with the German magazine Der Spiegel. He criticised the FFE scheme, the Fifa peace prize and, most significantly in his opinion, the overturning of Folarin Balogun’s suspension for a red card during the World Cup.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Sport in Focus Our picture editors select their favourite sporting images from the past week, from the spectacular to the powerful, and with a little bit of fun thrown in Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

“Fifa is suffering,” Blatter said. “It is currently led by a person who has allowed himself to be blinded.” He described the peace prize as “embarrassing”, saying: “Why would he do something like that? Infantino awards a peace prize to someone who wages war against Iran shortly afterwards?”

In assessing the FFE scheme, which was abandoned after an international outcry, Blatter said: “Infantino no longer knows any borders. He doesn’t understand any of this.” He described the Balogun controversy as “the worst”, saying: “Statutes can be interpreted. But rules of the game must apply to everyone, you can’t interpret them.”

FIfa has been approached for comment.

Sports.title: Danny Kelly, football broadcaster and renowned editor, dies aged 69
Sports.content:
The journalist and broadcaster Danny Kelly, who helped define coverage of music and football in the UK for a generation, has died at the age of 69.

Kelly edited the NME and Q magazine, and launched the Football 365 website before going on to be a presenter and pundit on the BBC and TalkSport. He had been receiving treatment for oesophageal cancer.

Tributes were led by Kelly’s longstanding broadcast partner Danny Baker. “My great friend, supreme broadcaster and funniest man I ever knew, Danny Kelly, died yesterday afternoon,” Baker wrote on social media, the pair having worked together on any number of radio, TV shows and podcasts. “I cannot believe I will never hear his voice again.”

Tottenham Hotspur paid emotional tribute to Kelly, a lifelong Spurs fan. A statement said: “The entire Tottenham family mourns the loss of one of our own, broadcasting legend Danny Kelly. Our thoughts and love are with his family and friends at this incredibly sad time.”

TalkSport, for which Kelly worked as a presenter for nearly two decades, said it was “heartbroken” by the news. “A cherished part of TalkSport for so many years, Danny brought extraordinary wit, warmth and knowledge to our airwaves,” the station said. “His passion for football, music and life was infectious, and his kindness touched everyone around him.”

Another broadcaster, the former Sky Sports host Richard Keys, said Kelly “was all of the things – and more – being said about him – ‘warm, witty and knowledgable’”.

View image in fullscreen Danny Kelly at the launch of the Football365 website in 1998. Photograph: Patrick Barth/Shutterstock

Kelly was born in north London in 1956 and first made his name writing about music. He began contributing to the NME in his 20s and went on to edit the agenda-setting weekly newspaper at the end of the 1980s. From there he took charge of the top-selling music monthly Q magazine, where he was named British magazine editor of the year.

Manic Street Preachers paid tribute to “a brilliant broadcaster-writer-ideas factory. Danny was editor of the NME when we first started getting press, a wonderful man, his musical knowledge was vast and deep, his radio voice has been part of our lives for so long … We will all miss him.”

In the second half of the 1990s, Kelly threw himself into the nascent world of digital media and launched Football365, which became one of the leading online voices on the sport. In the noughties, he spotted another development – podcasts – and launched the Game, a weekly football podcast, for the Times.

Over the past 15 years Kelly became best known as a radio presenter and podcast host, including presenting the Tottenham-focused show View from The Lane. Paying tribute to “our host, our leader” on its X account, the View from the Lane said: “We all loved him as much as he loved Spurs.”

Sports.title: ‘I’ve had to prove people wrong’: Kane still striving before record England cap
Sports.content:
Harry Kane says he still feels a pressure to prove his worth, even as he prepares to become England’s most capped men’s player, as he outlined his determination to set records that will stand for years.

The captain will make his 126th appearance against Croatia at ­Wembley on Thursday night, moving him ahead of Peter Shilton on the all-time list. Kane is England’s record ­goalscorer with 91, comfortably clear of Wayne Rooney, who retired with 53.

Kane will be presented with a memento of his historic cap by ­Shilton before kick-off against ­Croatia. ­Shilton has held the record since 1990 when he finished his 20-year career. Kane’s achievement of winning the Ballon d’Or last month will also be recognised.

“I don’t think it will ever leave me,” Kane said, when asked whether he continued to have points to prove. “It’s probably part of what makes me push myself to the limits that I do because in football, you’ve never completed it. No matter what you’ve achieved, there is always a trophy that someone else has won or a goal record that someone else has.

“Whether it’s noise from the outside, from media or the fans … it just helps motivate me to realise there’s a lot more to achieve. My biggest fear is finishing my career and thinking I could have done a bit more … if I could have just done that or done that. I want to make sure I cross every bridge and do everything possible so that whenever that day does come, I can say I’ve done everything possible. And I can sleep well at night.”

The 33-year-old is conscious that two of his England teammates have won a significant number of caps. Declan Rice has 80 at the age of 27; Jude Bellingham 60 at 23. “I’ll try to give them a good number to catch,” Kane said. “The goal record, of course, is going to be one that’s difficult to beat for a while.

“I’ve spoken about leading by example and pushing a lot of these younger players. It’s by setting standards, being available every time, getting the caps and scoring the goals. That should help motivate the younger players. If I was younger and I had a player in front of me doing what I was doing, I know that would push me to think: ‘OK, I can score those goals, I can win the Ballon d’Or, I can break the cap record.’ Whilst I’m in this place, it is to try to set these records as high as I can and one day look back to see if anyone can catch them.”

View image in fullscreen Harry Kane receives the Ballon d'Or in London. Photograph: Franck Fife/AFP/Getty Images

Kane has been doubted at ­numerous points of his career, ­starting when he was released by Arsenal as an eight-year-old. He had difficult loans from Tottenham to Norwich and Leicester in 2012‑13 and there were the one‑season‑wonder jibes after his breakthrough campaign for Spurs and England in 2014-15.

Kane has been ridiculed for ­setting lofty targets: such as in 2017, when he said he wanted to replicate the numbers of Lionel Messi and ­Cristiano Ronaldo; when he stated his ambition to win the 2018 World Cup Golden Boot. Or when he stood on the verge of his 100th England cap in September 2024 with 66 goals and said he wanted to score 100. There were questions about his place in the team after Euro 2024 when his performances were underwhelming and he was substituted in the final. Every time, he answered back.

“It’s just my mindset,” Kane said. “Because I’ve had to prove people wrong my whole career. From early academy days proving coaches wrong, proving scouts wrong – it has just been instilled in me. If someone tells me I can’t do something it motivates me more to do it.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

“When you look at all the great athletes, I’ve spoken before about Tom Brady [the NFL icon] and it’s that unwavering mentality to be the best. Maybe with me, because I’m a calm person and you don’t see … like, the ego of some of these great players and I’m a bit more relaxed … but it doesn’t mean I don’t want it as much as everyone else. That I don’t put in the work and drive myself and everyone around me to be the best.

“Maybe getting released that early [by Arsenal] and ­proving them wrong and then maybe ­proving [wrong] my early coaches at ­Tottenham, who I wasn’t playing as much [under]. The loan moves that didn’t go well. Same thing: ‘I’m going to show them.’”

Kane brought up surely the lowest individual moment of his England career – the penalty miss against France in the 2-1 World Cup ­quarter‑final defeat in 2022. “That was really tough but again it was the way I bounced back,” he said.

“And even the fact I scored the next 30 [actually 31] penalties of my career. I changed the technique a little bit and it made me improve. There have been a lot of low points but maybe they are things that have helped me get to where I am now.”

Sports.title: Thomas Tuchel keeps laser focus on ‘unfinished business’ with England
Sports.content:
Thomas Tuchel will not be going anywhere before Euro 2028. Mauricio Pochettino is expected to leave his role as the USA men’s head coach to replace Michael Carrick at Manchester United, but Tuchel has not lost his passion for international football and has revealed he did not insert a release clause when he extended his deal as England’s manager this year.

It will not matter whether there is an approach from a big club before the next tournament. United can pay about £7m to get Pochettino out of his deal, but the Football Association does not have to worry about being forced to let Tuchel go. “There’s no intention [of leaving],” Tuchel said. “I signed the contract. I want to stay until the Euros. I want to do the Euros. We have unfinished business.”

Tuchel, a Champions League winner with Chelsea in 2021, did not rule out a return to club management one day. He admitted to missing “the 50 matches” a season, “these two minutes when everything is done, before the whistle goes … it’s like the best two minutes”. But while he loves the daily grind, he added there were downsides to playing every four days and there was a twinkle in his eye when he was asked about potentially staying with England beyond the European Championship.

“I am open to everything,” he said, perhaps reflecting that it is not so long ago that people were calling for his head after England’s World Cup semi-final defeat by Argentina.

The mood has improved. Tuchel sounds energised after England’s bright start to their Nations League campaign. His contract contains a performance-related clause that would have allowed the FA to sack him had England underperformed at the World Cup, but Tuchel has support from Mark Bullingham, the chief executive, and Dan Ashworth, the chief football officer.

View image in fullscreen Jobe Bellingham (right) and Jude Bellingham will by aiming to earn England a point against Croatia or Spain to make the Nations League quarter-finals. Photograph: Justin Setterfield/Getty Images

Ashworth and Bullingham reinforced the message in person during the summer. “They made it very early in the World Cup,” Tuchel said, explaining that the backing came while the sacking clause remained active. “They just made it very clear and it comes from a place of trust, and that’s what you look for as a coach.

“I love my players. I love my staff and I have bosses who trust me. I know how to appreciate it a lot. I miss my players, and I miss my team, and I miss the 50 matches that I’m not involved in a year. But I’m desperate to win the Nations League and to try to win the Euros.”

Tuchel, who is preparing for the Nations League game at home against Croatia on Thursday night, is thinking ahead. He is gearing up for a European Championship staged mainly in England, who would also like to be chosen to host the Nations League finals next summer. “To have it here would be exciting,” Tuchel said. “First of all, we need to reach the final.”

England need one point from their final two games in Group A3 to finish in the top two and qualify for the quarter-finals in March. Victory against Croatia would give them a chance of finishing top when they visit Spain on Sunday. The Croatia game will not merely be a celebration of Harry Kane’s Ballon d’Or. Wembley will watch the captain break the England men’s appearance record, but other issues are at play.

Tuchel needs Jude Bellingham to be careful given that England’s No 10 is on a booking and at risk of missing the Spain game through suspension. There are unknowns in central defence after Marc Guéhi’s withdrawal. Ezri Konsa is unavailable against Croatia and targeting a return against Spain. Tuchel, who added James Hill and Dan Burn to his squad this week, will use a new partnership against Slaven Bilic’s side.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

View image in fullscreen Dan Burn (second right) is likely to play at left-back for England. Photograph: Eddie Keogh/The FA/Getty Images

It is likely to be Jarell Quansah as the right centre-back while Jarrad Branthwaite could miss out to Burn on the left. “Jarrad is doing very well but it’s a very different style of play for him from Everton towards us,” Tuchel said. “Dan Burn is more used to the style with Newcastle from the last two seasons where they followed in a high press.”

Burn led the team out when England trained on Wednesday. Among the group are exciting newcomers who inevitably command the attention. Tuchel has Rio Ngumoha and Josh King in attack. He is the first senior manager to work with the Bellingham brothers. Jobe Bellingham, who has impressed with his physicality and calmness on the ball, plays a deeper midfield role than Jude. Jobe is likely to start on the bench.

Tuchel wants to reconnect with the values from the previous camp. It featured England impressing in a narrow defeat by Spain, before they crushed Croatia 7-0 in Rijeka. One big highlight from the Croatia win was Alex Scott’s performance alongside Elliot Anderson in midfield.

Scott, who is out with a thigh injury, can challenge Declan Rice. The competition for places is fierce. Rice is back after missing the last camp. Tuchel said the Arsenal midfielder remained crucial.

“Declan understands the game like he’s almost a coach on the field,” Tuchel said, but a new identity is forming. It was interesting that Tuchel mentioned the young Chelsea defender Josh Acheampong, whose first call-up may not be far away. It seems Tuchel 2.0 is taking shape.

Sports.title: US withdraw from U-17 World Cup in Qatar due to safety concerns
Sports.content:
The US men’s national team have pulled out of the Fifa U-17 World Cup, which is due to kick off in Qatar in just over a week. In a letter sent to players explaining the decision, the US Soccer Federation cited safety concerns for players and staff, referring them to the US state department’s travel advisory for Qatar, which encourages citizens to reconsider travel to the country “due to risk of armed conflict” and asks government employees to obtain special authorization to do so.

“Unfortunately, in light of current circumstances … we are no longer able to participate in the tournament,” US Soccer’s letter to players reads. “The wellbeing of our players and staff will always be our top priority.

“Please accept our deepest appreciation for your commitment to US Soccer and our shared disappointment about these circumstances.”

A US Soccer spokesperson said the federation would not go into details about how it reached its decision. The Guardian understands Fifa was informed of the federation’s decision on Wednesday.

Fifa’s regulations for the U-17 World Cups stipulate that qualified nations must participate in the tournament or be fined, with withdrawal within 30 days of the tournament’s start resulting in a fine of CHF20,000 (about $24,000). Fifa has been approached for comment.

The ongoing situation in the Middle East – involving interconnected conflicts among multiple states – has already led to postponements or cancellations of international sporting events. The 2027 Asian Cup, the continental soccer championship, was due to be held in Saudi Arabia in January 2027 but has been postponed nearly a year due to the conflict between the Saudis and the Houthi rebels, and the Iran war. More recently, Qatar pulled out of hosting rugby’s 2028 Nations Championship finals due to uncertainty around the conflicts. The final races of the Formula One season are still going ahead in the Middle East, on 29 November in Qatar and then 6 December in Abu Dhabi.

Multiple missile strikes by the Houthis on Riyadh’s international airport killed 13 people and wounded hundreds in October. Later that month, US diplomats were told to leave Saudi Arabia amid ongoing Houthi attacks.

Qatar has been acting as a mediator in talks between the US and Iran aimed at ending the countries’ conflict, which started with attacks by the US and Israel on Iran earlier this year. A tanker off the coast of Qatar was attacked in October amid thetensions.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Twice weekly Sign up to Soccer Desk Jonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer. Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

The U-17 World Cup is still due to begin on 19 November in Doha. The US were placed in Group J along with Montenegro, Algeria and Chile. The US roster that was due to compete in the tournament does not contain any household names, but features a number of promising young players in MLS and abroad.

Sports.title: Top four teams in Fifa rankings set to be kept apart until semi-finals at 2027 Women’s World Cup
Sports.content:
The top four ranked teams will be separated until the semi-finals at the 2027 Women’s World Cup, ­provided they each win their group, after a change to the tournament’s draw procedure was confirmed by Fifa.

Spain, USA, Germany and England are ranked one to four in the world respectively, although USA and England still need to qualify for the tournament. The seedings will be based on the 7 December updated rankings, meaning the standings could change before the draw, which will take place on 11 December in Rio de Janeiro.

The top four sides were also ­separated until the semi-finals of the 2026 men’s World Cup, which consisted of 48 teams, but it was not announced until Wednesday that the same rule would apply to the 32-team ­women’s tournament. In the men’s World Cup the top four – Spain, Argentina, France, and England – all reached the semi-finals.

The record four-time champions USA face El Salvador on 27 November as they aim to confirm their place at the tournament next summer. A victory, coupled with no changes to the world rankings, would ensure USA would be placed in the opposite half of the draw to the defending cham­pions, Spain. That would mean if they win their groups the two teams could not meet until the final, which will be played at the ­Maracanã Stadium on 25 July. Neither Spain nor USA finished top of their group at the previous World Cup.

England, the 2023 runners-up, must beat Ukraine over two legs on 1 and 5 December to ensure their qualification. The European ­champions hold a 31-point advantage over fifth-placed Japan in the world rankings before the upcoming round of internationals.

France, the hosts Brazil and ­Sweden – who finished third at three of the past four World Cups, and face Scotland in their qualifying playoff in December – would complete the set of eight Pot 1 seeds for the eight groups, if the top eight remains as it is. ­Canada, ranked ninth in the world, could pounce on a Pot 1 spot if anyone slips up.

Fifa has also confirmed that the draw will take place at 1.30pm local time (11.30am EST/4.30pm GMT) on 11 December, at Rio de Janeiro’s Museum of Modern Art. Brazil, as hosts, will be placed in Group A and will contest the opening match at the Maracanã on 24 June.

After the eight Pot 1 sides, the next eight highest-ranked teams involved will be in Pot 2, with the next eight below them in Pot 3. Pot 4 will include three places for the winners of the inter-confederation playoff ­tournament that will conclude in March, along with the lowest-ranked sides involved. No group will be permitted to include more than one team from the same continent, except for European teams, of whom there can be a maximum of two per group.

Fifa also confirmed later on Wednesday that the uncontested bids to host the 2031 and 2035 Women’s World Cups have both passed their extensive bid evaluations.

The US, Mexico, Costa Rica and Jamaica are bidding to jointly host the 2031 event and they received an overall score of 4.4 out of 5. The UK is the sole bidder for 2035 and the bid – which includes a proposal for Wembley to host the final – received a score of 4.3 out of 5.

No venue has yet been specified to stage the 2031 final. Both bids’ infrastructure, stadiums and accommodation were praised by Fifa. Fifa’s congress is expected to formally appoint them as hosts on 23 November.

Sports.title: League One clubs aim for further curbs on spending as budgets continue to spiral
Sports.content:
League One clubs want to introduce new spending restrictions to reduce losses by limiting investment from owners.

Clubs in the division voted to tighten the rules last summer by reducing spending limits from 60% to 50% of turnover, and removed a staggered approach to owner investment, so that only 50% of equity injections can be spent on squad costs, with the rest assigned to infrastructure projects. Less than six months later many want to go further.

The Guardian has learned that two proposed models are being ­con­sidered: a fixed cap on owner investment or introducing a version of the Premier League’s squad cost rules, with a £1 levy on clubs for every £1 spent above 50% of their revenue. Sporting sanctions would be applied if spending reached 60%, with the money raised from the levy redistri­buted to other clubs in the division.

The move to introduce more spending curbs comes despite a legal challenge to the existing rules from the Professional ­Footballers’ Association, which launched proceedings in August on the grounds that the clubs had failed to abide by the terms of their membership of the ­professional negotiating and consultative committee.

An attempt by League One and League Two to introduce salary caps of £2.5m and £1.5m respectively was withdrawn in 2021 after the PFA took them to an independent arbitration panel.

Discussions over stricter controls have been taking place for some time, but have been given fresh impetus by the publication last month of the State of the Game report. The first piece of work by the ­Independent Football Regulator showed that 94% of clubs in the EFL and National League are loss-making, and that 32 of the 96 would not survive for a month without owner funding.

The changes last summer reduced the percentage of clubs’ income that can be spent on wages, with mana­gers’ salaries included for the first time, but there is a renewed move to reduce losses, which averaged £7.5m per club in League One last season, up from £5.3m the previous season.

One owner said that further regulation was ­necessary because the clubs had shown ­repeatedly that they could not restrain themselves, pointing out that League One wage bills have increased by 15% this season, and that a top-six budget in the division five years ago would now rank in the bottom three.

Reading and Peterborough have long campaigned for tighter spending controls, but face opposition from clubs such as MK Dons and Wycombe, and it is unclear whether any proposal would gain the two-thirds majority required to be introduced.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

A source at another League One club warned that an unintended consequence would be to create a cliff edge in terms of financial resources with the Championship, which loosened its regulations last season by permitting owners an inject up to £33m over three years, an equity allowance that does not count towards the 85% wage spending/revenue limit.

League Two clubs are also involved in the discussions, although it is unclear whether they will choose to align with League One.

The EFL confirmed discussions were ongoing, although formal proposals have yet to be put to the clubs.

Sports.title: £75m-rated Chelsea star could spark Man United vs Man City transfer tug of war
Sports.content:
Manchester United and Manchester City are both keeping tabs on Malo Gusto, talkSPORT understands.

The Chelsea defender has seen his role reduced since Xabi Alonso's arrival at Stamford Bridge, leading him to be linked with an exit.



4 Malo Gusto has not been a regular starter for Chelsea this season Credit: Getty

Gusto has not started a Premier League match since September 12 and has increasingly lost his place to Josh Acheampong at right-back, despite captain Reece James being injured.

Two-horse race?

Two of Chelsea's rivals could now be set to pounce, with both City and United understood to be interested in Gusto.

It is not currently clear whether either side will make an official approach in the January transfer window.



Man City were previously linked with a move for Gusto in the summer, who were keen for a reunion between the 23-year-old and former Chelsea boss Enzo Maresca.

talkSPORT understands Chelsea value the Frenchman at £75million, however their efforts to sign him could be affected by other matters.



City are still awaiting the outcome of their appeal against the Premier League following their guilty verdict on 114 charges of breaching financial rules.

The Premier League giants were adjudged to have artificially inflated their revenue by £900million via 'sham' contracts over a nine-year period between 2009 and 2018.



While City have since launched an appeal, they are yet to learn the outcome of this, and their pending sanctions hearing will complicate any pursuit of Gusto.

Man United also find themselves at a crossroads amid their interest in the full-back.

The Red Devils look poised for a change in management, with a deal agreed in principle for USA boss Mauricio Pochettino to replace Michael Carrick at Old Trafford.

4 Gusto made 49 appearances in all competitions for Chelsea in the 2025/26 season Credit: Getty



4 Maresca previously managed Gusto between 2024 and 2026 at Chelsea Credit: Getty

Gusto's Chelsea career so far

Gusto joined Chelsea in 2023 from Lyon for around £26m.

He has been a regular fixture in the team ever since, making 144 appearances and scoring three goals in all competitions.

However, this season he has slipped down the pecking order under new manager Alonso, starting just three of his seven Premier League appearances this term.

Other than this, Gusto started all three of the Blues' Carabao Cup fixtures, before their fourth-round exit to Liverpool on penalties.



His performance in the defeat did little to help his case for more minutes, with concerns being raised over him.

Gusto was the target of plenty of Chelsea fan ire as he was booed off when he was replaced in the 67th minute, and talkSPORT's Adrian Durham and Andy Townsend both weighed in on this.

4 Gusto's theatrics in Chelsea's Carabao Cup exit to Liverpool left talkSPORT's Townsend unimpressed Credit: Getty

Durham said: “There were cheers from the Chelsea fans at Anfield when he was taken off. He was awful.



“One Chelsea fan messaged me saying I don't want to see him in a Chelsea shirt again.

“Players go through this, but it feels like it could be the end of the road. He was actually linked with Man City in the summer, and they're talking about him going Man City in January.

“I don't really understand what City see, but I'm being a very harsh critic of a footballer here.”

Townsend, meanwhile, accused Gusto of going 'a little soft', criticising for him going to ground easily and playing for free-kicks.

Sports.title: Thomas Tuchel reveals double injury blow on eve of England clash
Sports.content:
Thomas Tuchel has confirmed England will be without both Djed Spence and Ezri Konsa against Croatia.

The Three Lions return to action on Thursday at Wembley, with kick-off at 7:45pm, live on talkSPORT.



4 Tuchel has confirmed Spence and Konsa will miss the match against Croatia Credit: Getty

However, they have been dealt an early blow in defence, with two potential starters in Spence and Konsa ruled out.

Konsa has been managing his fitness after suffering a knee issue during Arsenal’s 2-1 win away to Slavia Prague.

The 29-year-old then played the full 90 minutes in a 1-0 victory over Hull three days later, but has been following an individual training programme since linking up with England.



While Spence has no clear injury, the full-back struggled for fitness following his £30million move to Inter Milan and has only recently began to star regularly, making it likely he is still getting up to speed.

Despite being without the two for the Croatia clash, Tuchel revealed both players could return against Spain on Sunday.



Tuchel: Not risking Konsa and Spence

Speaking to reporters on Wednesday, Tuchel explained: "It’s my understanding at the moment that they will both be available (for Spain).

"But we will not take the risk tomorrow (vs Croatia), they are out tomorrow.



"The hope and belief is they are in individual training on Friday, team training on Saturday and available on Sunday."

With Konsa's absence for the Croatia clash becoming clear on Tuesday, Tuchel moved quickly to bring in cover.

Uncapped Bournemouth defender James Hill received his first England call-up, having previously been on the 55-man shortlist.

4 Konsa has been a virtual ever-present for Arsenal this term, making 15 appearances in all competitions Credit: Getty



4 Spence has two assists in seven games for Inter Milan this term Credit: Getty

Konsa and Spence's absences aren't the only defensive headache Tuchel has faced in the international break.

Manchester City’s Marc Guehi pulled out of the squad through injury leading to Dan Burn’s late inclusion.

Fortunately though, Jarrad Branthwaite, Jarell Quansah and Ben White are all available and capable of playing at centre-back.



Tuchel will certainly be hoping both Konsa and Spence are ultimately fit for the Croatia clash, particularly with the latter heading into the international break in fine form.

After establishing himself at Inter Milan following a fitness-affected start to life, Spence has earned rave reviews with his recent displays.

The full-back completed his third straight 90 minutes on Sunday in a 2-0 victory over Cesc Fabregas' in form Como side.

4 Spence will have to wait slightly longer for his first England appearance since this summer's World Cup Credit: Getty



As well as keeping a clean sheet, his impact going forward was hailed after he provided his second assist in as many games in the win.

Spence's impact in Italy has drawn widespread praise, with Premier League icon Paolo Di Canio going as far to claim he can play 'blindfolded'

Sports.title: Michael Beale resigns from management role after just 12 games in charge
Sports.content:
Michael Beale resigns from management role after just 12 games in charge

Michael Beale has resigned as head coach of Zulte Waregem after just six months in charge, talkSPORT understands.

The ex-Rangers boss penned a two-year deal with the Belgian side in May - his first managerial role since he was sacked by Sunderland in February 2024.



4 Beale has left his position at Zulte Waregem after a nightmare run of form Credit: Getty

However, Beale's return to the dugout has quickly turned into a nightmare, as he departs with his side on a six-match losing run.

The Englishman's final game in charge saw his side get thumped 4-1 by Sint-Truidense on Saturday, leaving them just four points clear of the Belgian Pro League relegation zone.

Beale leaves his post

Beale's resignation comes after a breakdown in relations with senior figures at the club.
