Sports.title: WBA Orders Floyd Schofield to Face José Valenzuela
Sports.content:
Floyd Schofield has until December 11 to reach a deal with José Valenzuela after the WBA ordered the lightweight champion to make his first mandatory defense. Valenzuela’s southpaw counterpunching could make it an awkward fight for Schofield, who won the title on October 10 and does some of his best work when he can close distance quickly.

The WBA opened a 30-day negotiating period on November 11. Its Championships Committee can call a purse bid if the camps fail to reach an agreement by the close of business on December 11 or if either side says it is unwilling to negotiate or take part. The WBA announcement gave no fight date or venue.

Schofield’s speed gives him a way to take the initiative against Valenzuela. The harder part will be getting back out after he attacks. Valenzuela can give ground as Schofield comes forward and look for the straight left once Schofield has committed his feet. If Schofield finishes a combination directly in front of him, Valenzuela will have a chance to answer before the champion gets back to punching range.

Schofield can make those counters harder to time by changing how much he commits on each entry. A quick jab to the chest can score and make Valenzuela show how he plans to respond. A feint can draw the left hand early and give Schofield an opening to step in behind it. Those small decisions could let him dictate the pace without having to throw a full combination every time he gets close.

Valenzuela has a decision to make about how much ground he can afford to give away. If he waits too long for a clean counter, Schofield can touch him with single shots and move off before the left hand comes back. Valenzuela’s best stretches could come when he makes Schofield lead, catches him at the end of an attack and then steps forward before the champion can start again. Landing that left early would give Schofield something to think about on every entry that follows.

The WBA cited Rule C.11, which requires the champion to face the official challenger designated by the organization. It also cited Rule C.12, which limits whom a champion can face in the 60 days before the mandatory defense period expires. The December 11 deadline applies to negotiations, giving the camps a month to settle terms before the committee can move to a purse bid.

Schofield’s first mandatory will test how much he can get done with his speed when the other man is waiting for him to commit. He can win stretches of the fight by getting in first. If Valenzuela can regularly land the last clean punch in those sequences, Schofield may have to spend more of the fight making the challenger come to him.

Sports.title: Arnold Barboza Jr vs. Oscar Duarte Set for Jan. 23 in Anaheim
Sports.content:
Arnold Barboza Jr. and Oscar Duarte are set to meet on January 23 in Anaheim, California, in a junior welterweight bout built around a classic clash of styles. Golden Boy Promotions announced the date and location during the WBC convention, according to reporter Darshan Desai.

The Anaheim card is also expected to showcase top junior middleweight talent. WBC number one contender Brandon Adams is slated to appear in either an interim title bout or a final eliminator, alongside fellow contender Charles Conwell. Specific venues and opponents for the undercard fighters have not yet been revealed.

For Barboza, the biggest danger against a relentless pressure fighter like Duarte lies in his defensive exits. Barboza has the tools to score consistently with his jab and crisp combinations, yet retreating in a straight line will allow Duarte to march right behind him and force him against the ropes.

Lateral movement is the key adjustment here. Every time Barboza pivots off the center line after landing a punch, Duarte is forced to reset his feet and start his attack from scratch. How well Barboza maintains that spatial discipline will dictate whether this fight happens at his preferred distance or in a phone booth.

Duarte’s path to victory depends on cutting off the ring with patience rather than reckless aggression. Charging in from the outside gives Barboza plenty of time to read the attack and fire counters before Duarte is even set to punch. Instead, Duarte needs to inch forward behind a tight guard until he is close enough to target the midsection.

Barboza is slick enough to slip wide hooks upstairs, but his torso remains an accessible target when he leans back. Investing in heavy body work early will pay major dividends by slowing Barboza’s legs and making it much harder for him to escape the ropes in the second half of the fight.

Meanwhile, Barboza cannot afford to rely purely on defense to win rounds. While his jab and straight right hand can punish Duarte for overreaching, making an aggressive opponent miss is rarely enough on the scorecards if the aggressor is landing the harder, more eye-catching shots during brief exchanges on the inside. Barboza must throw enough volume to bank rounds decisively.

This makes the opening stanzas crucial for setting the physical terms of the night. If Barboza establishes his jab and glides back to open canvas after every exchange, Duarte will burn tremendous energy just trying to close the gap. Conversely, if Duarte traps Barboza on the perimeter within the first three rounds, Barboza will be dragged into heavy trenches he would much rather avoid.

Further down the bill, the stakes for Brandon Adams hinge entirely on the sanctioning body’s final ruling. Depending on how the WBC structures the matchup, Adams will walk into Anaheim fighting either for an interim championship belt or for the mandatory challenger spot that guarantees a future shot at the full world title.

Sports.title: Can Josh Kelly’s Speed Solve Jaron Ennis in Atlanta Unification?
Sports.content:
Josh Kelly pulled off his title win over Bakhram Murtazaliev by picking his spots with surgical precision. He’s going to need every ounce of that timing when he steps in with Jaron “Boots” Ennis on February 27, 2027, for a three-belt junior middleweight unification at State Farm Arena in Atlanta.

Matchroom just made it official: Ennis (36-0, 32 KOs) is putting his WBA and WBO belts on the line against IBF champion Kelly (19-1-1, 9 KOs) in the promoter’s first-ever show in Atlanta. Fans in the U.S. can catch the action on TNT, truTV, and DAZN, while DAZN will stream it everywhere else around the globe.

Ennis grabbed his two 154-pound straps by stopping Xander Zayas in seven rounds at Barclays Center last June, picking up right where he left off after unifying at welterweight against Eimantas Stanionis the year before. Meanwhile, Kelly upset Murtazaliev in Newcastle back in January to win the IBF belt and successfully defended it against Caoimhin Agyarko in July.

Against Murtazaliev, Kelly showed he knows how to frustrate a dangerous puncher into long stretches of inactivity, baiting leads and resetting the pace after landing his own counter. The problem is that Ennis brings a completely different kind of speed in the split second right after an exchange. Boots closes the gap in a flash, switches stances mid-combination, and unloads before you even have a chance to reset your feet.

Kelly’s best shot is to make Ennis pay early every time the Philly star marches forward. A crisp counter on the way in can buy Kelly just enough breathing room to angle out and force Ennis to start over from the outside. If Kelly backs straight up after throwing, Ennis will happily walk him to the ropes and start tearing up the body. Once Kelly gets pinned there, climbing back out to his preferred range gets awfully tough.

“I’ve waited a very long time to prove myself at the highest level – finally I have that moment!” Kelly said.

Even if Kelly stays off the ropes all night, he still has a scorecard problem to solve. Ennis can steal a quiet round with a three-second burst that gives the judges plenty of clean, eye-catching shots to remember. Kelly definitely has the hand speed to catch Ennis coming in, so how often he dares to pull the trigger between those flurries will decide just how competitive this fight gets.

Whoever leaves Atlanta with their hand raised will hold three of the four major belts at 154 pounds. WBC champion Sebastian Fundora still holds the fourth piece of the puzzle, though Matchroom’s announcement didn’t include any deal for him to fight the winner. Ennis and Kelly will get their first look at each other this Friday at a kickoff press conference in Los Angeles.

Sports.title: The Three Kings: Shakur, Devin, And Ryan Keep Fumbling The Crown
Sports.content:
Currently, world champions Shakur Stevenson, Devin Haney, and Ryan Garcia are the premier boxing names, but each time one of the stars gets in position to assume the role of the king, they end up fumbling the crown.

Back in 2023, Gervonta “Tank” Davis, Teofimo Lopez, Devin Haney, and Ryan Garcia were tagged with the moniker “The Four Kings.” All four boxers have achieved success, but the landscape has experienced a slight shift.

As of now, Shakur Stevenson, Devin Haney, and Ryan Garcia are the Top Dogs. From lightweight all the way up to welterweight, many hungry boxers have placed these top names on their radars.

In past decades, fight fans witnessed the Mike Tyson Era, the Roy Jones Jr. Era, the Floyd “Money” Mayweather Era, and the Canelo Era. With the current crop of talent, we’re still waiting for one of them to step up and claim this time period.

After outpointing Vasiliy Lomachenko, Devin Haney moved up to super-lightweight, defeated Regis Prograis, and won the WBC title. In his next fight, Haney was dropped three times by Ryan Garcia and lost via majority decision.

A month later, the New York State Athletic Commission overturned the win to a no-contest because Garcia tested positive for ostarine. Haney would go on to move up to welterweight, outpoint Brian Norman Jr., and win the WBO world title.

Instead of immediately following up on the big November 2025 victory, Haney wasted most of 2026 having a Twitter battle with Shakur Stevenson. It would have made more sense for Devin to rematch Ryan or fight Rolly Romero.

Shakur Stevenson looked spectacular in January 2026 when he thoroughly outclassed Teofimo Lopez and won the WBO super-lightweight title. The boxing pundits praised Shakur’s performance, and they were ready to crown him.

Unfortunately, Shakur fumbled the crown by being inactive for the remainder of 2026. Shakur Stevenson wasted a considerable amount of time going back and forth with Devin Haney over two pounds.

At one point in October, it seemed like Stevenson and Haney agreed to fight at 145, and then suddenly, the negotiations stalled. Shakur could have claimed the crown by defeating Haney at 147 and becoming a five-division world champion.

After losing to Rolly Romero, Ryan Garcia bounced back by scoring a unanimous decision victory over Mario Barrios. With the win, Garcia became the new WBC world welterweight champion.

Seven months later, in September 2026, Garcia looked extremely impressive as he stopped Conor Benn in the second round. The victory put Garcia in position to grab that elusive crown.

According to media reports, it appears as if Garcia is going to fumble the crown by placing himself in a lose-lose situation. If Garcia loses to Floyd Mayweather, he’s going to get trolled.

If he defeats Mayweather, nobody is going to give him credit for beating a 50-year-old man. Garcia has more eye-catching options such as Teofimo Lopez, a rematch with Devin Haney, or avenging the loss he suffered against Rolly Romero.

Once upon a time, star boxers used to thrive on claiming ownership of a particular time period. Those days appear to be gone because nowadays, it seems like none of the elite boxers want to step up and take ownership of this current era.

Sports.title: William Zepeda Faces Jadier Herrera’s Power March 13
Sports.content:
William Zepeda will defend his WBC lightweight championship against interim titleholder Jadier Herrera in Mexico on March 13, 2027, according to ESPN’s Salvador Rodríguez. Herrera easily carries the rawest punch Zepeda has encountered in the pro ranks.

Still, Ricardo Núñez sent the Cuban southpaw to the canvas in the opening frame of their clash, exposing technical cracks before Herrera managed to close the show in the eighth round.

Boasting 16 knockouts across 18 bouts, the 24-year-old proved that a single blow can bail him out of trouble. Yet the nature of that knockdown against Núñez highlights a glaring liability. Núñez baited Herrera late in the first round by faking low with the left, drawing Herrera’s eyes down before looping a clean right hand upstairs. That willingness to bite on basic level-change feints could prove fatal against Zepeda, whose entire offense is built around digging to the beltline before detonating hooks around a dropping guard.

Surviving the Storm Before the Stoppage

While Herrera recovered from only the second knockdown of his career by relying on jabs and forward pressure to halt Núñez in round eight, surviving Zepeda demands a far tighter defensive shell. Relying on dramatic second-half rescues rarely works against an engine that throws 80 to 100 punches per frame. Herrera cannot afford to spend minutes waiting for the perfect counter while Zepeda piles up triple-digit punch totals.

Zepeda shines deepest into his sequences. He crowds the pocket, alternates targets between ribs and chin, and continues firing even when his rival shells up. Herrera’s clearest route to slowing that machine is timing his counters directly between the incoming shots. Catching the champion cleanly during the level-change from head to body could make Zepeda hesitate before launching extended combinations.

With both men operating from the southpaw stance, Zepeda anticipates an aggressive challenger. The champion noted in remarks to the WBC that Herrera comes forward rather than circling away. Holding real estate in the center of the ring gives Herrera punch-for-punch trades, but it leaves him vulnerable to the exact high-low sequences that made him vulnerable against Núñez.

A single sharp counter might steal a frame for Herrera if it rattles Zepeda and yields room to follow up. Yet if Zepeda simply absorbs the shot and resumes digging to the liver, Herrera risks landing the prettiest single punch while dropping the round on raw work rate. Núñez troubled him with basic feints; Zepeda will amplify that pressure exponentially from the opening bell.

Rodríguez added that the WBC plans to mandate two lightweight eliminators featuring its top available contenders, though specific pairings remain unconfirmed. Herrera has his title shot locked down, and the opening rounds will reveal whether his vaunted power can keep Zepeda off him or if his defensive lapses will cut the night short.

Sports.title: Willy Hutchinson Can Borrow Bivol’s Blueprint Against Canelo
Sports.content:
Matchroom wants the WBC to install Ben Whittaker as the mandatory challenger for newly minted light heavyweight champion Willy Hutchinson. The promotional outfit envisions Whittaker taking an interim bout in February before stepping into a title shot. That route quickly hits a snag if Saul Canelo Alvarez enters the picture.

During the WBC convention, president Mauricio Sulaiman agreed to pause discussions to let promotional teams negotiate behind closed doors, per reporting from Tris Dixon shared by EverythingBoxing’s Darshan Desai. An additional report reveals Whittaker sits among four contenders under consideration for title eliminators, joining Artur Beterbiev, Radivoje Kalajdzic, and Imam Khataev. Because of that, Whittaker might need to secure another win before he gets anywhere near a mandatory distinction.

Hutchinson captured the vacant green belt on Saturday by defeating Joshua Buatsi on points in Manchester, successfully avenging his 2024 loss. Shortly after, Canelo trainer Eddy Reynoso pointed to the Scottish champion as a realistic target during a conversation with ESPN KnockOut. Alvarez reclaimed his WBC super middleweight belt against Christian Mbilli last month, so jumping to 175 pounds gives him a shot at securing yet another division crown.

Hutchinson made his stance clear during an appearance on Sky Sports’ Toe2Toe podcast, confirming rumors that Canelo is considering moving up to challenge him. The Scotsman embraced the prospect, knowing a fight against Alvarez offers massive global attention and an enormous payday compared to a purely domestic clash with Whittaker. Whittaker brings guaranteed British interest, yet Canelo represents superstardom. That reality gives the champion every incentive to keep his schedule open while his management sees if Reynoso follows through with an official contract.

The calendar works in the champion’s favor. Matchroom wants Whittaker active in February regardless. Should the sanctioning body sanction an Alvarez defense first, Whittaker might pick up a winter victory only to end up stuck in a holding pattern. A Canelo triumph would shuffle the deck completely, forcing Matchroom to chase an entirely different champion.

Ordering a final eliminator creates a separate hurdle for Matchroom. Depending on whom the WBC tabs as Whittaker’s opponent, that proposed February date might turn into a mandatory qualifier rather than a routine tune-up. Sulaiman’s committee controls the bracket, while Canelo holds the cards on Hutchinson’s next move. Until Alvarez locks in his plans, Hutchinson can comfortably wait out the market before looking at Whittaker.

Hutchinson taking Whittaker over Canelo would be leaving generational money on the table. In boxing economics, the math is not even close.

Whittaker brings standard domestic revenue. A fight with Canelo is an immediate life-altering purse, plus a mandatory rematch clause if Hutchinson pulls off the upset. Beating Alvarez turns Hutchinson from a newly crowned British champion into an international pay-per-view fixture overnight. He would control the terms for a rematch that generates double the revenue of the first fight.

Stylistically, Hutchinson is a nightmare for where Canelo sits at this stage of his career: Hutchinson is a true 175-pounder who operates with significant height and length advantages over a blown-up super middleweight.

Canelo struggles when opponents force a high work rate, pump a consistent jab from distance, and refuse to sit along the ropes. Bivol wrote the blueprint on how a rangy, busy light heavyweight neutralizes Canelo’s low-volume counterpunching.

Canelo simply does not carry one-punch equalizer power against durable, full-sized light heavyweights. He has to walk them down, absorb leather, and land clean hooks to the body. Hutchinson throws with volume from odd angles and keeps opponents guessing.

Whittaker will still be floating around the UK scene whenever Hutchinson is finished with the Alvarez business. Taking a risky domestic defense against an unproven contender for a fraction of the purse when the biggest cash cow in boxing is sniffing around would be promotional negligence.

Sports.title: Frank Warren Must Protect Moses Itauma From Himself
Sports.content:
Moses Itauma wasted no time seeking redemption after suffering his first career loss, immediately lobbying promoter Frank Warren for a direct return bout with Filip Hrgovic. Warren, however, has other plans.

Warren revealed that the young heavyweight blew up his phone following the August stoppage.

“He was on the phone the day after, and the day after that, and the day after that, but as I said to him, we had to pay Frank Sanchez to step aside, and that’s the position,” Warren said to DAZN News.

Sanchez originally stepped aside to allow the initial clash to happen, securing his spot as the mandatory challenger for Hrgovic’s IBF heavyweight title. Reports indicate Hrgovic and Sanchez will likely collide in Croatia during early 2027. Itauma is slated to return to action early next year against a ranked contender.

Warren taking his foot off the gas is the only sensible move. Itauma looked sharp out of the gate against Hrgovic, banking the opening stanzas with poise. The wheels fell off in round 3 once Hrgovic began putting hands on him.

Itauma did not react well to incoming fire. A look of panic crept across his face, exposing a young fighter utterly bewildered by an experience he never anticipated. That reaction is the direct byproduct of soft matchmaking. Having bypassed elite amateur competition, Itauma spent his developmental run feasting on fragile opposition that fell apart under early pressure.

When Hrgovic stood firm, Itauma tried a Shakur Stevenson step back, giving up ground in a straight line with his head stuck on the center line. Hrgovic recognized the amateur defensive flaw instantly, closing the distance like a shark stalking injured prey. Trapped along the ropes, Itauma abandoned his boxing technique, loading up on wild individual bombs in a desperate bid to punch his way out of trouble. Hrgovic timed the predictable swings, walked him down, and closed the show.

Warren will not fix these glaring deficiencies in a single training camp. A lone confidence builder against a hand-picked opponent solves nothing. Itauma needs five to ten genuine, grueling learning fights against durable, prime contenders who will test his chin, force him past six rounds, and make him solve problems under real fire.

Rushing Itauma back into a rematch after blasting out an overmatched opponent would be promotional negligence. Until he learns how to survive under distress, another date with Hrgovic will produce the identical outcome.

Sports.title: Ben Shalom Says Chris Eubank Jr vs Kell Brook Terms Nearly Agreed
Sports.content:
Ben Shalom says terms are nearly agreed for Chris Eubank Jr. to fight Kell Brook, with Boxxer targeting February for a DAZN pay-per-view. Brook is 40. He has been out of the ring for more than four years. Boxxer is banking on domestic nostalgia to sell a bout detached from any legitimate world title picture.

“I think the fight happens. I think pretty much terms are agreed on both sides,” Shalom told Pro Boxing Fans. The Boxxer promoter expects Eubank to headline the February card, pitching Brook as the opponent fans want to see. The fight remains unannounced, and Shalom mentioned no weight limit.

Brook won his IBF belt at 147 pounds. He finished Amir Khan at a 149-pound catchweight in February 2022. Eubank operates at middleweight and super middleweight. Brook ventured to 160 pounds against Gennadiy Golovkin, suffering a stoppage loss along with a shattered orbital bone. Errol Spence Jr. fractured Brook’s other eye socket the following year. A strict catchweight below 160 pounds forces Eubank to cut harder, yet Brook still enters the ring against a naturally bigger man who leans, roughs up opponents inside, and unloads heavy volume.

Brook relies on his straight right hand to halt aggressive opponents. A timed counter over a lazy jab forces fighters to hesitate. Trouble arrives if Brook reacts a split second late. Eubank closes distance rapidly, chaining flurries together before an older opponent sets his feet. A four-year layoff destroys spatial timing and depth perception faster than punch resistance. Brook must measure distance against a larger fighter closing the gap, then absorb the return fire when the tempo accelerates.

Boxxer capitalized on Khan against Brook because British fans spent a decade arguing over the rivalry. That personal animosity made the pay-per-view an event. Eubank and Brook share zero history. Boxxer assumes name recognition alone generates buys, testing whether casual viewers will pay for an opportunistic, manufactured pairing.

Shalom cited Anthony Joshua against Tyson Fury as reason to shift the card off a crowded December calendar into February. Moving dates avoids domestic clashes, yet February puts the event directly into post-holiday consumer fatigue. Streaming subscribers must justify paying an extra fee for a non-title showcase between veterans.

For Eubank, the event represents a safe payday over risky bouts against active middleweight champions like Janibek Alimkhanuly or Carlos Adames. Beating an inactive 40-year-old former welterweight proves nothing at world level. A Brook win produces a memorable upset, yet offers nowhere to go next. Boxxer is simply wagering that old memories can carry a pay-per-view broadcast.

Ghana News.title: Accra after Sunset: El Niño, a heating city and the sky above us
Ghana News.content:
By Petras Anaab Ali (MPhil)

The sun has gone down, but the room still feels hot. The fan is running, yet sleep does not come easily. Outside, people seek relief on verandas, in compound yards and along the roadside. For anyone who has spent such an evening in Accra, the question is simple: why does sunset bring so little comfort?

That question has become more urgent. On 30 October 2026, the Ghana Meteorological Agency (GMet) warned that a very strong and still intensifying El Niño is developing, and that Ghana should prepare for a hotter, drier and dustier dry season. Heat stress is expected to peak between February and April 2027, especially in the north. The ocean data behind that warning are striking. In mid-October, the weekly Niño 3.4 index, the standard measure of El Niño, reached +3.3°C. Scientists classify anything above +2.0°C as "very strong."

For Accra, the warning raises a practical question: how prepared is a densely built city for additional heat? Answering it means looking at three things together: the global climate, the city we have built, and, less obviously, the whole column of atmosphere above us. My MPhil research in Physics at the University of Ghana followed the last strong El Niño upwards through that column. What it found is that El Niño does not only change the weather at ground level. It disturbs the entire sky.

A distant ocean, a connected atmosphere

El Niño begins with unusually warm surface water in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific. Normally, trade winds push warm water westward towards Asia. During El Niño those winds weaken, and the warm pool spreads east. Warm water heats the air above it, the air rises, and storm clouds form where they normally would not. That shift in where the atmosphere draws its heat rearranges winds and rainfall across the globe. Scientists call these long-distance links teleconnections.

El Niño strength Niño 3.4 sea surface temperature anomaly Weak +0.5°C to +0.9°C Moderate +1.0°C to +1.4°C Strong +1.5°C to +1.9°C Very strong +2.0°C or higher

The present event is far beyond the top of that scale. In September, the US Climate Prediction Center put the chance at 75% that it would exceed every El Niño recorded since 1950. The great events of 1982/83, 1997/98 and 2015/16 are remembered in Ghana for drought and bushfires, and the first two were followed by power rationing.

Two cautions belong here, because they keep the argument honest. First, El Niño changes the odds; it does not dictate the weather of every community. Ghana's seasons also depend on the tropical Atlantic, and GMet notes that a cool Gulf of Guinea could shape how the 2027 rains behave. Second, the heat people feel today cannot automatically be blamed on a forecast for the coming months. Establishing how unusual Accra's present heat is requires local observations compared with the same season in earlier years.

The planet is already running hot

According to the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), September 2026 was the second-warmest September on record, with the global surface temperature 1.33°C above average. NOAA's map for that month shows a bright red tongue of warm water stretching along the equator from South America across the Pacific: El Niño itself. Northern Canada and Siberia are deep red. Cooler-than-normal blue is now confined mostly to Antarctica and a few small patches.

Ghana and the Gulf of Guinea appear in light pink, roughly half a degree to one degree above normal. That should not reassure us. Global temperatures usually peak a few months after El Niño itself peaks, because the heat released by the Pacific takes time to spread through the atmosphere. That is what happened after the 2023/24 El Niño, when 2024 went on to break global temperature records. On the evidence so far, West Africa's turn is still coming.

Accra already has a heat problem

El Niño will not arrive in a cool city. Local evidence over the past year gives the discussion a firm foundation.

Surfaces have heated sharply: A peer-reviewed study of the Greater Accra Metropolitan Area found that urban land surface temperature rose by an average of 4.07°C between 1991 and 2020 , as built-up land grew from about 31% to 73% of the area and forest cover fell from about 21% to 11%.

A peer-reviewed study of the Greater Accra Metropolitan Area found that urban land surface temperature rose by an average of , as built-up land grew from about 31% to 73% of the area and forest cover fell from about 21% to 11%. Heat is now on the city's agenda: In October 2025, the Accra Metropolitan Assembly (AMA) trained 30 data collectors to survey households, hawkers and outdoor workers in heat-vulnerable zones including Chorkor, Mamprobi, Korle Gonno, Kaneshie, Makola, Agbogbloshie, Old Fadama and Jamestown, to inform the city's first operational Heat Action Plan.

In October 2025, the Accra Metropolitan Assembly (AMA) trained to survey households, hawkers and outdoor workers in heat-vulnerable zones including Chorkor, Mamprobi, Korle Gonno, Kaneshie, Makola, Agbogbloshie, Old Fadama and Jamestown, to inform the city's first operational Heat Action Plan. Vulnerability is rising: In December 2025, AMA reported preliminary findings from its Urban Heat Vulnerability Assessment showing a sharp rise in land surface temperatures over three decades. The lead researcher said Accra is "heating faster than many imagine."

In December 2025, AMA reported preliminary findings from its Urban Heat Vulnerability Assessment showing a sharp rise in land surface temperatures over three decades. The lead researcher said Accra is "heating faster than many imagine." No neighborhood is spared: A study presented in June 2026 found rising heat in low-, middle- and high-income communities alike, from East Legon and Cantonments to Chorkor and Abossey Okai. It found women more affected than men, and, perhaps surprisingly, indoor workers more vulnerable than outdoor workers.

One clarification matters. Land surface temperature is the temperature of roofs, roads and soil as seen by satellites. A 4°C rise in surface temperature does not mean the air everywhere in Accra has warmed by 4°C. But hot surfaces are exactly what keep a city warm after dark, which brings us back to that sleepless evening.

Why sunset brings little relief

The physics begins with the energy received during the day. Sunlight heats roofs, roads and walls. Dark surfaces absorb more of it, and dense materials such as concrete and block store it. After sunset, that stored energy keeps flowing into the surrounding air and into rooms, partly as infrared radiation we cannot see but can certainly feel. A room can stay uncomfortable long after the sun has gone because it is still releasing the day's heat.

How fast that heat escapes depend on ventilation, shade, roof design and how closely buildings are packed. Iron roofing sheets heat quickly under the sun; poorly ventilated rooms hold heat in. Trees and wetlands work the other way: they shade surfaces and cool the air through evaporation. As Accra has replaced vegetation with concrete, it has removed some of its own natural cooling.

Humidity adds another layer. Our bodies cool mainly by evaporating sweat. In Accra's humid coastal air, sweat evaporates slowly, so a night at 27°C can feel far more oppressive than the number suggests. A thermometer reading alone cannot describe the experience of heat.

Who can afford relief?

Heat is shared, but the ability to escape it is not. One household can run an air conditioner all night. Another depends on a single fan in a poorly ventilated room. A trader may have to stay at a roadside stall through the hottest hours because leaving means losing income. That helps explain why indoor workers in crowded, unventilated spaces can be more exposed than people working outside.

Accra's authorities have begun to document this. AMA's citywide Extreme Heat Perceptions Survey asks residents how heat affects their health, livelihoods, productivity, sleep, transport and daily routines. It complements a heat-mapping exercise in which temperature sensors were installed across the city to identify hotspots. Publishing those results in an accessible form would let residents understand their own exposure and let the public judge whether interventions reach the places of greatest need.

Electricity sits at the centre of this. Every fan and air conditioner draws power, and a hotter dry season will push demand up. The supply side carries its own El Niño risk. GMet says Lake Volta is in good shape for now, but warns that the real risk falls on the 2027 rainy season, which determines how much water will be available for hydropower in 2028. When power fails on a hot night, the fan stops, and the people with the fewest alternatives suffer most.

Following the last El Niño upwards

The heat we feel is only the bottom of the story. For my MPhil thesis, Investigation of the Potential Changes in Ionospheric Patterns Due to Climate Variability (University of Ghana, 2024), I compared the strong La Niña of 2020/21 with the strong El Niño of 2023/24. I used temperature profiles from the COSMIC-2 satellites, covering the atmosphere from the ground to 60 km, and navigation-satellite signals recorded in Bogotá (Colombia), Antananarivo (Madagascar) and Baie-Comeau (Canada). Those signals reveal the Total Electron Content (TEC) of the ionosphere, the electrically charged layer roughly 100 to 1,000 km up that every GPS signal must cross.

To be clear, that work did not measure temperatures in Accra's streets or homes. But it showed that El Niño leaves a fingerprint at every level of the atmosphere.

Layer What was measured La Niña (2020/21) El Niño (2023/24) Lower atmosphere (2–5 km) Strength of early-morning temperature inversion 5–8 K 3–5 K Lower atmosphere Time the morning inversion breaks up Baseline 30–45 minutes earlier Upper troposphere Size of wave-driven temperature disturbances 1–2 K 3–4 K Stratosphere (20–30 km) Tropical stratospheric temperature Baseline About 2–3 K warmer Ionosphere Irregularity in electron content 1.7–2.1 TECU 2.4–2.8 TECU (25–40% higher) Ionosphere Night-time electron content Baseline 30–40% higher

In plain terms: during El Niño, the stable morning layer of air that acts as a lid on the lower atmosphere was weaker and broke up earlier, so convection started sooner and reached higher. That churning launches atmospheric gravity waves, ripples in the air that grow as they climb into thinner air, much as a whip's crack builds towards its tip. A warmer stratosphere let more of those waves through, and when they reached the ionosphere, they stirred up its charged gas.

The Sun is the ionosphere's main driver, so the two had to be separated. My La Niña year fell near solar minimum and my El Niño year near solar maximum. After statistically removing solar activity, El Niño still explained an additional 17–27% of the variation in the ionosphere's electron content. The study was among the first systematic analyses of El Niño's effect on the African equatorial ionosphere, and the African station responded as strongly as stations elsewhere in the tropics.

The Sun has been active this season too. The provisional Dst index, which tracks geomagnetic storms, recorded six disturbances between September and October 2026. The strongest, on 11 October, reached about −93 nanotesla, a moderate storm just short of the intense threshold. My thesis concluded that El Niño-linked ionospheric variability can rival a moderate geomagnetic storm of that kind. The difference is duration: a solar storm passes in a day or two, while El Niño's influence persists for months.

Why should anyone in Accra care? Because a disturbed ionosphere bends and delays satellite signals. My analysis suggests El Niño-linked changes can produce position errors of a meter or more, and vertical errors of 2 to 3 meters for single-frequency receivers, the kind found in most everyday devices. That will not stop anyone finding a trotro station, but it matters for satellite-guided aircraft approaches, land surveying, precision farming, drones and radio communications. West Africa sits beneath the equatorial ionization anomaly, one of the most turbulent parts of the ionosphere, where irregularities after sunset are already common. My data showed night-time electron content rising 30 to 40% during El Niño, precisely when those irregularities are worst.

I must add one honest note. None of my stations was in Ghana, because long, continuous, publicly available records of the kind this study needed were not available here. A Ghanaian physicist studying the African sky had to use data from Madagascar.

What the next set of numbers should show

Good decisions need better local data. Four things would sharpen the picture considerably:

Night-time temperatures: Daily minimum temperatures are a good start. Hourly records would show how quickly Accra cools after sunset and how long uncomfortable conditions last. Fair comparisons: This season's readings should be compared with the same calendar period in earlier years, including past El Niño dry seasons (1997/98, 2015/16, 2023/24) and neutral years. Otherwise, normal seasonal change can be mistaken for exceptional warming. Humidity and neighborhood context: Humidity should be reported alongside temperature, and comparisons between neighborhoods should account for trees, building density and distance from the coast. More than one El Niño: My own thesis compared a single El Niño with a single La Niña. Any firm conclusion about El Niño and Ghana should cover several events and account for the long-term warming trend.

The purpose is to give residents a clear account of what is changing, where exposure is greatest, and which responses the evidence justifies.

Turning warnings into cooler places

There is a foundation to build on. In April 2026, the Mayor of Accra announced plans to amend AMA's bye-laws to formally recognize heat as a public health risk, after a review found major gaps in how the city handles extreme heat. The new provisions are to focus on markets, transport terminals and temporary structures. AMA's public health leadership has also called for reforms covering ventilation standards, roofing requirements, shade and green infrastructure. The task now is delivery. I would urge the following:

Set up GMet's proposed National El Niño and Dry-Season Preparedness Task Force without delay. GMet recommends one bringing together the relevant ministries, the Volta River Authority and local government, reporting monthly to Cabinet. The peak heat period is weeks away. Get heat advisories into homes and workplaces, not only onto websites. Use radio, churches, mosques, markets and SMS, and name practical steps: drink water often, avoid strenuous activity in the hottest hours, and check on older people, young children and the sick. Make the bye-law reforms visible. Shaded waiting areas at lorry stations, cooler market spaces and better-ventilated buildings are outcomes residents can see and judge. Plant trees that survive. Tree planting must come with maintenance budgets and evidence that the trees are alive where shade is needed. Plan electricity for 2028, not only 2027. The Volta River Authority and the Energy Commission should model cooling demand now and prepare for weaker inflows into Lake Volta next year. Measure our own sky. As my thesis recommended, a network of dual-frequency satellite receivers across Africa, with Ghanaian universities and GMet as partners, would let us monitor the ionosphere ourselves, and a West African space weather advisory service would warn aviation, surveyors and farmers when it is disturbed.

Africa needs to study Africa. The atmosphere does not stop at the top of the clouds, and neither should our science.

One atmosphere, from our bedrooms to space

The warm room after sunset and the disturbed ionosphere 300 km overhead are not separate stories. They are the same atmosphere responding to the same warm ocean. The data are clear: a Pacific running more than 3°C above normal, a planet in its second-warmest September on record, a city whose surfaces have heated by about 4°C in three decades, and a measurable El Niño fingerprint from the lowest kilometers of air to the top of the ionosphere.

We cannot stop El Niño, but we can measure it, forecast it and prepare for it. GMet's warning gives Ghana a few months before the peak heat arrives. The sun will keep setting over Accra. Whether its residents find relief afterwards depends partly on decisions we make before the next hot day begins.

His MPhil research investigated how El Niño and other forms of climate variability affect the ionosphere. His academic interests lie at the intersection of cosmology, quantum theory, philosophy of science and Christian theology. He is also a Sports Analyst, Researcher, Writer and Commentator with Radio Univers and Legon Today.

Ghana News.title: 9 in 10 sexual and gender minority people feared stigma in Ghana’s 2024 elections – Study finds
Ghana News.content:
A study by Rightify Ghana says 94.3 per cent of the sexual and gender minority people it surveyed feared stigma and discrimination during Ghana’s 2024 elections.

The human rights group shared the findings in the Ashanti Region as it trained volunteers to record rights abuses before the 2028 elections.

The study, called Navigating Democracy, looked at safety, inclusion and political participation. It covered 218 people in six regions. Of these, 176 answered a survey and 42 took part in focus groups and key informant interviews.

Fear did not stop most people from voting. About two in three respondents, 64.8 per cent, voted in 2024. Fewer took part in other ways. 26.1 per cent joined campaigns and 20.5 per cent took part in policy discussions. 30.1 per cent never took part.

Ebenezer Peegah, the Executive Director of Rightify Ghana, said people voted but met barriers.

“Our democracy is not inclusive. If we want to deepen our democracy, we need to make it inclusive,” he said.

The study found that 56.8 per cent of respondents said political campaigns affected them negatively. 42.6 per cent said very negatively.

Respondents could name more than one barrier to taking part. After stigma, 61.9 per cent named safety concerns, 47.2 per cent named family or community pressure, and 36.9 per cent named perceived legal restrictions. Lack of information was named by 33.5 per cent, and economic barriers by 32.4 per cent.

Other findings show the same pattern. 78.4 per cent said they feel unsafe taking part in civic life. 75.6 per cent said they faced or witnessed discrimination. 72.7 per cent said they see misinformation very often.

Mr Peegah said messages about key populations ran through the 2024 campaigns. He said presidential and parliamentary candidates used them, as did political leaders, sports figures and people in culture.

He said the targeting of minority groups is a sign of democratic backsliding.

The Constitution gives every person the right to vote and to be voted for. Mr Peegah said that right applies to key populations.

“These are citizens of this country who pay taxes,” he said. He said their number is enough to decide votes.

He asked political parties to campaign on issues, not on groups of people.

“We want political parties to campaign on issues that improve the lives of Ghanaians and solve problems, like unemployment and bad roads,” he said.

The volunteers, known as Equality Envoys, will record cases, follow them up and report on happenings in their own regions. They will also report when politicians make statements that put fear in people.

Rightify Ghana also runs an early warning system that teaches people the signs of democratic backsliding.

Mr Peegah cited one example. He said some traditional authorities banish people from their communities, and that only the courts can limit a person’s movement.

“There are some traditional authorities who just banish people, and that is against the law,” he said.

Ghana News.title: Appoint Clowns. Get a Circus
Ghana News.content:
Kwame Sowu Jnr., the writer

By Kwame Sowu

One of the biggest obstacles to Ghana’s economic and social development is not a shortage of ideas, policies or even resources. It is the chronic appointment of incompetent people to positions that demand competence, leadership and results.

Take our Metropolitan, Municipal and District Chief Executives. For decades, many have presided over communities that remain filthy, poorly planned, environmentally deplorable and barely liveable. Roads are neglected, drains remain choked, sanitation is appalling, public spaces are abandoned and basic urban management appears to be an alien concept.

Yet, somehow, we keep changing governments without changing the conditions in which people live.

What exactly do some of these appointees do? Beyond occupying offices, attending meetings, making political appearances and distributing photographs of themselves, what measurable difference have they made to the communities entrusted to them?

We must confront an uncomfortable truth: political loyalty is not a qualification for administrative competence. Being a party activist, campaign financier or familiar face in the corridors of political power does not automatically make anyone capable of managing a district, municipality or metropolis.

A government can have the most brilliant manifesto, the most ambitious development agenda and the most eloquent presidential speeches. But if the people entrusted with implementation lack imagination, discipline, initiative and basic managerial competence, the outcome is predictable: grand promises, mediocre execution and another four years of excuses.

Development is not delivered by manifestos. It is delivered by people who know what they are doing.

We must stop treating public appointments as political compensation packages. Critical positions must be occupied by people who can think, organise, innovate, mobilise resources and deliver measurable outcomes.

Ghana does not need more ceremonial officeholders. It needs problem-solvers.

If we keep appointing people who cannot transform their immediate surroundings, we should stop pretending they will transform a nation.

Ghana News.title: Ablekuma West: Roni Nicol declares third bid for NPP parliamentary candidacy
Ghana News.content:
Roni Nicol

Roni Nicol, a long-standing member of the New Patriotic Party (NPP), has declared his intention to contest the party’s parliamentary primary in Ablekuma West ahead of the 2028 general elections.

The declaration marks his third attempt to become the party’s parliamentary candidate for the constituency, having contested the position in 2016 and 2024.

Mr Nicol said his decision was informed by more than 20 years of service to the party, which he described as loyal, selfless and humble.

He also highlighted his longstanding connection to the constituency, saying he had lived, schooled and worshipped there for more than 30 years.

“For over 30 years, Ablekuma West has been my home. I schooled here, I worship here, I grew here. Ablekuma West is my heart,” he said.

Mr Nicol said his previous electoral contests and grassroots political experience had prepared him to lead the NPP in its bid to reclaim the parliamentary seat from the National Democratic Congress (NDC).

He pledged to pursue an inclusive campaign focused on job creation for young people, support for businesses and unity within the party.

He also called for accountable leadership and urged party members to work together towards victory in the 2028 elections.

“Together, let us win back Ablekuma West. Together, let us give our people a united, humble and accountable representation they deserve,” he said.

He appealed to delegates and constituents for their support and prayers as the party prepares for the 2028 electoral contest.

Ghana News.title: Jimmy Aglah takes the fight against galamsey into Ghanaian classrooms
Ghana News.content:
Kumasi, Ghana — Ghanaian author and media executive Jimmy Aglah is taking the national conversation on illegal mining, environmental destruction and responsible citizenship into the classroom following the approval of his novel, When the River Testified, by the National Council for Curriculum and Assessment (NaCCA) as supplementary reading material for Ghanaian students.

The NaCCA verification system lists the book as officially approved, identifying it as a supplementary reader for JHS/SHS and confirming that it meets the Council’s standards.

At a time when Ghana continues to grapple with the devastating consequences of illegal and irresponsible mining, popularly known as galamsey, When the River Testified seeks to help young people understand not only the environmental damage involved, but also the deeper questions of responsibility, leadership, silence, greed and the choices communities make when confronted with wrongdoing.

Set in the fictional Ghanaian town of Asempa Nkwanta, the novel follows broadcast journalist Kofi Densu, whose investigation into a deteriorating river gradually uncovers a much wider environmental and public health crisis.

Scientific tests conducted by Dr Mensima reveal elevated levels of mercury and lead in water and food crops. Evidence from the clinic, borehole, palace and surrounding community gradually comes together, forcing residents to confront the consequences of environmental degradation and the failure of individuals and institutions to act.

Although fictional, the issues explored in the novel mirror a national challenge that has become increasingly urgent.

For Aglah, bringing the subject into literature for young readers is an attempt to move the conversation beyond enforcement and political debate.

“We cannot wait until our children become adults before teaching them why the rivers matter, why forests matter and why individual choices have consequences for entire communities,” he said.

“The fight for our environment must also be fought in the classroom, in the imagination and in the values we pass on to the next generation.”

Aglah believes fiction offers a particularly powerful way of engaging young people because it allows them to encounter environmental issues through characters, consequences and moral choices rather than through statistics alone.

The approval of When the River Testified also places the book within Ghana’s broader educational objective of developing learners who can think critically, solve problems, exercise responsible citizenship and apply knowledge to real-life challenges.

The book also speaks directly to the international agenda on Education for Sustainable Development.

Under Sustainable Development Goal 4.7, the United Nations calls for all learners to acquire the knowledge and skills needed to promote sustainable development, sustainable lifestyles, responsible citizenship and an appreciation of humanity’s relationship with the wider world.

The themes of When the River Testified also connect naturally with SDG 6, which seeks access to clean water and sustainable management of water resources, while its treatment of environmental stewardship, degraded land and community responsibility touches on the broader sustainability agenda.

Aglah argues that the long-term solution to environmental destruction cannot depend exclusively on arrests, task forces and regulation.

“Laws are important, enforcement is important, but sustainability ultimately depends on what a generation believes,” he said.

“If young people grow up understanding that poisoning a river is not simply an environmental offence but an attack on health, livelihoods, food security and the future, we begin to build a different kind of citizen.”

The author hopes the novel will be used not simply for individual reading, but also as a resource for guided classroom discussion, literature lessons, reading clubs, environmental clubs and values-based education.

Teachers, he believes, can use the story to encourage learners to interrogate competing interests, examine evidence, discuss moral responsibility and propose solutions to environmental problems within their own communities.

The approval therefore comes at a significant moment in Ghana’s continuing debate over galamsey and the sustainability of the country’s natural resources.

Rather than presenting environmental protection as an abstract national policy issue, When the River Testified brings the consequences home through the lives of ordinary people living beside a river whose condition becomes a testimony against human choices.

For Aglah, that is ultimately the purpose of the book.

“The river in the story cannot walk into a courtroom. It cannot organise a demonstration or hold a press conference. But it can testify through what happens to the people who depend on it. I want young readers to understand that nature eventually presents its evidence.”

With NaCCA approval secured, attention now turns to publishing, nationwide distribution and partnerships that can make the book available to schools and young readers across Ghana.

Aglah is currently engaging publishers and organisations interested in education, literacy, environmental sustainability and youth development to support the production and wider distribution of the book.

When the River Testified is written by Jimmy Aglah and has been officially verified by NaCCA under Book ID NaCCA/G.42/Vol.8/366.

Ghana News.title: Ghana’s Gold has finally come home, and your pocket knows it
Ghana News.content:
For years Ghana lived with a strange contradiction in which it was Africa's largest gold producer yet struggled to find the dollars needed to pay for fuel, medicine and machinery. The cedi weakened and prices climbed while businesses planned around the next bout of exchange rate panic. The gold kept leaving the country but too much of its value never came back.

A report by the Swiss development organisation Swissaid found that about 229 tonnes of Ghanaian gold worth US$11.4 billion went unrecorded in official exports over the five years to 2023. That is not merely a mining statistic, because it represents dollars that never reached our banks, royalties and taxes that never reached the state and stability that never reached ordinary households.

The Ghana Gold Board (GoldBod), established in 2025 under Act 1140, was created to confront that contradiction. The public argument about it has been loud and some of the questions are legitimate, but the noise has often hidden a simpler question about what the country has actually gained. The answer is substantial and it reaches well beyond the mining pits.

More of our gold now counts

The first gain lies in bringing a scattered trade into the formal economy, and it also gives the state records on which serious oversight can rest. GoldBod exported 104 tonnes of gold from artisanal and small scale miners in 2025 worth more than US$10 billion, and a further 85.4 tonnes worth US$11.6 billion between 1 January and 20 October 2026. These figures are export values rather than profit, and their importance is that the trade now passes through official channels where it is recorded and where its foreign exchange can serve the wider economy.

A stronger shield for the economy

The national accounts show the scale of the change since GoldBod began operating. Gross international reserves rose from about US$8.98 billion in December 2024 to US$13.8 billion a year later, and the current account surplus jumped from US$1.47 billion in 2024 to US$9.08 billion in 2025. By August 2026 total exports had reached US$22.4 billion and the trade surplus stood at US$8.86 billion, with gold earning about two thirds of all export receipts.

World gold prices were exceptionally favourable during this period and cocoa and oil also played their part, so the credit must be shared. Yet high prices only help a country to the extent that it captures the proceeds. Reserves serve as the national shock absorber because they reassure investors, support the currency and give the country room to respond when the world turns difficult.

A steadier cedi

The benefit Ghanaians watch most closely is the value of the cedi, which comes under pressure whenever dollars are scarce. Every legally exported consignment of gold helps to ease that scarcity, since foreign currency from gold supports the banks that trade dollars and builds the reserves the Bank of Ghana can draw on to calm the market.

The cedi gained about 41 percent against the dollar in 2025, its first sustained annual gain in three decades, and the Finance Ministry has credited GoldBod's exports as a major driver of that recovery. The steadiness that followed matters even more than the size of the gain. The cedi has given back some ground in 2026, yet the Bank of Ghana reports lower volatility in the first 140 trading days of this year than in the same period of previous years, and the rate in September was still stronger than a year earlier. People can plan around a currency that moves less sharply.

When Gold Pays the Import Bill

Nowhere are these gains felt more directly than in international trade, because Ghana is an import dependent economy with an almost constant demand for United States dollars. The country spent US$5.87 billion on imports in the first four months of 2026 alone, and about US$2 billion of that went on oil, with diesel the single largest item on the national import bill. Rice, wheat, sugar, vehicles, spare parts, medicines and industrial inputs all have to be paid for in foreign currency, and that demand peaks in the fourth quarter when importers stock up for Christmas and manufacturers settle their overseas suppliers.

Reserves built partly from gold give this trade a firmer footing, and at the end of 2025 Ghana's reserves covered 5.7 months of imports, a buffer that reassures foreign suppliers, shipping lines and lenders that Ghanaian buyers will be able to pay. Banks with better access to dollars can open letters of credit more readily, and importers spend less time chasing foreign exchange and more time moving goods.

A stable cedi matters just as much at the point of payment, since an importer commits to a dollar price months before the cargo arrives and then pays duties and charges at whatever rate prevails on the day of clearance. The Importers and Exporters Association of Ghana reported that clearance costs during the 2025 Christmas peak were significantly lower than in previous years because a stronger cedi reduced the foreign exchange component of duties, freight bills and port charges. A consignment valued at US$10,000 cost about GH¢124,200 to settle in September 2025 and about GH¢115,500 in September 2026, and that difference of GH¢8,700 is working capital a trader can put into the next order.

Tema Port handled 2.29 million twenty foot equivalent units in 2025 according to Lloyd's List, an increase of 34.6 percent on the previous year. New terminal capacity and the diversion of vessels around the Cape of Good Hope drove much of that growth, but a better supplied foreign exchange market made it easier for importers to use the capacity that had been built. Shipping lines, freight forwarders and haulage firms whose costs are largely priced in dollars benefit as well, and predictable costs strengthen Ghana's hand against Abidjan and Lomé in the contest for transit cargo bound for Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger.

Relief in the household and the market

Most Ghanaians will never read a reserve report, but they feel the effect of a steadier currency in their daily lives. Inflation fell to 3.4 percent by April 2026, and while the Bank of Ghana's tight policy and fiscal discipline under the IMF supported programme deserve their share of the credit, a calmer exchange rate removed one of the main sources of imported inflation. In a country that buys so much of what it consumes from abroad, that shows up in the price of fuel, medicines, school supplies and spare parts.

Room for business to plan and grow

For business owners a calmer economy has proved as valuable as a cheaper dollar, and the cost of credit tells much of the story. Average lending rates fell from 27.40 percent to 16.33 percent in the year to April 2026, easing one of the heaviest burdens on Ghanaian enterprise, while the Ghana Stock Exchange Composite Index was up 72.5 percent for the year by that same month. A manufacturer can now quote a customer with more certainty, and a trader at Makola or Kumasi Central Market can restock without guessing what the dollar will do by Friday.

A wider foundation for development

The benefits may also prove more durable than a single good year because several reforms now point toward lasting change. The ban on exporting unrefined doré from 1 September 2026 encourages more refining, testing and skilled work at home, so that Ghana keeps more of the value of its own resource. Reclamation of mined forest land has also begun, although on a modest scale.

Government states that its Big Push infrastructure programme, covering roads, energy, water and housing, is being funded from domestic resources including revenue tied to gold and mining royalties rather than new borrowing on international capital markets. After the debt restructuring Ghana has just endured, that direction deserves serious attention provided it is pursued with care.

Credit, with eyes open

Honest praise must also acknowledge the limits of what has been achieved so far. The cedi depreciated by 9.5 percent in the first nine months of 2026, and reserves fell to US$11.07 billion in August, partly because of a pause in GoldBod exports, before recovering to US$12.05 billion by 22 September. Gold export volumes fell slightly in the first half of the year even as values rose 49 percent, a reminder that much of the gain has come from price and that a correction would be felt widely.

Protect the gain, then build on it

None of these concerns argues for reversing course, but they do argue for finishing the job. Ghana should publish an analysis of what a fall in gold prices would mean for reserves and public investment, and GoldBod should keep exports flowing steadily rather than allowing pauses that drain reserves just before the busy fourth quarter. Consumers and importers should receive the benefit whenever the currency strengthens, and above all the breathing space must be used to build what gold cannot provide on its own in the form of more factories, more exports and more jobs.

GoldBod did not create Ghana's gold, but it has given the nation a far better chance of keeping what that gold earns. For the family at the market, the entrepreneur at the bank and the young Ghanaian looking for work, that is the reform's real promise. Gold has always been in our ground, and the task now is to make sure that its value stays in our economy.

By: Albert Derrick Fiatui

Albert Derrick Fiatui is the Executive Director of the Centre for International Maritime Affairs, Ghana (CIMAG).

Ghana News.title: Ahead of 2027 Budget: Techiman drivers complain about fuel prices as traders lament slow sales and delays in Women’s Development Bank
Ghana News.content:
As Finance Minister Dr Cassiel Ato Forson prepares to present the 2027 Budget Statement and Economic Policy to Parliament tomorrow, Thursday, November 12, at 6:00 pm, the mood in Techiman reflects a mixture of hope and frustration.

The budget is expected to outline the government's “New Economy Agenda” – a strategic shift from economic stabilisation to productivity, competitiveness, job creation and infrastructure development.

It is also expected to include plans to fully fund the Accra-Kumasi Expressway using oil revenues. The government has promised not to introduce new taxes, opting instead for expenditure rationalisation and spending cuts.

However, at the Techiman Central Market and the main lorry terminals, residents say their concerns go beyond policy documents, as they look forward to measures that will provide tangible relief.

Drivers: Fuel prices are squeezing us

For drivers who ply the busy Techiman-Kumasi-Kintampo routes, the rising cost of fuel remains their biggest concern.

“Fuel prices keep going up every week,” one driver at the main terminal said.

“Every time we hear there's a budget, we pray it brings relief. The government must do something about fuel prices – that's our biggest problem. If fuel goes up, everything goes up for us.”

Another driver appealed for stability in fuel prices.

“We are not asking for too much. Just stabilise fuel prices so we can plan. When fuel is high, passengers complain, and we also suffer. The budget should address this,” he said.

Market women: Goods are available, but buyers say there's no money

At the Techiman Central Market, traders said prices of goods had remained relatively stable, but sales were slow because, according to them, customers had little money to spend.

“The goods are here, prices haven't changed much, but nobody is buying,” one trader lamented.

“Customers keep telling us there's no money. How do we survive like this?” she asked.

Disappointment over Women's Development Bank

Several market women also expressed disappointment over the delay in rolling out the government's proposed Women's Development Bank, which they expected would provide access to affordable loans to expand their businesses.

“We were promised the Women's Development Bank. We voted for it. We waited for it. Where is it?” one trader asked.

“If that bank had come, we would have accessed soft loans to expand our businesses. We are disappointed,” she added.

Hope for tomorrow

Despite their frustrations, many traders said they were looking forward to the budget with cautious optimism.

“Tomorrow we will listen to the budget. We want to hear something for the ordinary trader,” one market woman said.

“No new taxes is good, but we need real support – affordable credit and a market that moves,” she added.

Others believe investment in infrastructure could help ease their challenges.

“If they fix the roads, it helps us. Our goods travel from Accra, from Kumasi. Good roads mean lower transport costs. That would be something,” another trader said.

What to expect from the 2027 Budget

The budget is expected to focus on the government's “New Economy Agenda”, with an emphasis on moving from economic stabilisation to productivity, competitiveness, job creation and infrastructure development.

It is also expected to outline plans for funding the Accra-Kumasi Expressway with oil revenues, while the government has pledged not to introduce new taxes and instead rely on expenditure rationalisation and spending cuts.

Dr Ato Forson is scheduled to present the budget to Parliament on Thursday, November 12, 2026, at 6:00 pm.

For the people of Techiman, the budget is more than a policy document; it is a test of promises made and expectations yet to be fulfilled.

“We are watching,” one driver said.

“We voted for change. Tomorrow, we will listen carefully. The budget must speak to our pockets.”

World.title: Trump pleads not guilty to 34 felony counts
World.content:
News outlets will not be allowed to broadcast former President Donald Trump’s arraignment on Tuesday in a New York state court, a judge said Monday night, but he will allow some photographers to take pictures in the courtroom before the proceedings formally begin.

Acting New York Supreme Court Judge Juan Merchan rejected the request by several media organizations, including CNN, for permission to broadcast the historic proceedings. Trump’s arraignment — like most arraignments in the Manhattan courthouse — is a public proceeding, but news cameras are not usually allowed to broadcast from inside the courtroom.

However, the judge is allowing five pool photographers to take still photos at the beginning of the proceedings “until such time as they are directed to vacate the jury box by court personnel.”

Earlier on Monday, Trump’s lawyers urged the judge to reject the media’s request for live cameras in the courtroom. The Manhattan District Attorney’s office told the judge they didn’t have a position.

The media outlets that tried to get cameras into the courtroom argued that “the gravity of this proceeding … and, consequently, the need for the broadest possible public access, cannot be overstated.”

Trump is now in Manhattan ahead of the arraignment. A grand jury indicted the former president last week.

The arraignment is also expected to bring the unsealing of the criminal charges against Trump, which have not yet been seen by his lawyers or the public.

The indictment stems from Manhattan District Attorney Alvin Bragg’s investigation into hush-money payments, made during the 2016 presidential campaign, to women who claimed they had extramarital affairs with Trump, which he denies.

Trump denies all wrongdoing and his lawyers said last week that they’ll fight to get the charges dropped.

World.content:
A Ukrainian tank is seen near the frontline area amid the Russia-Ukraine war, in Bakhmut, Ukraine, on April 02. (Muhammed Enes Yildirim/Anadolu Agency/Getty Images)

The Ukrainian military has reported little change to the front lines but heavy fire from Russian forces at various parts of the front line in the Donetsk region.

The General Staff said that more than 45 enemy attacks had been repelled over the past day, with the focus on Lyman, Bakhmut, Avdiivka and Mariinka.

It said there were 17 air strikes and more than 20 strikes by multiple launch rocket systems.

“In the Bakhmut direction, the enemy is trying to take full control over the city of Bakhmut and continues to storm it,” the General Staff said.

West of the city, Ukrainian defense forces repelled about 20 enemy attacks, according to the General Staff.

Oleksandr Syrskyi, commander of Ukrainian Land Forces, posted on Telegram that in Bakhmut he had met with “soldiers and commanders who destroyed the myth of invincibility of the Wagner fighters and Russian paratroopers.”

“The enemy is weakening and trying to cover up its failures with new fakes about the capture of Bakhmut,” Syrskyi said.

Syrskyi referenced the possibility of a future counter-offensive, saying that “the forward movement of our entire army depends on what every soldier is doing right now on their section of the front.”

Some of the most intense fighting is to the northwest and west of the city of Donetsk – as the Russians continue months-long efforts to dislodge Ukrainian defenses in Avdiivka and Mariinka. The General Staff said that some 20 assaults had been repelled.

“There are also some operational successes of our military in the Donetsk area. Our military have taken some positions. They have taken a more strategic and favourable position,” said Oleksii Dmytrashkivskyi, spokesperson for the military in that zone.

He also noted that Russian special forces had been introduced in the area.

“The enemy is trying to attack our positions between Avdiivka and Marinka. These attempts do not stop. It should be noted that the enemy has suffered quite significant losses,” Dmytrashkivskyi said.

He also claimed that the Russians “don’t have the same amount of equipment and, as they themselves say, they are on a ‘diet’ of ammunition for assaults.”

Social media video showed both sides engaged in heavy fire in the Avdiivka area, which the Russians have surrounded on three sides.

Denis Pushilin, the leader of the self-declared Donetsk People’s Republic, claimed that Russian forces were still advancing in the Avdiivka direction.

“It is still premature to speak of encirclement, but the situation is being created, if not critical, then extremely difficult for the enemy… After clearing Kamianka, our units are moving further. There are difficulties both with the terrain, which must also be overcome, and there are also similarities with weather conditions. But these difficulties are mutual — both for the enemy and for us,” Pushilin said.
