Recently, I asked a group of young people in Abuja who had travelled from the North, West, South and Eastern parts of Nigeria whether drug use is reducing or increasing in their various neighbourhoods. The answer was unanimous- “Increasing!”. They are obviously not lying, and the answer is what we can all see in our communities. The many years of the war on drugs in Nigeria and across many African countries have not led to drug use abating while the human cost is also not yet fully quantified.

In 2014, the West Africa Commission on Drugs led by the Former President of Nigeria, Olusegun Obasanjo, launched a report “Not just in Transit: Drugs, State and Society in West Africa”. A report that detailed the reality of illicit drug trade, increasing consumption and health related challenges among the burgeoning population of West African countries. The report emphasised the need for national laws to evolve from the prevailing “war on Drugs” to a pragmatic approach that consider the realities of drug use in our communities.

More than ever before, we are seeing how drug laws disproportionately affect the most vulnerable in our society. In Nigeria, our drug law does not differentiate between people who traffic drugs and those who use drugs with the NDLEA Act (2004) prescribing minimum of 15 years and maximum of 25 years’ imprisonments for people caught using illicit drugs. While the national policies have evolved with less emphasis on prosecuting people who use drugs, the general principle of using the criminal justice system and law enforcement to address a public health problem persists. This has led to series of human rights violation of people who use drugs, incessant arrests, extortions, limited treatment and rehabilitation facilities and reduced government funding for health and harm reduction programs which are proven public health interventions approved by the World Health Organization. Year after year we celebrate arrests and seizures of drugs and crack down on organised crimes which are very much commendable, the human cost of paying less attention to the other side of the response where health and development ought to be the centre of our response to drug control among both young and adults who use drugs is becoming too difficult to ignore. A nation where over 14.3 million people are using illicit drugs, according to 2019 survey; and where HIV prevalence among people who inject drugs increased from 4.4% to 10.9% based on 2020 national survey do not need a further debate to discontinue the narrow fixation on law enforcement to manage a public health need.

Drug control response in Nigeria and Africa should embrace a developmental approach. Africa’s drug-control response requires developmental justice rather than continuing the conventional “war on drugs”. Punitive enforcement alone does not address the conditions that shape vulnerability. Experts have documented how poverty, exclusion, stigma and limited access to health care have aggravated the impact of drug use on individuals and communities. Poverty brings food insecurity and stress; unemployment brings economic insecurity, and limited schooling means less knowledge of risk and fewer routes to help. In a survey on drug use disorders, including alcohol and drug use disorders, conducted in twenty six countries, only 1.0% of affected people in low & lower-middle-income countries received minimally adequate treatment, compared with 10.3% in high-income countries. A developmental-justice approach would combine proportionate law enforcement with prevention, harm reduction, treatment, social protection and meaningful participation by affected communities. It would distribute responsibilities and resources fairly, while protecting health, dignity and future of our youths.

As member states gather in Luanda, Angola from the 15th-16th of November to discuss and adopt the next African Union Plan of Action on Drug Control, leaders need to look beyond the rhetorics of the war on drugs. There is need for a plan that no longer justify punishment as a response for an issue that require public health experts to manage. Policy makers need to hold themselves accountable and tell themselves the truth that the war on drugs as a response for drug use is completely a failure. National response needs to invest in public health interventions by focusing on evidence-based prevention, treatment, rehabilitation, harm reduction and community development. Legal frameworks and political actions cannot continue to neglect the root causes of the rising tide of drug use and the impact on health and community development. The evidence is clear. What we need now is the political will to act on what we already know. This is when real change will happen, and we hope this new plan of action will be robust enough and be the needed catalyst for member states.

* Dr. Adeolu Adebiyi is Member West Africa Commission on Drugs.

World.title: Late Architecture Benjamin Afakwu: Celebrating a Life of Impact 20 Years After
World.content:
Royce Okolie

Twenty years after his passing, the remarkable life, professional accomplishments, philanthropic disposition and enduring legacy of Late Architect Benjamin Sunday Afakwu remain worthy of celebration.

A man of immense charm and charisma, he was a distinguished professional, philanthropist, sports enthusiast, devoted family man and committed Catholic whose contributions touched lives across different generations.

Twenty years may have passed since the departure of Late Architect Benjamin Afakwu, but the memories of his remarkable life, professional accomplishments and contributions to humanity remain indelible in the hearts of those who knew him.

Indeed, his family, the people of Onicha-Ugbo in Delta State, the University of Port Harcourt community and the nation at large lost a rare gem when he passed on November 13, 2006, at the age of 57.

An achiever in several ramifications of life, Afakwu was a man whose story represented resilience, determination, intellectual curiosity and an uncommon commitment to personal development.

From his humble beginnings in Onicha-Ugbo to his professional accomplishments in the built environment and his eventual rise to the position of Chief Technical Officer at the University of Port Harcourt, his journey was one of courage, hard work and perseverance.

Born on April 10, 1949, in Onicha-Ugbo, Delta State, he was the last of five children of the late Mr. Monye Afakwu and late Madam Ugom Afakwu. His childhood, however, was marked by personal tragedy. At just four years old, he lost his father, and two years later, at the age of six, he also lost his mother.

Following the loss of their parents, he and his siblings had to confront the realities of life and fend for themselves. Despite these difficult circumstances, young Benjamin refused to allow the challenges of his early years to define his future. Rather, they became part of the foundation upon which he built a life characterised by determination, discipline and an enduring quest for knowledge.

A Journey Defined by Education and Excellence

Afakwu began his formal education at the age of six at CMS Primary School, Onicha-Ugbo. In 1955, he gained admission into Niger Technical College (NTC), Asaba, where he studied Building Science and Construction.

His passion for knowledge and professional excellence subsequently took him beyond Nigeria’s shores. In 1973, he proceeded to City and Guilds, London, where he obtained a Full Technological Certificate (FTC) in Building Construction.

Not content with his accomplishments, he continued his academic pursuit at the Early School of Building, London, where he obtained an IAAS in Building. He later gained admission into the PGDAA School of Architecture, London, where he obtained a Postgraduate Diploma in Urban Planning.

His intellectual curiosity remained undiminished even after establishing himself professionally. In 2000, he obtained a Postgraduate Diploma in Technology Education (PGDTE) from Rivers State University of Science and Technology (RSUST).

Two years later, in 2002, he earned a Master of Science degree in Environmental Management from Enugu State University of Science and Technology (ESUT). In 2004, he further obtained a Master of Education degree in Industrial Education (Building) from Rivers State University of Science and Technology.

These academic qualifications reflected more than his desire to accumulate certificates. They demonstrated his belief in continuous learning, professional development and the importance of acquiring knowledge to make meaningful contributions to society.

A Distinguished Career at the University of Port Harcourt

Professionally, Afakwu found an important platform for expressing his technical expertise and commitment to service at the University of Port Harcourt, where he was employed.

Through dedication, experience and professional competence, he rose through the ranks to become Chief Technical Officer in the University’s Works and Services Department before his demise.

His position placed him within an important institutional structure responsible for the university’s physical infrastructure and technical services. His professional journey at the institution remains an important part of his legacy, particularly among members of the University of Port Harcourt community.

Beyond the designation he held, his career represented years of commitment to an institution that played a significant role in the development of higher education in Nigeria.

Marriage, Family and the Values of Togetherness

Away from his professional engagements, Afakwu was a devoted husband and father who cherished his family.

In 1979, he married his beloved wife, Mrs. Rita Ngozi Afakwu, at All Saints Catholic Church, Onicha-Ugbo, Delta State.

Their marriage was blessed with four children. His family remained an important part of his life, and the memories of his devotion, discipline and commitment to his responsibilities continue to form an enduring part of his family’s story.

For a man who experienced the painful loss of both parents at a tender age, building and nurturing his own family represented an important chapter of his life’s journey.

A Man of Character, Philanthropy and Passion for Sports

Perhaps one of the most remarkable aspects of Afakwu’s personality was the combination of professional discipline and an amiable disposition.

He was widely remembered as a man of immense charm and charisma, a philanthropist and a passionate lover of sports. His interest in sports reflected his appreciation for recreation, competition and the values of teamwork.

He was also a devoted Catholic who believed in peace and harmonious relationships. His commitment to his faith was reflected in his disposition towards life and his interactions with people.

Those who encountered him remembered him as a strict timekeeper, a dedicated professional and someone who took his responsibilities seriously. He valued punctuality, discipline and commitment, qualities that were evident in both his professional and personal life.

Despite his accomplishments and professional standing, he was known for treating people equally, irrespective of age or social standing. Whether dealing with the young or the old, he demonstrated a disposition that earned him affection and respect.

His philanthropic nature further distinguished him. He understood the importance of reaching out to others and making a difference in the lives of people around him.

Indeed, the true measure of a man’s greatness is not limited to his professional achievements or material accomplishments, but also to the lives he touches and the memories he leaves behind.

Twenty Years After: A Legacy Worth Celebrating

On November 13, 2026, it will be exactly 20 years since Architect Benjamin Sunday Afakwu passed on to glory. Yet, two decades have not diminished the significance of his life or the memories he left behind.

For his wife, children and extended family, the anniversary represents an opportunity to reflect on the life of a man whose presence meant so much to them. For the people of Onicha-Ugbo, it is an occasion to remember a son of the community who rose above difficult childhood circumstances to achieve remarkable milestones.

For the University of Port Harcourt community, his professional journey remains part of the institution’s history, while his story offers inspiration to younger generations about the importance of education, determination, professional commitment and personal discipline.

His life also teaches an important lesson about resilience. Having lost both parents before reaching the age of seven, he could easily have been overwhelmed by the difficulties of his early years. Instead, he pursued education, developed his professional capabilities, built a family and established a career that earned him recognition and respect.

As family members, friends, associates and well-wishers gather to commemorate his 20th remembrance anniversary, the occasion goes beyond mourning his departure. It is a celebration of a life that demonstrated the possibilities of determination, hard work, faith and service to humanity.

Twenty years after his passing, his story remains relevant, his memories remain cherished and his legacy deserves to be preserved for generations yet unborn.

Late Architect Benjamin Sunday Afakwu may have departed this world at the age of 57, but the values he represented, the professional milestones he achieved, the family he nurtured and the lives he touched remain enduring testimonies to his existence.

He was a man of vision, character, compassion and achievement. Twenty years after, his memory lives on, his contributions are remembered, and his life remains worthy of celebration.

World.title: The Fight for Africa’s Stomach Health Begins In Lusaka as O’Morain, Yamaoka, Leja Lead the Charge
World.content:
Helicobacter pylori is silent, widespread, and deadly, fuelling ulcers and gastric cancer across Africa. Now the continent is fighting back as world-leading experts are converging on Lusaka to rewrite the battle plan. Writes MARY NNAH

For millions of Africans, a silent bacteria is quietly destroying stomach health, causing ulcers and fuelling gastric cancer. Yet the guidelines used to fight it were never built for Africa.That is why the world’s leading experts are heading to Lusaka, to launch a battle plan made in Africa, for Africa.

A Silent Bacteria Ravaging Africa

Africa is rising in a fierce battle against Helicobacter pylori, the silent stomach bacteria behind ulcers and gastric cancer.For millions across the continent, H. pylori is not just an infection. It is a daily threat to stomach health, a driver of chronic pain, ulcers, and a major risk factor for gastric cancer. Yet for years, the fight against it has been fought with borrowed tools.Medical experts recognized that existing international medical guidelines failed to account for Africa’s distinct socioeconomic realities such as limited local funding, poor health care access and underdeveloped diagnostic infrastructure.That failure is the core issue driving the 2nd African Helicobacter Pylori and Microbiota International Scientific Conference in Lusaka, Zambia.

Lusaka Becomes The War-Room

Global Professors, Prof. Emeritus Colm O’Morain and Prof. Yoshio Yamaoka lead a world-class charge to speak at the conference. The two-day war-room conference will hold at the Grand Palace Hotel Lusaka, Zambia from November 27 to 28, 2026.

Prof. Colm O’ Morain, renowned Emeritus Professor of Medicine at the Trinity College Dublin & Tallagent University Hospital Ireland, is the keynote speaker and will be speaking on “The next 40 years of H. pylori – Opportunities & Challenges.”

Another globally renowned Physician, Microbiologist & research specialist in Helicobacter /gastro cancer pathogens, Prof. Yoshio Yamaoka will be speaking on “Collaborative Research in Africa: Current Progress & Future Perspective, while Prof. Marcis Leja will be speaking on “Gastric Cancer Prevention Initiatives in Europe”.

“The President, AHMSG, Prof. Mashiko Setshedi in a press release said the international conference will also feature, good will messages from Prof. Peter Malfertheiner, President, ZAGAN, Prof. Kelly, Richen Symposium, oral presentations, panel discussions, award/prize presentations for best oral presentation, AHMSG Presidential handover and AHMSG Board Members meeting.

Built In Africa, For Africa

The African Helicobacter & Microbiota Study Group was established and launched in Lagos, Nigeria, in 2022 through a series of collaborative steps to tackle the specific challenges of Helicobacter pylori (H. pylori) infections and gastric health across the African Continent.

Prof. Stella Smith, a Director of Research at the Nigerian Institute of Medical Research (NIMR) and prominent microbiologist, spearheaded the initiative and was appointed the founding President.

The Group was built to create tailored continent specific guidelines for diagnosing, preventing and treating H. pylori infections to ultimately reduce related conditions like stomach ulcers and gastric cancer.It was formed as an international coalition originally bringing together leading medical scholars and board members across multiple African countries including Nigeria, South Africa, Cameroon, Egypt, Kenya, Morocco, Senegal and Tanzania. However, the Group has expanded with additional three countries such as Zambia, Namibia and Democratic Republic of Congo.

Innovation That Must Reach Patients

Richen Medical Sciences, based in China, supported the Group’s official establishment with major sponsorship. According to Dr. Attilio Citrino, the Global Marketing R & D Director, Richen Medical Group, “Medical innovation has real value only when it reaches patients and makes a difference in their lives. Our commitment is not simply to develop advanced diagnostic technologies, but to build meaningful scientific partnerships, share knowledge and support healthcare professionals in improving early diagnosis and disease prevention. We believe that cooperation with the African medical and scientific community represents an important opportunity to advance gastrointestinal healthcare and create lasting benefits for patients.”

Dr. A. Citrino and Mr. S. Jiangs, further emphasized that, “Richen Medical Science Group considers Africa an important region for the development of sustainable scientific and healthcare collaborations. The company aims to strengthen relationships with African medical institutions, universities and healthcare professionals, supporting greater awareness of Helicobacter pylori infection, earlier diagnosis and improved prevention of gastrointestinal diseases, including gastric cancer.

Through scientific cooperation, medical education and access to advanced non-invasive diagnostic technologies, Richen seeks to contribute to the continuous improvement of healthcare services and patient outcomes, promoting a shared vision in which technological progress and medical knowledge work together to improve global health.”

They stressed that Richen Medical Science Group is an international medical technology company headquartered in Beijing, China, founded in 2002 and specialising in the research, development, manufacturing and commercialization of innovative diagnostic solutions. With a strong focus on gastroenterology, the company has developed extensive expertise in non-invasive diagnostic technologies, particularly the Carbon-13 Urea Breath Test (¹³C-UBT) for the detection of Helicobacter pylori infection.

Its product portfolio includes advanced infrared spectrometry systems and hydrogen and methane breath-testing technologies for the assessment of gastrointestinal disorders. Through its international operations, including its European subsidiary in Italy, Richen is committed to providing reliable, accurate and patient-friendly diagnostic solutions to healthcare professionals worldwide, and that scientific research, technological innovation and international medical cooperation are fundamental pillars of Richen’s development strategy.

The company actively supports clinical research, scientific education and collaboration with leading academic institutions and professional organisations, including its longstanding partnership with the European Helicobacter and Microbiota Study Group (EHMSG).

World.title: Pochettino Set to Replace Carrick at Troubled Man Utd
World.content:
Mauricio Pochettino is ready to accept an offer from Manchester United to become their next head coach.

United have opened talks with the Argentine about him potentially replacing Michael Carrick(45), who is expected to be relieved of his duties in the next 48 hours.

Once Carrick’s future is clarified, sources have told BBC Sport that USA manager Pochettino wants to take the job.

US Soccer officials are expecting an official approach from United – and sources have told BBC Sport they have a contingency plan for their manager leaving, which includes a succession plan.

Former Tottenham and Chelsea boss Pochettino wants to remain respectful to the US Soccer Federation and will wait for United to make their approach.

The Red Devils would be required to pay $10m (£7.5m) to release Pochettino from his contract, which he only signed in August.

The USA have a two-legged Concacaf Nations League quarter-final against Haiti over the next week.

With confidence over a succession plan, it raises the possibility that Pochettino may not take charge of those games.

On Thursday, US Soccer cancelled planned media with players citing a clash with Veterans Day, though some reports claimed it was to stop the squad being asked about their manager.

Pochettino, 54, is understood to view the prospect of managing United as a serious opportunity, with the expectation being he would accept the job were it formally offered.

United have spoken to the ex-Argentina defender about their managerial position on three previous occasions – when Jose Mourinho was sacked in 2018, then in 2022 before the club appointed Erik ten Hag and again when the Dutchman was sacked in 2024.

Carrick’s future at United was top on the agenda of a meeting in Monaco last night expected to be attended by chief executive Omar Berrada, director of football Jason Wilcox and co-owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe.

United are 18th in the Premier League – inside the relegation zone – after winning just one of their first 10 games and none since August.

It is the club’s lowest position at this stage of a top-flight season since 1986-87, when they were 20th.

World.title: Shaibu Describes Tinubu’s Reward to Flamingos as Bold Statement on Sports, Youth Devt
World.content:
The Director-General of the National Institute for Sports (NIS), Comrade Philip Shaibu, has praised President Bola Ahmed Tinubu for rewarding Nigeria’s U-17 women’s national football team, the Flamingos, with ₦100 million each following their historic FIFA U-17 Women’s World Cup victory in Morocco.

The financial packages were officially announced yesterday by the First Lady, Senator Oluremi Tinubu, during a reception for the team at the Presidential Villa in Abuja

According to the monetary incentives announced, each of the players is to receive ₦100 million to be held in trust in a designated bank to secure their financial futures. The Head Coach Akeem Busari is to also get ₦100 million, while the Technical Crew Members get ₦50 million each.

Comrade Philip Shaibu in his reaction to the largesse from the Federal Government described the reward as a bold statement on the value of sports and youth development in Nigeria.

He noted that the gesture serves as “leadership rewarding excellence” and will inspire grassroots athletes to aim for national recognition.

Senator Oluremi Tinubu in his message to the champions advised them to maintain their focus, discipline, and role as positive ambassadors for Nigeria as they transition into higher levels of their football careers.

The Flamingos secured their place in history after defeating Japan 3-1 to become the first African team to ever win the FIFA U-17 Women’s World Cup last Saturday in Rabat, Morocco.

Earlier on their arrival to Abuja, the Flamingos were promised a ₦100million donation by Senate President, Godswill Akpabio in behalf of the Red Chambers of the National Assembly.

The players and officials were also serenaded at a special dinner organised by Premium Trust Bank with promises of Naira rain to follow.

World.title: Black Friday: Is ‘Buy Now, Pay Later’ option worth it?
World.content:
Black Friday is around the corner. Image via Canva

Black Friday is around the corner, and shoppers around the world are looking forward to getting their hands on their most-wanted items. To sweeten the deal with additional discounts, merchants are offering “Buy Now, Pay Later” (BNPL) at checkout.

The option allows consumers to split the cost of a large purchase into smaller, often interest-free instalments, providing convenience and flexibility. However, a shopping spree can soon turn into a debt trap if the model is misused.

WHEN IS BLACK FRIDAY?

Black Friday takes place on Friday, 27 November.



The shopping extravaganza occurs on the fourth Friday in November, after the US holiday, Thanksgiving.

Although it originated in the US, over the years Black Friday has become a major shopping event in South Africa and other countries. Retailers offer discounts on everything from electronics and appliances to clothing, furniture and groceries.

WHAT ARE BUY NOW, PAY LATER OPTIONS?

Currently, South Africans can pay for items such as clothing, household appliances, beauty services, furniture, and even food in instalments rather than making traditional upfront purchases.

Buy Now, Pay Later (BNPL) service providers include the following:

Payflex

Pay Just Now

Happy Pay

Zero Pay

Microbed

Float

Several banks, including Tyme, Standard Bank, Nedbank, and Absa, are also offering similar instalment repayment options.

The interest-free instalments are short-term. However, late payments can incur hefty penalties and bank fees, and, if unpaid, even legal action.



When it comes to Black Friday shopping, is the BNPL option worth the fuss?

The model works in consumers’ interest if it is managed responsibly. However, if misused, it can create a sense of false affordability.

Take a look at the pros and cons before checking out…

World.title: Gonubie Beach closed as sharks feed on whale carcass
World.content:
A beach near KuGompo City (formerly East London) has been temporarily closed following reported sightings of sharks.

Per a public safety notice issued by the Buffalo City Metropolitan Municipality, Gonubie Beach has been closed to the public after sharks were observed feeding off a whale carcass floating offshore near Black Rock.

“For the safety of beachgoers and the public,” the safety notice reads, “swimming and other water activities are prohibited until further notice.”



As such, members of the public are strongly urged to keep out of the water. They are also asked to adhere to all safety instructions issued by lifeguards and local authorities.

No reopening date has been announced as of the time of publishing. However, the municipality stressed that the beach will remain closed until it’s deemed safe to do so.

PRESENCE OF SHARKS

The closure of Gonubie Beach comes nearly a month after a 65-year-old woman was tragically killed in a shark attack at Orient Beach in KuGompo City.

Janine Lochrenberg, a retired nuclear radiographer and musician, had been swimming in open water alongside others when a shark fatally attacked her.

Nearly two weeks after Lochrenberg’s death, a shark was sighted at Nahoon Beach in KuGompo City, prompting a temporary closure of the beach.

TAKE PRECAUTIONS

While shark attacks are rare, taking a few simple precautions can reduce the risk further. Coast KZN recommends that you follow these safety tips:



Swim in a group, as attacks are often directed towards individuals.

Swim at beaches with lifeguards and stay within the safe swimming areas.

Avoid swimming at night, dawn or dusk, as sharks are most active during these times.

Sharks can smell and taste blood, so avoid swimming if you are bleeding.

Refrain from swimming at sewage-contaminated beaches, as sewage attracts baitfish, which in turn attracts sharks.

Obey warnings/requests to leave the water by lifeguards and shark spotters if sharks are seen.

Stay safe out there, folks!

World.title: Oswin Appollis continue to struggle at Pirates this season
World.content:
Orlando Pirates winger Oswin Appollis has struggled to replicate last season’s form.

The 25-year-old has managed just two goals and three assists this campaign, a poor return for a player of his calibre.

In his first year with the Buccaneers, Appollis was consistent throughout the season, netting 10 goals across all competitions and also adding eight assists.



In recent matches, Pirates head coach Abdeslam Ouaddou decided to start him from the bench. The Moroccan has defended his decision to bench the star, saying it was not the lack of form but player management.

“Appollis is one of our best players. Appollis is one of the best players in South Africa. He is full of quality, but Appollis we don’t have to forget is a human, he is not a robot,” Ouaddou said.

“So Appollis played a fantastic season for his first season in Pirates. He comes from Polokwane, where you know a lot of things have changed for him, and he managed to handle all these things. He did a wonderful, a fantastic season.

“Straight away, he went to the World Cup, and it’s not only him, many players in Europe, many players in other clubs. He played the games. He gave everything for his country. So it’s a guy who is not cheating. So we can understand one moment that sometimes a player can maybe have this fatigue.

Appollis yet to have a solid match for Pirates this season

With Relebohile Mofokeng gone, Appollis has struggled this season. In terms of goals, he has taken more shots at goal than any Pirates player but often failed to find the target.

At Bafana, he also failed to recapture his form, which helped the team in the 2025 AFCON.



Will Appollis find his form?

World.title: Zimbabwe targets South African tourists in fresh Victoria Falls tourism drive
World.content:
South African travel agents participated in a Familiarisation (FAM) Tour of Victoria Falls. Image: ZTA

Zimbabwe is stepping up efforts to attract more holidaymakers from neighbouring South Africa through a tourism marketing initiative targeting travel agents who sell international holiday packages.

The Zimbabwe Tourism Authority (ZTA) said South African travel agents recently participated in a familiarisation (FAM) tour of Victoria Falls, organised in partnership with South African Airways (SAA) and local tourism industry players.

The programme gave the agents first-hand exposure to the resort town’s tourism products and experiences, which they can use to package and recommend Zimbabwe to prospective travellers.



Zimbabwe strengthens tourism ties with South Africa

According to the ZTA, the initiative aims to strengthen business relationships between South African travel agents and Zimbabwean tourism operators.

The authority said the programme would help agents better understand the country’s tourism offerings and promote them to customers in the South African market.

The initiative also seeks to turn greater destination awareness into increased bookings, tourist expenditure and economic returns for Zimbabwe’s tourism industry.

South Africa is an important source market for Zimbabwe’s tourism sector.

In March 2025, The Herald reported that Zimbabwe had hosted another group of South African travel agents on a three-day familiarisation tour of Victoria Falls.

The earlier programme included visits to hotels, a guided tour of Victoria Falls, a Zambezi River sunset cruise, game drives and helicopter excursions.



South Africa remains an important tourism market

Zimbabwe’s tourism industry continues to attract international visitors, with South Africa playing a significant role in regional travel.

According to figures from the Zimbabwe Tourism Authority cited by the United States International Trade Administration, the country recorded 1,613,901 international tourist arrivals in 2024, compared with 1,602,781 in 2023.

This represented a one percent increase in international arrivals.

The tourism sector generated an estimated US$1.2 billion (approximately R19.86 billion) in revenue during 2024, highlighting its contribution to the country’s economy.

Meanwhile, SAA’s route information lists Victoria Falls connections with Johannesburg, Cape Town and Durban, giving South African holidaymakers several air travel options.

The airline’s involvement in the latest familiarisation programme could help strengthen links between travel agents and Zimbabwean tourism suppliers.

Victoria Falls remains one of Zimbabwe’s major attractions, alongside Hwange National Park, Lake Kariba, Matobo National Park and the Great Zimbabwe Monuments.

By targeting travel professionals who influence holiday bookings, Zimbabwe hopes to increase its visibility among South African travellers and generate more business for local tourism operators.

World.title: Bryanston homeowner racks up R800 000 in municipal debt; home goes to auction
World.content:
Bryanston home goes to auction. For illustration purpose. Image: Pexels

A homeowner of an upper-middle-class property in Bryanston faced the unfortunate reality of having their home go to auction today.

According to a recent listing by Absa’s Sale in Execution division, the homeowner’s municipal rates and taxes bill has exceeded R800 000, and they had failed to pay their bond.

couple’s home repossessed after separation



The 4-bedroom home on Shepherd Avenue went to auction today with a R6 million reserve.



The auction took place at 11:00 on Wednesday morning at the Randburg South West Sheriff’s Office.

Besides the municipal debt, the owners of the lavish 4-garage property fell into arrears and failed to remedy it before the bank took the matter to court.

Beyond falling into arrears with the bank, the couple also racked up R801 469 in municipal debt.



When the matter went to court, the pair, who had separated, failed to appear.

The husband argued that his financial circumstances had changed and that the bank shouldn’t be allowed to execute the sale.

However, the wife hadn’t been served, and the case was removed from the roll.



Later, judgment was handed down that Absa could execute on the property.

Today, the bank will try to retrieve its losses at auction on the lavish 1 200-square-metre property.

Buying the property at auction

To get the property, any successful bidder would have had to pay R40 000 in Sheriff’s commission.



They would also be required to deposit 10% (R600 000+) into the Sheriff’s trust account.

And then, within 21 business days, the buyer would need to pay the balance on the sale, roughly R5.4 million.

However, the buyer may also have to pay municipal debts once the property transfers into their name.



If the home isn’t sold at auction, Absa will take possession of it. At that point, the property will transfer from a sale in execution to a property in possession.

At the time of writing, Absa has 69 such properties in its possession.

All have failed to sell at auction, and some have been in the bank’s possession for years.



If the bank can’t recoup the bond balance and legal fees when the home eventually sells, the original homeowners may still be on the hook for the difference.

World.title: Number Of The Day | 68,000 | 11 November 2026
World.content:
The Economy Inside Our Homes Is More Fragile Than We Think

Domestic workers are part of the invisible infrastructure that keeps South African households functioning. When that infrastructure begins to shrink, the consequences extend far beyond cleaning and childcare.

Every morning, an extraordinary amount of economic activity takes place before most South Africans even arrive at work. Children are prepared for school, meals are organised, homes are maintained and care arrangements are negotiated. These responsibilities rarely feature in conversations about productivity, yet they determine how easily millions of people can participate in the economy.

Much of this work happens without pay, performed by family members whose time is assumed to be endlessly available. Some of it is transferred to domestic workers, whose labour allows other members of a household to pursue employment, run businesses or meet professional obligations.

This arrangement creates an economy within the home, one that is essential to the functioning of the formal economy but often remains invisible until something goes wrong.

When Household Support Disappears

Consider a working parent who employs someone to help with childcare and household responsibilities. The arrangement allows the parent to work longer hours, attend meetings and maintain a predictable schedule. The domestic worker receives an income that supports another household.

Now imagine that rising expenses make the arrangement unaffordable. The parent may reduce working hours, take on additional unpaid responsibilities or rely on relatives for assistance. The domestic worker loses some or all of their earnings. Their own family must then absorb the financial consequences.

One budget decision has redistributed work, time and economic insecurity across several people.

This is why domestic employment cannot be understood purely as a private transaction between an employer and an employee. It is part of a wider network of financial and caregiving relationships, where the stability of one household can depend on the labour of someone from another.

The Hidden Cost Of Unpaid Work

When paid household support disappears, the work itself usually does not. Floors still need cleaning, children still need supervision and elderly relatives may still require care.

Those responsibilities return to the household, where they must be absorbed by somebody else's time.

That time has economic value, even when no money changes hands. Hours devoted to additional caregiving may reduce opportunities for paid work, education, rest or professional advancement. The burden will not necessarily be shared equally, particularly in families where existing expectations already place most domestic responsibilities on women.

The result is an important paradox. A household may appear to save money by reducing paid assistance while simultaneously increasing the unpaid labour required to keep its daily life functioning.

The saving is visible in the budget. The transferred cost is much harder to measure.

A Warning Hidden In Employment Figures

South Africa's reported loss of 68,000 private-household jobs between July and September 2026 brings the fragility of this arrangement into focus. The figures do not establish why those positions disappeared, and they cannot tell us how each affected household reorganised its responsibilities.

Nevertheless, they raise questions that reach beyond the employment category itself.

If fewer households can sustain paid domestic work, what happens to the people who previously depended on those incomes? Who absorbs the work left behind? And how much additional unpaid labour can families accommodate before their own participation in the economy is affected?

Flexible domestic services and occasional work may provide alternatives for some people, but they do not automatically replace the stability of regular employment. A worker who moves from a dependable schedule to scattered assignments may remain employed intermittently while experiencing greater financial uncertainty.

Recognising The Infrastructure We Depend On

South Africa's conversations about employment tend to focus on the jobs businesses create and destroy. Far less attention is paid to the labour that makes those jobs possible in the first place.

Yet the ability to participate in paid employment often depends on reliable arrangements for care, transport and household management. These are not peripheral concerns. They are part of the conditions that make productive work possible.

That recognition has implications for how employers, policymakers and households think about economic resilience. Affordable care services, fair domestic employment

and practical support for working families are connected questions, not separate social issues.

The work taking place inside our homes may be largely invisible to the broader economy, but its consequences are not. When households lose the capacity to support that work, the disruption can travel much further than their front doors.

Editorial source note: The reported quarterly job-loss figure is drawn from the 11 November 2026 Number of the Day transcript, which attributes the employment data to Statistics South Africa. The article's wider analysis of unpaid care and economic interdependence is an original editorial argument, not a finding established by those figures.

World.title: IEC sets 18 November as revote day for Douglas residents
World.content:
DOUGLAS - Residents of Douglas in the Northern Cape will return to the polls on 18 November.

This comes as the Electoral Commission of South Africa (IEC) ordered a revote in Ward Three of the Siyancuma Local Municipality after ballot papers were destroyed before counting could be completed.

According to IEC deputy CEO for elections operations Masego Sheburi, the voters roll as certified and used on 4 November will be the voters roll used for the revote.

“For purposes of the recount, the processes of 4 November are preserved. In other words, candidates as they were certified will be the candidates in this election," Sheburi explained.

He further indicated that the IEC has reopened applications for special votes to be given to eligible voters.

The applications opened this Wednesday and are set to close on Saturday.

World.title: COGTA issues guidelines to help coalition talks
World.content:
JOHANNESBURG - The Cooperative Governance and Traditional Affairs (COGTA) Department has published guidelines to help parties navigate coalition talks following the Local Government Elections.

It follows a Technical MINMEC held on 9 November 2026, during which the draft guidelines were considered, and technical inputs were made to strengthen and improve the document.

The enhanced guidelines were presented to the Political MINMEC on Wednesday for consideration and approval.

READ | 14 days for coalition discussions start on Wednesday

The framework guides political parties and municipalities in navigating coalition arrangements, managing potential disagreements, and setting up stable governance structures as the new municipal councils are formed.

Approximately 138 metropolitan and local municipalities did not secure outright majorities, making power-sharing arrangements necessary.

COGTA Minister, Velenkosini Hlabisa, has called on provincial and local departments to support municipalities in implementing agreements.

Hlabisa has also called on leaders to intervene where political instability threatens municipal operations.
