World.title: COP31 Launches Electrification Finance Coalition; Separate $15 Million Guarantee Announced for Liberia Solar Program
World.content:
Aerial view of Liberia’s first utility-scale, 20-megawatt solar power plant located alongside the Saint Paul River at the Mount Coffee Hydropower complex in Montserrado County. Photo: International Consolidated Contractors

A new international coalition launched at COP31 will bring together governments, development banks and private financiers to support electrification in developing economies.

Separately, the Climate Investment Funds announced a $15 million guarantee for Liberia’s solar and battery-storage program, expected to help mobilize about $200 million.

Liberia’s electricity access remains low, with only 34.9 percent of the population connected in 2024, according to World Bank data.

By Aria Deemie | Climate and Environment Reporter

A new international financing coalition launched at the 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference aims to bring governments, development banks and private investors together to expand access to electricity in developing countries.

The Electrify Now Finance Coalition is expected to help countries prepare investment projects, address barriers to private investment and improve access to financing for clean electricity.



“Policies only show direction; they don’t make customers.”

The statement came from Emmanuel D. Wilson, Manager of Policy and Programs at Liberian Youth for Climate Actions Liberia, made the remark in an interview with FrontPage Africa after participating in a COP31 side event on youth-led clean energy investment at the Liberia Pavilion on November 10.

Emmanuel D. Wilson, Manager of Policy and Programs at Liberian Youth for Climate Actions Liberia (far right), speaks during a COP31 side event on youth-led clean energy investment at the Liberia Pavilion. Photo: Aria Deemie

His concern comes as Liberia continues to face a major electricity access gap. World Bank data show that 34.9 percent of the country’s population had access to electricity in 2024. In rural areas, the figure was just 9.2 percent, compared with 35.7 percent across sub-Saharan Africa. For households without electricity, access to reliable lighting and the ability to use electrical appliances remain limited. Businesses and public facilities also depend on dependable power to operate equipment and provide services.

The new coalition is intended to help mobilize investment for electricity expansion, but questions remain about how countries such as Liberia will access its support and what financing will become available.

The coalition was launched alongside the 35-by-35 Global Electrification Pledge, which aims to increase electricity’s share of global final energy consumption from about 23 percent to 35 percent by 2035. The African Development Bank and World Bank are expected to co-lead the coalition from 2027, bringing together development institutions, governments and private financiers.

The initiative is expected to work with developing countries to identify priority projects, build investment pipelines, reduce risks and address regulatory barriers that can discourage private investment. However, details of country eligibility, application procedures and the amount of financing that could be mobilized for individual countries were not specified in the launch announcement.

FrontPage Africa sought clarification from the African Development Bank on how Liberia could benefit from the coalition, what countries would need to do to access its financing, and whether the initiative would mobilize new funding or coordinate existing resources.

The questions were sent through Sonia Borrini, the bank’s Communication and Knowledge Management Specialist, whom this publication contacted at the Africa Pavilion during the conference. Borrini said she had forwarded the questions to the person responsible for responding. The bank had not provided a response by publication time. FrontPage Africa will update this story in its online version once a response is received.

Separately, the Climate Investment Funds announced a $15 million first-loss payment guarantee for Liberia’s utility-scale solar and battery-storage program. The guarantee is not a $15 million cash grant to the Liberian government. Instead, it is designed to cover certain payment risks associated with the electricity off-taker under the second phase of the Liberia Electricity Sector Strengthening and Access Project, which will be implemented with the World Bank.The guarantee is expected to help attract about $200 million in investment for solar and battery projects by reducing some of the financial risks investors may face and encouraging private-sector participation.

Solar panels installed at a Salesian center in Monrovia in 2020, when unreliable and expensive electricity supply posed challenges across Liberia. Photo: Agenzia Info Salesiana

Solar plants generate electricity from sunlight, while battery systems store electricity for use when generation is lower, including after sunset.

The financing announcements come as Liberia seeks international support to implement its climate and energy plans.

Emmanuel K. Urey Yarkpawolo, Executive Director of Liberia’s Environmental Protection Agency, said financing remains the main obstacle to implementing the country’s climate and energy plans.

“We have the policies. I think we have the political will. I think what is needed is the financing.”

Liberia’s latest national climate action plan targets a 64 percent reduction in emissions by 2035, with about 90 percent of the planned reduction dependent on international support, according to Yarkpawolo. Investment in renewable energy, he said, would be important to achieving the target. He also called for a simpler process for accessing climate finance.

“We hope that this new financing mechanism can help Liberia to be able to meet its target,” he said, adding that the process should be “transparent and simplified.”

Yarkpawolo described the Environmental Protection Agency’s role in ensuring that energy projects meet environmental requirements and undergo environmental and social impact assessments. He also pointed to the development of net-metering policies and regulations as part of efforts to support renewable energy.

Net metering allows households and businesses with solar systems to supply surplus electricity to the public grid and receive credits for the power they contribute. Liberia has taken steps towards establishing the framework. The Ministry of Mines and Energy validated a draft national policy in 2025, while the electricity regulator gazetted Embedded Generation Regulations in July 2026.

But having the rules in place does not necessarily mean households and businesses can afford solar systems or that the grid can accommodate electricity from privately owned installations. Wilson also highlighted affordability and the financial risks facing young entrepreneurs as barriers to expanding clean-energy solutions.

The question of access to climate finance was also raised by Dr. Hakima El Haite, COP22 High-Level Climate Champion, during an Economic Commission for Africa event at the Africa Pavilion on November 10.

“Our projects fail not because of the risk. We are not as risky as any other country. It is because of the perception of the risk,” she said.

Speaking at the event, titled From Pledges to Implementation: Delivering on Presidential Initiatives – Lessons for Africa on the Road to COP32, El Haite addressed Mr. Amer Baig, Chief Investment Officer of the Green Climate Fund, who was seated beside her. She called on the Fund to make its financing more accessible to African countries.

Dr. Hakima El Haite, COP22 High-Level Climate Champion, speaks during an Economic Commission for Africa event at the Africa Pavilion, with Green Climate Fund Chief Investment Officer Amer Baig seated second from right. Photo: Aria Deemie

“Our projects fail not because of the risk. We are not as risky as any other country. It is because of the perception of the risk,” she said.

She urged Baig and the Fund to help African countries overcome difficulties in accessing climate finance, pointing to the limited number of accredited institutions across the continent and the complexity of the application process.

“Please make it simple for Africans to implement climate actions,” she said.

El Haite also raised concerns about the debt burden facing African countries, saying governments were spending time negotiating and taking loans while trying to finance climate action.

For Liberia, the financing challenge extends beyond large-scale electricity projects to the ability of local businesses and communities to participate in the energy transition.

An earlier FrontPage Africa investigation documented how changing rainfall patterns and difficulties sustaining farming had pushed some rural residents towards charcoal production. Another investigation also found that a project involving women producing briquettes from palm-kernel shells in Todee District, Montserrado County, stalled after equipment broke down and the women struggled to find buyers. Without repairs and a market for their products, they returned to producing wood charcoal.

A mini steel (zinc) oven once used by women in Todee to char palm-kernel shells for briquette production. Photo: Aria Deemie

Charred palm kernel briquettes lie unprocessed after equipment failure ended a clean energy project in Liberia. Photo: Aria Deemie

Wilson said his organization’s clean-cooking survey in a rural community found that charcoal production was an important source of income for some households, helping them pay for food and school fees. He said switching to cleaner alternatives could be difficult if households lost that income without other livelihood options.

He said young entrepreneurs also face difficulties obtaining loans because they often lack collateral and an established business record. He called for financing that takes account of what households can afford and gives young businesses technical support and room to test their products before taking on major debt. He added that young people should have a role in implementing and monitoring climate policies, not only in consultations.

Liberia is also part of Mission 300 , a separate initiative led by the African Development Bank and World Bank that aims to connect 300 million people in Africa to electricity by 2030. The country has a National Energy Compact outlining its energy access priorities. The new Electrify Now Finance Coalition is a separate initiative, and its launch does not by itself guarantee additional funding for Liberia under Mission 300.

The announcements at COP31 have placed new attention on the role of finance in expanding electricity access. For Liberia, the next questions are how its proposed projects will qualify for support, whether the new coalition will bring additional financing and how the planned investments will translate into more reliable electricity for households, businesses and public services.

This story was produced as part of the COP31 Climate Change Media Partnership ,a journalism fellowship organized by Internews’ Earth Journalism Network, Informed Earth and the Stanley Center for Peace and Security.

World.title: Liberia: Monrovia City Mayor Siafa Dismissed, James Mulbah In
World.content:
Monrovia City Mayor Siafa Dismissed, James Mulbah In

Monrovia– President Joseph Nyuma Boakai has dismissed Monrovia City Mayor, John-Charuk Saah Siafa, nominating the General Manager of the Roberts International Airport (RIA) James K. Mulbah, has his replacement as new Mayor.

By Jaheim T. Tumu- [email protected]

His replacement, Mulbah joined the ruling Unity Party (UP) last December, declaring his confidence in the leadership and direction of President Boakai. Mulbah made the announcement during the Unity Party’s Homecoming Program, where he arrived at the party’s national headquarters accompanied by a large group of supporters.



In a endorsement said, he said, “My joining Unity Party today is not a political game.” He added that the UP was the first political party he had ever joined and that President Boakai’s stance against corruption was a major reason for his decision.

Asked then whether he harbored ambitions for elected office, he said he could not predict the future and that his focus was on joining the party. Mulbah would require confirmation by the Liberian Senate.

FrontPageAfrica reported early Monday that a prestigious source has informed the Siafa was out of favor with the Unity Party hierarchy after persistent complaints that the his institution was being starved.

However, Siafa has been axed after nearly three years of persistent public criticism of his handling of the capital — over piling garbage, unpaid workers and contractors, and allegations of financial irregularities — even as the mayor and his supporters have argued that the national government has never given the MCC the money it needs to do its job.

Siafa was nominated by President Boakai on January 27, 2024, and commissioned in March that year as Monrovia’s 28th mayor, succeeded Jefferson Tamba Koijee with promises to clean the city, restore transparency and depoliticize the MCC. He has been widely reported to be a close relative of the President.

But his tenure has been dogged by controversy. In June 2025, allegations of financial and procurement irregularities at the MCC surfaced in the press, including claims about the rapid elevation of staff to senior paid positions.

Earlier that year, MCC contractors protested in front of City Hall on UN Drive over unpaid wages, and the mayor and the Civil Service Agency came under fire from civil society over the dismissal of civil servants that critics described as political retaliation.

Some of the sharpest attacks have come from within the ruling party itself. In September 2025, Queen Johnson, Deputy Director for Records at the National Port Authority and a staunch UP member, publicly called for Siafa’s dismissal, labeling him corrupt and incompetent. Days later, MCC employees planned a protest demanding his resignation over the city’s persistent sanitation problems. In March 2026, another UP loyalist publicly branded the mayor a criminal amid allegations tied to an audit of the MCC.

World.title: Washington’s Blunt Verdict on Liberia’s Investment Climate
World.content:
MONROVIA — On paper, Liberia has rarely looked better. The economy grew 5.1 percent in 2025, mining and panning expanded by 17 percent, export volumes jumped 31.5 percent, and headline inflation eased to an average of 8.5 percent by December, down from a peak of 11.6 percent. The International Monetary Fund, the World Bank, the African Development Bank and the European Union are all underwriting the recovery.

By Rodney D. Sieh

Yet the United States government’s newest assessment of Liberia as a place to put money, published in early November in the State Department’s 2026 Investment Climate Statements, reads less like a sales brochure than a warning label.



Strip away the diplomatic packaging and the message to American companies is plain: the opportunities are real, the minerals are in the ground, the coastline is strategic — but bring patience, bring lawyers, and bring a plan for dealing with officials who expect to be paid.

Corruption as the “primary brake”.

The report’s harshest language is reserved for governance. It describes corruption as the main obstacle to both Liberia’s democratic consolidation and its economic growth, saying it raises costs, causes delays and exposes investors to legal and reputational risk.

Citing business surveys and U.S. Embassy reporting, the statement says some officials put short-term personal gain ahead of the investment climate, and that political cronyism often shapes decisions that should rest on merit. In one of its most striking passages, it says businesses can find it easy to operate illegally if the right political interests are paid — while companies that follow the rules get little help at best and, at worst, become targets for bribe demands.

Multinational firms, the report adds, frequently say they are charged fees that appear nowhere in their investment agreements, and accounts of extortion “at multiple levels of government” are common. The worst areas, it says, are procurement, contract and concession awards, customs and tax administration, regulatory approvals and government payment systems.

Liberia has signed the relevant regional, continental and United Nations anti-corruption conventions. The State Department’s assessment is that membership “has not produced measurable reductions in corruption.” Enforcement of domestic anti-graft laws, it says, is inconsistent, and even-handed application is “the exception rather than the rule.”

The report does give President Joseph Boakai’s administration some credit: asset declaration requirements, investigations into irregularly awarded contracts, a push by the Liberia Anti-Corruption Commission for a specialized criminal court for corruption cases, and a proposed amendment that would remove the statute of limitations on corruption prosecutions. But it labels these “nascent” efforts — a polite way of saying the results are not yet visible.

Courts that cannot keep up

For investors, a corruption problem becomes a courtroom problem the moment a contract goes wrong. Here the report is equally blunt.

The Commercial Court, which handles disputes of $15,000 and above, is described as severely backlogged, with cases taking two to five years. Judgments — especially against government entities — are hard to enforce. The report notes regular media accounts of executive interference in judicial and legislative matters, and widespread reports that court officials solicit bribes to act on cases. Appeals land at a five-member Supreme Court that is buckling under the volume.

The consequences ripple into the wider economy. Because collateral is so hard to recover through the courts, banks demand more of it and lend less, which feeds high rates of bad loans. Unsurprisingly, the report says, investment contracts with the government often specify arbitration outside Liberia, and investors prefer not to rely on local courts at all.

Liberia does belong to the ICSID and New York conventions, which oblige its courts to recognize foreign and international arbitration awards. But even there, enforcement can take years.

Land: the oldest fault line

No issue in Liberia is more combustible than land, and the report treats it as a core investment risk.

The constitution limits land ownership to citizens of “Negro descent,” so foreign investors lease — typically for 25 to 50 years. The difficulty is knowing who actually owns what.

According to the Liberia Land Authority, less than a quarter of the country’s land is formally registered, and conflicting records are common.

The report also states that much land has been allocated to commercial companies through agriculture, forestry and mining concessions, often without local communities’ knowledge or consent. Investors, it warns, can face costly disputes even after signing agreements with the government — or after years in operation. The 2018 Land Rights Act was meant to settle historical claims, but public awareness of it remains limited.

A thin, expensive financial system

Liberia has no stock exchange. It has nine commercial banks, mostly foreign-owned, and four deposit-taking microfinance institutions. The Central Bank reports a comfortable liquidity ratio of 50 percent, well above the 15 percent minimum, and calls the sector resilient.

But the State Department notes that bad loans account for about 16 percent of total lending, that commercial interest rates run between 18 and 25 percent, and that lenders often demand collateral worth 150 to 200 percent of a loan. Some Liberian banks struggle to keep correspondent relationships with international banks. The banking system, the report concludes, is adequately capitalized but “not well positioned to withstand shocks.”

There are bright spots. The Central Bank switched on a national instant-payment system in December 2025 that lets money move in real time between mobile networks, and all government-to-person payments now run through the new national electronic payment platform, which is due to be fully operational by December 2026. Investors can also repatriate 100 percent of their funds, with no exchange controls, in a country where the U.S. dollar is legal tender.

State firms in the shadows

Liberia’s 46 state-owned enterprises employ more than 10,000 people in ports, power, water, petroleum, fisheries, forestry and telecommunications. The report describes them as politically governed, financially weak, inefficient and opaque.

It says senior officials, including some who sit on SOE boards, reportedly steer these companies in ways inconsistent with sound corporate governance; that not all of them pay taxes, or do so transparently; and that their revenues and debts are not always properly reflected in national budgets. There is no formal privatization program, despite public calls to privatize the Liberia Electricity Corporation, the Liberia Water and Sewer Corporation, Roberts International Airport and the Liberia Petroleum Refining Company.

The welcome mat, with conditions

The report does not suggest Liberia is closed. Its corporate law, modeled in part on Delaware’s, allows 100 percent foreign ownership with no residency requirements for directors. Tax incentives — duty and GST exemptions, tax holidays and deductions of up to 30 percent on qualifying equipment — are on offer in sectors from agriculture and energy to tourism, health and waste management. Extra incentives apply to projects in poorer regions, those creating more than 100 jobs, and those using at least 60 percent local materials.

Infrastructure is moving, too. APM Terminals is pushing the Freeport of Monrovia toward round-the-clock operations and aims to raise activity by 40 percent. A $40 million World Bank trade project is building a single window for customs. Special economic zones are planned, including a 94-acre free zone beside the Monrovia port and a 200-hectare agro-processing zone at Buchanan funded by the African Development Bank.

But the doors are not open everywhere. Sixteen lines of business — from sand supply and block making to taxis, gas stations, used clothing and used cars — are reserved for Liberians. Fully foreign-owned firms in other sectors must invest at least $500,000; joint ventures need $300,000 and at least 25 percent Liberian ownership. In September 2025, the Labour Ministry tripled work permit fees for foreigners from $1,000 to $3,000 to push companies toward local hiring.

That local hiring is not easy. The report puts the population at 5.3 million and the labor force at 2.1 million, with functional literacy just under 50 percent and as many as nine in ten people working in the informal economy. Employers, it says, should expect to invest heavily in training.

The American angle

For a country with Liberia’s historic ties to the United States, the commercial relationship is strikingly small. Central Bank data cited in the report show $57 million in exports to the United States against $63 million in imports. There is no bilateral tax treaty, meaning U.S. companies may face double taxation, and the report notes there has been no recorded investment dispute involving a U.S. investor in a decade — a sign, perhaps, of how few have tried.

Washington’s advice to American firms is cautious: do thorough due diligence, find strong local partners, stay close to the U.S. Embassy, and expect licenses and projects to take longer than planned. Mining and energy are flagged as the most promising sectors.

What it means

The 2026 statement captures the paradox at the heart of Liberia’s economy. The headline numbers show a country recovering; the fine print shows a state whose institutions have not caught up with its resources.

None of the individual criticisms will surprise Liberians — they are the stuff of daily headlines. What gives this report weight is its source and its audience. It is read by boardrooms, development financiers and risk analysts deciding where capital goes. When the U.S. government tells its own companies that rule-breakers can thrive if they pay the right people, and that rule-followers risk being shaken down, that sentence travels further than any investment conference speech.

For the Boakai administration, which has staked its reputation on fighting corruption and reviving the economy, the report is both a mirror and a test. The reforms it cites — asset declarations, contract probes, a proposed anti-corruption court — are the right ones. The question investors will ask is whether they become convictions, cleaner concessions and faster courts before the next edition of this report is written.

World.title: Five Years, $25.6M Pledged: West Point Still at the Mercy of the Atlantic
World.content:
Monrovia – At West Point, the sea works to its own timetable, and it is not waiting for anyone.

The crowded fishing township sits on a narrow spit of sand where the Mesurado River meets the Atlantic Ocean, on the edge of Liberia’s capital. For years its residents have watched the shoreline move inland, taking homes, walkways and the beaches where fishermen pull up their canoes. Each rainy season brings the same worry: which houses will still be standing when the season ends.

By Rodney D. Sieh



In 2021 an international climate fund made the township a promise. A sloping wall of heavy rock would be built along its exposed shore to break the waves before they reached the houses, with landing points so the fishing fleet could still get to sea.

Five years and four months later, that wall exists in drawings, approvals and contract talks, but not yet on the beach.

A promise made in 2021

The Monrovia Metropolitan Climate Resilience Project (MMCRP) was approved in March 2021 and took effect that July. It is a Government of Liberia initiative funded mainly by the Green Climate Fund (GCF), the world’s largest dedicated climate fund. The GCF pools money mostly from wealthy nations to help poorer countries adapt to a warming planet. The United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) manages the grant money. Liberia’s Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) runs the project day to day, working with the Ministries of Finance, Mines and Energy, and Public Works.

The ambitions are large. The project aims to reach about 250,000 people directly, and about one million more through better management of Liberia’s coastline.

It has three parts. The centrepiece is the West Point sea defence, known as a rock revetment. The second is a national plan for managing the coast, which includes mapping the areas most at risk and training government staff to use that information.

The third supports communities: protecting mangrove forests, helping people earn a living through clean-cookstove manufacturing and cold storage for fish processors, and building an Education and Innovation Center in West Point.

In total, US$25.6 million has been committed. Of that, US$21.4 million is cash and US$4.27 million is the estimated value of rock the government has pledged from the Mount Coffee quarry.

Five years of preparation

In its public update, dated November 8, 2026, the EPA says much of the groundwork has been done.

Engineers studied West Point’s currents, coastline and the ground beneath the planned wall in 2023. The GCF approved the detailed design in 2024, and stakeholders validated the construction plan in 2025. The Environmental and Social Impact Assessment, which sets out how the works may affect fishing, trading and access, won GCF approval in the last quarter of 2025.

An agreement covering the rock has been signed by the EPA, the Ministry of Mines and Energy and the Liberia Electricity Corporation, which operates Mount Coffee. Mangrove mapping is finished. Ten community stewards have been hired, six of them women. Twelve billboards on coastal risk now stand in four communities, and livelihood surveys have begun in Topoe Village, Jacob Town, Fiamah and Plunkor. Renovation of the West Point Education and Innovation Center is under way, supervised by the Ministry of Public Works, and is expected to be finished around the start of 2027.

The agency puts it plainly: “The main protection works had not yet begun.”

Following the money

The financial figures show how slowly the project has moved.

By the end of October 2026, US$5.35 million of the US$21.4 million in committed cash had been released to the project.

That is about one dollar in four. Of the money released, US$2.07 million had been spent, or 9.68 per cent of all cash committed.

The GCF grant, the largest single source of money, shows the gap most clearly. The fund has committed US$17.26 million but has sent only US$2.78 million so far, in two transfers: US$523,932 in November 2021 and US$2.26 million in August 2025. Just over US$1 million of that has been spent, which is 6 per cent of the full grant. UNDP is holding the remaining US$1.74 million to start the West Point construction.

The EPA stresses that an approved grant is not money sitting in a bank account. The GCF pays in stages, and only after agreed conditions and milestones are met. Most of the money, the agency notes, is budgeted for the sea wall itself, so spending will stay low until construction starts.

Liberia’s own contribution

One of those conditions involves Liberia’s own money, and here the statement points to a long gap.

The government promised

US$2.54 million in cash. The EPA says that by the time the Boakai-Koung administration took office in early 2024, only US$50,000 had arrived, in a single payment in 2022. The new government paid US$500,000 in December 2024 and another US$800,000 in 2026, bringing the total to US$1.35 million, or 53 per cent of what was promised.

The agency links the delay directly to the project’s slow pace. Larger GCF payments depend on government co-financing and on completing early engineering milestones. “Limited co-financing before 2024 had constrained the pace of work,” the statement says.

Even so, most of the government’s money has not yet been used. Of the US$1.35 million received, about US$253,500 had been spent by the end of October, leaving almost US$1.1 million in the EPA’s project account. A further US$1.19 million of the government’s cash pledge is still to be paid.

The 20 per cent problem

The newest obstacle is the price of the wall itself.

The EPA says the prospective contractor for the West Point revetment has asked for a one-time 20 per cent increase in its price before signing. It cites inflation and higher fuel and material costs since it submitted its financial proposal in December 2025.

The statement does not name the contractor or give the contract value, so it is not yet possible to say how much the increase would cost in dollars. It does say that no adjustment has been approved. The EPA and UNDP are reviewing the contractor’s calculations and talking to the Ministry of Finance and Development Planning about how any extra cost might be covered, along with the government’s outstanding co-financing.

The agency warns that the request “could further delay contract finalization and mobilization,” and that any price change must be “adequately justified, funded and processed” under procurement rules.

Why it has taken so long

The EPA lists a familiar set of reasons: slow early hiring and work planning, COVID-19 restrictions, later staffing gaps, complicated procurement, long technical reviews, rising construction costs and late government co-financing, especially between 2021 and 2024.

Other steps are also still waiting. A Livelihood Restoration Plan, meant to protect traders and fishing families whose income could be disrupted during construction even if they do not have to move, has been prepared but had not yet been submitted to or cleared by the GCF. Bids for the national coastal management plan and risk mapping closed only in October 2026. A request to extend the project and a catch-up plan are awaiting the GCF’s decision.

“Implementation has taken longer than anticipated,” the agency acknowledges. It adds that it “recognizes the urgency for residents and the importance of reporting physical progress alongside expenditure.”

A wider pattern

West Point’s experience reflects a common pattern in climate finance. Pledges are announced in large round numbers. The money then moves in small, conditional amounts through layers of accredited agencies, safeguards and procurement rules. Those rules exist to protect communities and public funds, but each step takes time, and the coastline keeps eroding throughout.

The EPA says the immediate tasks are to finalise the construction contract, complete the outstanding safeguards, begin the coastal planning work and turn livelihood surveys into real support for families.

For West Point, the measure of success will be visible on the beach. The design is approved, the rock is pledged and much of the money has been promised. The township is still waiting for the first truckload of stone.

World.title: Liberia: CDC Supporters Push for Former Chairman’s Return
World.content:
MONROVIA – Three years before Liberians return to the polls to elect a new president and members of the Legislature, a conversation is emerging within the opposition Congress for Democratic Change (CDC), with supporters of its former National Chairman, Mulbah K. Morlu Jr., increasingly making the case for his return to the party’s highest administrative position.

By Selma Lomax, [email protected]

Across several counties, including Bong, Margibi, Grand Bassa and Montserrado, individuals identifying with Morlu’s political leadership are said to be organizing themselves around a common demand that the former chairman return to the position he resigned from in February 2024.



Their campaign is expected to take a more visible form on November 14, when supporters say they intend to present a petition urging Morlu to reconsider his departure and return to the chairmanship.

Although the proposed mobilization is being described by its organizers as a grassroots initiative, its broader political significance lies in what it reveals about the internal conversations taking place within the CDC as the party considers its future.

For a political movement that rose from opposition politics to the presidency in 2017, the challenge is not merely to remain politically relevant. It is to demonstrate that it can reorganize itself after losing power and convince Liberians that it has the leadership, structure and national appeal to return to government.

Morlu’s supporters believe he is among the few figures within the party capable of undertaking that assignment. They point to his years of involvement in the CDC, his experience coordinating nationwide political structures, his role in the party’s 2017 electoral campaign and his ability to mobilize supporters beyond traditional party boundaries.

But beyond the arguments about his political résumé, the campaign also appears to be driven by a sentiment among some partisans that the CDC needs to rediscover the organizational energy that characterized its years in opposition.

A political movement looking for direction

The CDC’s defeat in the 2023 presidential runoff remains a defining moment in the party’s recent political history. Former President George Manneh Weah received 793,914 votes against 814,481 for Joseph Nyuma Boakai, who contested on the ticket of the Unity Party. The difference of 20,567 votes delivered the presidency to Boakai after a closely contested election.

While the CDC lost the presidency, it retained considerable political influence, emerging as the largest single party in the House of Representatives with 25 of the 73 seats.

For Morlu’s supporters, those figures demonstrate that the party’s political foundation was not destroyed by the electoral defeat. Instead, they argue that the CDC possesses a substantial electoral constituency that needs to be reorganized, motivated and expanded.

Their argument is that the party should not approach 2029 as a political organization starting from nothing. Rather, it should build upon the support it accumulated during its years in government and opposition.

That process, they believe, requires leadership capable of understanding the party from the grassroots to its national executive level. Morlu’s supporters say his experience in different positions within the CDC gives him an institutional understanding that would be difficult to replace.

They also argue that his return would provide an opportunity to reconcile members who may have become politically distant following the party’s loss of power and his eventual resignation.

Bong County: A call for organizational experience

In Bong County, where the CDC has maintained a considerable political presence over the years, supporters say the party needs a chairman who understands the importance of building its structures beyond Monrovia.

Samuel K. Nyumah, representing the Bong County constituency, argues that the CDC’s political strength has historically depended on its ability to maintain relationships with ordinary partisans in towns, villages and communities.

According to Nyumah, the party cannot prepare for another presidential election by concentrating its political activities around national headquarters while grassroots supporters remain disconnected from the leadership.

He believes Morlu’s experience in rebuilding the party’s structures following the 2011 elections makes him a suitable candidate to lead another organizational exercise. “Mulbah Morlu understands how the CDC is built. He understands the people who sacrificed their time and resources to make the party what it became. We are not saying that other members do not have leadership qualities, but we believe that, at this particular moment, the party needs someone who understands its structures and knows how to bring people together. We want him to return because the work ahead

requires experience, commitment and a clear understanding of the grassroots,” Nyumah said in an illustrative statement.

Margibi County: The question of political mobilization

In Margibi County, supporters are placing particular emphasis on Morlu’s reputation as a political mobilizer and his ability to organize people around issues that extend beyond party politics.

Patricia W. Kollie argues that the CDC needs a chairman who can transform political dissatisfaction into organized participation and give younger partisans a meaningful role in the party’s future. Kollie believes that the political environment leading to the 2029 elections will require more than speeches, press conferences and occasional rallies.

She argues that the party must begin preparing its supporters through sustained community engagement, political education, recruitment and the establishment of functional county and district structures.

“Politics is not only about having a popular presidential candidate. It is also about having people who can take the party’s message to the communities, listen to ordinary Liberians and organize supporters around a common vision. We believe Morlu has demonstrated that capacity over the years. His ability to mobilize people and communicate political issues is something the CDC should not take for granted. We want him back because we believe he can help restore the energy that made the party a formidable political force,” Kollie said in an illustrative statement.

Grand Bassa County: Rebuilding unity after political disagreements

In Grand Bassa County, the argument for Morlu’s return is being framed around reconciliation and the need to prevent internal disagreements from weakening the party ahead of the next electoral cycle.

James T. Wleh believes that the CDC must find a way to bring together members whose relationships may have been affected by disagreements over leadership, political direction and the management of party affairs.

Morlu resigned from the chairmanship in February 2024, citing disagreements and concerns about constraints on his ability to perform his responsibilities.

Although his departure was voluntary, supporters now argue that political differences should not permanently separate individuals who contributed to building the party. Wleh believes that Morlu’s return could provide an opportunity for the party to open a new chapter in its internal relations.

“We cannot continue to allow disagreements to determine the future of a party that so many Liberians worked hard to build. People have their differences, and political organizations will always experience disagreements, but those differences should not become permanent divisions. We believe Morlu has a role to play in bringing people together again. His return would send a message that the CDC is prepared to put personal interests aside and focus on the bigger responsibility of rebuilding the party,” Wleh said in an illustrative statement.

Montserrado County: Beyond party politics

In Montserrado County, where the CDC maintains its most visible political presence, supporters are highlighting Morlu’s activities since leaving the party’s chairmanship.

They argue that his leadership of Solidarity and Trust for a New Day (STAND) demonstrates that he has retained the ability to organize people and engage in national political conversations even outside the CDC’s formal leadership structure.

Michael B. Dolo believes the former chairman’s political activities since 2024 show that his influence is not limited to the traditional CDC membership.

Dolo points particularly to the July 17, 2026, “Lead or Leave” demonstration, which was organized amid growing public demands for accountability and concerns about governance. The Independent National Commission on Human Rights reported that the demonstration attracted more than 1,500 participants and was largely peaceful.

Supporters also point to the participation of student organizations, including the Student Unification Party, the Progressive Students Alliance and the Student Integration Movement, as evidence of the potential for broader political cooperation.

For Dolo, these developments demonstrate that Morlu can engage people from different backgrounds around issues of national interest. “One of the things the CDC needs going into 2029 is a chairman who can communicate beyond the party’s traditional supporters. We need somebody who can bring young people, students, community leaders and ordinary citizens into national conversations. What Morlu has demonstrated through STAND is that he can mobilize people around issues that concern the country, even when they do not necessarily belong to the CDC. We believe that experience can be useful to the party as it prepares for the next elections,” Dolo said in an illustrative statement.

A record supporters say should not be overlooked

Much of the campaign for Morlu’s return rests on his history within the CDC. Supporters trace his involvement to 2005, when he served as chairman of the Progressive Action for Change, a CDC-aligned auxiliary.

They say he subsequently served as assistant public relations director before becoming director of public relations that same year. Over the years, he occupied several positions, including chairman of the Policy Response Committee in 2009, chairman of the Mobilization and Recruitment Committee in 2010 and chairman of the Nationwide Restructuring Committee in 2012.

He later served as vice chairman for operations from 2012 to 2018 and chaired the party’s convention committee in 2014. Supporters consider his role in the 2012 restructuring exercise particularly important.

Following the CDC’s defeat in the 2011 elections, the party faced the challenge of reorganizing its county structures after widespread resignations among county-level leadership. According to supporters, Morlu’s restructuring committee worked to rebuild those structures and restore the party’s organizational presence across the country.

They contend that the exercise provided the foundation for the political machinery that subsequently supported the CDC’s successful 2017 presidential campaign. Morlu later became National Chairman and served for approximately six years, including during the period when the CDC controlled the Executive Branch.

For his supporters, that experience provides an important basis for their argument that he understands the demands of leading a political organization through both opposition and government. They also cite vocational training initiatives reportedly organized for ordinary partisans at the party’s headquarters as evidence that his leadership sought to provide opportunities beyond political mobilization.

Whether those experiences would translate into another successful period at the helm of the CDC remains a question that only the party’s political process and Morlu himself can ultimately answer.

The STAND factor

Morlu’s supporters also believe his work outside the CDC has added another dimension to his political profile. Through STAND, he has continued to participate in national political discussions, particularly those involving governance, accountability and public institutions.

The July 17 demonstration remains one of the events frequently cited by his backers. The “Lead or Leave” protest brought together different categories of participants and attracted attention because of its demands for accountability amid concerns surrounding governance and the country’s response to a major narcotics investigation.

For Morlu’s supporters, the demonstration illustrated the importance of political organization in shaping public discourse. They argue that a party preparing for 2029 must be capable of connecting its political objectives with the concerns of ordinary citizens.

However, they also acknowledge that leading a civic movement and managing a political party are different responsibilities. While STAND can mobilize around particular national issues, the CDC must manage internal elections, membership disputes, candidate selection, legislative coordination and the broader responsibilities associated with electoral politics.

Supporters believe Morlu’s previous experience as chairman gives him an advantage in understanding those institutional demands.

They say the combination of his experience within the CDC and his continued engagement in national affairs could help the party strengthen its political relevance.

Will Morlu accept the call?

Despite the growing enthusiasm among his supporters, the biggest question surrounding the proposed November 14 petition is whether Morlu himself is prepared to return. His resignation in February 2024 came amid disagreements over the direction and management of the party.

Those circumstances remain relevant to any discussion about his possible return, particularly because supporters acknowledge that reconciliation would require more than a public petition.

It would require engagement between Morlu and the party’s current leadership, an understanding of the concerns that contributed to his departure and a willingness among different factions to find common ground.

There is also the question of the CDC’s constitution and the procedures governing the selection of its national chairman. A petition from supporters, regardless of its size, cannot by itself confer the chairmanship. Any leadership change must follow the party’s established constitutional and electoral processes.

The position of the current national leadership will therefore be important in determining whether the proposed initiative develops into a broader internal discussion about the party’s future.

Morlu’s response will also matter. If he accepts the appeal, the party could be confronted with a renewed debate about its leadership direction and the possibility of an internal contest.

If he declines, supporters will have to decide whether to continue pressing for his return or channel their efforts into another form of political engagement.

As of November 8, no confirmed response from Morlu concerning the proposed petition has been provided in the information available for this report.

World.title: Liberia: Cuttington, Bong County University Graduates’ Clean Cities Experience Exposes Liberia’s Unemployment Challenge
World.content:
Ultimately, the country’s development will not be measured only by how many graduates its universities produce or how fast its economy grows. It will depend on whether educated young people can find decent work, support their families, and put their knowledge to use for their country. Until that happens more consistently, the stories of graduates like Tokpah and Kien will remain a stark reminder that in Liberia, earning a degree and finding a job are still two very different achievements

MONROVIA – Every morning, young men and women across Liberia’s towns and cities pick up cutlasses, brooms and wheelbarrows to clear roadsides and drains. Among them are two university graduates who once pictured themselves in offices, laboratories and farms, applying what they learned in lecture halls. Instead, they are part of a government sanitation program that offers short-term work to unemployed youth.

By Selma Lomax, [email protected]

Their names are Aloysius Tokpah and Jonathan Kien. Their paths to the program differ in detail, but they share a common thread: both did what Liberian families have long told their children to do. They went to university, finished their studies, and waited for the doors that a degree is supposed to open.



A degree in public service, a job on the roadside

When Tokpah enrolled at Cuttington University, the plan seemed straightforward. He would study hard, graduate, and move into a professional career where his knowledge could serve both his own future and his country’s development.

He majored in Public Administration, with a minor in Economics, and graduated in the 2024/2025 academic year. It is a combination suited to work in government institutions, public service, policy planning and economic development, the very fields in which Liberia says it needs capable people.

But the months after graduation did not unfold as he had hoped. Instead of landing a role in his field, Tokpah found himself doing roadside brushing under the Government of Liberia’s Presidential Clean Cities Initiative, a program designed to improve urban sanitation while giving young people temporary income. On November 10, he shared his feelings on Facebook. He wrote about the sacrifices behind his education, the hope that came with it, and the strangeness of finding himself doing roadside work simply to survive. Life, he reflected, sometimes takes people in directions they never imagined.

The post struck a chord because it spoke for many. It offered a glimpse of the distance between academic ambition and the realities of Liberia’s job market. There is an irony in his situation that is hard to miss. A graduate trained in public administration and economics could, in principle, contribute to planning, managing and evaluating public programs, including the sort of initiative in which he now works with his hands. Rather than sitting in an administrative office, he is helping to clean public spaces.

Supporting a family after graduation

Kien’s story is rooted in a different, equally pressing concern. A 2024/2025 graduate of Bong County University, he studied Agriculture, a field with obvious relevance for a country that wants to raise food production and strengthen rural livelihoods.

Yet since completing his studies, Kien has not found a job. With no income and a mother and other relatives depending on him, he said he accepted a place in the sanitation programme because he needed a way to support them.

For Kien, the decision was less about career than about responsibility. Waiting for the perfect opportunity in his field might mean months more without earnings, and family needs do not wait. Taking available work, however modest, became the practical choice.

His situation reflects a reality confronting many young Liberians: graduating does not automatically lead to employment, and a certificate does not guarantee economic independence.

These stories also point to something less often discussed, the sacrifices families make to educate their children. Tuition, transport, books and daily upkeep are often paid for through great effort. When graduation does not bring a job, the disappointment is felt well beyond the graduate.

What the numbers say

The experiences of Tokpah and Kien arrive at a moment when the World Bank is urging Liberia to look beyond headline growth. In the seventh edition of its Liberia Economic Update, titled Beyond Growth: Addressing Structural Constraints to Job-Rich Growth in Liberia, launched in Monrovia on November 3, 2026, the Bank reported that the economy grew by 5.1 percent in 2025.

That growth was driven largely by a strong rebound in mining, which expanded by 17 percent, and by continued gains in services, which grew by 4.6 percent. Agriculture, the sector where Kien trained, lagged behind at 2.6 percent.

The Bank’s message was that good growth figures are not enough. For expansion to improve ordinary lives, it said, the economy must generate more and better jobs. It pointed to constraints that hold businesses back and limit hiring: high production costs, unreliable infrastructure, limited access to financing, and weak links to markets. Its recommendations included sustained macroeconomic stability, stronger private-sector development, better governance, and policies that widen productive opportunities.

World Bank Country Manager for Liberia Georgia Wallen stressed that the central challenge is converting economic gains into opportunities that improve people’s lives. For graduates, that challenge is concrete. A country can post solid growth while sectors that create the most visible wealth employ relatively few people.

A labour market dominated by informal work

The problem is not only how many people lack jobs, but what kind of work is available. In a May 2026 analysis of the private sector, the World Bank found that about 87 percent of Liberian workers were in informal employment, including smallholder farming and unregistered micro-enterprises. It also reported that roughly 14.8 percent of people aged 15 to 24 were neither in education, employment nor training, and cautioned that, given the scale of informality, youth underemployment may be far larger than conventional unemployment figures suggest.

A different picture comes from Liberia’s 2024 Labour Force Survey, cited in an International Monetary Fund assessment. It recorded an unemployment rate of 12.6 percent and found that 44.2 percent of young people aged 15 to 24 were neither in education, employment nor training.

The figures differ because the datasets and measurements differ, but they tell the same story: the labour market offers too few stable, productive opportunities for young people entering it.

For graduates like Tokpah and Kien, then, the obstacle is not unwillingness to work. It is the difficulty of finding work that pays enough and makes use of what they studied. How a sanitation drive became a lifeline

The Presidential Clean Cities Initiative is a Government of Liberia intervention championed by President Joseph Nyuma Boakai Sr. It aims to improve sanitation in urban communities while providing structured, short-term jobs for young Liberians. It also seeks to encourage community ownership of public spaces and deepen cooperation among citizens, youth groups, community-based organisations and local authorities.

The first phase began on November 10, covering eight counties, 14 cities and one township. Participating locations include Monrovia and Paynesville in Montserrado County; Ganta, Sanniquellie and Tappita in Nimba; Gbarnga and Totota in Bong; Foya and Voinjama in Lofa; Buchanan in Grand Bassa; Kakata City, Unification City and Schieffelin Township in Margibi; Tubmanburg in Bomi; and Zwedru in Grand Gedeh.

The targets are specific. Government plans to engage 1,250 young people and 30 community-based organisations, with at least 40 percent of participants expected to be women. The programme aims to clean and maintain at least 120 public spaces and 100 drainage systems, support the disposal of at least 2,000 metric tonnes of solid waste, and reach at least 500,000 citizens through sanitation and awareness activities.

The first phase is expected to last three months, with participants reportedly receiving US$100 a month, or US$300 in total if those terms hold. The programme is fully funded by the Ministry of State for Presidential Affairs. Its implementing partners include the Ministries of Local Government, Information, and Youth and Sports; the Environmental Protection Agency; county and city authorities; community-based organisations; and the President Delivery Unit, which is expected to independently track progress.

For participants, the stipend may bring genuine if temporary relief. For Kien, it can help meet family needs. For Zlatan, it is a way to earn while his professional path remains uncertain.

After the three months

The harder question is what happens when the programme ends. Three months of work, and a modest stipend, cannot by themselves solve a structural jobs shortage. Participants will return to the same labour market, with the same competition and the same limited openings.

None of this diminishes the work itself. There is dignity in honest labour, and clean public spaces and clear drains protect communities from environmental hazards and support public health. No one should look down on the young people doing it.

The real issue is why graduates who invested years in higher education must so often rely on temporary work far from their fields to meet basic needs. Producing graduates is only half of a development strategy. The other half is building an economy that can absorb them.

Liberia needs trained public administrators to strengthen state institutions, economists to guide development planning, and agricultural professionals to raise food production and productivity. These are exactly the areas where Tokpah and Kien studied, and where they could contribute if the right openings existed.

That points back to the World Bank’s argument. Businesses need cheaper operating conditions, dependable infrastructure, access to finance and stronger market connections if they are to expand and hire. A healthier private sector, supported by stable macroeconomic policy and good governance, is where lasting jobs for graduates are most likely to come from.

For the Boakai-Koung administration, the Clean Cities Initiative offers a chance to tackle immediate sanitation problems while giving young people temporary support. The test will be whether such programmes sit within an employment strategy that creates sustainable opportunities rather than standing alone.

Behind every broom

As the first phase continues, Tokpah and Kien remind the country that behind every sanitation worker is a person with ambitions, responsibilities and, sometimes, years of university study.

For Tokpah, the road from Cuttington’s classrooms to roadside brushing is not the one he planned. For Kien, accepting the work was about supporting his mother and family after months without a job. Both made a choice that many young graduates face when survival becomes more urgent than professional expectations.

Ultimately, Liberia’s development will not be measured only by how many graduates its universities produce or how fast its economy grows. It will depend on whether educated young people can find decent work, support their families, and put their knowledge to use for their country.

Until that happens more consistently, the stories of graduates like Tokpah and Kien will remain a stark reminder that in Liberia, earning a degree and finding a job are still two very different achievements.

World.title: Mporokoso Records Increase in Suicide Cases Among Young People
World.content:
Mporokoso Town Council Chairperson Daniel Lushinga has expressed concern over the rising number of suicide cases among young people in the district.

Mr Lushinga says it is worrying that despite youths making up a significant proportion of Zambia’s population, many are increasingly resorting to taking their own lives.

He has cited drug and substance abuse, among other factors, as contributing to the growing cases of suicide.

“I am saddened by the high number of youths committing suicide in our district. A week does not go by without hearing reports of young people taking their own lives,” he said.

Mr Lushinga told media in Mporokoso that suicide should never be considered a solution to life’s challenges, regardless of how difficult or unbearable a situation may seem.

He has urged young people to engage in productive ventures such as farming and to take advantage of skills training bursaries under the Constituency Development Fund (CDF) to improve their livelihoods.

“I want to appeal to our youths to consider farming. I know some may raise concerns about the cost of fertiliser, but there are crops such as pineapples that do not require fertiliser, which they can venture into to improve their livelihoods,” he said.

Mr Lushinga has further cautioned youths against engaging in betting and drug and substance abuse, saying such activities do not provide solutions to the mental health challenges they may be facing.

He has called for concerted efforts from various stakeholders, including the Church, in addressing the growing cases of suicide in the district.

The Council Chairperson has also appealed to organisations working in mental health and drug abuse prevention to consider establishing a presence in Mporokoso to provide support and help address the situation.

World.title: Mpika to Conduct Social Cash Transfer Headcount
World.content:
Government has called on stakeholders in Mpika District to support the forthcoming Social Cash Transfer beneficiary headcount exercise aimed at verifying beneficiaries and ensuring that financial assistance reaches households that are genuinely vulnerable.

Mpika District Administrative Officer, Steven Mulenga said the exercise was important in strengthening the integrity of the programme by identifying beneficiaries who have died, relocated or whose socio-economic circumstances have changed, making them no longer eligible for assistance.

Mr Mulenga said the Social Cash Transfer Programme, implemented by the Ministry of Community Development and Social Services, remains one of government’s key interventions in combating extreme poverty.

He explained that the progarmme is providing regular financial support to labour-constrained and vulnerable households, including elderly persons, persons with severe disabilities, chronically ill individuals and child-headed households.

Mr Mulenga explained that although the transition to digital payments had improved the efficiency and security of disbursements, it had reduced direct interaction between social welfare officers and beneficiaries, making regular verification exercises necessary to establish their identities, confirm their eligibility and update beneficiary records.

He emphasised that the headcount exercise was not intended to punish or unfairly remove deserving households from the programme but to safeguard public resources, eliminate irregularities and create room for other vulnerable households to benefit from the intervention.

He urged beneficiaries to cooperate with officials during the exercise by remaining in their respective communities and presenting their National Registration Cards and disability cards, where applicable, to facilitate verification.

The District Administrative Officer also called on government departments and other stakeholders to provide accurate information on deaths, relocations and other changes affecting beneficiaries.

Mr Mulenga further urged members of the District Development Coordinating Committee (DDCC) to actively participate in the exercise by sensitising communities, reporting irregularities and supporting the verification process.

He noted that an accurate beneficiary register would ensure that every kwacha allocated to the programme reached its intended recipients.

Mpika District Social Welfare Officer Mazhina Chipota has called for regular reassessment of Social Cash Transfer beneficiaries to ensure that only eligible and genuinely vulnerable households continue receiving financial assistance.

Ms Chipota said the ongoing beneficiary headcount exercise would help identify individuals whose socio-economic circumstances had improved, children who had attained adulthood and beneficiaries who had died, so that they could be graduated or removed from the programme accordingly.

She explained that the Social Cash Transfer Programme was not intended to provide lifelong assistance, but rather to support vulnerable households until they attained a level of self-reliance, citing beneficiaries who had improved their livelihoods through the acquisition of livestock and construction of houses.

Ms Chipota said the exercise would also strengthen accountability, improve the accuracy of beneficiary records and address payment challenges arising from incorrect personal details, mismatched National Registration Card information and blocked SIM cards.

She urged stakeholders, including community structures and government departments, to support community mobilisation and sensitisation, adding that beneficiaries would be required to present their National Registration Cards and disability cards, where applicable, during verification.

The District Social Welfare Officer disclosed that beneficiaries who were temporarily away from their communities would be guided on alternative ways of submitting photographs holding their National Registration Cards to facilitate verification.

Ms Chipota has further called on stakeholders to collaborate in the dissemination of information to the beneficiaries as a way to rid of misinformation.

Social Welfare Assistant Kaula Nyirenda said stakeholders were key to the success of the programme because of their regular engagement with community members, particularly vulnerable households benefiting from Government’s social protection interventions.

Ms Nyirenda said the Social Cash Transfer Programme, implemented by the Ministry of Community Development and Social Services, provides regular financial assistance to extremely poor and labour-constrained households, with Mpika District currently recording 14,213 beneficiaries under 66 Community Welfare Assistance Committees (CWACs).

She said the district was targeting to migrate all beneficiaries to the urban payment system by December 2026, noting that 13,251 beneficiaries were already on the urban system, while 980 remained under the rural arrangement.

World.title: Government Calls for Concerted Efforts to Curb Illegal Mining
World.content:
Muchinga Province Deputy Permanent Secretary Grants Chisapa says the formalisation of gold mining activities in the province will bring significant benefits to both Muchinga and the country at large.

Mr Chisapa said the government is committed to formalising all gold mining activities in the province and to ensure the process is undertaken without delay.

He, however, indicated the need for all miners to first vacate the mining sites before the formalisation process could commence.

Mr Chisapa said this during a stakeholders’ engagement on mineral regulation, compliance and formalisation of artisanal and small-scale mining held at Northern Rock Hotels in Mpika today.

He said formalisation would help bring sanity to the mining sector by ensuring that all mining companies operating in the province were properly identified and regulated.

Mr Chisapa said this would also make it easier for authorities to hold mining companies accountable whenever they violated mining regulations.

He expressed concern that unregulated mining activities had contributed to water pollution and exposed miners to unsafe working conditions.

Mr Chisapa further noted that illegal mining activities had provided a haven for prohibited immigrants and facilitated other illegal activities.

He called for concerted efforts among stakeholders to curb illegal gold mining in Muchinga Province.

Meanwhile, Minerals Regulation Commission Minerals Security and Protection Manager Malfred Moola said illegal mining deprived the Government of much-needed revenue that could otherwise contribute to national development.

Mr Moola said illegal gold mining needed to be stopped without delay to ensure that the benefits from the country’s mineral resources reached all citizens.

He emphasised that the government would not discriminate against anyone during the removal of illegal miners from mining sites.

Meanwhile, Chief Chikwanda of the Bemba speaking people in Mpika expressed concern over the conduct of some mining companies operating in the area.

The traditional leader said some companies had been granted licenses to undertake mineral exploration but had instead engaged in actual gold mining in violation of the law.

Chief Chikwanda called on the government to urgently intervene and stop the companies from engaging in illegal mining activities.

“What these people are doing is a serious violation of the law,” he said.

The engagement was held under the theme of mineral regulation, compliance and formalisation of artisanal and small-scale mining.

Gold deposits have been discovered in several districts of Muchinga Province, presenting economic opportunities for local communities while also raising concerns that require urgent regulatory intervention.

World.title: Government Reiterates Commitment to Youth Skills Development
World.content:
Government has reaffirmed its commitment to empowering young people through enhanced skills development programmes funded under the Constituency Development Fund (CDF).

Acting Chinsali District Commissioner Brenda Silwembe, says the government remains determined to expand access to skills training through the CDF Skills Development Bursary Component and Technical Education, Vocational and Entrepreneurship Training (TEVET) programmes.

Speaking during the 2nd graduation ceremony of the Chinsali Youth Resource Centre held in Chinsali today, Ms Silwembe stated that the event is a testimony of the government’s resolve to decentralise skills development opportunities and ensure that youths from all parts of the country acquire practical skills for sustainable livelihoods.

Ms Silwembe noted that the initiative is in line with the Grow Zambia Agenda which seeks to strengthen the country’s economic growth through skills development, entrepreneurship and productivity.

“As you leave this institution equipped with practical competencies in trades such as carpentry, tailoring, bricklaying and other disciplines, I challenge you to embrace a fundamental mindset shift and utilise the skills acquired here to improve your livelihoods and contribute to national development,” she said.

And Muchinga Provincial Youth Coordinator Malikana Akatama, disclosed that a total of 232 youths among them 14 in-mates, had successfully completed training in various fields under Government-supported youth empowerment programmes.

Ms Akatama said the beneficiaries were drawn from different parts of Chinsali District and were selected on merit to benefit from the CDF-sponsored skills training programme.

She charged that the government will continue supporting young people, particularly vulnerable but ambitious youths to access vocational and tertiary education opportunities.

“I also wish to encourage our graduating youths to take advantage of the many empowerment programmes that the Government has continued to provide in order to improve their lives and become productive citizens,” she said.

Meanwhile, Chinsali Youth Resource Centre Manager Benson Mambunji, commended the government for providing scholarships to all the graduates through the CDF Skills Development Bursary Component.

Mr Mambunji explained that the support had significantly improved access to skills training among youths in the district, enabling many of them to acquire competencies that will help them become self-reliant.

He also appealed for increased stakeholder support towards expanding the institution’s training capacity in order to accommodate more youths.

“I urge our graduates to value this opportunity and utilise the skills acquired to create meaningful change in their communities through entrepreneurship, creativity and innovation,” he added.

And one of the graduates in tailoring, Emma Siatwinda, praised the government for introducing the CDF Skills Development Bursary Component, describing it as a life-changing initiative for many vulnerable youths.

Ms Siatwinda said the programme enabled her to complete her studies without financial challenges and acquire skills that will help her pursue a sustainable livelihood.

“If it was not for CDF, I do not think I would have managed to complete my studies because the Government provided everything I needed to reach this stage,” she stated.

She further urged her fellow graduates to utilise their newly acquired skills through entrepreneurship and innovation to improve their living standards and contribute to national development.

The 2026 graduation ceremony was held under the theme: “Equipped with Skills, Empowered for the Future.”

World.title: OPINION: This is Chipolopolo’s true test without Daka
World.content:
There is a temptation to panic when Germany based striker Patson Daka is ruled out ahead of crucial matches.

He is Zambia’s biggest name, captain in spirit if not always in armband. Losing him, plus Lameck Banda and Gamphani Lungu, for both legs against Burundi feels like a cruel twist just when Chipolopolo needs momentum.

If Zambia cannot beat Burundi without Daka, then it does not deserve to be at AFCON PAMOJA 2027.

Burundi are bottom of Group I with one point. They are not Algeria. They are not a team Zambia should fear. They are a team Zambia should beat – home and away – to show seriousness about returning to Africa’s biggest stage.

This double-header is not about who is missing. It is about who steps up.

This is Edward Chilufya’s chance to remind fans why he was once the next big thing. This is Derrick Bulaya and Prince Mumba’s chance to prove the local league and the less glamorous leagues abroad still produce Chipolopolo quality. This is Kennedy Musonda’s moment – the in-form Zesco striker who has been scoring while others have been on treatment tables.

Interim coach George ‘Chicken’ Lwandamina did not ask for this injury crisis, but he now has a perfect excuse to do what Zambia has needed for years: build a team, not a collection of stars.

For too long, Zambia have played like Chipolopolo is Daka plus ten others. When he is fit, Zambia looks to him. When he is not, the squad some times looks lost.

Friday at Levy Mwanawasa Stadium must be different.

Zambia must press high, move the ball quickly, and trust the system. Burundi will come to Ndola to frustrate, to waste time, to snatch a draw. The National Team cannot allow them to dictate the tempo. Zambia must score early, kill the game, and go to Bujumbura with confidence, not anxiety.

The maths is simple. Algeria lead on four points. Zambia are on three, level with Togo. Six points from Burundi puts Lwandamina’s side on nine and in command. Anything less – a draw in Ndola, a loss in Bujumbura – and Chipolopolo hand the initiative to Togo and Algeria.

Lwandamina is coaching for his future too. An interim tag is a heavy shirt to wear. Win both games, and he forces FAZ to take him seriously. Drop points, and the whispers will start again about needing a foreign coach.

World.title: Three Kalomo Clubs Set to Benefit Over K1 Million Under TRALARD II Project
World.content:
Three clubs in Kalomo district are set to benefit from climate-resilient livelihood interventions valued at over 1 million kwacha under the Transforming Landscapes for Resilience and Development Phase II (TRALARD II) Project.

The interventions seek to strengthen community resilience, improve household livelihoods and promote sustainable management of natural resources ahead of the anticipated Super El Niño conditions.

Project manager James Siakakaba says the interventions are designed to support vulnerable communities with affordable and practical livelihood opportunities that can help them cope with possible drought conditions.

Mr Siakakaba says the project also aims to address challenges associated with water scarcity, reduced agricultural production and the impact of climate variability on household incomes.

The beneficiary groups are Kamudoti Women’s Club, Tubeleke Women’s Club and Kalonda Agro-forestry and Beekeeping Association in Siachitema chiefdom.

Kamudoti Women’s Club will benefit a water reticulation system and horticultural production, small livestock support and the establishment of a tree nursery.

While Tubeleke Women’s Club has been earmarked for horticultural development, goat rearing, establishment of a tree nursery and a solar-powered borehole.

The proposed support is aimed at strengthening the group’s livelihood activities while providing a more reliable water source to support production and improve its ability to withstand climate-related shocks.

And Kalonda Agro-forestry and Beekeeping Association is expected to receive support towards horticulture, water reticulation, beekeeping and tree nursery establishment as part of its agroforestry activities.

The interventions are intended to promote sustainable land-use practices, conserve biodiversity, diversify income sources and improve the economic well-being of its members.

“The selected activities have been considered because they can be rolled out within the current year as they have the potential to deliver immediate and practical benefits to the targeted communities and be rolled out in the coming years,” Mr Sikakaba said.

These interventions are expected to contribute to increased household incomes, improved food and livelihood security, better environmental management and enhanced capacity among communities in the district to respond to climate-related risks and other livelihood challenges

TRALARD II is a five-year World Bank funded programme running from January 2026 to December 2030 in ten districts of Southern Province.

The project is being implemented by line government departments from the Council, Forestry, Agriculture, Fisheries and Livestock, Water Resources, Cooperatives and Community Development.
