World.title: Democrat Scott Colom wins Mississippi Senate race
World.content:
Democrat Scott Colom wins Mississippi Senate race

toggle caption i Sarah Warnock/AP

Democrat Scott Colom has won election to the U.S. Senate from Mississippi, according to a race call by the Associated Press, narrowly defeating Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith.

After more than a week of counting outstanding, absentee ballots and affidavit — or provisional — ballots, Colom won the closest Senate race in the country by just a few thousand votes. His victory expands the majority Democrats will have in the new Congress to 55 seats, with the race in Alaska still undecided.

Sponsor Message

Loading...

In a midterm full of stunning upsets for Democrats, Colom's victory underscores a dramatic shift in the political landscape across the South driven by a surge of Black voter turnout.

Mississippi has the highest share of Black voters in the country, at close to 40%, but President Trump won the state by 23 points in 2024. Mississippi hasn't elected a Democrat to the U.S. Senate in more than 40 years and hasn't sent a Black senator to Washington since Reconstruction.

The state's rural, agriculture-heavy economy was disproportionately impacted by rising prices, and saw millions in investment from both parties, particularly in the final weeks of the race. Colom, a district attorney, made cost of living a centerpiece of his campaign message, decrying "Cindy High-Prices" as bad for Mississippi.

Hyde-Smith conceded the race in a video posted to social media shortly after the AP's race call on Wednesday.

"While this is not the outcome we worked for or hoped for, I respect the decision of Mississippi voters," she said. "I want to congratulate Scott Colom and wish him well as he takes on the tremendous responsibility of representing our great state."

Unlike most other contested Senate races that flipped, Mississippi did not see much national money or attention until the closing days of the election. That included a rally in the final week by President Trump and high-profile visits from former Vice President Kamala Harris, Georgia Sen. Raphael Warnock and other Democrats. The Cook Political Report had the race rated as Likely Republican going into election night.

Sponsor Message

Colom told NPR earlier this month that a lack of investment from national Democrats until the last minute was a mistake.

"The reality is, Mississippi has never been a lost cause, we've been a betrayed cause," he said. "The Democratic Party has not been trying to win Mississippi. Let's stop kidding ourselves, right? They spent hundreds of millions of dollars in other states. They spent almost nothing in Mississippi."

Colom's campaign was a contrast in style from Hyde-Smith, who rarely spoke to reporters in Washington and had minimal presence in the state.

When asked about high beef prices earlier this year, Hyde-Smith — a cattle rancher and onetime state agriculture commissioner — said that "you have so many other proteins to choose from."

That led to a viral campaign ad from Colom, which featured several people expressing disbelief at the senator's suggestion to "pick another protein." Instead, the ad said, it was time to "pick another senator."

World.title: Why is gasoline suddenly under $4 a gallon?
World.content:
Why is gasoline suddenly under $4 a gallon?

toggle caption i Brandon Bell/Getty Images

Stay up to date with our Up First newsletter, sent every weekday morning.

Drivers are starting to see some relief from high fuel prices. For the first time in months, the average price of a gallon of gasoline has dipped below $4, according to AAA .

The price crossed below the $4 threshold on Tuesday, and is currently down to a national average of $3.94 for a gallon of regular. Prices have dipped about 40 cents over the past month, with much of that decline happening in the past two weeks.

"Many will assume the election had something to do with it, but that's a myth," Patrick De Haan, head of petroleum analysis at GasBuddy, wrote in his industry newsletter .

Sponsor Message

Instead, he continued, gasoline prices are dropping for a more banal reason: "For now, it's the seasonal shift, not politics, driving the relief at the pump."

Gas prices often ease in the fall.

One reason: It's no longer summer, which is the peak season for gas. (Fewer people drive in colder weather, AAA points out .) With less demand, there's a touch more gas on the market.

Refineries also finish their annual maintenance by late fall. So that adds a bit more gas to go around.

And the blend of gasoline that's on the market gets cheaper.

Refineries make two types of gasoline every year: summer and winter blends. The summer blend produces less smog, because it evaporates less quickly in the heat; the winter blend helps engines start up in freezing weather, and uses a bit more butane, which helps lower its cost.

(Normally, the switch happens around September 15. This year, the Environmental Protection Agency and the Department of Energy said the switch would happen on September 1, citing gasoline prices that have been driven up by the war in Iran.)

But none of those are the biggest reason why gas prices are falling, says Jorge León, head of geopolitics at the research group Rystad Energy. The main driver is the falling price of Brent crude oil, which is now down to about $90 a barrel, and which is what refineries need to make gasoline, diesel and jet fuel.

That price is falling because there's a bit more oil coming out of the Middle East via pipelines, and because market traders have rejoiced at the intensifying diplomatic efforts between the U.S. and Iran.

Sponsor Message

That progress could easily be reversed if the war escalates, León wrote in an email to NPR. "President Trump may see further military action as a way to regain negotiating leverage before Democrats take control of Congress in January. If we see renewed escalation, much of last week's oil price decline could quickly reverse," he wrote. The same would be true for gas prices.

Congressional Democrats have expressed their support for ending the war in Iran. While they have limited power to do that, they do control the power of the purse, and can withhold additional war funding or hold back confirmations of key officials.

For now, if the price of Brent crude keeps falling, so could prices at the pump. "However, this does not mean a complete 'normalization,' a return to the price levels we had before this conflict started," Jaime Brito, executive director of refining and oil markets for Dow Jones Energy, wrote in an email to NPR.

To get back to pre-Iran war gas prices, the whole oil supply chain would have to recover. Ships that have been running long alternative routes to avoid the Strait of Hormuz would have to return to their points of origin, then resume their normal routes, taking crude oil to refineries. Those refineries would have to pump out enough fuel to alleviate global demand — and depleted stockpiles. The whole process could take months after a lasting peace deal.

"Coming back to those levels will require a return to normal crude production, shipping and refining of the entire global supply chain," Brito continued.

World.title: Greetings from Senegal, where breakdancers are competing in the Youth Olympics
World.content:
Greetings from Senegal, where breakdancers are competing in the Youth Olympics

Ricci Shryock for NPR

Hip-hop music blasted over a portable speaker while half-a-dozen teenagers practiced their best breakdancing moves in Senagal's capital Dakar. They glided on their shins and jumped into the air, clutched their heels and struck midair poses.

Senegal's breakdancers were honing their craft ahead of the country's historic hosting of the Youth Olympic Games this month. It's the first time an Olympic event is being held on African soil.

I took the photo above last month as 15-year-old Suzanne Toure struck a breakdancing pose. She is the only girl on the Senegal National Sport Dance and Break Team. Three years ago, her little brother introduced her to breakdancing.

Sponsor Message

Dancers on the Senegalese team mix traditional moves into their routines from national styles such as mbalax and Yela, swirling their arms and legs in a windmill-like motion. "You can sense some American and European influence in our routines, yes, but there are also African dances. It's about mixing these African dances into the breaking," says coach Francis Siméon Gomis.

They see this as their chance to show the world what their nation can offer on the dance floor, and hope to win a medal on home turf.

World.title: Kennedy relatives join the fight against Trump's arch, alleging harm to JFK's grave
World.content:
Kennedy relatives join the fight against Trump's arch, alleging harm to JFK's grave

toggle caption i Jewel Samad/AFP via Getty Images

One of America's most prominent political dynasties has waded into the growing fight against President Trump's proposed arch in Washington, D.C.

Nine members of the Kennedy family filed suit in federal court on Tuesday to block the 250-foot structure, saying it would obstruct their relatives' gravesites — including the John F. Kennedy Eternal Flame — at nearby Arlington National Cemetery.

"A towering arch casting shadows across the graves of our father, mother, and uncles, as well as the graves of so many who have served our country, would also cast a shadow over our democratic principles, undermining the safeguards established by our elected representatives to protect this hallowed ground for generations to come," Rory Kennedy and Maxwell Kennedy said in a statement on behalf of the family.

Sponsor Message

The plaintiffs include children of Sen. Robert F. Kennedy and Ethel Kennedy and a son of Sen. Edward M. Kennedy, all three of whom are buried at Arlington National Cemetery. There is one noticeable absence: Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., did not join his siblings in the lawsuit against his own administration.

"It is unfortunate to see that some members of the Kennedy family have joined the litigation against the Arch as the project is intended to honor our heroes who rest in Arlington Cemetery," White House spokesperson Davis Ingle told NPR in a statement. "We will continue making the case for this beautiful and fitting monument and are confident we will be fully vindicated as this litigation proceeds."

Max Kennedy, one of RFK's sons, told NPR's All Things Considered on Wednesday that his family is acting to protect Arlington National Cemetery from "the arbitrary, capricious vanity of one man."

"This is one man who wants to build this arch," he said. "He's violated every rule. If this is a great idea, then bring it before Congress, follow the rules and get it approved."

The Kennedys' motion, filed hours before Veterans' Day, adds a highly personal layer to the ongoing legal fight.

Sponsor Message

"[The arch] constitutes nothing less than a permanent denigration of the Kennedy Gravesites and the final resting place for Plaintiffs' parents and grandparents," they wrote in their 27-page filing. "Plaintiffs would never again be able to appreciate both sites as they always have before, and as the Kennedy family always intended."

The Kennedys seek to join the existing federal lawsuit against the arch, which combines two cases: one brought by Vietnam War veterans and an architectural historian earlier this year, and another filed by the governments of D.C. and Virginia late last month. The Arlington County Board has also filed a lawsuit in Virginia.

Loading...

The Trump administration has raced its arch through the federal approvals process over the past year, culminating in a final green light from the National Capital Planning Commission on Thursday. Officials had previously said they could break ground in Memorial Circle that same day.

But within moments of the late-night approval, District Court Judge Tanya Chutkan stepped in with an order blocking construction for two weeks while she evaluates the broader legal challenges.

One of the main arguments against the arch is that its construction is unlawful without congressional approval, which the Trump administration has not sought. The administration maintains that the arch is justified by a century-old authorization of two never-built columns at that same location, which did not seem to convince the judge: Chutkan wrote last week that "merely to state this argument is to reveal its flaws."

The administration has also argued that the case should be thrown out because of plaintiffs' lack of standing, which was the Supreme Court's reasoning in the White House ballroom case. But Chutkan has said D.C. and Virginia likely have standing to sue over the arch, given the financial and logistical harms they would suffer.

Sponsor Message

David Super, a Georgetown University law professor, told NPR in an email that he believes the Kennedys' involvement only strengthens the plaintiffs' standing.

"I can imagine ... that a judge on any level would feel uncomfortable denigrating their concerns over their family graves the way the Supreme Court denigrated the plaintiffs' interest in the White House ballroom case," he wrote. "And coming at a time when the Administration is hinting that it might tear down the Kennedy Center, this certainly makes the President look insensitive or even hostile to his revered predecessor."

Several Kennedy family members have spoken out against Trump's attempted takeover of the Kennedy Center, which is the subject of a separate lawsuit.

Kennedy told NPR that his family acted here in part because they have the unique legal standing to argue the arch will harm them directly. In doing so, he said they can "stand in for the American people because ... this injures everyone in America."

He said his family would have no problem with the arch if it had followed the standard rules and regulations for adding new memorials to D.C., a process that typically includes years of expert and public input.

"All of that has been ignored in this case," Kennedy said. "This arch is being constructed at the whim and whimsy of an autocrat. It's a vanity project, and it's completely different than the memorials that dot the city and that enrich the life of the city."

Arlington National Cemetery is central to the arch fight

toggle caption i Brendan Smialowksi/AFP via Getty Images

The cemetery says JFK's gravesite is one of its two most-visited locations, along with the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier.

The Kennedys explain in their legal filing that JFK's family chose Arlington as his final resting place so that his gravesite could be accessible to the public.

"President Kennedy himself visited the Cemetery and stood where he is now buried," they wrote. "The vista looking back toward the District from the spot where his grave now stands was one of his favorites. While looking out, he remarked, 'I could stay here forever.'"

The grave was intentionally placed on the same axis as the bridge connecting Arlington House (the former home of Confederate Gen. Robert E. Lee) to the Lincoln Memorial, with Kennedy's personal secretary remarking that he was "the link between Lincoln and Lee."

Sponsor Message

Kennedy's gravesite is topped with an eternal flame, which has burned since his funeral in November 1963. The Kennedys said their ancestors were "assured that all aspects of the design would safeguard visibility of the Eternal Flame" from the bridge, even with its intentionally low profile to preserve views of Arlington House.

The arch, they say, would block those views. The Trump administration has acknowledged that the arch would disrupt the historic significance of many nearby memorials, but has said building it anywhere else would defeat its purpose.

The Kennedy complaint goes a step further, citing a recent forensic analysis by the Washington Post that shows the arch would cast shadows over tens of thousands of graves. It would darken JFK's memorial on 50 days of the year, and briefly block the eternal flame on almost half of those.

toggle caption i Abbie Rowe. White House Photographs. John F. Kennedy Presidential Library and Museum, Boston

The Trump administration has said the arch will be topped with its own eternal flame, per the controversial lighting recommendations of the Federal Aviation Administration.

The Kennedys said they often visit their family's graves in the morning for extra privacy — exactly the time of day that the Post analysis found the shadows would be most pronounced.

"Plaintiffs' visits to these would literally be shadowed by the Arch, an unlawfully-created structure," the filing reads. "The shadow the Arch would leave over the Kennedy Gravesites would fundamentally alter the experience of visiting the Gravesites."

Arlington National Cemetery is the final resting place for more than 400,000 service members, veterans and their relatives.

The White House has characterized the arch as a tribute to the nation's military heritage, saying it will "enhance the visitor experience at Arlington National Cemetery for veterans, the families of the fallen, and all Americans alike."

But many of those veterans and their family members have spoken out vehemently against the arch: at protests in Memorial Circle, in tens of thousands of written comments as part of the federal review process, over nearly nine impassioned hours of public testimony during last Thursday's planning commission meeting.

Sponsor Message

Critics say the arch would disrespect those buried at Arlington and disrupt the solemnity of the space for the loved ones who visit them. They say construction — which the Trump administration estimates would involve 20-hour days — would interfere with the 24 to 27 funeral services held there every weekday.

Veterans have said that if Trump — who got five draft deferments during the Vietnam War — really wants to honor their service, he would stop cutting resources for them.

A flurry of court filings argue for a more permanent ban on the arch

The Trump administration has also recast the arch as a military structure (on a public-facing website and in recent court filings), though the plan that received final approval last week has no details about national security. The judge did not seem to find that late-stage argument compelling in her order last week.

In a 10-page declaration filed Tuesday, a retired military general argued that the arch would actually endanger national security.

Ret. U.S. Army Brig. Gen. Steven Anderson warned that storing ammunition in a tourist attraction would constitute a "tremendous risk," and that launching drones in that area — especially so close to D.C.'s airport — "poses clear hazards" to civilians.

"Not only is the Arch not suitable for any practical military facility, but it actually degrades security in the National Capital Region by placing a high-payoff target for our enemies just a few meters from a major road network and the traffic circle that surrounds the Arch," Anderson wrote.

toggle caption i Tom Brenner/Getty Images

He pointed to bombings in Beirut in 1983 and Oklahoma in 1995 as "two examples of the danger posed by allowing vehicles within close proximity of comparable military or law enforcement targets."

Anderson's declaration was part of a slew of documents that the veterans filed this week in their quest for a more permanent ban on the arch.

Sponsor Message

Democrats have also vowed to use their forthcoming majority in Congress to block Trump's construction projects and investigate potential wrongdoing.

But experts told NPR earlier this week that given Trump's veto power, Congress is better positioned to tackle that fight through oversight hearings and funding restrictions. The future of the arch, they say, will likely be up to the Supreme Court.

World.title: What's behind democratic socialists' historic victories in the midterms?
World.content:
What's behind democratic socialists' historic victories in the midterms?

Historian and The New Yorker writer Jill Lepore says the DSA, once maligned, is no longer "beyond the political pale." She discusses the history of socialism in America, and its current resurgence.

Transcript

TERRY GROSS, HOST:

This is FRESH AIR. I'm Terry Gross. American socialists are having their best year since 1912. In last week's midterms, six socialists were elected to Congress, and three were elected mayor, which means New York, LA, Washington, D.C., Seattle, Ann Arbor and Providence, Rhode Island, are now led by socialists. And you could spend your day, you know, walking your dog and, you know, doing finger painting with your kids and making homemade pizza.

And it's really freaky to me that the visions converge, right? A kind of socialist utopianism converges with a techno-utopianism. You know, it kind of just has to do with a couple different forces - right? - like a planned economy, which, when you think about it, is much more likely in an AI-driven state where, like, you can have a very efficiently planned economy, and the idea that the best thing is to not have to work. And you go back to 1912 - those socialists were fighting for, like, let's at least have half a day off, right? Like, they were fighting for a 5 1/2-day workweek, right? A day and a half at most, right? The labor movement fought for the weekend. But we're talking about something different with the AI vision, which is never working.

GROSS: Yeah. Why is the AI vision of how you're going to get your leisure time becoming more dystopian to so many people?

LEPORE: Because it's not about choice and because there is, you know what people describe as the purpose problem, right? It'd be nice to not have to - you know, that nurse who has three jobs on top of regular nursing hours? It'd be nice to not have that. But what if all the nurses are robots and nobody nurses anymore? What are you doing with your day? I think people find that mind-numbing. And even just thinking about the crisis of mathematicians, right? We're like, well, these math problems have been solved by AI. What - these mathematicians having kind of a crisis of meaningless- and purposelessness. I see that with my college students. Like, a lot of things that they're training to do, they feel like machines are going to be able to do better or already can do better. What's their meaning and purpose in life? And that has actually always been a kind of crisis around socialism as well.

But I think it kind of goes way back, this sort of fantasy that the great thing would be if no one had anything to do and machines could do it all for us. That was - like, that was a lot of socialist vision of the 19-teens. It was also a vision in the 1930s, of an alternative to socialism called technocracy, which was led by Elon Musk's grandfather, Joshua Haldeman. He was the national chairmen of the thing called Technocracy Incorporated in the 1930s. And he proposed getting rid of the nation state and democracy and banks and elections and prices and work and everybody would live in a technate. It's not that different from a kind of weird socialist vision.

GROSS: The thing I wonder about, too, sure you'll have plenty of leisure time if AI is doing everything. How are you going to have an income if you don't have a job?

LEPORE: It will be provided - in a socialist vision - by the state. It would be provided - in the Musk vision - by corporations, right? That's what the universal, you know, there'd be - I've written a whole book about what I call the artificial state, right? It's not really. A nation state, it's not a democracy, it's not liberal. It's just a world in which there are six big corporations, AI corporations, that are responsible for all production, and for not working, you are paid to live. The plan for universal income has been, certainly in the vision of someone like Musk or someone like Altman, is that it is a hedge against revolution. If you don't pay people to not work and there is no work, they will revolt against the political system in which they are trapped. So if you don't want a revolution, you have to advocate for universal basic income. Terry, I have to say, I find this dystopian in the extreme, but that is actually the vision.

GROSS: Well, let me reintroduce you here. My guest is Jill Lepore, a professor of American history and a law professor at Harvard. We're talking about her new piece in The New Yorker, where she's a staff writer. It's titled "Can American Socialism Survive It's Success?" We'll be right back. This is FRESH AIR.

(SOUNDBITE OF MARY LOU WILLIAMS' "A GRAND NITE FOR SWINGING")

GROSS: This is FRESH AIR. Let's get back to my interview with Harvard professor and New Yorker staff writer Jill Lepore. Her latest article is about the Democratic Socialists of America. It's called "Can American Socialism Survive It's Success?"

Has Trump's attempts to rewrite and, in some instances, censor history, affected you personally? Affected books of yours that were maybe taught in schools or in school libraries or in public libraries? Has it affected your invitations to speak at schools or at other places?

LEPORE: Yeah, it has. But to be clear, like, I'm not on the front lines of that. You know, K-12 public school teachers deal with that all the time, and they have very little power to fight back against it. So do libraries, public librarians. So yeah, I've experienced it. Like, my book "These Truths" is also a textbook edition. And in states where you have to call the Gulf of Mexico the Gulf of America, if you don't make that change to your textbook, either it won't be adopted or you have to sticker it and put in a sticker that covers up Gulf of Mexico with Gulf of America. So I've contended with that. Last year, I went to speak in Boise, Idaho, this wonderful event where all the kids who are taking history classes across the whole city were going to be bussed to the biggest school, and it was going to be on a tour of like 9,000 kids, and I was going to give a lecture on the history of the Constitution.

And I guess some parents got wind of that and thought that that constituted liberal indoctrination and said their kids couldn't be required to go. So it was an audience of kids who had decided that they wanted to go, so it was kind of an opt-in. I'd really not experienced that before. I found that fascinating. I mean, I talked about it with the kids 'cause I was like, this is a - how does this happen? It has been a fearsome, fearsome moment, and I really do think that the world of the incredibly important work of public education, public librarianship, museum curatorship has lost a lot of talent. I know a lot of people who have quit their jobs, gone into a different profession. It's really tough to be in a classroom where kids have been told by their parents to report something that, you know, looks, I guess, red to them in the sense of communist red, not Republican red. It's very much like the campaigns in the 1930s, where - again in the 1950s, where young people disguised themselves as students and went into college classrooms and reported on professors.

GROSS: You write that last year, the Sandra Day O'Connor Institute published the results of a nationwide study that found that, quote, "teachers now approach subjects like elections, the economy or Civil Rights with caution, if at all," and also that more than three out of four civics teachers surveyed reported having censored themselves out of fear of pushback or controversy. More than one in three had removed or altered lesson plans, and more than one in four had considered quitting, and you wrote, so have I. What do you mean? What have you considered quitting?

LEPORE: You know, it's not what you expect when you go into the world of teaching that - certainly at a university level, that you'll encounter struggles over what you should be teaching, what you're allowed to teach. And I think, you know, to be fair, a lot of this pressure has come from the other side, as well. I mean, in the height of kind of the George Floyd moment, you know, which is a really important moment of racial reckoning in the United States but was also kind of a crazy time, you know, I had students who would say - I assigned the Dred Scott decision, the infamous Supreme Court decision from 1857 that ultimately leads to the Civil War that declares that Black people can never be citizens of the United States. I had student who wouldn't read the assigned reading. They just wouldn't read Dred Scott.

There were faculty at my own institution who were required to apologize to their students for this, that and the other thing. And there was, you know, a huge right-wing campaign to call attention to that as a kind of left-wing McCarthyism, which was then followed by right-wing McCarthyism - right? - these tremendous persecution of school teachers around the country for doing things like teaching the history of immigration, for teaching about slavery and segregation. So there's just been a really tremendous amount of vengeance in the supervision of education in this country. And I really hope that we are past that and that we are in a new moment.

GROSS: And you mentioned that you thought if you assign reading about Dred Scott that some of your students would refuse to read it. Why?

LEPORE: It's a very racist opinion, and they would say that it would cause them harm. Well, you know, we're not reading historical documents for the pleasure they give us. I mean, we often find pleasure in them. But even in the introduction to that book, I say, you know, the reason that I spent so much time quoting from primary documents and the way that I write history is that people should be allowed to speak for themselves in the historical record. And sometimes they say beautiful, soaring, hallowed things. You know, the Gettysburg Address - we need to really listen to that and appreciate the beauty of the prose, the poetry of it. And sometimes they say hideous things, and Dred Scott opinion is one of them.

And it doesn't serve anybody's interests for us to shield ourselves from positions that we disagree with. It doesn't empower us. It doesn't improve our analytical skills. It narrows our understanding of the world. It impedes our ability to counter arguments with which we disagree. Like, everything about refusing to do a course reading is crazy to me and in complete defiance of the objective of a liberal arts education.

GROSS: So have you really considered quitting teaching?

LEPORE: Yeah, I have. I think about it a lot.

GROSS: Because of what we've been talking about, because of all the conflict?

LEPORE: Yeah, yeah. You know, and again, like, let me be clear. I have the best job. Like, I'm very - I have, like, this blessed job. Like, I have nothing to complain about. But both my parents were public school teachers, and I saw them go through a lot of agony. We were living in Massachusetts during the busing debates in the 1970s. Public school teachers bear a lot of the burden of polarized political issues. And I just think our concern should be how to help support public school teachers, not, like, whether I - what my own views about teaching are definitely beside the point.

But we have really imperiled the profession of public school teaching in this country by treating it so cavalierly and by legislators just, you know, offering up decrees about what can and cannot be taught and by supporting a kind of parents' rights mentality that allows for moral crusades against public school districts. I think it's incredibly destructive of civil society, and so far from attacking public schools, we should be holding them up as the guardians of our democracy.

GROSS: Well, Jill Lepore, I really appreciate your approach to writing about history and how it helps us understand the present. So thank you for that. I know, in addition to teaching, you write so well in the New Yorker, and I really appreciate those pieces. Thanks for being on our show today.

LEPORE: Oh, thanks so much. It's really an honor, Terry.

GROSS: Jill Lepore's article, "Can American Socialism Survive Its Success?" is published in the current issue of the New Yorker. Her latest book, "The Rise And Fall Of The Artificial State," is about how AI and data are changing politics and government.

Tomorrow on FRESH AIR, our guest will be Steve Buscemi. His breakout role was in Quentin Tarantino's "Reservoir Dogs" as Mr. Pink, a smart-mouth criminal who, among other things, didn't believe in tipping.

(SOUNDBITE OF FILM, "RESERVOIR DOGS")

STEVE BUSCEMI: (As Mr. Pink) If they really put forth the effort, I'll give them something extra, but, I mean, this tipping automatically, it's for the birds.

GROSS: Since then, Buscemi's acted in more than a hundred movies and TV shows. He now appears in two new films, "Wild Horse Nine" and "The Only Living Pickpocket In New York." I hope you'll join us.

FRESH AIR's executive producer is Sam Briger. Our technical director and engineer is Audrey Bentham. Our interviews and reviews are produced and edited by Phyllis Myers, Ann Marie Baldonado, Lauren Krenzel, Therese Madden, Monique Nazareth, Thea Chaloner, Susan Nyakundi, Anna Bauman and Nico Gonzalez-Wisler. Our digital media producer is Molly Seavy-Nesper. Roberta Shorrock directs the show. Our co-host is Tonya Mosley. I'm Terry Gross.

(SOUNDBITE OF THE WESTERLIES' "ENTROPY, PT. 1")

World.title: Following big Democratic wins, these swing voters are looking for results
World.content:
Following big Democratic wins, these swing voters are looking for results

toggle caption i Tara Anand for NPR

Republicans were dealt a stunning rebuke in last week's midterms. But swing voters, who could be decisive in the next election, are more interested in results than investigations or impeachment as Democrats prepare to take power in Congress.

"I am hoping that we don't experience a bunch of gridlock and a lot of whining and crying and just political infighting for the next two years," said Theresa, a voter from Pennsylvania who is participating in NPR's Swing Shift project. "I'm hoping we don't have that. I fear that we will have that."

NPR has agreed not to use the full names of the Swing Shift voters, so they can speak freely about politics without fear of personal or professional repercussions.

Sponsor Message

Loading...

Theresa voted for President Biden in 2020, President Trump in 2024 and split her ticket in this year's midterms. Like many voters, her top issue this year was affordability. In a voice memo sent to NPR days after the midterms, Theresa said she is eager for the cost of living to come down.

"I just don't remember it ever being as bad in our time," Theresa said. "And I'm just hoping we get some relief and we get some relief soon."

At 9:56 PM on election night, Wally in Georgia hit send on his voice memo. He had seen enough.

"Just checking in here with a quick note. I'm not surprised at all by the outcome tonight," Wally said. "I believe that this is a lot of Trump's doing and pushback on his style of politics and how he governs."

Wally voted for Trump in 2024 but swung back to Democrats in this year's midterms. He had initially supported Trump in hopes that a Trump presidency would shake up the political system, but that didn't happen and now he says the second Trump term has been exhausting. As he sees it, the decisive Democratic wins signal that the country is ready to move on.

Sponsor Message

"Trump has been shooting himself in the foot for many months now," Wally said. "But voting isn't the end of the game here. We have to hold Democrats to some sort of tangible change and not just promises about what they want to do."

For several of the Swing Shift voters, Tuesday's results came as a surprise.

Jason from North Carolina split his ticket, voting for Democrat Roy Cooper for Senate and the Republican incumbent for the House.

"My congressman was defeated this time by someone that no one's really ever heard of," said Jason, sounding almost puzzled by the blue wave that crashed on North Carolina.

That happened in a lot of places. Jason wants the incoming Democratic Congress to focus on the cost of living and steer clear of impeachment.

"My fear is that the Democrats now are going to spend the next 2 years not focusing on any of the things that they say Trump didn't do," said Jason.

Michelle in Michigan, voted for President Biden in 2020 but chose Republicans in 2024 and again in this year's midterms.

"This is the first time I think ever since I've been voting that not one of the people that I voted for won their election," Michelle said.

Michelle says she understands why so many people voted for Democrats, even if she didn't. Americans are tired, she said, of high gas prices, the cost of living and not being able to afford their groceries. They voted for change.

John from Pennsylvania said it felt like his state went from purple to blue overnight.

"I'm just very surprised," John said. "Not surprised that Democrats had a good night, but they had a very good night. Absolutely amazed that they won in Texas and places that just seemed like they were really red."

He voted for President Biden in 2020 and President Trump in 2024. In the most recent midterms, he stuck with Republicans despite concerns about the cost of living and the war with Iran.

Sponsor Message

Gerald in Georgia ran through the list of states where Democrats won senate races in disbelief.

"Come on man, Texas turned blue," Gerald said. "South Carolina turned blue, Ohio, Kansas. Like, this was a referendum of epic proportions."

Gerald is a Biden to Trump voter from Georgia, who has gone all in on MAGA. He's already looking ahead to a future without Trump leading Republicans.

"The Donald Trump era for all intents and purposes is coming to an end in 2028 for certain, if not before that," Gerald said.

Before that, though, Democrats will take power in Washington, at least in part.

Swing Shift voters said again and again when asked about their hopes and fears following these midterms that they hope that the incoming Democratic Congress will focus on the issues that impact their daily lives but fear more of the same broken politics.

"I will choose to hope because that's really all we can do is hope," said Michelle. "Hope that the politicians that were voted in will live up to the promises they made and that change will truly be made."

Even though John didn't vote for Democrats this year, he still wants them to tackle the cost of living.

"Over these next 2 years I hope they are concerned with and concentrate on the affordability issue," John said. "I hope they work with President Trump to try to lower prices. I just hope it's not two years of investigations and impeachment hearings."

Anything Democrats pass in a divided government would have to be signed by President Trump. The president has been inconsistent in recent days about whether he wants cooperation or combat with the new Congress.

World.title: Russia and Ukraine agree to a prisoner exchange as talks end with no big breakthrough
World.content:
Russia and Ukraine agree to a prisoner exchange as talks end with no big breakthrough

toggle caption i Altaf Qadri/AP

ABU DHABI, United Arab Emirates — Russia and Ukraine agreed to a large exchange of prisoners of war, both sides said Wednesday as two days of U.S. mediated talks concluded with no major breakthrough on ending Moscow's nearly 5-year-old full-scale invasion.

Hopes had been low for any significant development in the first meeting in nine months between the delegations. Russia and Ukraine have from time to time swapped POWs but have remained far apart in their demands for accepting a peace settlement.

U.S. officials say they are determined to revive Washington's peace efforts that so far have failed to deliver significant results.

Sponsor Message

Along with postwar security guarantees for both countries, other key hurdles are the fate of Russian-occupied Ukrainian territory and what role European countries will play in an eventual settlement.

U.S. envoys to meet with Putin and Zelenskyy

The session was the first such meeting since February on Russia's invasion, which analysts and humanitarian organizations say has killed hundreds of thousands of soldiers and thousands of civilians.

The talks lasted just under two hours Wednesday, after a four-hour session the previous day.

"One of the positives is we agreed that we're going to have the biggest humanitarian release of prisoners, which we're going to finalize the numbers tomorrow," said Jared Kushner, U.S. President Donald Trump's son-in-law, after the Abu Dhabi talks ended.

toggle caption i Altaf Qadri/AP

Vladimir Medinsky, head of the Russian delegation, and Rustem Umerov, who led Kyiv's contingent, confirmed the planned POW exchange, although Medinsky noted the agreement was "in principle."

Alexander Zorin, a deputy chief of the General Staff's information department who attended the talks, told Russian state TV it would be one of the biggest such swaps after the 1,000 soldiers returned home last year.

The latest exchange could take place in the next two or three weeks, he said.

Kushner said he and U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff will travel to Moscow on Thursday to meet with President Vladimir Putin, then fly to Dublin, Ireland, to meet Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

Sponsor Message

Medinsky said he felt the meeting helped Moscow and Kyiv edge closer to peace, while Kremlin foreign affairs adviser Yuri Ushakov described the talks as "substantive and quite useful."

European officials were excluded by Moscow from the talks

Umerov said Kyiv's delegation was expected to meet later Wednesday with representatives of European governments, the European Union and NATO who were in the capital of the United Arab Emirates but did not attend the three-way talks.

Moscow doesn't want European countries, which are concerned about Russia's conduct and broader intentions on the continent, involved in the direct negotiations. Kushner said one of the goals of the Moscow meeting is to try to get Europeans added to the talks.

"Ukraine's priority is to end the war as soon as possible with a dignified peace," Zelenskyy said on X. "We believe that Europe must be represented at every stage of real diplomacy. It is essential that the United States have a strong position and exert influence on the source of this war — that is Russia."

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said European representatives could eventually join peace talks but added their current statements "don't indicate any desire on their part to contribute to movement along the path toward peace." Moscow complains that Europe is financing and supplying weaponry to Ukraine.

Kushner said both Ukraine and Russia needed clarity on postwar security arrangements. He said European countries, the EU and NATO have to be involved in those discussions to build consensus on next steps.

Ukraine wants to ensure that Moscow doesn't invade again, and EU officials say any discussions on Europe's security arrangements could only start after a ceasefire. Many in Europe see the inclusion of Russia in those plans as a concession to Putin, who has described NATO's eastward expansion as a top threat to its security. Russia has demanded that the alliance pull back its troops from its borders.

Sponsor Message

Russia's security concerns were discussed at the talks, Kushner said, adding that Moscow was told it needs to provide different de-escalation proposals acceptable to Europe.

"The reality is, is there's no trust right now between the sides. And that's to be expected after a conflict like this," he said. But he posted on X later that the POW exchange "will reunite families, build trust and create momentum toward peace."

The talks were held in a new political atmosphere

The context of the negotiations has changed since the February meeting in Geneva. The Trump administration now must reckon with Democrats taking over the U.S. Congress in January following the U.S. midterm elections, and they could demand more support for Ukraine.

Also, Russia's wartime economy is under heavy strain, and Ukraine is reeling from devastating aerial attacks on its power grid.

Fighting continues on the front line, where little territory has changed hands this year. Both countries are battering each other with long-range missiles and drones.

Three people died and 11 were injured after Russia launched a daytime attack on a market in the southern Odesa region, local authorities said. Residential buildings were damaged, said Oleh Kiper, head of the regional military administration.

Overnight, Russia struck the Zaporizhzhia region in southern Ukraine and the eastern city of Kharkiv, wounding seven civilians and damaging property, Ukrainian officials said.

Russia's Defense Ministry said it downed 627 Ukrainian drones overnight, 150 of them over the region around St. Petersburg. Regional Gov. Alexander Drozdenko said the drones started a fire at the port of Ust-Luga, a main facility for Russian oil exports, injuring three workers.

An Indonesian man is reportedly captured on the battlefield

Meanwhile, a 49-year-old Indonesian man reportedly was captured on the battlefield in southern Ukraine's Zaporizhzhia region after he claimed he was unknowingly recruited to fight for the Russian military.

Sponsor Message

The Indonesian Embassy in Kyiv was seeking access to the man, who was in Ukrainian custody, according to Yvonne Mewengkang, a spokesperson for the Indonesian Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

According to Ukraine's "I Want to Live" project that offers Russian troops the opportunity to surrender, the man was taken to occupied Donetsk with no military training and then to the Zaporizhzhia region, where his unit was attacked and he was captured, according to the group's post on Telegram.

The man said he signed what he believed to be a contract to work in construction for one year in Moscow, the group said.

Ukrainian and Russian officials made no immediate comment.

World.title: Ottawa had been aware of Stellantis-Roshel talks for months, source says
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The federal government had been made aware for months about the possibility that Stellantis would sell its Brampton, Ont., assembly plant to a light armoured vehicle manufacturer, a source has told CBC News.

The automaker announced on Monday that it plans to sell the plant to Roshel Inc., a move Prime Minister Mark Carney characterized as a "betrayal of the workers as it is a betrayal of the obligations to Canada."

A source with direct knowledge of the sale of the Stellantis Brampton plant said the federal government had been engaged regularly on the deal since August. The source said both the Prime Minister's Office and Industry Minister Mélanie Joly's office had been briefed on the details of what was going to be announced. CTV News first reported the government's involvement in the talks.

More than 2,000 workers were laid off from the Brampton plant when Stellantis halted operations in 2023 to refit the facility to produce the Jeep Compass.

Both Carney and Joly have blasted the potential sale to Roshel. The minister is expected to hold a meeting of all stakeholders in Toronto on Thursday in an attempt to find a way forward for the laid-off Stellantis workers.

WATCH | Did Stellantis violate its deals with the federal government?: CBC speaks with Flavio Volpe about funding contract given to Stellantis by government | Duration closed caption 8:48 Get the latest on CBCNews.ca, the CBC News App, and CBC News Network for breaking news and analysis.

Ottawa didn't facilitate deal: government source

A separate senior government source told CBC News that Joly didn't facilitate the deal between Roshel and Stellantis and that the minister would never have approved of a deal that wasn't supported by the union.

The minister was unable to block the deal before it happened, the source said.

In a deal announced by the former Trudeau government in 2022, Ottawa said it would inject up to $529 million in Stellantis plants in Brampton and Windsor, Ont., to help them retool to increase production of electric and gas-powered vehicles.

The government source also said Joly wouldn't have approved of the deal with Roshel because it would break Stellantis's commitments under the 2022 deal.

That same agreement also saw Ontario Premier Doug Ford's government pledge to support the plants with an investment of up to $513 million.

CBC News confirmed on Tuesday that Ontario has not provided the company with any funding for its Brampton retooling initiative because it didn't meet conditions related to job creation and project milestones.

Ford cautions against Chinese 'knock-down kits'

Ford wrote a letter to Carney on Tuesday, a copy of which has been obtained by CBC News, warning against the possibility that the plant would be used to assemble "Chinese-made knock-down kits" — where a Chinese auto manufacturer imports parts from overseas just to be assembled in Canada.

"We cannot undermine the future of Canada and Ontario’s automotive sector by allowing the introduction of Chinese-made knock-down kits at the Stellantis Brampton facility," Ford wrote in the letter, adding that he is pleased the federal government is aligned on that position.

"The economic impact of introducing kits to Ontario’s automotive sector would be devastating to Canadian automotive workers and to the thousands of businesses and workers across the Canadian automotive and auto parts supply chain."

WATCH | Poilievre calls on Joly to be fired over Stellantis plant closure: Poilievre calls on Joly to be fired over Stellantis Brampton plant closure | Duration closed caption 2:02 Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre blamed the Liberal government for failing to prevent the closure of the Stellantis auto plant in Brampton, Ont., and called on Prime Minister Carney to fire Industry Minister Mélanie Joly for her handling of the file.

Ford has come out aggressively against the idea of the Brampton plant being used as an assembly station for Chinese vehicles since the possibility was first suggested in a February report by Bloomberg News. The outlet suggested Stellantis was in talks with Zhejiang ‌Leapmotor Technology, a Chinese automobile manufacturer with headquarters in Hangzhou, China, at that time.

Asked about the Stellantis sale during an unrelated news conference on Monday, Ford again raised concerns about Chinese assembly kits.

"We can't bring in kits from China. Can't happen," the premier said. "That will bastardize the whole sector. Unacceptable. We need them to find a vehicle, a model that works."

World.title: Sleeping driver in self-driving vehicle woken up, stopped and charged in Ottawa
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Ontario Provincial Police say a Tesla driver who had their self-driving mode activated has been charged after they were found asleep at the wheel on Highway 417 during rush hour.

Police charge driver for being asleep at the wheel of self-driving car

Provincial police in Ottawa say they stopped and charged a sleeping driver who had the self-driving mode activated in her vehicle on Highway 417 during morning rush hour Tuesday.

The Tesla driver faces a careless driving charge, according to Ontario Provincial Police (OPP).

"Even though your vehicle has an autonomous driving feature, drivers are still required to pay due care and attention when behind the wheel," OPP wrote on social media on Wednesday.

Const. Michael Fathi told CBC News an officer was able to see that the woman in the driver's seat had her eyes closed and her hands weren't on the steering wheel.

The officer didn't use sirens to wake the driver and pull them over, Fathi said. Rather, they had pulled very close to get evidence on a body camera and it's possible that triggered an alert in the driver's Tesla.

A first for Ottawa OPP

Fathi said he believes it's the first time the Ottawa OPP detachment has charged a motorist with sleeping in a self-driving vehicle.

Several other drivers have been caught dozing behind the wheel in B.C. recently, with police there warning the "potential for serious injury or death is too high" and pointing out the law requires people to be alert and focused on the road.

"The law still clearly states that a driver has to be in in due care and control of a motor vehicle even if it's in self-driving mode," Fathi said Wednesday.

Drivers have to be able to take control of a car with a self-driving feature if there's a malfunction or other emergency, he explained.

That means not sleeping and not being impaired.

"The same driving laws apply to you when using driver assistance technologies. Even if your vehicle is equipped with driver assistance technology, always keep your eyes on the road and your hands on the wheel," according to Ontario Ministry of Transportation guidelines.

"You are responsible for any traffic incidents or collisions, not the advanced driver assistance systems features."

World.title: 2 dead, 4 critically injured after building collapse in New York City
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Firefighters dug through the rubble of a three-storey building in New York City's Brooklyn neighbourhood on Wednesday after it collapsed at the edge of a construction site, killing at least one person and trapping others beneath the wreckage.

Firefighters were called to the scene in the borough's Flatbush section around 4 p.m. News helicopter footage showed dozens of firefighters scouring the debris, with a group honing in on one area and appearing to use a saw to cut through the wreckage.

One person died, and four others were rushed to a hospital in critical condition, according to the New York City Fire Department.

Six additional people were taken to hospitals with minor injuries.

Firefighters search through the rubble on Wednesday. (Ryan Murphy/The Associated Press)

The aerial videos showed firefighters digging at least one person out of the rubble and removing them on a stretcher.

The building that collapsed had been perched at the edge of a lot where another one-storey building had been torn down for a construction project. The site was being excavated, and the building that fell down filled the construction pit with bricks and wood.

Another building that shared a wall with the collapsed structure remained standing, but its wall was shorn off, exposing the rooms inside, including a bedroom and closets filled with clothing.

A wall was shorn off the Brooklyn building, exposing a bedroom and closets filled with clothing inside. (Ryan Murphy/The Associated Press)

A drone hovered over the site as firefighters dug by hand, tossing chunks of rubble aside. Rescuers also used dogs to sniff for survivors. As darkness fell, firefighters used flashlights to illuminate the area where they worked.

Phone and email messages seeking comment were left with the architect, property owner and general contractor listed in city records as being associated with the construction project.

A soldier guarding the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier at Arlington National Cemetery issued a verbal reprimand to a group of advisers and staffers with U.S. War Secretary Pete Hegseth following a Veterans Day ceremony.

Video shows Hegseth taking photos on the empty steps in front of the tomb with his wife, Jennifer, chief of staff Ricky Buria, deputy chief of staff Patrick Weaver and senior adviser Tami Radabaugh.

As the group broke from taking photos, a loud laugh could be heard, and the soldier guarding the tomb shouted that "all visitors will maintain an atmosphere of silence and respect at all times."

Sean Parnell, the Pentagon's top spokesman, said that "while commemorating this solemn day, a soldier correctly and respectfully reminded everyone to maintain decorum."

"The Secretary and the entire Department have always honoured — and will always honour — the sacrifices our military men and women have made to keep America safe," he added.

WATCH | Hegseth and group appear to be rebuked: Hegseth delegation appears to be rebuked at Tomb of the Unknown Soldier | Duration closed caption 0:43 A U.S. army sentinel guarding the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier appeared to rebuke War Secretary Pete Hegseth, his wife and aides after loud laughter was heard from the group.

Incident follows near impeachment of Hegseth

The tomb is considered to be one of the most solemn and revered war memorials in the U.S., being the final resting place of unidentified soldiers from the First and Second World Wars and the Korean War. It has been guarded around the clock — rain or shine — by a soldier from the Army's 3rd Infantry Regiment, also known as "The Old Guard," since 1948.

Hegseth and his staff were at the tomb as part of a larger ceremony commemorating Veterans Day that also was attended by U.S. President Donald Trump and Vice-President JD Vance.

The incident comes a day after Hegseth narrowly survived an effort to impeach him by lawmakers in Congress.

The effort was led by Republican Rep. Thomas Massie, and backed by Democrats. However, while Hegseth's critics were not successful in Tuesday's vote, Republicans may have only delayed efforts to impeach him. With Democrats set to take control of the House and Senate in January, those efforts are likely to be renewed.

Hegseth slammed the effort Tuesday in his first news conference in months, arguing that he had committed none of the high crimes required in the Constitution for his removal.

WATCH | Hegseth survives impeachment vote: Republicans block impeachment push against Hegseth | Duration closed caption 2:43 The House of Representatives voted on Tuesday to shelve impeachment articles against Secretary of War Pete Hegseth. Shortly after, U.S. President Donald Trump called outgoing Kentucky Republican Thomas Massie, who put forward the motion, a 'major loser.'

A core part of his argument included the assertion that criticisms of him and his handling of the U.S. military were tantamount to an indictment against the nation's service members and their successes.

"On the eve of Veterans Day, these resolutions tell every one of them that their service was a crime," Hegseth said Tuesday.

"This is not patriotism," Hegseth argued. "This is sabotage."

Following the reprimand at Arlington National Cemetery on Wednesday, the reaction from Democrats was swift.

Rep. Gwen Moore said Hegseth demonstrated "his utter lack of fitness for his office."

"One day after narrowly avoiding impeachment, he shows his contempt for our men and women in uniform by disrespecting the sanctity of the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier," she wrote in a social media post.

Pete Hegseth continues to demonstrate his utter lack of fitness for his office. One day after narrowly avoiding impeachment, he shows his contempt for our men and women in uniform by disrespecting the sanctity of the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier. —RepGwenMoore

It was not the first time members of Trump's team have caused controversy at Arlington National Cemetery.

During his campaign for a second term, Trump attended a ceremony in 2024 to honour U.S. forces killed in the Iraq and Afghanistan wars. A campaign staffer reportedly shoved a cemetery employee trying to prevent two people from filming and photographing the event.

WATCH | U.S. army confirms worker shoved by Trump staffer: U.S. army confirms Arlington cemetery worker 'pushed aside' by Trump staff | Duration 1:57 The U.S. army has confirmed claims that a member of Donald Trump's campaign 'pushed aside' a worker at Arlington National Cemetery who attempted to enforce rules against political activities there.

Trump, who had been invited by troops' families, later shared a video on TikTok showing him at the cemetery with a voiceover blaming the Biden administration for the "disaster" of the Afghanistan withdrawal.

U.S. law prohibits campaign or election-related activities within national military cemeteries.
