World.title: Series of storms leaves B.C. woman with tree stuck on her house for days
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

As B.C. continues to batten down its hatches amid the third in a series of major fall storms, one resident who saw a tree fall onto her house last Friday says it'll have to remain in place as high winds continue to batter the province.

Environment and Climate Change Canada (ECCC) has posted a swath of weather warnings throughout B.C., warning of high winds and rainfall, with more than 250 millimetres of rain possible locally on Vancouver Island.

In the Central Interior and Prince George area, thousands have remained without power for multiple days, as B.C. Hydro says the ongoing series of storms has made cleanup challenging.

Prince George resident Olivia Power lost power for three days, from last Friday to Sunday, due to one of the windstorms — which toppled a tree onto her house.

"We couldn't really go outside to look at what had happened. We were just worried with the windstorm that more trees were going to fall down," she said.

Power and her husband went into a basement hallway after the tree fell onto her house last Friday, not wanting to stay near windows as winds picked up. She said there is no water damage currently due to the fallen tree. (Submitted by Olivia Power)

Power said that a tree removal service she called wasn't available until Wednesday at the earliest — but with winds picking up again, the tree would have to stay in place until at least Thursday.

ECCC said in an orange wind warning on Wednesday that winds could gust up to 90 km/h in the Prince George region.

B.C. Hydro said in an update for the Central Interior that crews were having trouble accessing areas due to fallen trees and debris.

"Additional contractors, specialized equipment and resources have been brought into the region to support restoration efforts," the utility wrote.

#BCStorm update: Crews have made significant progress restoring power in the Central Interior, with most main electrical lines in and around #CityofPG now restored. More than 180 workers continue restoration efforts around the clock as crews focus on remaining outages and areas with significant damage. Strong winds are expected through late afternoon and early evening and may cause additional outages. Stay back at least 10 metres from downed power lines and call 9-1-1 immediately. Read our latest operational update: https://t.co/MoKGIMYFbp —bchydro

Power said that she spoke to some neighbours who told her the windstorms that struck Prince George and the Interior were unprecedented in nature.

"The community has really come together though," she said.

"It's been really nice to see a lot of people wanting to help clear trees and and whatnot, so it's nice knowing that the community got each other's back. Even if we do get hit by another strong storm."

WATCH | Sea-to-Sky Highway rockslide after storm: Rainstorm causes Sea-to-Sky Highway rockslide, traffic delays | Duration closed caption 2:05

Luke Lamplugh, who runs Prince George Property Cleanup, said the winds were so high last week that garbage from a nearby dump flew into trees and roof shingles fell into ditches.

He said he hauled over 1,300 kilograms of tree branches to the dump after the first storm hit Prince George late last week, and had some advice for residents as they continue to deal with high winds.

"If you're on natural gas [heating], and the fans don't work because the power is out, then you need to keep your windows closed and try and retain heat in the house," he said.

"That's really important for a lot of folks, especially seniors around here."

Lamplugh also advised residents to store jugs of water in their freezer in case they lose power for multiple days.

World.title: The remarkable story behind the secret Canadian guerrilla force you've never heard of
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Brent G. Hoy's father, Charles Hoy, didn't talk much about what he did during the Second World War.

It wasn't just that it was difficult. He also was part of a covert Chinese Canadian force, sworn to secrecy.

Force 136, part of Britain's Special Operations Executive, was trained in espionage, guerilla warfare and jungle survival for parachute deployment behind enemy lines in Southeast Asia.

These soldiers wore a Canadian uniform and were prepared to sacrifice their lives, despite being shunned by their country, both in law and daily discrimination.

"Fighting for a country that really didn't want you, but nevertheless having that deep sense to contribute," Hoy said of his father.

That complicated legacy is being spotlighted in a black and white photograph selected by Canada Post for a new stamp, to commemorate the country's military history.

It shows 10 out of about 150 Chinese Canadian soldiers who served the Allied war effort with Force 136 and, after the war was won in 1945, came home to become part of a broader push to change how their community was treated. In 1947, the Chinese Exclusion Act was repealed and the entrenched racism Chinese Canadians experienced began to shift.

It was a double victory, says Catherine Clement, a historian and curator whose work excavates stories of the Chinese Canadian experience.

"Helping the Allies win the war, but also helping the Chinese community to win the right, like equal rights, full rights of citizens of Canada".

Canada Post's new Remembrance Day stamp shows 10 soldiers from Force 136 awaiting repatriation in 1945. Brent G. Hoy's father, Charles Hoy, is in the bottom row, second from the right. (Canada Post)

Between 1885 and 1923, Chinese immigrants who came to Canada had to pay at least $50 to enter. The head tax was later raised to $100, then $500, before all Chinese immigration was banned in July 1923.

From then until 1947, all Chinese people — even those born in Canada — were required to register with the government or risk fines, detainment or deportation. They were segregated within society too, like being prevented from working in some professions or swimming in some public pools.

Operation Oblivion

It was under those laws, designed to exclude or ostracize people on the basis of their Chinese ethnicity, that Hoy's father, at the age of 26, still decided to volunteer in the war effort for Canada.

It was the same story for Rick Wong's father, Hank Wong, the son of a head tax payer and a member of Force 136, also called Operation Oblivion. Hank, who died in 2019, was the last surviving member of the original 13 members of the top secret mission to sabotage supply lines and equipment within Japanese-occupied territory in the Pacific.

Wong says despite first being rejected from the navy, because it was "for white men only," his father eventually joined the Kent Regiment and learned to parachute out of planes and rapidly deploy from moving trucks.

It was in the 1940s, when Japan entered the Second World War and began to quickly invade and occupy large parts of Southeast Asia, that the British realised it needed agents in the region to support local resistance fighters.

Undercover resistance

An undated photo of the first recruits of Force 136 training in Darwin, Australia. (Chinese Canadian Military Museum)

Chinese Canadians were the perfect recruits, from the perspective of Britain's Special Operations Executive, easily blending in with local populations with language skills in English and Cantonese.

Force 136 was born.

Then began intense training in Canada and abroad, including in espionage, wireless operation and jungle survival. Their mission was to gather intelligence, support local resistance fighters and carry out sabotage operations.

They were told to expect extreme heat, insects and disease, alongside the dangers of capture, torture or death.

Members of Force 136 training in Queensland, Australia in 1945. (Chinese Canadian Military Museum)

'A suicide mission'

One recruit, dropped into Borneo, recalled living on crocodile meat, monkeys and wild pigs, in a story highlighted by the Chinese Canadian Military Museum.

"They were told to save your last bullet for yourself, carry cyanide, if you're captured don't reveal any secrets," said Wong.

He says he once asked his father if he was afraid about what was "essentially a suicide mission" while he was awaiting his deployment in Australia.

His father replied, "you gotta do what you gotta do."

Then the Americans, under President Harry Truman, dropped the atomic bomb on Hiroshima and Nagasaki, in early August 1945. There's long been difficulty in estimating total casualties, but more than 120,000 people were killed instantly in both cities, with many more dying from radiation in the years following, according to the Harry S. Truman Presidential Library & Museum. A few days later, the war ended and so too did Operation Oblivion.

While most of Force 136 sailed back to Canada through England, some men, including Wong's father, were abandoned in Australia.

" They had to work their way back on a freighter in order to get back," said Wong.

When they did get back to Canada, it took another two years until discriminatory laws were repealed. Many see Force 136 and the dismembering of legislation like the Chinese Exclusion Act as inseparably linked.

When those men returned they continued fighting, says Melissa Karmen Lee, the CEO of the Chinese Canadian Museum in Vancouver. It's the only place in Canada, including the War Museum in Ottawa, where the public can see a permanent exhibit on Chinese Canadian soldiers.

"Their faces belong on a Canadian stamp, their stories belong in our history books, and their legacy belongs to every Canadian," Lee said.

Rick Wong, left, and Brent G. Hoy unveil the new Canada Post stamp in Vancouver on Nov. 3. (Spill Studios)

'That's my dad there'

Hoy told an audience at the unveiling of the stamp in Vancouver that he could visualize his father's "broad and knowing closed lip smile of approval" that the contributions of Force 136 would be memorialized in such a way.

His father, who died in 2002, appears in the stamp in the bottom row, second from the right.

Hoy says he was thrilled "beyond words" when he was sent a mock-up of the stamp.

"I thought, hey gee, you know that's my dad there."

While the stamp features only a handful of the faces behind Force 136, Hoy says it marks an acknowledgement of gratitude for the Chinese Canadians that were prepared to sacrifice their lives. None lived long enough to see this commemoration.

"This selfless sense of duty shines a bright light on the fact that we, as a generation after them, are the offspring of our ancestors' courage, persistence, commitment and sacrifice."

World.title: Canada says Russian hockey players with visas will still be barred from world junior championship
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The federal government says Russian hockey players will not be permitted to compete at next month's world junior championship in Alberta, even if they already hold valid Canadian visas.

A statement provided Wednesday by Secretary of State for Sport Adam van Koeverden says Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada will take measures to individually assess and prevent Russian and Belarusian athletes and officials from entering Canada to compete.

There are Russians with valid visas playing in the Canadian Hockey League, the umbrella organization for the country's three top major junior hockey leagues.

Russians and Belarusians were banned from the CHL's import draft from 2022-24 before being allowed back in. According to the CHL, Russia led this year's draft with 32 of the 114 players selected.

Wednesday's statement appears to close the door on Russia's return to the world juniors following last month's Court of Arbitration for Sport ruling that the International Ice Hockey Federation (IIHF) must reinstate the country in international hockey.

Norway's hockey federation said Sunday the IIHF had informed it that Russia would be added to the tournament at Norway's expense.

Norway qualified for the tournament and has said it still hopes to compete.

The IIHF has not formally announced any changes to the tournament field. Its website continues to list Norway among the 10 participating teams.

Hockey federations from several nations, including Finland, Sweden, Czechia and Norway, have said their teams will refuse to compete against Russian players.

Russia and Belarus have been banned from international hockey competition since Russia invaded Ukraine with Belarusian assistance in 2022.

Prime Minister Mark Carney said last week that Russian and Belarusian athletes could not compete in Canada while representing their countries as long as the war continues.

The government's earlier position allowed individual athletes to compete as neutrals, leaving open the question of whether a Russian team could participate under a neutral designation.

Van Koeverden clarified Monday that the neutral designation applied to individual athletes, not teams.

The government said its position would not change as long as Russia continues its war in Ukraine with Belarus's complicity.

The world junior championship begins Dec. 26 in Edmonton and Red Deer.

World.title: De la Espriella failed to make Colombia secure in 90 days
World.content:
Colombia’s far-right President Abelardo de la Espriella failed to live up to his promise to “recuperate” state-control of conflict regions through a “shockwave” of hardline security measures within 90 days in office.

His first three months in office ended this week, and by almost every metric violence is rising.

Non-state armed groups and organized criminal groups alike have staged a series of attacks on security forces and their infrastructure, likely in retaliation for aggressive security actions that have included bombings carried out by Colombian aerial forces (which have killed at least 8 minors).

It would seem the shockwave is being carried out by not-state, rather than state forces.

According to new data published by the country’s Ombudsman’s Office and police, extortion, homicides, acts of “terrorism”, kidnappings, and attacks on security forces have all risen since De la Espriella assumed the presidency. Thirty-eight members of the police or military have been killed, and 213 wounded in attacks by criminal groups.

Child-recruitment by non-state armed groups has also risen dramatically: 131% higher than former President Gustavo Petro’s first 90 days in office.

Although De la Espriella has made concrete changes from the policy of his predecessor — destruction of coca is up, and the right-wing president has dismantled previously ongoing negotiations and peace processes with some criminal groups — much of his administration’s security policy has been more about optics than substance.

The president has released videos of himself walking among the bodies killed by aerial bombings, and has taken to showing up in affected cities wearing a pistol on his hip, and carrying a walkie-talkie.

During an operation in Cucuta, in the province of Norte de Santander, on November 10, De la Espriella spoke with military officials armed, wearing a military uniform and a red military-style beret.

The same day, The National Liberation Army, ELN, the largest remaining rebel group in the country, carried out a drone attack on a military base in the north of the same department that killed at least one soldier and wounded 4 others.

His Ministry of Defense released a video of him interrogating and mocking a member of FARC-dissident group the 33rd Front, telling him “welcome to Patria Milagro,” the miracle country —a slogan from his campaign during elections.

In September, paramilitary group the ACSN shut down large parts of the northern coast, including the city of Santa Marta. In a show of power, the ACSN even defied a response-deployment by Colombian military forces to the region to continue the forceful shutdown as the military largely stood by powerless.

De la Espriella has since militarized both Santa Marta and Cucuta, a measure which seems to have had little effect on the day-to-day operations of non-state armed groups in the regions.

De la Espriella has also repeatedly requested help from the US, and invited them to participate in his security crackdowns. In September, the President met with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio to sign a series of agreements he calls the “Barranquilla Accords.” Colombia agreed to give US companies preferential treatment regarding mining contracts, particularly involving rare earth minerals, in return for US security assistance and drone technology, among other things.

De la Espriella has attempted to align Colombian and US interests in security in the region, and talked repeatedly of extraditing “high priority targets,” to the US rather than charge them under Colombian law.

At a press conference with Rubio, De la Espriella announced what he called a “21st-Century Plan Patriot.”

Named after an aggressive security operation by former right-wing President Alvaro Uribe, the president said the agreement with the US will “modernize aircraft, radars, drones, helicopters, anti-drone systems, air defense, mobility, intelligence, cyber defense, special forces, and maintenance and operations.”

Armed groups currently operate in 24 of Colombia’s 32 provinces — roughly 75% of the country. That was true before De la Espriella took office, and the president’s promise to change that within three months has so far yielded little to change that.

World.title: Three months after 7.5M earthquake struck Colombia, “reconstruction hasn’t begun”
World.content:
Human rights officials warned on Tuesday that the reconstruction of west Colombia, which was partially destroyed by an August 10 earthquake, fails to show progress.

In a statement, the Ombudsman’s Office warned that “difficulties persist in providing assistance to and supporting the recovery of affected communities, particularly with regard to housing, access to essential services, the protection of rights, and funding for response measures.”

The top human rights official of Pereira, Leonardo Fabio Reales, told Caracol Radio that “the reconstruction of the city has not begun. There isn’t even a rough outline of what is planned to be done after the earthquake.”

Pereira is among the hardest hit by the 7.4M earthquake that destroyed more than 123,000 homes, and hundreds of hospitals and schools.

More than 450 people continue to live in tents in temporary camps that were set up in Pereira and cities like Buenaventura, according to the Ombudsman, which raised the alarm over “the lack of clear protocols for closing shelters and providing housing alternatives for departing residents, alongside infrastructure and security deficiencies in several facilities.”

Promised rent assistance, which would allow those who lost their homes to temporarily find residence, has also been insufficient.

“More than a month ago I received a million pesos ($304) stipend, although this was supposed to be three, I haven’t received any news,” Pereira resident Christian Castañeda told France 24.

“They’ve announced a so-called ‘Miracle Fund,’ but so far we’ve only seen billboards—no major progress,” said Castañeda, whose mother is one of more than 3,000 people who have yet to receive financial aid.

This Miracle Fund was set up a few weeks ago with an initial COP625 billion ($190 million) budget, which is only a drop in the COP59.29 trillion (18 billion) bucket that the government must get together for the reconstruction process.

“I’m not sure whether the Miracle Fund is working with the diligence and sense of urgency that are required, nor am I sure that they are doing so in the most transparent way,” said House Representative Catherine Juvinao, a member of the congressional commission that monitors the recovery process.

According to Senator Alejandro Toro, local governments from parts of the country that weren’t affected by the earthquake have also tried to receive emergency funds.

Sixteen departments were listed as affected—16, when everyone knows only 5 were actually impacted. It turns out that among these 16, certain departments reported every single public building and school as damaged. For instance: in Caqueta, according to the governor, there are more affected municipalities than families. No one knows the true number of victims in Caqueta; the press didn’t cover a single damaged house there. In Bolivar, along the Atlantic Coast, 11 families were reported affected—and do you know how many total people were listed under those 11 families? 467 people from 11 families! That averages to 43 people per family! Come on, that is completely false! That is a lie; it’s not as if every household belongs to [vallenato singer] Diomedes. They also reported about 189 damaged schools, which would mean 12 or 13 damaged schools per family… impossible. This same issue occurred across other departments—16 departments, including Sucre!

Senator Alejandro Ocampo

Ocampo said he would continue his lawsuits against the foundation of First Lady Ana Lucia Pineda, Colombia Luz y Sonrisas, which has failed to comply with court orders ordering transparency on what it has done with money collected in response to the earthquake.

World.title: De la Espriella claims ELN plans to attack Colombia’s corporate media
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella ordered State forces to protect corporate media, claiming alerts over “possible terrorist attacks by the ELN” guerrilla group.

De la Espriella said he issued “specific instructions to ensure that the full capacity of the State is directed toward protecting” private television networks RCN and Caracol, “their journalists, employees, and families” on social media platform X.

The president said he also ordered to increase the protection of Semana, a far-right magazine owned by the main sponsor of his campaign, the Gilinksi family.

Freedom of the press is sacred and must be respected! No narco-terrorist group will silence the media through threats, intimidation, or acts of violence. President Abelardo de la Espriella

According to the Bogota Mayor’s Office, the orders were issued hours after the prosecution’s Technical Investigations Unit issued a “security alert” to the media outlets and the local government.

In a response, Caracol evacuated its main office in the capital and allowed police to search the premise for bombs without result.

Press freedom foundation FLIP said that “we reject and express our profound concerns over the alerts of possible attacks against media in Bogota.”

“The fact that no explosives have been found does not mean that the risk has ended. These alerts require monitoring and effective protection,” the FLIP said on X.

The alert was issued amid increased violence between guerrilla groups and State forces, who have been ordered to carry out an offensive against insurgencies and organized crime groups by the president.

World.title: Colombia’s war crimes tribunal JEP announces steep measures after being forced to cut $53M from its budget
World.content:
The president of the JEP announced radical cuts in the war crimes tribunal’s spending, which was forced to cut $53 million (COP170 billion) from its annual budget by Colombia’s Congress.

In a press statement, JEP president Danilo Rojas said that the court would abandon its 15,000m² main office in Bogota and move to a much smaller building in March of next year.

The court president additionally announced that it would eliminate 85% of its temporary employees and force staff to absorb administrative, technical defense, and psychosocial tasks previously handled by external contractors.

Many of the remaining workers will largely be working from home to facilitate the aforementioned move.

The court will also abandon personal security details for magistrates and the court directors and ask the National Protection Unit to take on the protection of victims, witnesses and defendants.

Last but not least, the court announced partnerships with universities, the Inspector General’s Office and local governments to secure regional presence, which is necessary to investigate war crimes.

The radical austerity measures became a necessity after Congress agreed with President Abelardo de la Espriella and hi far-right National Salvation party to slash the JEP’s budget.

The war crimes tribunal seeks justice for millions of victims of the military and the now-defunct guerrilla group FARC, which agreed to demobilize and disarm in 2016.

The JEP has long been the target of criticism of the far-right, which has historically downplayed the war crimes committed by the State and regional elites that used the armed conflict to accumulate wealth.

World.title: Colombia’s labor unions and social organizations call national strike on November 19
World.content:
Colombia’s main labor unions and a collection of civil society organizations called a national strike “against the fascist government of Abelardo de la Espriella and his tax reform” bill.

In a press statement, the organizations accused De la Espriella of, among other things, dismantling the “social, environmental, trade union, and labor rights achieved during the government of Gustavo Petro,” and surrendering sovereignty and kneeling before the imperialist government of the United States.”

The government of Abelardo, like that of Duque and Carrasquilla, intends to reach into the pockets of the people and privilege the ultra-rich with its “economic rescue” bill, which imposes a 19% VAT on food and other basic goods in the family basket, higher taxes on earned income, raises health contributions up to 8%, and conversely reduces the corporate capital income tax from 35% to 31%, eliminates the wealth tax in 2031, and reduces the capital gains tax to 20% for investments in 2027 and 2028. Civil society organizations

The organizations additionally accused the government of seeking special powers to facilitate the privatization of state-controlled companies like oil firm Ecopetrol.

The organizations said they united with the main opposition party, the Historic Pact, “with the purpose of opposing this fascist government and decisively participating in the National Strike.”

The National Strike on November 19 constitutes a new stage in the organization and expression of growing popular discontent, which was also manifested in the successful national mobilization day of October 14. It is about strengthening a collective action process capable of confronting the Government’s regressive measures, demanding respect for hard-won rights, and opposing the deepening of its neoliberal and authoritarian project. Civil society organizations

The last time a national strike was organized was in 2021 when the labor unions and their allies from civil society shut down parts of the country for months.

At the time, a tax reform propose by former President Ivan Duque triggered the initiative.

World.title: Colombia’s government presents “Economic Rescue Bill”
World.content:
Colombia’s Vice-President Jose Manuel Restrepo on Thursday presented an Economic Rescue Bill that seeks to reduce government spending and increase its revenue.

The bill grants extraordinary powers to President Abelardo de la Espriella to slash government spending by decree and includes a tax reform that includes higher sales tax rates on gasoline, coffee, cigarettes and vegetables.

The bill also includes tax breaks for corporations in an attempt to increase investment.

Abelardo’s extraordinary powers

While on campaign, De la Espriella powers vowed a 40% reduction of the State, which the bill falls short of doing.

Article 7 of the bill does grant the president extraordinary powers to “abolish, merge, and split ministries and administrative departments, as well as to determine or modify their names, objectives, and organizational structure,” and allows De la Espriella to “abolish, merge, split, and change the legal status” of other State bodies like the superintendencies, agencies, special administrative units, and public institutions.

Article 96 allows the government to change the personnel hiring of tax agency DIAN, which “would allow for the elimination of annual competitive exams for entry into the DIAN and a return to the practice of appointing thousands of officials,” according to former DIAN director Luis Carlos Reyes.

Last but not least, the bill mandates a 20% reduction in salaries of State employees, excluding the security forces, and cut half of the costs in temporary contracts.

VAT reforms and squeezing the middle class

The bill seeks to remove popular products like cocoa, coffee, sugar and fruits from a VAT exemption list and introduce a 19% sales tac on them.

An increase in taxes on gasoline will inflate its price.

The bill additionally seeks to charge VAT on vice products like liquor and cigarettes, which would make them up to 53% more expensive.

The bulk of these tax increases wouldn’t take fore until after the November 2027 local and regional elections in an apparent compromise to Congress and Colombia’s political forces.

In an attempt to not impoverish the poor, the bill seeks a mechanism that would refund up to 100% of IVA payments to some 19 million of the country’s poorest citizens.

The increased pressure on the middle class has already resulted in opposition from within De la Espriella’s congressional coalition.

Tax benefits for the capitalists

The government seeks to gradually lower the corporate income tax from 35% to 31% and offer a reduced tax rate for large companies that decide to invest in new enterprises.

According to the Inter-American Development Bank, a similar scheme introduced by former President Alvaro Uribe “was ineffective in promoting investment.”

World.title: Accusations over De la Espriella’s narco ties “lack conclusive or solid evidence,” says Colombia’s justice minister
World.content:
Colombia’s Justice Minister, Ivan Cancino, downplayed the evidence of ties between President Abelardo de la Espriella and drug traffickers that was displayed in Congress by opposition Senator Ivan Cepeda.

In a video, Cancino said that “political oversight is a fundamental tool of our democracy. However, it cannot become an arena for launching accusations without proving and substantiating them.”

The justice minister admitted that the pieces of evidence provided to Congress “may seem serious,” but “lack conclusive or solid evidence, as well as any support that could jeopardize the innocence and the presumption of innocence of our president.”

It is not just about displaying organizational charts, deeds from over a decade ago, and business transactions to construct a narrative that supports neither judicial decisions nor the documentary, testimonial, circumstantial, or expert backing required for these types of accusations. Ivan Cancino

Cancino accused the opposition of remaining “silent regarding the grave scandals involving corruption, drug trafficking, and even alleged sexual abuse, as well as fiscal irresponsibility and possible links to criminal organizations that surrounded the previous government. ”

The justice minister was forced to come out after Cepeda showed Congress evidence of De la Espriella’s business ties with multiple convicted drug traffickers and announced criminal complaints against the president.

De la Espriella’s law firm rose to prominence during the demobilization of paramilitary organization AUC with whom he created a foundation that sought to justify the paramilitary violence that terrorized much of Colombia in the 1990’s and 2000s.

Once the ties between the AUC and elected politicians became known, the president ended up defending many of the “parapoliticians” in court.

According to Cepeda, De la Espriella plays a key role in a “revolving door” system that could end up benefiting the very drug traffickers and corrupt politicians that have paid the president for his legal defense in the past.

World.title: Colombia’s opposition announces criminal charges against De la Espriella over ties to drug traffickers
World.content:
Colombia’s opposition leader, senator Ian Cepeda, accused President Abelardo de la Espriella of leading an agrarian counter-reform designed to benefit land-owning clans and convicted drug traffickers.

During a congressional debate, Cepeda claimed that De la Espriella put allies of drug traffickers and paramilitaries in charge of key state institutions responsible for land distribution and asset forfeiture.

The president and his appointees are part of a revolving door system of people who, before being appointed to government positions, defended the interests of drug traffickers and paramilitaries associated with De la Espriella and his businesses, according to the opposition leader.

For example, the president put Diana Patrica Bravo, a former prosecutor and partner at his law firm De la Espriella Lawyers, in charge of The Society of Special Assets (SAE), which controls assets that were seized from drug traffickers.

The leader of the leftist Historic Pact party showed financial statements of one of De la Espriella’s companies, Dominio De la Espriella, that would prove that in between 38% and 40% of its capital deposits came from the family and corporate network of Hugues Rodríguez, a.k.a. Comandante Barbie, a former paramilitary financier who was charged with drug trafficking in the US.

The SAE would control more than 130 properties of Comandante Barbie.

De la Espriella family construction firm, Cosenza S.A.S., made property purchases in the city of Monteria directly with individuals under investigation for money laundering and illicit enrichment, according to Cepeda.

The president’s ex-wife, Yoly Beatriz Illidge, was appointed Superintendent of Notaries, making her “directly responsible for inspecting and monitoring all land entries and records issued by restitution judges throughout the country,” according to Cepeda.

De la Espriella is an associate of drug traffickers, owns assets purchased from drug traffickers, and defends drug traffickers from within the national government. Senator Ivan Cepeda

Last but not least, Agriculture Minister Indalecio Dangond “arrived at this post to execute an agrarian counter-reform at the service of paramilitary land-grabbers, foreign capital, and agro-industrial partners” while blocking investments for small farmers and displacement victims, the opposition leader stated.

Cepeda vowed that he would give the dossier to the United States Department of Justcie and to “Congressmen of the Democratic Party, given that mister De la Espriella is a US citizen.”

The opposition leader additionally promised to file criminal charges against the president and his agriculture minister in Colombia.

World.title: Chile: Fatherhood Under Threat or Masculinity on the Defensive?
World.content:
A critique of Chile’s proposed False Accusations Law

By Andres Kogan Valderrama

HAVANA TIMES – Regarding a bill in the Chilean legislature which addresses false accusations and reports in family court proceedings, I would like to discuss how this initiative fits into antifeminist discourse and the activities of organizations seeking to perpetuate gender inequalities. I have worked on issues of masculinity for years, and as a father, I am particularly interested in discussing what we are defending when we talk about fatherhood.

First, I want to express my support for Colectiva Resistencia Materna Chile and Movimiento FemNNA, as well as the many other organizations and individuals who have warned about the risks this initiative poses to women who report violence and who have signed the letter opposing the proposed false accusations law (1). I believe their concerns must be heard. I worry that, in the name of children’s rights, we may end up casting even more suspicion on women seeking protection for themselves and their children.

One of my main concerns is the role of the Fundación Crianza Compartida Chile (Shared Parenting Foundation). Under concepts such as shared parental responsibility and children’s rights, it has promoted a narrative in which false accusations and alleged maternal manipulation occupy a central place. In my view, its discourse is part of the antifeminist currents within fathers’ rights movements and the manosphere. It is no coincidence that men are repeatedly portrayed as victims of feminism and women as responsible for their problems.

From my own experience as a father, I understand that raising children involves much more than claiming the right to spend time with our sons and daughters. It means getting up, being present, showing concern, being available, and taking responsibility for everyday needs. It also means giving up some of our own time and taking on tasks that have historically been left to women. That is why I find it difficult to understand a defense of fatherhood that places so much emphasis on men’s rights and so little on our responsibilities.

Australian sociologist Michael Flood has spent years researching fathers’ rights movements and their connections to antifeminist discourse (2). His work helps us understand that not all organizations promoting fathers’ involvement pursue the same objectives. The problem arises when defending fatherhood becomes a platform for attacking feminism, discrediting women, and asserting an alleged loss of male authority. I believe Fundación Crianza Compartida and this bill should be examined from that perspective.

This criticism is not new. In November 2025, I published a column titled “The Antifeminist Discourse Hidden Within Fundación Crianza Compartida” (3). In it, I questioned how this organization uses the defense of fatherhood to promote positions opposed to feminism. Today, faced with this proposed legislation, I find myself confronting the same concerns. I cannot help but notice how children’s rights are invoked while women who report violence are placed under suspicion.

The bill in question also deserves a much more rigorous discussion of its provisions. It does not merely seek to punish deliberately false accusations; it also introduces changes related to expert reports, precautionary measures, child custody, and visitation rights. There is something we should never forget: the fact that an allegation cannot be substantiated in court does not mean it is false. Confusing these two situations could ultimately discourage women who need to report abuse and seek protection.

There is something I have been observing for some time in my workplace, my family, and the spaces where I talk with other men: women are often more willing to discuss male privilege. Among men, it is considerably more difficult. We talk about our rights as fathers, but we are not always willing to discuss who cooks, cleans, takes the children to the doctor, or cares for them when they are sick. That contradiction should also be part of the discussion about fatherhood.

I am also concerned that concepts such as parental alienation are being used to discredit the testimony of women and children. The United Nations has warned about the risks of using this concept in custody disputes, particularly when it ends up overshadowing allegations of violence. Children are not their parents’ property, nor are they instruments for resolving conflicts between adults (4). Listening to their experiences and protecting their well-being should take precedence over any dispute.

For these reasons, I support Colectiva Resistencia Materna Chile, Movimiento FemNNA, and the many other organizations and individuals who have questioned this bill. As a father, I do not see fatherhood as a struggle against women or as a means of reasserting male authority. I want men to be able to participate fully in raising their children, but I also want us to be capable of examining our own practices and responsibilities. Because if there is something that should concern us, it is not that feminism challenges our authority, but rather that so many men still do not feel personally called upon to take responsibility for caregiving.

Read more from Chile here on Havana Times.

World.title: Paraguay’s Ueno Bank Scandal Spreads Its Effects to Panama
World.content:
The official explained that the business structure is complex, consisting of nearly 40 companies that provided various services to Ueno Bank. Photo: RODRIGO BUENDIA | AFP

By Manuel Vega Loo (La Estrella de Panama)

HAVANA TIMES – Paraguay’s Minister of Labor, Monica Recalde, said she had received communications from workers in Panama, Nicaragua, Argentina, and Mexico who provided services to the company Itti and received their salaries from Paraguay.

Workers in Panama are among those affected by the crisis involving companies linked to Ueno Bank in Paraguay, which has impacted approximately 7,000 direct employees, both in Paraguay and abroad, Monica Recalde told radio station Universo 970 AM.

In an interview, Recalde explained that the impact of the situation extends to several countries because companies associated with the business group provided technology and IT support services from Paraguay while employing workers in other markets.

The minister said she had received communications from workers in Panama, Nicaragua, Argentina, and Mexico who provided services to the company Itti and received their salaries from Paraguay.

Itti is a Paraguayan technology company founded in 2004 and owned by Grupo Vazquez. It specializes in software development and digital solutions for the financial and corporate sectors.

Recalde clarified that these employees are subject to the labor laws of their respective countries, although their employment relationships were connected to the Paraguayan business structure.

The minister told Universo 970 AM that the Paraguayan government’s updated estimate is approximately 7,000 workers affected by the crisis, including employees of the bank, affiliated companies, and nonbank correspondent operations.

Of that total, around 6,000 are workers associated with the bank and companies operating in Paraguay, while the remainder are linked to international operations.

The minister explained that the business structure is complex, consisting of nearly 40 companies that provided various services to Ueno Bank.

According to Recalde, some employees had contracts with one company but, in practice, performed duties for another company within the same corporate network or directly for the bank. She noted that some workers even used the bank’s uniforms, email accounts, and equipment, although they were formally employed by third parties.

Among the first measures adopted by Paraguay’s Ministry of Labor was the elimination of contractual restrictions that prevented employees from providing services to other companies.

Recalde explained that several companies maintained exclusivity clauses prohibiting their employees from working for another company, in some cases for up to six months after their employment ended.

The Ministry issued a ruling releasing workers from that obligation and allowing them to seek other employment opportunities or work independently, even if they remain on the companies’ payrolls.

The minister justified the decision on the grounds of the right to work and the lack of actual work assignments, since many of these companies had ceased operations and their employees were no longer being assigned duties.

The ruling was delivered to representatives of 37 companies linked to the group.

Recalde also reported that the Ministry of Labor had asked the Board of Directors of the Social Security Institute to evaluate exceptional measures to protect access to medical care for affected workers.

Concerns include pregnant women and people requiring medical treatment, given the uncertainty surrounding the continuation of their social security contributions.

The minister said the last employer contributions recorded by the companies corresponded to September and that the government is seeking to coordinate mechanisms to prevent employees from losing access to medical services.

She also noted that working groups continue to review the legal situation of each employee and determine the conditions for paying their severance and other employment benefits.

Regarding the possibility of the state helping keep some of the affiliated companies operating, Recalde said the government is examining the issue but cautioned that it must first understand how the business model functioned and the legal circumstances of each company.

First published in Spanish by La Estrella de Panama and translated and posted in English by Havana Times.

Read more news here on Havana Times.

World.title: Cuba’s Revolution Is Even Taking Away Our Vices
World.content:
By Fabiana del Valle

HAVANA TIMES – There comes a day when you realize there are things you don’t need, and you decide to give them up as a voluntary, personal choice. But in Cuba, there are things you give up because they have become economically impossible.

My husband, for example, is discovering that the “Revolution” has found a way to force him to quit smoking. Not through anti-smoking campaigns, a terminal illness, the image of a lung reduced to a rag, or a personal decision born of a desire to be healthier.

Here, even vices are subject to inflation, and existential questions begin when, before lighting a cigarette, you look at it as if it were a diamond. Do I really need to smoke? Should I save the money to buy food, or just buy three cigarettes and save a little that way?

Every cigarette becomes an equation, and getting even the most die-hard smoker to develop the skills of an economist when lighting up a Popular brand cigarette is quite a revolutionary achievement.

The famous Popular cigarette, or “ration-store cigarette,” as all Cubans know it, deserves a special chapter in the life of anyone born on this island who has ever smoked.

It’s a domestic product made with so few resources that it seems to have been manufactured from the leftovers of a cigarette someone else already smoked. Sometimes you even find a tobacco stem or a cockroach wing in the filling. Its packaging, white paper with blue lettering, makes you suspect it has been through a war before reaching the consumer’s hands.

It turns up on the informal market at a frightening price, as though every cigarette were wrapped in gold leaf. One thing is for a product to be unavailable; quite another is for it to show up where it shouldn’t be, at a price far above its actual value.

It’s the same old game with every product manufactured in this country. It all begins in the warehouse of some factory, with a worker who knows someone else who knows how to get hold of the merchandise. Then there’s the famous “buddy” who always manages to obtain a few boxes, moves them around, resells them, and at the end of the chain are the same people as always: those trying to survive on wages that are laughable.

I’m not going to blame the person selling them. Unfortunately, that person is also trying to survive. This country’s economy resembles a game of dominoes in which everyone tries to play their tile and move forward however they can before night falls. And while some manage to get their hands on merchandise, others can barely afford to breathe.

I know smoking isn’t a basic necessity. It would never occur to me to convince anyone that a cigarette should take priority over rice, medicine, or electricity. Smoking is bad for your health, and if it’s also expensive, well, you just quit. Simple as that.

Except that the same thing is happening with anything that still gives us a little pleasure. We don’t smoke, we don’t drink coffee, we don’t eat meat because it costs too much, traveling is an impossible dream, and we don’t buy clothes. There are always other priorities. The sad thing is that when someone asks how we’re doing, we answer without hesitation: “We’re fine.” We’ve learned to survive without complaining too much.

In this tropical version of the Holy Trinity, the land of rum, sugar, and tobacco, you’d better have your wallet ready. My husband has the right to decide to quit smoking because he wants to, rather than having his choices dictated by economic misery.

Cigarette packs warn that smoking is harmful to your health, but in Cuba, smoking seriously damages your wallet, leaving it sick, very sick, with no chance of getting an appointment with a specialist.

Read more from the diary of Fabiana del Valle here on Havana Times.

World.title: Camaguey, Cuba, Governor Exposed for Corruption Resigns
World.content:
Sutil Sarabia had held the position since May 28, 2023. / Radio Agramonte

An independent journalist exposes serious irregularities, while readers of Cubadebate demand explanations about Jorge Enrique Sutil Sarabia’s “mistakes.”

By 14ymedio

HAVANA TIMES – Jorge Enrique Sutil Sarabia, governor of Camagüey, submitted his resignation, which was accepted by Miguel Diaz-Canel on Tuesday, according to a statement published in official media. According to the official version, the resignation came “after acknowledging mistakes made in the performance of his duties that were incompatible with his responsibilities,” an explanation that has failed to satisfy public opinion.

The public is well aware that the word “corruption” is hidden behind this euphemism, and even some comments on the pro-government Cubadebate website demand transparency. Still fresh in everyone’s memory is the dismissal of former Minister of Economy and Planning Alejandro Gil in February 2024, which was initially presented as a “personnel reshuffle.” A few days later, however, it was announced that his removal was the result of “serious mistakes made in the performance of his duties.” The former high-ranking official was sentenced in December 2025 to life imprisonment for espionage and to 20 years in prison in a second trial for economic and administrative crimes.

Probably with that precedent in mind, citizens have not hesitated to demand clarity to prevent speculation. “The reason for the resignation, without euphemisms or secrecy. We’re not living in the 1970s. Nowadays everything is known, and the truth will come out in the coming days, but I’d rather hear the Government’s version,” wrote one reader. “Why not report the whole story, including the reasons for his resignation, and thus prevent speculation, lies, etc., from other media outlets?” urged another.

A third commenter was even more explicit: “Some time ago, the Social Communication Law was approved, and one of its provisions guaranteed citizens the right to transparency of information. However, there is ever greater secrecy. For some time now, corruption involving this official has been denounced on social media. Once again, they are beating us in the communications war. Credibility remains in crisis,” the reader lamented.

On social media, independent journalist Jose Luis Tan Estrada, a native of Camagüey, has claimed the governor’s removal as a success of his investigations, attributing it to the information he has published about the official. The reporter, now exiled in Mexico, says that a colonel from the province traveled to Havana to participate in the investigation into Sutil, which was based on his allegations.

“Why was it necessary to bring an investigator from the province to participate in an investigation of this magnitude? Was there distrust about the possibility of investigating these events independently from Camagüey? Now they will try to prevent all of this from turning into a public scandal,” he says.

Tan Estrada maintains that “among the matters under investigation is the fuel allocated to several private businesses in quantities exceeding established limits,” allegedly diverted from public services, including ambulances and taxis used to transport dialysis patients.

“Amid this scandal, and because of other acts of corruption that are under investigation and that we exposed, the director of Taxis Cuba in Camagüey has also been removed. Another case of corruption uncovered by the investigative commission involves resources belonging to state-owned companies that produce food and beverages. Certain contracts favored some private businesses, which ended up purchasing practically all of the production,” he adds.

Tan Estrada identifies the Beverage and Soft Drink Company, La Vaquita Dairy Industry, and the Meat Processing Industry as entities under investigation. These companies produced food and beverages but allegedly diverted their products to private businesses.

He adds that construction materials were also diverted, along with another specific case that “involves the Provincial Directorate of Community Services. Huge budgets allocated to repairing the vehicle fleet, purchasing spare parts and fuel, as well as resources used to support the private business Almaley, which is linked to that entity, are under investigation.”

The journalist directly implicates several executives from a wide range of sectors, including the cultural sector, through a project run by the Provincial Book Center that served to divert “millions of pesos.”

“Thanks to my sources for their courage. Several years of investigation and risk, and in the end we succeeded,” Tan Estrada concludes.

According to the official statement, Sutil Sarabia will be replaced by the current deputy governor until a new governor is chosen, a decision that the public finds difficult to understand, judging by the comments.

“I don’t understand anything. The deputy governors, who are the governor’s right-hand people, had nothing to do with the mistakes?”

Sutil Sarabia had held the position since May 28, 2023.

First published in Spanish by 14ymedio and translated and posted in English by Havana Times.

Read more news from Cuba here on Havana Times.

World.title: Prices in Today’s Cuba and Who Can Pay Them
World.content:
Photo Feature by Irina Pino

HAVANA TIMES – Several times a week, I visit private businesses in my neighborhood and surrounding areas, looking for the most affordable prices for my budget. And believe me, prices keep rising every day, going through the roof. And I’m certainly not talking about heaven, but rather prices that are outrageously high for anyone who doesn’t have dollars to exchange for Cuban pesos, a currency that has become completely devalued.

Today, the exchange rate is 915 Cuban pesos to 1 US dollar. No one could have imagined this happening, even in their worst nightmares.

We live on an island that no longer has an economy. It produces nothing. Factories and sugar mills have disappeared, and the same has happened to Cuban coffee. All products are imported. State control over agriculture prevents productive forces from being unleashed. Dante Alighieri’s Inferno is child’s play compared to the hell we are living through.

Now I ask myself: How does a retiree survive on less than 4,000 pesos a month? What can they do to eat and buy the medicines they need? They won’t even be able to afford rice, because now one kilogram of the cheapest white rice costs 1,200 pesos. And eggs cost 150 pesos each.

Many people are dying from curable diseases. Soon we will see people lying dead in the streets from starvation.

Meanwhile, the state-run ration stores and the ration books have practically ceased to exist. Sometimes they offer a little bread that employees sell at 200 pesos for 10 small rolls.

Who can survive in this disaster? Only those who receive substantial remittances from abroad and those who own profitable businesses. I’ve seen many of my friends grow thin, and I’ve lost weight myself. It’s difficult to eat two meals a day, let alone have a simple glass of milk for breakfast when one kilogram of powdered milk costs 5,000 pesos.

How much longer will the state turn its back on what is happening to the people? Nobody controls prices. They couldn’t care less about us.

Here are some photos showing the prices at a nearby private store. Look at what things have come to in this country.

See more photo features here at Havana Times.

World.title: International News Briefs for Wednesday, November 11, 2026
World.content:
HAVANA TIMES – We bring you some of the top international news stories compiled by Democracy Now on Wednesday, November 11, 2026.

House GOP Blocks Impeachment Charges Against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth

Nov 11, 2026

House Republicans on Tuesday blocked impeachment charges against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. By a margin of just seven votes, Republicans managed to bury the charges in committee through a 211-204 party-line procedural vote. Eleven Democrats skipped the vote, including Democratic Congressmember Nancy Pelosi of California. While House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, who is vying for the speakership in January, expressed support for Hegseth’s impeachment, many wondered how it was such a surprise that he was unable to corral Democratic votes to impeach Hegseth. President Trump hailed the outcome as an “exoneration.” Hours before the vote, Hegseth blasted the impeachment articles and said he’d carry out the same operations again.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth: “Let’s be clear about what this resolution actually does. It tells our enemies, Iran, the cartels, every adversary watching, that the United States will actually punish its own warriors and its own civilian leadership for successfully executing lawful military operations.”

Sanders Says He Will Not Back Schumer for Senate Majority Leader

Nov 11, 2026

Vermont’s independent Senator Bernie Sanders said Tuesday he will not back Senator Chuck Schumer for Senate majority leader. Democratic Senator Elissa Slotkin of Michigan also said she won’t support Schumer until he presents a plan to govern differently. Senators-elect Peggy Flanagan of Minnesota, Troy Jackson of Maine, Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan, Juliana Stratton of Illinois and Adam Hamilton of Kansas have all said they won’t support Schumer, as has Senate candidate Scott Colom of Mississippi. This comes as Democratic Senator Chris Van Hollen of Maryland indicated Monday he’s open to running for Senate majority leader when the new Congress convenes in January. This is Senator Sanders.

Sen. Bernie Sanders: “If this campaign was about anything, it was about change and the need for the Democratic Party, in my view, to move in a new and bold direction. I personally have known Chuck Schumer for over 30 years, and I like Chuck. Nobody who works harder than Chuck Schumer. But in my view, the time is now for change, and I will not be supporting Chuck to be reelected as the Democratic leader.”

Rep. Jordan Elected as House GOP Leader as Senator Thune Reelected as Senate Republican Leader

Nov 11, 2026

House Republicans elected Congressmember Jim Jordan, a staunch Trump ally, as their leader after last week’s sweeping midterm losses. Jordan will replace Speaker Mike Johnson come January when a new Democratic majority takes office with at least 256 seats in the House. In the Senate, Republicans reelected Senator John Thune of South Dakota as leader. Democrats currently have a 54-seat majority in the Senate, with the races in Alaska and Mississippi leaning toward Democrats. The Democratic Senate candidate in Mississippi, Scott Colom, leads his Republican opponent by 3,000 votes.

Trump’s Former Lawyer Alina Habba Mildon Fired by Concord Partners

Nov 11, 2026

Image Credit: Gage Skidmore

President Trump’s former lawyer Alina Habba Mildon has been fired by Concord Partners, a secretive company with no public profile, set up by a prominent and wealthy Venezuelan family, which had previously signed Habba Mildon to a $50 million deal. Habba Mildon had received the contract shortly before Trump pardoned the head of the family, Julio Herrera Velutini, who was facing felony bribery charges in Puerto Rico. According to The New York Times, Trump recently erupted in anger after learning about Habba Mildon’s $50 million contract. In a letter from last week, Concord Partners said that Habba Mildon was fired due to a “failure to perform duties.” She will still keep $6.5 million that was paid to her, as well as an $8 million signing bonus.

U.S. Gov’t Received Over $12 Billion in Revenue from Venezuela’s Oil Exports

Nov 11, 2026

The U.S. government received over $12 billion in revenue from exports of Venezuela’s natural resources in the first nine months of this year, following the abduction of Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro. That’s according to a report by the global financial firm KPMG, which is among the first to provide detailed insight into the Trump administration’s financial holdings in Venezuela. The report was reviewed by The New York Times. After the U.S. removed Maduro from power in January, the Treasury Department reportedly established a “Venezuela Custody Account,” initially based in Qatar and then moved to Citibank in New York.

NYT: Immigrants Deported Back to Home Countries Despite Court Orders

Nov 11, 2026

The New York Times reports that foreign governments are accepting U.S. deportees and then sending them to their home countries, where they risk torture, sexual abuse or persecution. The Times identified more than 110 immigrants who were deported from the U.S. to third-party countries and then passed on to their home countries despite U.S. court orders. Alma David, a consultant with the National Immigration Litigation Alliance, said, “It’s immigration colonialism — making these governments do the dirty work.”

WaPo: ICE Hired 19 Officers with Past Allegations of Misconduct, Violence and Criminal Charges

Nov 11, 2026

An investigation by The Washington Post reveals ICE hired at least 19 officers who had past allegations of misconduct, violence and criminal charges during a mass hiring spree after Trump took office in 2025. The findings come after a Homeland Security Department data breach in October leaked the names of an estimated 1,500 new ICE hires. The Washington Post ran a background check on about 300 of them, with over a dozen officers coming back with red flags, including a former Detroit police officer involved in a fatal shooting that resulted in a $2.5 million wrongful-death settlement.

Immigrants Jailed at Northwest Detention Center in Washington Hold Hunger Strike

Nov 11, 2026

Image Credit: La Resistencia

A group of immigrants jailed at the troubled Northwest Detention Center in Tacoma, Washington, have been on a hunger strike for over eight days denouncing due process violations, medical neglect and inhumane conditions. They’re also demanding all ICE jails be shut down. This is at least the 22nd hunger strike inside the Northwest ICE jail this year alone. Despite mounting reports of abuse, Northwest will continue to operate for another 10 years, after the for-profit prison company GEO Group signed a $1.5 billion contract with the federal government in October.

Israeli Forces Kill at Least Eight Palestinians in Gaza

Nov 11, 2026

In news from Gaza, Israeli forces have killed ⁠at least eight Palestinians, including a father and his 13-year-old son, in attacks on Gaza City and Khan Younis. Israel has conducted near-daily attacks on Gaza despite a so-called ceasefire brokered by the U.S., killing more than 1,600 Palestinians since the deal went into effect last October. This comes as damage and destruction caused by Israel’s relentless bombings on Gaza’s infrastructure since 2023 have contributed to worsening flash floods as the enclave faces another winter with torrential rains. Gaza’s stormwater and sewage networks are so deteriorated that thousands of tents are being flooded. This is UNICEF spokesperson James Elder.

James Elder: “So, toxic sewage could flow into the streets and tents of Gaza City, forcing children and families from their makeshift home once more and grossly increasing the threat of disease. So we’re a bit baffled. Let’s do the rehabilitation before this becomes another entirely preventable killer of girls and boys in Gaza.”

Israeli Soldiers Kill 14-Year-Old Palestinian Boy in West Bank

Nov 11, 2026

In the occupied West Bank, Israeli soldiers have killed a 14-year-old Palestinian boy and wounded two other teens during a raid on the village of Burqa Tuesday. The boy was identified as Moataz Iyad Daghlas. This comes as more than 50 illegal Israeli settlers attacked a village south of Nablus, setting vehicles on fire. The U.N. has warned that attacks by Israeli settlers have escalated to an “unprecedented level,” with at least 1,143 Palestinians killed in the occupied West Bank since October 2023, including 250 children.

Russia and Ukraine Hold First Peace Talks in Nine Months

Nov 11, 2026

Russia and Ukraine on Tuesday held their first peace talks in nine months in Abu Dhabi. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky was not in attendance at the summit, where Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner and envoy Steve Witkoff renewed pressure to end the war.

In related news, a senior U.S. Army soldier was arrested in Britain for allegedly attempting to steal secret NATO information and deliver it to Russia. The 41-year-old has not been identified. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov denied any links between Russia and the suspect.

Independent Russian Newspaper Novaya Gazeta Closes Moscow Office

Nov 11, 2026

In more news from Russia, the independent newspaper Novaya Gazeta closed its Moscow office on Monday, saying it was not able to continue operating due to a campaign of state persecution. The investigative outlet was co-founded by the last Soviet leader, Mikhail Gorbachev, with money from his 1990 Nobel Peace Prize. Russian President Vladimir Putin had designated the paper as a “foreign agent.” Last month, Novaya Gazeta’s landlord refused to renew the news outlet’s lease. Also, Russian banks said that they would stop processing donations from readers. In October, Russian authorities raided the home of editor-in-chief Sergei Sokolov and took him in for questioning. Another editor, Oleg Roldugin, was arrested in April.

Dmitry Muratov, the Nobel Peace Prize-winning editor of Novaya Gazeta, said, “Those in our country who advocate for peace have been denied the right to read what they choose, as we see happening today. We are currently at a point where the section of the Russian constitution that guarantees political and civil rights has ceased to function.”

Egyptian Court Postpones Criminal Trial of Mada Masr’s Editor-in-Chief Lina Attalah

Nov 11, 2026

A court in Egypt has postponed proceedings in the criminal trial of Mada Masr’s editor-in-chief, Lina Attalah, until November 18. Attalah faces charges of publishing false news and managing a website without a license. Click here to see our recent interview with Lina Attalah.

Federal Appeals Court Rules Trump Admin Illegally Fired Head of Voice of America

Nov 11, 2026

Image Credit: J. David Ake/Getty Images

A federal appeals court panel ruled on Tuesday that the Trump administration illegally fired the head of Voice of America (VOA), Michael Abramowitz, last year. Earlier this year, a federal judge also revoked the firing of more than 1,000 journalists at VOA and voided Trump’s installment of his ally to serve as the interim chief of the United States Agency for Global Media, which is the parent agency of VOA. In a statement, Abramowitz said, “There is no longer any reason for the government to prevent me from doing the job for which I was legally installed on a bipartisan basis more than two years ago.”

Greta Thunberg Attends U.N. Climate Summit for the First Time Since 2021

Nov 11, 2026

As world leaders and delegates from over 190 nations kicked off the U.N. climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, this week, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan took the opportunity to celebrate the discovery of two new oil fields in the Gabar Mountains and the possibility of future fossil fuel projects. Phasing out fossil fuels has been a central proposal at the annual climate talks pushed by Indigenous and environmental activists who are again demanding urgent climate solutions.

Swedish activist Greta Thunberg arrived at COP31 on Tuesday. It is the first time she is attending the climate summit since 2021.

Greta Thunberg: “In all the catastrophes we are facing, it is scientific fact that if we continue like now, things like food, clean water, functioning infrastructure will become luxury.”

Thousands of Protesters Rally in Indonesia over Government’s Response to Fires

Nov 11, 2026

In Indonesia, thousands of students and activists rallied across the country on Tuesday over the government’s inadequate response to forest and land fires. They demanded that the government declare a national disaster and punish those responsible for the blazes. The protesters also called for more jobs and economic relief.

Faturrohman Jaguna: “We call on the local government and the Yogyakarta Regional House of Representatives to improve the welfare of small and medium-sized enterprises, pedicab drivers and all the people of Yogyakarta who today are facing hardships from a weakening economy. Therefore, we urge the government to restore the people’s economy in Yogyakarta and across Indonesia.”

Read more news here on Havana Times.

World.title: Milei in tears as he bids farewell to Leo XIV at Ezeiza, closing the Pope’s Argentina visit
World.content:
Milei in tears as he bids farewell to Leo XIV at Ezeiza, closing the Pope’s Argentina visit

11th Wednesday, November 2026 - 19:49 UTC Full article

The day had begun at the Devoto prison in Buenos Aires, where the Pope listened to some 70 inmates

President Javier Milei was moved to tears during Pope Leo XIV’s farewell at Ezeiza airport, at the end of a four-day visit, the first by a pontiff to Argentina in 39 years. The Pope left for Peru, the second leg of his South American tour, after celebrating his last Mass at the Basilica of Luján.

Milei, accompanied by his sister and presidential chief of staff, Karina Milei, and Foreign Minister Pablo Quirno, greeted the Pope and the bishops present and walked him to the steps of the plane, an Aerolíneas Argentinas Airbus A330. While the aircraft was still waiting to depart, the three embraced, as behind a fence a group of children waved small Vatican flags. The plane began taxiing at 2.14 p.m.

Javier Milei in tears, absolutely balling his eyes out, thanking Pope Leo XIV for his visit, as he asks the Pope repeatedly to pray for him. This has been an incredibly well organised trip. Everyone involved should rightly be praised. Argentina you won. https://t.co/1vAO8wZqXp — Catholic Sat (@CatholicSat) November 11, 2026

Earlier, in Luján, the Pope bade farewell to the faithful. “Thank you for receiving me with such affection. Thank you, Argentina, for receiving me with open arms. Farewell, my dear Argentina!” he said. Official figures reported by Argentine media put the crowd at the Mass at more than three million people, which have not been independently verified. At the start, he placed a Golden Rose, the highest honour the Vatican grants to Marian shrines, at the feet of the image of the Virgin. According to Infobae, he said in his farewell message that the country “now has two Popes, one born here and one by adoption”.

The day had begun at the Devoto prison in Buenos Aires, where the Pope listened to some 70 inmates. “I hope to take away the message that a new life is possible,” he said, according to the news site MDZ.

The visit began on Sunday with a speech to the authorities, with Milei present, in which the Pope said that “the economy must be at the service of the person”. On Monday he celebrated Mass in Palermo, with some 2.5 million people according to the authorities, and on Tuesday another in Córdoba, with some 650,000, according to El País. The visit was preceded by tensions between the government and the Catholic hierarchy over austerity policies. Milei, who harshly criticised Pope Francis in the past, described him on Sunday as “the most important Argentine in history”.

The Pope arrives in Lima tonight, where President Keiko Fujimori will receive him at the Government Palace. Between November 13 and 16 he will visit Chiclayo, Cusco and Pucallpa, among other places, and he will return to Rome on the 16th.

World.title: Prosecutors open the vault at Peña’s house and find it empty; two safes found at Ueno Bank
World.content:
Prosecutors open the vault at Peña’s house and find it empty; two safes found at Ueno Bank

11th Wednesday, November 2026 - 11:12 UTC Full article

Prosecutor Silvia González said Peña, through his lawyer, indicated where the key was, which made it possible to open the room. “We found nothing of value inside,” she said

Paraguayan prosecutors on Tuesday opened the armoured vault hidden in former President Santiago Peña’s summer house in San Bernardino, two days after finding it, and found it empty. In a second raid, at Ueno Bank’s headquarters, they found two more hidden safes, one containing about US$14,000 in cash.

Prosecutor Silvia González said Peña, through his lawyer, indicated where the key was, which made it possible to open the room despite its complex security system. “We found nothing of value inside,” she said. According to the defence, the space was built as a “panic room”. Images released show an empty space with ventilation and electrical connections, without furniture. The house, which cost about 7.7 billion guaraníes (US$1.25 million) financed with loans from Ueno Bank, has passed to the administration of Senabico, the state body that manages seized assets.

Neighbours say three SUVs left the residence several times on Friday, November 5, as the Senate began Peña’s impeachment trial, and surveillance cameras reportedly recorded the vehicles’ movements. It has not been reported what they were carrying.

At Ueno Bank’s headquarters, known as La Matrix, investigators found a safe about 1.70 metres tall hidden behind a wall in a rooftop bathroom, linked to the offices of former vice-president and chief executive Miguel Vázquez. It contained documents and drinks, but no money. A second safe was in a false bottom in the bathroom of his office. Prosecutor Jorge Arce opened it and found 87.1 million guaraníes, about US$14,000 in cash, along with documents and empty bags.

An appeals court meanwhile upheld Vázquez’s pre-trial detention and provisionally expanded the legal classification of his case to money laundering and criminal association, so he could face up to 15 years in prison, according to the newspaper La Nación of Paraguay. Peña, charged with breach of trust and self-serving administration, has been in pre-trial detention since Saturday and says he is innocent. Prosecutors estimate the damage at about US$809 million.

Opposition lawmakers criticise prosecutors for not having seized Peña’s mobile phone and for delaying the raids, which they say allowed evidence to be removed, and are calling for the impeachment of Attorney General Emiliano Rolón. The Colorado Party has the votes to block it.

World.title: EU-Mercosur deal, six months on: winners, losers and the question mark over Europe’s top court
World.content:
EU-Mercosur deal, six months on: winners, losers and the question mark over Europe’s top court

11th Wednesday, November 2026 - 11:02 UTC Full article

Supporters highlight tariff savings of about €4 billion and a market of more than 700 million consumers

Six months after it began to apply provisionally, the trade agreement between the European Union and Mercosur, made up of Argentina, Brazil, Paraguay and Uruguay, combines projected benefits for both blocs, opposition from part of Europe’s farming sector and a legal question mark: the opinion of the EU Court of Justice on its legality, which could take until early 2028.

The interim trade agreement, signed in January, has applied since May 1 and covers trade and investment liberalisation. Mercosur will gradually eliminate tariffs on 91% of imports from the EU and the EU on 92% of those from Mercosur. The European Commission specified that it applies to those South American countries that completed their ratification. The broader, political Association Agreement must be ratified by all 27 member states. On January 21, the European Parliament voted 334 to 324 to ask the court to review the deal. The Commission then said those doubts were unjustified, and provisional application continues in the meantime.

Supporters highlight tariff savings of about €4 billion and a market of more than 700 million consumers. BBVA Research estimates that bilateral trade will grow by 40% by the end of the 16-year implementation period. For Mercosur, the estimates cited by the newspaper point to a boost of up to half a percentage point of GDP in Argentina and one and a half in Brazil.

There are also sectors set to lose. According to BBVA Research economist Juan Ruiz, in Europe these will be extensive beef farming, sugar and bioethanol, and in Mercosur, industry and manufacturing. The agreement provides for closed quotas for beef and poultry, safeguards if prices fall by more than 5% and a €45 billion reserve to compensate European farmers. Ruiz acknowledges that these protections “distort the market”, but give time to adapt. Spanish farming organisation ASAJA argues that one cannot speak of “fair competition” while agreements are signed with countries that do not fully guarantee compliance with EU standards.

That debate was revived on September 3, when the Commission suspended imports of meat, eggs and honey from Brazil over antibiotic use incompatible with EU rules, pending an audit. For the specialists consulted, the measure shows that protection works. “There has been a lot of misinformation in the farming sector, which is the most protected in the world and has nothing to fear,” said Juan Moscoso del Prado of EsadeGeo.

Legal uncertainty worries businesses. “The uncertainty arising from the agreement’s legal status remains, which for now prevents companies from planning,” said Mar Guardiola, head of tax at Andersen. Her colleague Rafael Ripoll recalled that annulment has not been sought, only an opinion on three aspects, and that the formula of splitting the treaty in two was already used with the agreement with Canada.

On the geopolitical front, Moscoso del Prado considers it a deal “clearly alternative to the model imposed by both the US and China”. Experts concede that it arrives late, as China leads in goods trade, but argue it is not obsolete.

World.title: Leo XIV draws some 650,000 to Córdoba with a homily on holiness
World.content:
Leo XIV draws some 650,000 to Córdoba with a homily on holiness

11th Wednesday, November 2026 - 10:55 UTC Full article

On Wednesday, Leo XIV will celebrate his last Mass in Argentina in Luján, in Buenos Aires province, and then fly to Peru

Pope Leo XIV celebrated Mass on Tuesday in Córdoba, in central Argentina, before some 650,000 people, according to the newspaper El País, in a homily devoted to holiness and local saints. “There is no better way to teach than by setting an example with one’s own life,” he told the faithful, urging them to practise their faith concretely in daily life.

The pontiff left Buenos Aires at 7.30 a.m. and landed in Córdoba an hour and a half later.
