The Mass was held at the grounds of the Argentine Aircraft Factory, covering more than 200 hectares, with 50 giant screens. Many pilgrims came by bus from other provinces, walked the last stretch before dawn and camped in the open. Among them were 28 altar boys from a parish in Jujuy, 900 kilometres away, who raised the travel money by selling food and holding pet shows. “I was left with all my hopes,” said Dora Ponce, 76, who did not manage to see the popemobile pass and followed the ceremony on a screen.

In his homily, Leo XIV recalled figures such as Father Brochero and Mama Antula, venerated above all in the interior of the country, and highlighted Córdoba’s religious history, marked by the arrival of the Jesuits in the 16th century. Its Jesuit Block has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2000.

After the Mass the Pope privately received a group of about 20 people from various social struggles, among them Alba Camargo, who as a child was abducted during the last dictatorship (1976-1983) and lost relatives to forced disappearance. Camargo asked him to name the disappeared and for his words to encourage those who know something about those crimes, including members of the clergy, to come forward. The Vatican has not given details of the meeting.

In the afternoon, the Pope greeted crowds from the balcony of the Archbishopric, the same one John Paul II appeared on in 1987, and met members of religious orders at the Cathedral of Our Lady of the Assumption. “There are stages in priestly and consecrated life in which remaining is already a very concrete form of self-giving,” he told them. The meeting was especially moving for the cloistered nuns who prepared the celebration: they baked 400,000 hosts and polished the chalices and liturgical items.

Attendance at the Córdoba Mass was lower than in Buenos Aires, where authorities estimated some 2.5 million people, and than the million the provincial government had anticipated. On Wednesday, Leo XIV will celebrate his last Mass in Argentina in Luján, in Buenos Aires province, and then fly to Peru, where President Keiko Fujimori will receive him that night.

World.title: Hundreds march in Gibraltar against Pelagos data center plan and demand transparency
World.content:
Hundreds march in Gibraltar against Pelagos data center plan and demand transparency

11th Wednesday, November 2026 - 10:46 UTC Full article

Protesters gathered at Casemates Square on Saturday before marching along Main Street to Convent Place, where they delivered a letter to Economic Development Minister Sir Joe Bossano

By Jim Watt- Gibralter

This Saturday, there was a demonstration at Casemates Square organised to express public discontent with the endless construction projects in Gibraltar and the proposed mega data centre in particular.

Over 400 people gathered at 11:00 a.m., highlighting a wide range of grievances, from housing and environmental concerns to Government transparency and accountability.

The protest was addressed by the organiser, local activist Kaelan Joyce.

The demonstrators then marched down Main Street to Convent Place, where a letter setting out their complaints and grievances was delivered to Government Minister Sir Joe Bossano.

The main focus of the demonstration was the initiative by Pelagos Data Centres, which has applied for planning approval for a £1.8 billion data centre campus to be constructed on reclaimed land in the Port of Gibraltar.

The project's final power consumption is estimated at 250 megawatts (MW), starting in 2027 with five development phases finishing in 2033. The company has stated that it will not use the existing Gibraltar power infrastructure, which in any event does not have sufficient capacity.

While backed by the Government of Gibraltar as a transformative economic leap, the project has sparked local debate and strong opposition. Environmental organizations, including the Environmental Safety Group (ESG) and other community groups, have called for enhanced scrutiny, independent environmental impact assessments, and clear transparency regarding emissions, fuel sourcing, and land use. In response, developers maintain that off-grid power generation and advanced design will minimize local environmental impact while adhering to net-zero operational targets.

Gibraltar is one of the most densely populated territories in the world, ranking consistently among the top five globally. With a total land area of approximately 6.8 square kilometres (2.6 square miles) and a population of over 40,000 residents, its overall density exceeds 5,000 to 6,000 people per square kilometre.

However, the effective population density is significantly higher than these baseline figures suggest. Roughly 40% of Gibraltar's land mass consists of the Upper Rock Nature Reserve—an unpopulated, steep limestone promontory where development is restricted. Consequently, nearly the entire resident population is concentrated in urban areas along the western side of the peninsula, such as Westside and the historic Town Area. In addition, 15,000 workers cross daily into Gibraltar from neighbouring Spain, along with thousands of tourists, drastically raising the daytime human density.

Whilst Pelagos talks about using ‘renewable energy’, there is no space for a solar farm or wind generation facility in Gibraltar; in order to ensure continuity of supply, massive local generating capacity using fossil fuels would be needed.

While mega data centres involve significant capital investment and short-term construction employment, their ongoing operations require relatively few permanent employees (often fewer than 100 on-site technicians and security personnel for a multi-acre complex). Local communities sometimes feel the massive physical footprint does not yield proportional economic or employment benefits compared to traditional commercial developments.

Given the proximity to housing developments, there is considerable concern about noise. Data centre noise is relentless. Because Gibraltar’s dramatic landscape consists of a massive limestone ridge (the Rock of Gibraltar), sound reflects and reverberates rather than dissipating over flat ground.

Constant low-frequency hums (30–200 Hz) penetrate concrete walls, double-glazed windows, and structural foundations much more effectively than high-pitched sounds.

How this can be controlled is as much a mystery as where the electricity and water for cooling are coming from.

World.title: Nvidia investigates founder Jensen Huang over his relationship with an alleged Chinese agent
World.content:
Nvidia investigates founder Jensen Huang over his relationship with an alleged Chinese agent

11th Wednesday, November 2026 - 10:30 UTC Full article

The company announced on Sunday that it was starting the investigation “in light of recent reporting that founder and CEO Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort”

Nvidia’s board has opened an independent investigation into founder and chief executive Jensen Huang after it emerged that he had an extramarital relationship with a businesswoman of Chinese origin whom US intelligence services link to Beijing’s espionage. President Donald Trump said on Monday that the FBI is investigating the case. No one has been charged.

The company announced on Sunday that it was starting the investigation “in light of recent reporting that founder and CEO Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort”. Huang acknowledged the relationship with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based AI infrastructure company Megaspeed, to whom he is not related despite sharing a surname. “I am deeply sorry,” he wrote in a memo to employees, according to Yahoo Finance. Nvidia said in a statement that it has no “reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia’s secrets have been compromised”.

According to The New York Times, a classified intelligence report, overseen by Secretary of State Marco Rubio, linked Alice Huang to China’s Ministry of State Security and concluded that she sought information on advanced chips and to influence their large-scale distribution in China. Her whereabouts are unknown, according to U.S. News. A source cited by NBC News also said the Justice Department is conducting a criminal investigation into Megaspeed, which is suspected of shipping export-restricted Nvidia chips to China; the Commerce Department already had an inquiry open into the company. Lawmakers have called for a congressional hearing.

Trump, who said he had spoken with Huang, said Huang told him he did not know the woman was a spy. “We’ll look into it. I know the FBI is investigating, and I think he’ll come out fine,” he said at the White House, where he said he was “amazed” by the allegations.

The case affects the most important company in the artificial intelligence industry. Nvidia controls between 80% and 90% of the AI accelerator market, according to a Silicon Analyst study, and designs in California chips that Taiwan’s TSMC manufactures. Huang, 63, was born in Taiwan and raised in Oregon. The United States restricts sales of Nvidia’s most advanced chips to China, and Huang lobbied Trump this year to ease those controls; according to El País, Washington later allowed a series of H20 chips to be sold to Chinese companies in exchange for 25% of the revenue.

Nvidia shares came under renewed pressure on Tuesday, in a week when major tech stocks fell sharply after the US midterm elections.

World.title: Hamburg hearing opens as Argentina seeks to halt Sea Lion and the UK disputes jurisdiction
World.content:
Hamburg hearing opens as Argentina seeks to halt Sea Lion and the UK disputes jurisdiction

10th Tuesday, November 2026 - 15:31 UTC Full article

Because the United Kingdom chose the International Court of Justice for such disputes and Argentina opted for the Hamburg tribunal, the merits of the case must be settled by an arbitral tribunal

The International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea began hearing Argentina and the United Kingdom in Hamburg on Tuesday over Argentina’s request for provisional measures to halt the Sea Lion oil project north of the Falklands. Argentina argued that the resources of a disputed continental shelf cannot be exploited unilaterally, while the United Kingdom rejects the tribunal’s competence to rule on what it considers a question of sovereignty.

“The islanders cannot appropriate the resources of the disputed continental shelf,” said Argentina’s agent, Ambassador Mario Oyarzábal, presenting his country’s four requests: that the UK prevent the start or continuation of exploitation at Sea Lion, refrain from granting new permits, preserve information obtained during exploration and protect the marine environment. Oyarzábal cited the islands’ 2021 census, with 3,142 usual residents, of whom 1,625 hold the residence status granted by the Governor, and said those resources “belong to the Argentine people”.

Jurist Marcelo Kohen, an adviser to the delegation, said Argentina refers to sovereignty only to show that its claim to the continental shelf is plausible. “The land dominates the sea. That is why, and only why, we refer here to Argentine sovereignty,” he said, arguing that it is enough that the United Nations recognises the existence of the dispute. Argentina relies on UN General Assembly resolutions 2065 of 1965 and 31/49 of 1976, which call on the parties to avoid unilateral decisions, and warns that oil once extracted could not be restored by a later ruling. Dutch jurist Nico Schrijver, an expert on sovereignty over natural resources, also addressed the tribunal.

The United Kingdom is presenting its position in the afternoon session. Ahead of the hearing, Attorney General Ellie Reeves, who leads the British delegation, told The Times that the UK respects international law and the tribunal “but we don’t believe they have jurisdiction to hear a claim around sovereignty”. “We are absolutely clear that this is sovereign British territory,” she said. A spokesman for Prime Minister Andy Burnham insisted that “the hearing is not about the sovereignty of the Falklands” and that the islanders “have the right to develop their natural resources”, according to DPA.

Because the United Kingdom chose the International Court of Justice for such disputes and Argentina opted for the Hamburg tribunal, the merits of the case must be settled by an arbitral tribunal. Hamburg can only order provisional measures while that tribunal is being constituted, if it finds that the arbitral tribunal would have prima facie jurisdiction, that there is urgency and that the right invoked is plausible. Argentina’s Frida María Armas Pfirter, the tribunal’s vice-president, recused herself from the case, so Argentina appointed Raúl Vinuesa as judge ad hoc; the UK chose Vaughan Lowe. Both were sworn in on Monday.

The hearing concludes on Wednesday with a second round from each side. According to an expert consulted by Infobae, the decision could come around Friday, November 13. Sea Lion, operated by Israel’s Navitas Petroleum and Britain’s Rockhopper Exploration about 200 kilometres north of the archipelago, is expected to begin drilling in January 2027.

The hearing coincides with Princess Anne’s arrival in the islands on Monday and comes ahead of the debate on Argentina’s sovereignty defence bill in the Chamber of Deputies, scheduled for Thursday. The British government announced in October that it will introduce legislation to protect companies from possible Argentine sanctions.

World.title: Venezuela signs a memorandum with ExxonMobil for the oil major’s return after leaving in 2007
World.content:
Venezuela signs a memorandum with ExxonMobil for the oil major’s return after leaving in 2007

10th Tuesday, November 2026 - 14:52 UTC Full article

The signing took place in Caracas in the presence of acting President Delcy Rodríguez and ExxonMobil Upstream President Dan Ammann

Venezuela on Monday signed a memorandum of understanding with US oil company ExxonMobil with a view to its return to the country, which it left in 2007 after the nationalisation of the last privately held oilfields under Hugo Chávez’s government. The document is not a contract, and no investment figures or timelines have been disclosed.º

The signing took place in Caracas in the presence of acting President Delcy Rodríguez and ExxonMobil Upstream President Dan Ammann. Rodríguez called it a “very important signing”, reached after “months of negotiations for an effective return” of the Houston-based company. She said the memorandum covers “brownfield and greenfield” fields, that is, those already producing and those yet to be developed, with “billions of barrels of reserves”, and said ExxonMobil has “the capacity, technology and investment needed”. She also expressed hope that it would “very soon translate into concrete agreements”.

Ammann said the memorandum is “an important first step” in a process he hopes will lead to the company’s return. “We believe our unique capabilities, combined with this country’s extraordinary resources and Venezuela’s long history in oil and gas production, will bring significant benefits to all parties involved,” he said.

The rapprochement contrasts with Rodríguez’s position a little over a year ago. In March 2025, when she was Nicolás Maduro’s vice president, she accused ExxonMobil of “conspiring against Venezuela for more than a decade” to undermine its territorial integrity and take its resources.

Since Maduro’s removal from power following the US military operation on January 3, President Donald Trump has urged US energy companies to invest in Venezuela. In April, Rodríguez reported meetings with ExxonMobil and ConocoPhillips, among other companies, after a reform of the hydrocarbons law opened the sector to private and foreign investment.

World.title: Growing solar panel use drives Mexico’s 9.4% rise this year in distributed energy
World.content:
Distributed generation — electricity produced on a smaller scale near where it will be used — is on the rise in Mexico, having increased 9.4% in the first six months of the year, according to the National Energy Commission (CNE).

Driven by the growing use of rooftop solar panels, Mexico’s distributed generation reached 5,675 megawatts (MW) of cumulative installed capacity, with 485.76 MW and 54,766 new contracts added in the first half of the year

By generating electricity via modular systems located at or near the point of consumption, solar panels and other on-site systems don’t use large, centralized power plants or long-distance transmission lines, thereby helping reduce reliance on the national grid and supporting the nation’s transition to green energy-.

Distributed photovoltaic solar energy accounts for 5,640 MW of the distributed power and over 99.5% of the installed capacity under the CNE scheme. Cumulative investment in distributed generation reached a reported US $14.58 billion at the end of June.

“These investments reflect user confidence in these technologies and drive economic development, the creation of specialized jobs and the strengthening of supply chains linked to clean energy and high-value-added technologies,” the CNE stated.

Jalisco dominates in distributed electricity generation

The states with the largest installed capacity are Jalisco (808.58 MW), Nuevo León (596.22 MW) and Chihuahua (424.85 MW), together contributing 32% of the national total. Distributed generation is also growing in Guanajuato, Coahuila, México state, Sonora and Yucatán, demonstrating progress across various parts of Mexico.

In Jalisco, where distributed generation is expected to surpass 1,000 MW by 2030, the scheme is part of its Sustainable Energy Development Plan. The aim is for the state to generate at least as much energy as it consumes by 2030, with 60% of that energy coming from clean sources, up from 42% today.

“Every photovoltaic system installed in Jalisco frees up grid capacity, strengthens the supply chain, generates savings for families and businesses and reduces emissions,” Manuel Herrera Vega, head of the Jalisco Ministry of Energy and Sustainable Development, told the newspaper El Economista.

Those benefits cannot come too soon. The Mexican Institute for Competitiveness estimates that achieving the Plan México growth targets would increase electricity demand by 10.1% , or an additional 11.9 gigawatts (GW) of generation capacity than what is currently considered in the official planning for 2030.

With reports from El Economista

World.title: Indigenous language skills can now open the door to a career in Mexico’s Foreign Service
World.content:
For the first time, Mexico has begun counting Indigenous-language skills toward entry into its Foreign Service — aiming to improve consular assistance for Mexicans in the United States who speak those languages.

Applicants to the service’s technical-administrative branch can now demonstrate proficiency in specified varieties of Maya, Mixtec, Nahuatl or Zapotec to meet a language requirement.

The Ministry of Foreign Relations (SRE) published a recruitment notice Oct. 20 in Mexico’s Official Gazette (DOF), offering up to 80 positions: 44 in administration, 20 in consular affairs, communities and protection, and 16 in information technology and digitization.

Applicants do not have to prove Indigenous ancestry.

Ana Luisa Fajer, president of the Foreign Service Personnel Commission, said approximately 500,000 Mexicans of Indigenous origin live in the United States.

Recruiting speakers of their languages would improve access to documents, legal advice and consular protection, she added.

Rafael Laveaga, Mexico’s consul general in Atlanta, said language barriers complicate assistance for hospitalized patients, immigration detainees trying to understand their rights and crime victims communicating with lawyers.

Consulates provide that assistance, but finding interpreters can delay immediate help, he said. Hundreds of families speaking Mixtec, Zapotec and Nahuatl live in Georgia, Alabama and eastern Tennessee, he added.

The change follows a consular initiative launched last year to provide government information in 15 Indigenous languages at Mexican consulates, embassies and other offices abroad.

Mexico’s consulate in Los Angeles has worked with the local Indigenous advocacy organization CIELO since 2022 to provide interpretation, train staff, and promote Indigenous languages and cultures. CIELO is a women-led nonprofit that stands for Comunidades Indígenas en Liderazgo (Indigenous Communities in Leadership).

Language barriers also affect services inside Mexico. In a June article by Animal Político, specialists identified shortages of bilingual medical personnel and Indigenous-language educational materials among shortcomings limiting access to health care and education.

Though the change was widely reported only this week, the Oct. 26 to Nov. 3 registration period has already closed. Applicants accepted for the next step have until Nov. 17 to submit documents.

The first elimination round includes entrance exams in January; further evaluations and training will be held next spring.

Applicants must also pass a written Spanish exam, but those qualifying with an Indigenous language are not required to demonstrate proficiency in English or another foreign language.

With reports from Infobae, Animal Político and NX Noticias

World.title: Is violence in Mexico really falling, and by how much?
World.content:
The National Institute of Statistics and Geography (INEGI) reported over 5,000 more homicides in 2025 than the federal government’s Executive Secretariat of the National Public Security System (SESNSP), the largest gap in more than a decade.

INEGI reported on Tuesday that there were 29,488 homicides (or alleged homicides) in Mexico in 2025. According to INEGI’s “Registered Death Statistics” report, homicide was the eighth leading cause of death in Mexico last year.

INEGI’s homicide count is 5,140 higher than the combined number of homicides and femicides reported by the SESNSP in 2025. In percentage terms, the number of homicides reported by INEGI is 21.2% higher than the 24,348 homicides and femicides reported by the SESNSP.

The gap between the two numbers is the highest in the last 11 years, according to the news outlet Animal Político.

The difference is 95.3% higher than in 2024, when INEGI’s homicide total was 2,632 higher than the SESNSP count. It should be noted that the SESNSP’s homicide data is compiled from statistics it receives from the Attorney General’s Offices in Mexico’s 32 federal entities.

Marcela Figueroa, the head of the National Public Security System, reports the compiled data on a monthly basis at President Claudia Sheinbaum’s morning press conferences.

As Mexico News Daily reported in January, the reliability of the statistics the state-based Attorney General’s Offices provide to the SESNSP is considered by many to be questionable. There have also been claims that the decline in homicides during Sheinbaum’s presidency is related to an increase in disappearances.

“State Attorney General’s Offices don’t work in a vacuum,” Alberto Guerrero Baena, a public security consultant and academic, wrote in a column published by the news outlet Expansión in January.

“They operate under budgetary, political and media pressures. When a homicide is difficult to prove or requires lengthy investigation, there is an incentive to reclassify it as injury, accidental death or a lesser crime. … An unresolved homicide looks bad in the statistics. A [fatal] injury unrelated to homicide looks better,” Guerrero wrote.

The homicides reported by the SESNSP (and referred to above) are homicidios dolosos, or intentional homicides. Homicidios culposos — negligent or culpable homicides — are categorized separately by the federal government agency.

Why the discrepancy?

In a report published on Wednesday, Animal Político noted that the difference between INEGI’s homicide statistics and those of the SESNSP is not new, although it has increased significantly in recent years. The difference, the news outlet added, is explained, “in part,” by their methodologies.

For its homicide count, INEGI looks at death certificates and records as well as information from civil registry offices, forensic services and Attorney General’s Offices. In classifying a death as a homicide, INEGI looks closely at the cause of the death.

The SESNSP simply compiles the statistics it receives from the Attorney General’s Offices in Mexico’s 32 federal entities. It essentially takes the fiscalías, as the offices are called, at their word, despite allegations that they — or at least some of them — are fudging the numbers.

In an Oct. 30 column published by the Saltillo-based newspaper Vanguardia, Víctor Manuel Sánchez Valdés, a professor and researcher at the Autonomous University of Coahuila, wrote that INEGI’s statistics “are usually more reliable” than those of the SESNSP as INEGI “cross-checks various sources.”

Most of Mexico’s fiscalías — but not all— are formally autonomous of the governments in the states in which they operate. Still, there are claims by opposition politicians and others that fiscalías in states governed by Morena, Mexico’s ruling party, are manipulating data to make the country’s homicide toll appear lower than it actually is.

“Morena doesn’t fight violence, it covers it up,” National Action Party Senator Mayuli Martínez said in June.

“… It is concerning that in Quintana Roo there are six times as many homicides classified as negligent [homicidio culposo] as there are those classified as intentional [homicidio doloso],” she said.

“When more cases [involving the death of a person] are classified under categories other than intentional homicide, it creates an artificial impression of improvement in public safety indicators,” Martínez said.

Quintana Roo is one of 23 states governed by Morena. Data showing declining homicide numbers is, of course, politically beneficial to the federal government and Morena.

President Sheinbaum and other federal officials frequently cite the homicide statistics reported by the SESNSP as evidence that the government’s security strategy is working. On Tuesday, Figueroa, the National Public Security System chief, reported that homicides were down 50% in October compared to September 2024, the final month of Andrés Manuel López Obrador’s presidency.

Among the five states that recorded the biggest year-over-year reductions in homicides in the first 10 months of 2026, three are governed by Morena (Nayarit, Quintana Roo and Baja California Sur), one is governed by the Green Party (San Luis Potosí), an ally of Morena, and one is governed by the Citizens Movement Party (Nuevo León).

Sheinbaum has rejected claims that state fiscalías are manipulating statistics.

“Homicide is homicide, there is no manipulation. It’s not that there are crimes that go from [being classified as] one crime to another crime,” she said at her July 14 press conference.

At the same press conference, Figueroa said that the methodology that state Attorney General’s Offices are required to follow when classifying crimes is “very clear” and “public.”

Still, not everyone is buying federal officials’ assurances that state fiscalías’ homicide figures are accurate.

In his Oct. 30 column, Sánchez poses the question on many Mexicans’ lips: Is violence in Mexico really decreasing?

“The quick answer is yes, but we don’t know the exact extent [of the reduction],” he wrote.

“… Despite these [alleged] manipulations that seek to artificially reduce intentional homicides, everything indicates that there has been a reduction [in violence] since Claudia Sheinbaum came to power and the [new] security strategies were implemented by [Security Minister] Omar García Harfuch,” Sánchez wrote.

In other words, he (and many other Mexicans) believes that homicides have gone down, but not as much as the data compiled by the SESNSP indicates.

Security Ministry: SESNSP homicide numbers are ‘complementary’ and ‘show the same trend’

In early August, shortly after INEGI published preliminary homicide data for 2025, the federal Security Ministry (SSPC) released a statement titled “INEGI’s vital statistics confirm the decline in intentional homicides in 2025.”

INEGI’s preliminary statistics showed a 16.6% year-over-year reduction in homicides in 2025, more than four points higher than the 12.1% decline according to the final data published on Tuesday. According to SESNSP data, the year-over-year reduction in homicides in 2025 was 21.2%. At 9.1 percentage points, the difference between the reduction in homicides reported by INEGI and the decline reported by the SESNSP is not insignificant.

In its statement, the SSPC wrote that “the measurement of intentional homicide by INEGI and SESNSP are complementary exercises that use different methodologies and serve different purposes.”

The ministry said that the difference between their homicide numbers is “expected” as “each institution performs different functions, uses different [data] integration procedures, has different collection, validation, and publication periods, and generates information for specific purposes.”

Still, “the trend shown by both sources” is “consistent” with the progress made under the national security strategy, the SSPC said.

“Both sources show the same trend with respect to the evolution of intentional homicide,” the ministry said.

INEGI’s 2025 homicide data in brief

INEGI reported that there were 29,488 homicides in 2025, a reduction of 12.1% compared to the 33,550 homicides in 2024.

Almost nine in ten homicide victims in 2025 (87.5%) were men. Women accounted for 11.3% of victims while the sex of the deceased person wasn’t specified in 1.2% of cases.

Almost three in ten homicide victims (28.2%) were men aged 25 to 34.

Homicide was the leading cause of death in 2025 for men aged 25 to 34 and men aged 35 to 44.

Mexico recorded 22.6 homicides per 100,000 residents in 2025. There were 40.5 homicides per 100,000 men and 5 homicides per 100,000 women.

Among Mexico’s 32 federal entities, Guanajuato recorded the highest number of homicides in 2025 with 3,334. México state ranked second with 2,618 homicides, followed by Chihuahua (2,291), Baja California (2,144) and Sinaloa (1,966).

Mexico City recorded 830 homicides last year, the 16th highest total among the 32 federal entities.

Yucatán was the only entity that recorded fewer than 100 homicides in 2025. There were 59 homicides in the state.

Colima recorded the highest number of homicides per 100,000 residents in 2025, with 92.6. Sinaloa ranked second with 62.3 homicides per 100,000 people, followed by Morelos (58.6), Chihuahua (58) and Baja California (56.8).

The cause of death in 70.6% of homicides was a gunshot wound or wounds. Stabbings were the second most common means of homicide, accounting for 9.5% of cases. About one in 15 homicides (6.6%) involved hanging, strangling or suffocation.

By Mexico News Daily chief staff writer Peter Davies (peter.davies@mexiconewsdaily.com)

With reports from Animal Político

World.title: More foreign tourists are visiting Mexico for its culture than for any other reason — including beach resorts
World.content:
Tourism Minister Josefina Rodríguez Zamora told thousands of tourism industry professionals gathered in Guadalajara this week that Mexico’s total of 67.7 million foreign arrivals over the first eight months of the year was a two-decade high — and that the most common motive for their visit was to experience Mexican culture.

Rodríguez was speaking as the host of the opening ceremony of the first ITB Americas trade show, which will continue through Thursday. It is expected to attract 5,000 representatives from 61 countries, including participation from all 31 Mexican states plus Mexico City, 300 exhibiting companies and organizations and 300 specialized buyers. Its economic impact for Mexico should be around US $13 million.

In a true sign of the times, Rodríguez informed the gathering that approximately 36.3% of this year’s visitors said they came to Mexico for its cultural tourism. That percentage more than doubles the 15%-16% that came for beach tourism.

Meanwhile, sports tourism has been growing in popularity, getting a boost from the 2026 FIFA World Cup, but also traceable to the Mexican Formula 1 Grand Prix, several major international marathons, cycling events, open water swimming competitions and surfing opportunities, as well as tennis and golf tournaments.

Mexico is now the sixth most-visited country worldwide and No. 1 in the Americas, with hopes of moving up to the fifth most popular tourist destination by 2030 under the government’s Plan México national development strategy.

Mexico City has moved ahead of international cities such as London and Singapore in entertainment tourism, largely owing to hosting world-class concerts, said Rodríguez.

The tourism minister announced a planned investment of $42 billion in Mexico’s tourism sector by 2030, primarily directed at hotel and airport infrastructure, training for regional operators and strategies for enhancing tourist experiences across all states.

Rodríguez said that Mexico’s tourism model emphasizes regional service providers who had historically been marginalized.

With reports from LatinUS, Infobae and Informador

World.title: Opinion: Why (most of) Mexico’s elites dislike Sheinbaum
World.content:
There used to be an implicit social pact in Mexico.

The elites went to the same schools, ate at the same restaurants and knew one another. Access to power came by birthright: through the private school you attended if you were in Mexico City, or through your last name if you were in Guadalajara or Monterrey. The pact went something like this: we may think a little differently, but as long as you’re one of us, you’re all right. It made it very hard for outsiders to rise into the elite, and even harder for insiders to fall out of it, no matter how incompetent, corrupt or reckless they were.

The pact guaranteed a kind of social cohesion. Most of Mexico’s recent presidents, from Miguel de la Madrid, Carlos Salinas de Gortari and Ernesto Zedillo to Felipe Calderón and Enrique Peña Nieto, came from these closed circles. Even the “outsider” Vicente Fox was really one of them, just from the geographic periphery.

The PRI (Institutional Revolutionary Party), which governed Mexico for 71 years until 2000, did not create this elite; it inherited it and adapted it to its revolutionary story. Because the PRI was, at its core, a pragmatic political machine that used the Mexican Revolution to legitimize itself, Mexico’s elite ended up different from the rest of Latin America’s. While most Latin American elites were overwhelmingly right-wing, Mexico’s, at least in the capital, tolerated some pluralism. You couldn’t be too far right or too far left, but you could lean a little either way.

That broke down when Andrés Manuel López Obrador arrived on the scene. He hadn’t gone to a good private school, didn’t have a respected last name and wasn’t even from a major city. He was born in a small town in Tabasco, a place that looks more like Thailand and feels more like Costa Rica than the usual image of Mexico. He wasn’t exactly poor, but he was definitely not elite, and his political manners showed it. AMLO, as he is known, had not traveled the world, didn’t shop in Houston or spend summers in Spain. And whatever his politics (which are hard to pin down), moderation was not among them.

When he became mayor of Mexico City in 2000, the country’s main political goal was ending the PRI’s 71-year regime, and his freshness was welcome in a city that is huge, mostly progressive and the intellectual center of the country. He was audacious and, on balance, probably a good mayor: he changed the city’s political culture and paved the way for its later transformation. But when he ran for president, everything changed. The elites were alarmed to see an outsider so close to power. His razor-thin loss to Felipe Calderón in 2006, amid allegations of fraud, polarized the country, and his reaction, declaring himself the “legitimate president,” offended an elite that prized adherence to the unwritten rules of power.

By the time he won the presidency in 2018, López Obrador was more stubborn and polarizing than ever. But Mexico had also changed in the 18 years since he was elected mayor, and he understood that change better than almost anyone. Most Mexicans outside any elite were fed up. The “social mood” index of the Mexican polling firm Nodo showed alarming levels of anger. The Peña Nieto government had been so visibly corrupt and elitist that it finally woke up Mexico’s middle and lower classes.

AMLO used this to his advantage. He built a communication style based on constantly antagonizing the elite and its most visible figures, then waiting for them to lash back. What the elites didn’t understand was that every attack made him stronger. For his voters, AMLO was the legitimate voice of the people. The strategy also let him recreate the environment where he thrived most: the permanent campaign, fueled by friction.

AMLO was not a great president. To his credit, he reduced poverty as no one had before, and he took control of the public narrative so completely that he built a nearly unbeatable electoral machine. But he governed like an eternal candidate rather than a president. He decided with his gut more than with the vision of a statesman, polarized society, dismantled valuable institutions and infrastructure projects because he didn’t like them, and championed others that have yet to prove their worth. In many ways, his government was a huge missed opportunity. In that sense, though, it was no different from those of Peña Nieto, Calderón or Fox, which were also deeply flawed but never seemed to bother the elites.

A famous Mexican writer once told me that AMLO’s greatest contribution to Mexico City was paving the way for the mayors who came after him. So when he chose Claudia Sheinbaum, a successful former mayor of the capital with a PhD in engineering, as his party’s candidate, there was a lot of hope.

Sheinbaum is not AMLO. She comes from an elite I haven’t mentioned yet, the cultural elite, and above all, she was an effective mayor. She won the 2024 election by nearly 19 million votes over the runner-up, Xóchitl Gálvez, and her approval rating has stayed above 70%. Still, the elites don’t like her.

Her government looks nothing like AMLO’s. She has grown close to the business community and is promoting investment as few of her predecessors have. She has been pragmatic with the United States and has brought Mexico back onto the world stage. Her security policy is the opposite of AMLO’s: she has gone after the cartels and violence has dropped. And her infrastructure projects, including passenger rail lines connecting Mexico’s main industrial hubs, make sense for the country’s needs.

Part of the elite’s rejection has to do with style. Although her policies are very different from AMLO’s, her rhetoric is very similar, and that is deliberate: she knows how to speak to her large political base. But the elites wouldn’t like her even if she spoke differently. They dislike her emphasis on social programs and social justice, but above all they dislike what she represents. She represents otherness: a Mexico that doesn’t move in their circles, that doesn’t solve problems over coffee in Polanco or through class pacts. She isn’t interested in money or in pleasing Mexico’s powerful men. They don’t like that she wears Indigenous clothing, and they don’t like that she is the heir of López Obrador, whom they see as an uneducated, ill-mannered, far-left provincial.

Mexico has at least two elites: the cultural one, which more or less accepts Sheinbaum, and the economic one, which deeply dislikes her. And the economic elite’s rejection has less to do with her policies than with the otherness it cannot accept. That elite wants a sort of White Mexico, one that mirrors its Americanized or Europeanized values and aspirations, its social codes, the primacy of its class and even of its skin color. Sheinbaum reminds it that it is no longer in power, and that is unbearable. Mexico’s elites will keep disliking Sheinbaum no matter what she does. How much of that comes from an actual analysis of her government, and how much from a view shaped by class, is a question with a mixed answer, though one that leans heavily in one direction.

Emilio Lezama is a Mexican writer, political analyst and communications strategist based in Mexico City. As founder and director of Los Hijos de la Malinche, a strategic communications agency, he advises international companies and institutions on navigating Mexico’s political landscape, managing reputation and crises, and building public support for their projects. He is a columnist for El Universal, has written for The New York Times and El País and has published several books.

World.title: El Jalapeño: Mexico City man forced to buy event merchandise to obtain tortillas outside his own apartment
World.content:
All stories in El Jalapeño are satire and not real news. Check out the original article here.

MEXICO CITY — Municipal authorities confirmed Monday that Mexico City is on track to welcome a record-breaking 65.9 million tourists in 2026 — a massive influx driven by a packed calendar of international concerts and sporting events that has effectively transformed central residential neighborhoods into perpetual venue concourses.

The capital’s tourism boom, which has generated over 120 billion pesos in hotel revenue and a 16% jump in lodging tax collections, was fully on display Tuesday morning when local resident Rodrigo Morales was forced to purchase a 1,200-peso commemorative stadium tour hoodie just to reach the tortilleria on his own block.

Morales, 34, reportedly found himself cut off from basic domestic staples after event organizers erected a temporary VIP concourse, three wristband authentication checkpoints, and a corporate sponsor village outside his apartment building to accommodate back-to-back stadium shows and motorsport crowds.

“I simply wanted half a kilo of warm corn tortillas,” said Morales, standing in a two-hour credentialing queue while wearing a neon-laminated media pass. “However, security staff informed me that the sidewalk leading to the corner shop had been designated an exclusive artist-merchandise corridor. My options were either to buy the limited-edition tour fleece or attempt to breach the soundboard barricade.”

City tourism officials praised the interaction as proof of the capital’s booming hospitality economy, noting that as visitor volume reaches double its level from 10 years ago, public infrastructure must seamlessly integrate with event monetization.

“With tens of millions of visitors flooding the capital, our goal is to ensure every square block offers the vibrant commercial flow of an arena,” explained a spokesperson for the local tourism ministry. “When a local resident buys official tour merchandise just to step over an idling broadcast truck and retrieve his groceries, that represents a direct victory for our economic projections.”

At press time, Morales reported that while his tortillas were completely cold by the time he cleared the final security metal detector, he remained optimistic about his evening plans, provided he could secure a general-admission wristband to access his own bathroom.

World.title: Sheinbaum calls NYT report on CIA’s alleged bargain with Chihuahua prosecutor ‘very interesting’: Wednesday’s mañanera recapped
World.content:
Sheinbaum’s mañanera in 60 seconds

📰 NYT report spotlights ex-prosecutor who allegedly partnered with CIA: Sheinbaum called the Times article on Guillermo Zuany Portillo, a former special prosecutor in Chihuahua, “very interesting.” The report says Zuany’s revoked U.S. visa was reinstated after he helped CIA officers train state forces and join missions. Security Minister Omar García Harfuch said Tuesday that both the FGR and the Chihuahua Attorney General’s Office have outstanding arrest warrants for Zuany.

Sheinbaum called the Times article on Guillermo Zuany Portillo, a former special prosecutor in Chihuahua, “very interesting.” The report says Zuany’s revoked U.S. visa was reinstated after he helped CIA officers train state forces and join missions. Security Minister Omar García Harfuch said Tuesday that both the FGR and the Chihuahua Attorney General’s Office have outstanding arrest warrants for Zuany. ⚖️ “ It’s illegal because it violates the National Security Law”: Sheinbaum said her government flagged the CIA’s participation in an April drug lab raid in Chihuahua as illegal as soon as it found out about it. Former Chihuahua attorney general César Jáuregui was detained last month on a treason charge. She said any collaboration with foreign agencies must respect the Constitution and the National Security Law, and that “in this case, [the law] wasn’t obeyed.”

Sheinbaum said her government flagged the CIA’s participation in an April drug lab raid in Chihuahua as illegal as soon as it found out about it. Former Chihuahua attorney general César Jáuregui was detained last month on a treason charge. She said any collaboration with foreign agencies must respect the Constitution and the National Security Law, and that “in this case, [the law] wasn’t obeyed.” 🏥 IMSS Bienestar doctor’s appointments up 55% since 2023: Director Alejandro Svarch said the public healthcare service for people without social security is on track to provide 58.3 million free consultations this year, up from 37.3 million in 2023. Specialist appointments are projected to rise 105%.

Director Alejandro Svarch said the public healthcare service for people without social security is on track to provide 58.3 million free consultations this year, up from 37.3 million in 2023. Specialist appointments are projected to rise 105%. 📈 Opposition-governed states lag: Svarch said “general consultations” rose just 4% between 2023 and 2026 in the eight states that haven’t joined IMSS Bienestar, which operates in 24 of 32 federal entities, while specialist appointments are forecast to rise 27%. “It’s the same country, the same period, but you can see the results are vastly different,” he said.

Why today’s mañanera matters

At her Wednesday morning press conference, President Sheinbaum responded to a New York Times report headlined “The Man Who Helped the C.I.A. Secretly Operate in Mexico.”

Published on Tuesday, the article focuses on Guillermo Zuany Portillo, a former special prosecutor in Chihuahua, the state where U.S. Central Intelligence Agency officers allegedly participated in a drug lab raid in April without the authorization or knowledge of the Mexican government. Two CIA agents and two Chihuahua police officials died in a car accident after the raid, a tragedy that helped bring the CIA’s presence in the state to light.

The New York Times report states that “[w]hen the Central Intelligence Agency was looking to quietly expand its operations in Mexico last year, it found an especially useful partner.”

“… To the C.I.A., Guillermo Zuany Portillo, a prosecutor and former police commander in the border state of Chihuahua, offered a different kind of partnership,” the report says.

“He could pair C.I.A. officers with Mexican police units on counter-cartel operations — and he was in a bind that made him uniquely cooperative, Mexican and U.S. officials said.”

That bind, according to the Times, was that Zuany’s U.S. visa had been revoked “because of his suspected ties to the very cartels the C.I.A. wanted to root out.”

The Times reported that Zuany’s visa was reinstated after he “shepherded C.I.A. officers as they trained Chihuahua State forces, joined those forces on certain missions and provided expertise during ground operations” during a period of more than six months.

Beyond Sheinbaum’s response to the New York Times report, another notable topic at today’s mañanera was the performance of IMSS Bienestar, Mexico’s public healthcare service for people without social security coverage through institutions such as the Mexican Social Security Institute, or IMSS, and the State Workers’ Social Security Institute, or ISSSTE.

The IMSS Bienestar scheme was established by the previous federal government and now operates in 24 of Mexico’s 32 federal entities. Eight states have opted against signing onto the scheme. Those states — Nuevo León, Coahuila, Durango, Jalisco, Querétaro, Aguascalientes, Chihuahua and Guanajuato — are all governed by opposition parties, rather than by Morena, Mexico’s ruling party.

NYT report ‘very interesting,’ says Sheinbaum

A reporter raised the New York Times report about Zuany, noting that it quotes the former prosecutor as saying that Chihuahua Governor Maru Campos was aware of the CIA’s presence in the northern border state, something that Campos denies.

Sheinbaum, who has previously been critical of the Times’ reporting on Mexico, said she read the report and described it as “very interesting.”

🇲🇽#México | Claudia Sheinbaum se refirió al reportaje de The New York Times sobre la presunta facilitación de operaciones de la CIA por parte de Guillermo Zuany, fiscal especializado de Chihuahua. La presidenta calificó la publicación como “muy interesante” y sostuvo que los agentes estadounidenses deben apegarse a la Ley de Seguridad Nacional. “En este caso no se respetó”, afirmó. #ClaudiaSheinbaum #Chihuahua #CIA #SeguridadNacional 🌐 Consulta #ElPortalDeÁngulo7

➡️ https://t.co/14SVC19UGG — Ángulo7 Noticias (@angulosiete) November 11, 2026

She subsequently noted that the former attorney general of Chihuahua, César Jáuregui, was arrested in connection with the CIA’s presence in the state. Jáuregui, who was detained by federal authorities on a treason charge last month, is accused of allowing CIA officers to participate in the drug lab raid in Chihuahua in April without authorization from the Mexican government.

Sheinbaum said that the Federal Attorney General’s Office (FGR) has to continue its investigation of the case. Security Minister Omar García Harfuch said on Tuesday that both the FGR and the Chihuahua Attorney General’s Office have outstanding warrants for the arrest of Zuany.

Sheinbaum said that Zuany’s alleged conduct is “very relevant” to investigations into the CIA’s presence in Chihuahua.

“It’s worth learning about who this person is and how he collaborated with one of the U.S. agencies,” she said.

Although the New York Times report states that CIA officers joined Chihuahua state forces “on certain missions” and that the CIA “began working” with Zuany “around 2025,” Sheinbaum asserted that “the article doesn’t say that there were operations [with the CIA] since 2025.”

“It says there was [CIA] presence,” she said.

Sheinbaum highlighted that her government pointed out that the CIA’s participation in the drug lab raid in Chihuahua was illegal as soon as it found out about it.

“It’s illegal because it violates the National Security Law,” she said.

“And the Federal Attorney General’s Office opened an investigation,” Sheinbaum added.

“Today, the [former] attorney general of Chihuahua is detained for this reason. The important thing is that … any collaboration [with foreign authorities] has to guarantee respect for the [Mexican] Constitution and the National Security Law,” she said.

“Any agent from a U.S. agency in Mexico has to comply with the National Security Law,” Sheinbaum said.

“In this case, [the law] wasn’t obeyed,” she said.

IMSS Bienestar chief reports sharp increase in doctor’s appointments

At the start of his presentation, IMSS Bienestar director Alejandro Svarch said that “for decades, where a person was born and the job they held determined the range of medical care they were able to receive.”

“Three years ago, IMSS Bienestar began transforming this reality,” he said.

“Today we are the largest network of public health services in our country and above all we’re an institute that is achieving results,” Svarch said.

He went on to report that the number of medical consultations provided by IMSS Bienestar is projected to increase 55% this year compared to 2023. IMSS Bienestar is on track to provide 58.3 million free doctor’s appointments this year, according to the data presented by Svarch, up from 37.3 million in 2023.

“That’s why we say the model works. The results are clear and compelling,” the IMSS Bienestar chief said.

Svarch noted that IMSS Bienestar operates in 24 of Mexico’s 32 federal entities, while eight states have their own public healthcare systems for people without social security coverage.

He reported that “general consultations” increased just 4% this year compared to 2023 in the eight states that haven’t signed on to IMSS Bienestar.

“It’s the same country, the same period, but you can see the results are vastly different,” Svarch said.

He also reported that the number of specialist doctor’s appointments provided by IMSS Bienestar is projected to rise 105% this year compared to 2023, while the increase over the same period in states where IMSS Bienestar doesn’t operate is forecast to be 27%.

“These results are not the product of chance,” Svarch said.

“They are the product of actions and a very specific implementation plan,” he said.

World.title: MND Local Puerto Vallarta: Eat, dance, swim, run, repeat!
World.content:
One of the things I love most about living in Puerto Vallarta is the variety of entertainment and activities on offer. Case in point, this month you can 1) taste cuisine from some of Mexico’s top chefs at the 31st International Gourmet Festival; 2) listen to live jazz, rock and mariachi at one of Vallarta’s many great music venues; 3) compete in an open-water swimming race; or 4) run a half-marathon. OK, so the last two might not be for everyone, but you can cheer on the racers instead.

Read on to learn more about these exciting events.

31st International Gourmet Festival

Puerto Vallarta’s reputation as a culinary destination is on the rise. Earlier this year, two local restaurants, Icú and Pancho’s Takos, earned spots on the prestigious Michelin Guide’s recommended list, a first for the city. This month, Vallarta will host the 31st International Gourmet Festival from Nov. 12-22. The festival brings some of the most celebrated Mexican chefs together for 11 days of culinary events at more than 25 top-rated restaurants in Puerto Vallarta, Riviera Nayarit and Tepic.

Events include tasting experiences featuring food and wine from more than a dozen restaurants, dining “safaris” where you travel to a few selected restaurants in one night, multicourse fine dining at single restaurants featuring guest chefs and even a drag brunch.

On Nov. 17, the Technological University of Bahía de Banderas (UTBB) will host a panel of chefs who will discuss the latest trends shaping the culinary scene in Mexico. The panel discussion is free and open to the public. Tickets for the dining experiences are available for purchase on the festival website.

Live music up close and personal

I love listening to live music, especially in intimate settings where I can watch the performers up close. In my last events roundup, I promised to share some of my favorite venues. True to my word, here you go:

The Social Club: The Social Club is a modern-day speakeasy located at 447 Basilio Badillo in the Romantic Zone. Just a narrow black door marks its spot. If you’ve never been before, you could easily miss it. I feel transported to another era every time I visit. After entering the front door, you climb up a narrow staircase, pass through red velvet curtains and enter a small parlor-style room with tiny tables lit by tiny lamps. The “stage” is at the back of the room, just a few feet from the tables. Waiters clad in Prohibition-era outfits serve bespoke and classic cocktails. Doors open at 9 p.m., and music starts around 10 p.m., featuring many of the best local jazz musicians and many special events. This is one of our favorite date-night spots in all of Vallarta.

Aquí Nomás: In the mood for a Mexican folk music singalong? Then you want to go to Aquí Nomás in Versalles. On Friday and Saturday nights, the neighborhood cantina hosts a live mariachi band that plays all the classic songs that Mexicans seem to know by heart. On our first visit in early October, we had only planned on staying for dinner and venturing someplace for music. But, being early season, the other venues in Versalles were closed. Our waitress convinced us to stay, and we’re so glad we did. Around 10:30 in the evening, the band showed up — a full 10-person mariachi ensemble — and the tables filled up, too. Pretty soon, the band was passing the mic, and everyone was singing along. It was such a friendly, local vibe; we are looking forward to returning soon with the whole family.

Casita & Garden: Casita & Garden in the Romantic Zone offers a variety of live music from jazz to funk to rock and pop every night of the week except Sundays. Shows are held in its lovely outdoor courtyard during the winter season starting at 7 p.m. In addition to live music, you can sample wine and sake selected by their in-house sake sommelier, and fill up on sushi and wood-fired pizza. The venue also hosts private dinners and wine tastings, but they are popular, so it’s best to reserve well ahead of time.

For the sporting type

View this post on Instagram A post shared by CRUCE VALLARTA (@crucevallarta)

Coming from Boulder, Colorado — arguably the sporting capital of the United States — where every summer weekend is packed with running, biking and triathlon events, I was astounded to find a similar enthusiasm for sports in Puerto Vallarta. Grains — the daily wrap.

Key Facts Wheat led a quiet grains session on Wednesday, 11 November 2026: the wheat-tracking fund WEAT closed at US$22.18, up 2.02% on the day, a bounce after a long slide.

the wheat-tracking fund WEAT closed at US$22.18, up 2.02% on the day, a bounce after a long slide. Soybeans and corn barely moved: the soybean fund SOYB finished at US$25.95 (+0.12%) and the corn fund CORN at US$17.37 (+0.12%).

the soybean fund SOYB finished at US$25.95 (+0.12%) and the corn fund CORN at US$17.37 (+0.12%). The bigger story is the decline: corn is 14.4% below its 1 September high of 20.29, and wheat is 20.8% below its 28 August high of 28.00.

corn is 14.4% below its 1 September high of 20.29, and wheat is 20.8% below its 28 August high of 28.00. Brazil’s record crop is the main weight: the crop agency CONAB sees about 181.6 million tonnes of soybeans for 2026/27, and farmers are already selling ahead of it.

the crop agency CONAB sees about 181.6 million tonnes of soybeans for 2026/27, and farmers are already selling ahead of it. The dollar worked against grains: the US dollar index rose 0.60% to 102.84 and the 10-year Treasury yield stayed near 5%.

Today’s Focus Grain markets paused on Wednesday, 11 November 2026, after weeks of falling. Wheat bounced sharply, while soybeans and corn were almost flat. The pause follows the US agriculture department’s monthly supply report, which stopped a short rally in corn and soybeans. Behind it sits a simple fact: Brazil is about to harvest another giant soybean crop, and a weaker real encourages its farmers to sell dollars’ worth of beans early. Wheat’s jump looks like buyers covering bets after a steep drop. It is a bounce inside a downtrend, not yet a reversal. Think of the grain market as a very large warehouse that has just been told more stock is arriving. On Wednesday, 11 November 2026, prices stopped falling for a day but did not rise in any convincing way.

Wheat stood out. The wheat-tracking fund WEAT gained 2.02%, while the soybean fund SOYB and the corn fund CORN each rose 0.12%, barely enough to notice.

Assessment — A pause in a downtrend, not a turn MEDIUM Wednesday looks like a pause for soybeans and corn and a short-covering bounce for wheat, all inside a market weighed down by ample supply. Two things could change that: whether China keeps buying from both Brazil and the United States, and whether the dollar keeps rising. The variable to watch is the dollar index, because a stronger dollar makes American grain costlier for foreign buyers.

03 Why it moved

First, supply, with fairly high confidence. CONAB, Brazil’s crop agency, forecasts about 181.6 million tonnes of soybeans for 2026/27 on about 49.3 million hectares.

Second, the currency and the dollar, with medium confidence. A weaker Brazilian real makes each dollar of soybean sales worth more in local money, so farmers sell faster, and that pressure was a recurring theme in this week’s grain commentary. The stronger dollar on Wednesday, with the index up 0.60%, makes US exports pricier and caps any rebound.

Third, the wheat bounce, with medium confidence. The usual drivers pointed the wrong way, since the dollar and yields both rose, yet wheat still jumped. The best-supported reading is buyers closing bets on lower prices after a fall of 9.10% over 20 sessions.

Wider markets were calm rather than frightened: the S&P 500 rose 1.31% to 7,619 and the VIX fear gauge fell 10.12% to 17.49. Oil was flat. Nothing outside the grain complex forced the moves.

04 The trend behind it

Soybeans are 7.8% below their 10 September high of 28.14 and 19.5% above their 13 January low of 21.71. They are down 4.56% over 20 sessions, yet up 1.49% over five, so the damage has eased.

Corn is the weakest of the three on the 60-day view, down 5.7%, and sits 5.5% above its 29 June low of 16.47. Wheat has lost 10.2% over 60 sessions.

This is a continuation of the slide from the late-summer peaks, with a pause attached. Soybeans reached a three-year high in early September on strong export demand, and the harvest has been steadily eroding that rally since.

Our own price history adds perspective, though history is not a forecast. After earlier soybean falls this size, prices were higher 20 sessions later in 38 of 61 cases (62%), with a median gain of 0.7% and a worst case of a 10.1% fall. For corn it was 33 of 67 cases (49%), median a 0.1% fall, worst 15.1% down. For wheat it was 18 of 39 (46%), median 0.0%, worst a 23.9% fall.

05 What it means for Latin America

Brazil and Argentina are the export engine, so lower prices cut farm revenue even when volumes are large. Brazil’s record harvest is good for its trade balance in tonnes and bad for its price per tonne, while a weaker real softens the blow for growers paid in dollars and paying costs in reais.

Argentina, the world’s biggest exporter of soybean meal and oil, feels the same pressure through its export income and its hunt for foreign currency. Importers such as Mexico, Colombia and Peru gain, because cheaper corn and wheat lower feed and bread costs.

China matters most, because it buys most of the world’s traded soybeans, and Brazilian sellers watch whether it keeps buying from both Brazil and the United States.

06 The names to watch

The three funds, SOYB, CORN and WEAT, are the quickest read on the market for an ordinary investor. Remember that they track futures, so they can drift from the price of the physical grain.

Among companies, the farm owners SLC Agrícola and BrasilAgro in Brazil, and the global traders Bunge and ADM, move with crop prices and export margins. Itaú BBA, a Brazilian bank, has warned of a possible El Niño, a Pacific weather pattern that can disrupt South American crops, as a risk the market has not priced in.

07 What would end it

The slide would ease if soybeans hold above the January low of 21.71 and break back toward the 10 September high of 28.14, a long climb. For corn, the line to watch is the 29 June low of 16.47; for wheat, the 28 August high of 28.00 is far away.

The dated triggers are the next monthly USDA supply report in December, CONAB’s next crop estimate and any new Chinese purchase announcement. A weather scare in South America, such as El Niño, is the one event that could flip the story from surplus to shortage.

08 What to watch

The dollar: A further rise from 102.84 on the dollar index would make US grain dearer and keep prices capped.

A further rise from 102.84 on the dollar index would make US grain dearer and keep prices capped. China buying: Whether Beijing keeps taking Brazilian beans and also meets its 27 million tonne US pledge.

Whether Beijing keeps taking Brazilian beans and also meets its 27 million tonne US pledge. Brazil’s crop: CONAB’s next estimate against its 181.6 million tonne forecast.

CONAB’s next estimate against its 181.6 million tonne forecast. Weather: Any El Niño warning for South America, which could turn surplus into shortage.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why did wheat rise on Wednesday?

Most likely buyers covering bets after a long fall. This is a medium-confidence reading.

Why are soybeans under pressure?

Brazil is heading for a record crop of around 181.6 million tonnes, and a weaker real encourages farmers to sell early.

Do these funds show the grain price?

No. SOYB, CORN and WEAT track futures contracts, so they follow the direction of grains but are not the price of a bushel.

Does this make food cheaper?

Over time, yes, for feed and bread in importing countries such as Mexico and Colombia, though shops react slowly and currencies matter.

the fund tracking WTI crude (USO) ended Wednesday, 11 November 2026, up 0.01%, while Petrobras fell for an eighth session in a row. Petrobras is in a rout: its New York shares are down 31.30% over 20 sessions and 31.9% below their 23 October high of 26.16.

its New York shares are down 31.30% over 20 sessions and 31.9% below their 23 October high of 26.16. Crude is off its peak: USO sits 16.6% below its 12-month high of 169.53, set on 23 October, yet still 113.8% above its December 2025 low.

USO sits 16.6% below its 12-month high of 169.53, set on 23 October, yet still 113.8% above its December 2025 low. The Iran war still sets the tone: the Iran war keeps a risk premium in crude, and no end to it is in sight.

the Iran war keeps a risk premium in crude, and no end to it is in sight. Gulf supply is healing: Saudi Arabia’s October output jumped about 26% to near 10.56 million barrels a day, which caps rallies.

Saudi Arabia’s October output jumped about 26% to near 10.56 million barrels a day, which caps rallies. Latin American producers split: YPF rose and Ecopetrol edged up, while Brazil’s state giant carried a political discount.

Today’s Focus Oil went nowhere on Wednesday, 11 November 2026. The fund that tracks US crude, USO, gained 0.01%, as war risk pushed crude up and a recovery in Gulf supply pushed back. The real action was in Brazil. Petrobras, the state-controlled oil company, fell -2.52% to US$17.82 in New York, its eighth straight decline. That is a fall of 31.30% in 20 sessions for a company that holds some of the world’s richest offshore fields. Crude is not the cause: Brazilian politics is, and that is why oil and Petrobras have parted ways. Underneath, the war premium and returning supply pulled in opposite directions.

03 Why it moved

First, and heaviest for crude, is the Iran war. The war keeps a risk premium in the price. Confidence: medium.

Second, supply is coming back and caps the rally. Saudi Arabia’s October output jumped about 26% to near 10.56 million barrels a day, and Gulf crude exports are recovering, though refined products lag. Confidence: medium.

Third, for Petrobras, results and politics. The company reported third-quarter results on the day, with dividends below what investors expected. Investors tie the slide to Lula’s re-election and fears of heavier state influence over dividends and fuel prices. Medium confidence.

The usual drivers were mixed. The dollar index rose 0.60% to 102.84, and the US 10-year yield stayed near 5%, both usually negative for commodities, while the S&P 500 gained 1.31% to 7,619 and the VIX fear gauge fell 10.12% to 17.49.

04 The trend behind it

Crude is in a pullback within a larger climb. USO is 7.87% lower over 20 sessions and 2.71% lower over five, yet 8.3% higher over 60 sessions, and it stands 16.6% below its 23 October high of 169.53.

Petrobras is a new and harsher phase. It is 9.13% lower over five sessions, 31.30% lower over 20, and 54.4% above its 7 January low of 11.54, so most of its 12-month gain has been given back.

Our own history since 2007 adds context. After 84 earlier falls in USO as large as this one, the fund was higher 20 sessions later in 50 cases (60%), with a median gain of 2.2% and a worst case of 50.1% lower; for Petrobras, after 12 comparable falls it was higher in 7 (58%), median gain 7.3%, worst 21.6% lower. History is not a forecast.

05 What it means for Latin America

Brazil is the clearest case: high oil prices should enrich Petrobras, yet its shares fell, which shows investors price political risk above the barrel. For savers in São Paulo, a company that cannot pass on high prices to shareholders is a weaker bet than the headline price suggests.

Guyana’s boom rests on a single producer, ExxonMobil’s consortium, so Georgetown is seeking more investors. In Argentina, Chevron is preparing to expand drilling in Vaca Muerta and YPF chief executive Horacio Marín says more partners are needed for pipelines and plants.

Mexico’s Pemex, the world’s most indebted oil company, benefits from firm crude but still faces heavy short-term debt maturities. Colombia’s Ecopetrol sits 16.2% below its 15 September high of 18.26.

06 The names to watch

Petrobras is the stress test: eight straight falls leave it 31.9% below its high, so any hint of dividend clarity could trigger a sharp bounce. Our history suggests rebounds follow most such routs, but the worst case was 21.6% lower still.

YPF is the beneficiary of the shale story, with a partner-led model that investors like. Ecopetrol, 66.1% above its December 2025 low but far from its September high, depends on Colombian politics and the oil price in equal measure.

07 What would end it

For crude, the level to watch is the 23 October high of 169.53 on the upside and the recent 20-session lows on the downside, with a verified Iran-US negotiation the single event that would shake the war premium. The next marker is the EIA weekly inventory report on Thursday, 12 November.

For Petrobras, support is the 11.54 low from January, far below, and resistance is the 26.16 peak. The honest answer is that the slide ends when Brasília signals its dividend policy, or when oil makes the politics irrelevant.

08 What to watch

Iran diplomacy: Any confirmed US-Iran talks would drain the war premium from crude quickly.

Any confirmed US-Iran talks would drain the war premium from crude quickly. EIA inventories: The weekly US stock report on Thursday, 12 November tests the tight-supply story.

The weekly US stock report on Thursday, 12 November tests the tight-supply story. Brazil dividend policy: Government signals on Petrobras payouts and fuel pricing decide whether the slide ends.

These prices are bets, not polls. They show traders see a wide range for crude while the Iran war and returning Gulf supply pull in opposite directions.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why did Petrobras fall when oil was steady?

Press reports link the eight-session slide to Lula’s re-election and fears of state influence over dividends; the company’s chief executive has pushed back.

What does USO track?

USO is a US-listed fund that tracks WTI, the main US crude benchmark, so its price is a proxy and not the price of a barrel.

Is Saudi supply rising?

Yes. Saudi Arabia’s October output jumped about 26% to near 10.56 million barrels a day.

Will oil rebound?

In 84 earlier falls of this size in our history, USO was higher 20 sessions later 60% of the time, but history is not a forecast.

03 Why it moved

First and heaviest: Mexico’s protected market. Ternium’s Mexican shipments rose 18% on the year, and its realised prices climbed 3.0% on the previous quarter and 11.3% on the year.

Stricter trade-defence measures drove that, the company said, and it expects strong domestic sales and pricing through the first half of 2027. US tariffs of 50% on steel keep Mexican prices well below US levels, and no date has been set for a US-Mexico agreement.

Second: Wall Street. The S&P 500 rose 1.31% to 7,619 and the VIX fear gauge fell 10.12% to 17.49, which invites buying of cyclical shares such as steel.

The usual drivers pointed the other way: the dollar index rose 0.60% to 102.84 and the US 10-year Treasury yield stayed near 5%. Oil was flat. The best-supported reading is that equity appetite overrode the stronger dollar, with medium confidence.

Third, in Brazil: CSN’s bounce looks like a recovery after a 5-session gain of 6.33% from a deeply oversold level, not a change in fundamentals. Brazil’s anti-dumping duties were meant to ease pressure on the company, yet import penetration reached 22.5% in the first half of 2026.

Ternium says importers have shifted to Vietnam, South Korea and Egypt, which explains why the walls leak. Gerdau’s small fall after its steep decline reads as profit-taking, with low confidence.

04 The trend behind it

Over 12 months the SLX fund is 32.2% above its 20 November 2025 low but has slipped from its June peak, and it is 2.21% lower over 20 sessions. Gerdau is 40.8% above its 20 March low and has fallen 11.22% in 20 sessions.

CSN is the extreme: 60.9% below its 28 January high, it nearly touched a 12-month low on 3 November. This is a continuation of a split, with Mexico firm and Brazil’s flat-steel makers weak, not a new phase.

History offers a sober footnote. After earlier falls this large, Gerdau was higher 20 sessions later in 44 of 86 cases (51%), with a median gain of 0.9% and a worst case of 56.6% lower.

CSN was higher in 8 of 18 cases (44%), with a median of 2.1% lower and a worst case of 45.5% lower. History is not a forecast.

05 What it means for Latin America

In Brazil, protection is a transfer: builders and carmakers pay more for steel so that Gerdau, CSN and Usiminas keep factories running. China supplied 45.4% of Latin America’s steel imports in 2025, so the policy targets the region’s largest supplier.

In Mexico, the gain is sharper because Ternium sells most of its steel at home, behind trade barriers. Brazilian shipments for Ternium fell 1% to 984,000 tonnes, a reminder that its strength is Mexican.

For an investor, the lesson is that Brazilian construction demand helps Gerdau while imported sheet still hurts CSN.

06 The names to watch

Ternium: the cleanest earnings story, with fourth-quarter adjusted EBITDA (operating profit before some costs) guided broadly in line with the third quarter. The risk is a US-Mexico deal that changes the 50% tariff picture.

CSN and Gerdau: CSN is the high-risk rebound, Gerdau the steadier builder’s play. Usiminas follows CSN’s flat-steel fortunes.

07 What would end it

For the SLX fund, the round US$100 mark is the nearest support, then the 12-month low of US$75.82; resistance is the June peak of US$113.57. For Gerdau, resistance is the 20 October peak of US$5.24 and support the March low of US$3.26.

For CSN, support is the 3 November low of US$0.71, and the round US$1 mark is the first test of the rebound. The 12-month high is US$2.12.

No dated catalyst is confirmed. Brazil’s tariff runs to June 2027, and a US-Mexico steel agreement has no date.

The rally ends if Wall Street turns or Asian imports keep leaking into Brazil. It lasts if Ternium’s guidance holds.

08 What to watch

Brazil imports: Whether import penetration, 22.5% in the first half of 2026, falls after the duties.

Whether import penetration, 22.5% in the first half of 2026, falls after the duties. US-Mexico talks: Any deal on the 50% US steel tariff would reshape Ternium’s pricing.

Any deal on the 50% US steel tariff would reshape Ternium’s pricing. Asian substitutes: Shipments from Vietnam, South Korea and Egypt as importers move away from China.

Shipments from Vietnam, South Korea and Egypt as importers move away from China. Dollar and yields: A firmer dollar and a 5% Treasury yield are headwinds for metals if equities wobble.

Frequently Asked Questions

Investors were reacting to record Mexican shipments, a US$368 million quarterly profit and guidance for strong domestic sales and pricing through the first half of 2027.

Why is CSN so weak?

CSN makes flat steel, which competes directly with imported sheet and coil, and its shares remain far below their January high despite Wednesday’s bounce.

Do tariffs really help Brazilian steel?

Brazil’s 25% above-quota tariff and anti-dumping duties raise import costs, but importers have shifted to other Asian suppliers, so the relief is partial.
