World.title: Should Pula Airport Follow Zadar’s Model?
World.content:
November the 10th, 2026 – Pula Airport is notoriously empty during the winter season, and some are saying over-reliance on just Ryanair might be more of an issue than we realise – should it therefore follow Zadar’s model?

Much has been said recently about the business model employed by Pula Airport, and the debate even reached the Croatian Parliament recently. Boris Bilas reports for Glas Istre/Voice of Istria reports that SDP MP Sanja Radolović proposed an initiative to establish a route between Pula and nearby Venice. Given the previous management’s neglect of the airport, Pula Airport is still far from reaching the passenger numbers it recorded just under a decade ago. It’s therefore hardly surprising that Istrian politicians, as well as the general public in Istria, are becoming quite concerned.

The new airport director, Marko Ražem, has quickly demonstrated that he is the complete opposite of his predecessor, and it seems that Pula Airport finally has a chance to recover under his leadership. At the same time, many people in Pula are calling for the Zadar model to be adopted, wondering why Pula cannot have an airport just as successful as Zadar’s, especially given that Istria is a much stronger tourist region than the Zadar area.

However, Marko Ražem himself has already stated publicly that he doesn’t consider Zadar’s airport management model particularly appealing and would rather develop Pula Airport in a completely different direction. Indeed, the two airports have completely different business strategies, and a comparison of passenger traffic at Zadar and Pula airports reveals a fundamental divide in their approaches to route development. Zadar’s rapid rise, which saw passenger numbers exceed 1.6 million in 2025 and 2026, has been built on the back of one dominant partner, the ultra-popular Irish low-cost giant Ryanair.

Pula, on the other hand, records stable but more modest passenger traffic of around 554,000, approximately 200,000 fewer than its record year of 2019. However, its strength lies in spreading risk and maintaining a network of traditional and diverse airlines.

the two different strategies employed by zadar and pula

Zadar Airport has become one of Ryanair’s key hubs in this part of the Adriatic coastline. According to estimates, Ryanair accounts for between 75 and 80 percent of Zadar Airport’s total annual passenger traffic. The Irish airline group connects Zadar with more than 70 destinations, bringing record passenger numbers to the airport during the summer season, but also leaving it completely exposed to the business decisions of a single board of directors in Dublin.

Pula Airport, on the other hand, has historically maintained a more balanced portfolio. Although Ryanair first entered the Croatian market through Pula in 2006, Pula does not allow its future to be determined exclusively by the low-cost model. Germany and the United Kingdom account for more than half of all arrivals, while, alongside Ryanair, a significantly larger proportion of passengers travelling to Istria are brought in by other airlines and numerous charter operators.

In the aviation industry, having 80 percent of your traffic dependent on a single airline is considered an extremely high-risk gamble. Ryanair operates according to a highly aggressive business model: it has no particular loyalty to destinations. Its bases are established wherever subsidies from local tourism boards are highest and airport fees are lowest. When an airport refuses to reduce its charges or a government raises taxes, Ryanair does not hesitate to withdraw aircraft and shut down routes overnight. Zadar is currently undergoing a massive infrastructure expansion of its passenger terminal. Investments in increased capacity are justified by the current overcrowding. However, if Ryanair were to decide to drastically cut its operations or relocate its base, as it recently announced reductions and withdrawals from cities such as Berlin, Bremen and Thessaloniki due to disagreements over airport charges, Zadar Airport could be left with an enormous empty terminal, high fixed costs for maintaining unused facilities and a dramatic drop in revenue.

a broader airline range

This is precisely what the new director of Pula Airport, Marko Ražem, wants to avoid. He has announced that the airport will attempt to further expand its range of airlines in the future, even if this might mean slightly fewer passengers in the short term compared with Zadar.

In the long run, however, this would mean a much more stable and secure business model that does not depend on the whims of a single person in Dublin. All things considered, Zadar is currently enjoying the fruits of its tourism boom and making headlines with record-breaking passenger numbers. However, its Ryanair “monoculture” is unsustainable in the long run without a strong Plan B. Pula, despite having fewer passengers, can sleep much more peacefully because losing any individual airline would not automatically mean the end of the airport’s operations. The lesson for Croatian tourism and aviation authorities is clear: low-cost airline partners are an excellent engine for growth, but turning an airport into the private runway of a single airline creates a vulnerability that could bring an entire region’s air connectivity to a standstill in an instant.

ryanair’s cautionary tale…

The risks of depending on a single airline are not merely theoretical. Several smaller European airports have experienced complete collapse after becoming dependent on Ryanair and subsequently attempting to make the airline pay market-rate prices. It’s no secret that Ryanair offers the best prices for the vast majority of its routes, and that making sure it is present at your airport has become paramount across Europe, but it shouldn’t imply total reliance. There are a few cautionary tales to keep in mind…

Frankfurt-Hahn Airport (Germany): Once a textbook example of Ryanair’s success outside Frankfurt. When the Irish airline began transferring flights to Frankfurt’s main airport and cutting routes at Hahn, the airport sank into debts amounting to millions of euros and eventually declared bankruptcy.

Altenburg-Nobitz Airport (Germany): A regional airport that invested millions in modernisation to meet Ryanair’s requirements. Following disagreements over marketing funding, Ryanair completely abandoned the airport in 2011. The airport was left without commercial flights, and the project ended in business failure.

Ciudad Real Airport (Spain): Although it also suffered from other structural problems, this so-called “ghost airport” attracted Ryanair with millions in subsidies. When the subsidies dried up and Ryanair left, the airport closed and ended up in insolvency proceedings. The recent wave of base closures and capacity cuts across Germany and Belgium clearly demonstrates that O’Leary’s management is not afraid to make radical cuts.

World.title: Rally experts on Ott Tänak's WRC return: he has a hunger his rivals lack
World.content:
Ott Tänak is returning to the World Rally Championship stage after a year's absence, to the delight of Estonian rally fans.

Tänak made his public announcement last week and he will be joined by his compatriot and co-driver Martin Järveoja at the team with which the pair won the 2019 title – Toyota.

This followed a year's hiatus this year, after the Estonians finished the 2025 season for Hyundai, with Tänak fourth in the drivers' table.

More critical rally fans, however, are asking whether Tänak at 39 can still have the sharpness needed to compete for a further World Championship title or titles. Veteran and nine-time WRC title winner Sébastien Ogier was 41 when he won his most recent world title last year, they note; fellow Frenchman Sébastien Loeb was 38 when he won his ninth title, in 2012. Others say that experience matters. So what can be made of Tänak's chances this time around?

"Thirty-nine is no age at all in motorsport," rally expert Margus Murakas told "Spordipühapäev."

"If we are talking specifically about rallying, it is certainly a discipline where experience is required. Experienced drivers can objectively assess the situation and what is going to happen. Take the multiple French world champions, for instance, who have always had a clear plan. Ott and Martin also always have a clear plan on how to approach a race from the very first yard, be it tire choices or deciding where to attack, they stick to that plan and get to the finish line," Murakas said.

"Experienced drivers pick out those special stages where they feel comfortable and can see an opportunity to beat their rivals. They achieve a certain result or build up a lead, and then start defending it. I think it is impossible to drive the 300 competitive kilometers, which is currently the minimum for a WRC rally, flat out from the first meter to the finish," he added.

In Murakas' assessment, Tänak is even the leading favorite for this year's WRC title.

"Absolutely. I don't think he and Martin would have made this decision if they hadn't convinced themselves that they could compete for the very top spot," the expert noted.

Also appearing on "Spordipühapäev" was Margus Kiiver, who has followed rallying for years, worked at the EAL, the national autosport union, and the Estonian Olympic Committee, (EOK), and been involved in organizing Rally Estonia. He, too, believes Tänak and Järveoja have the potential to launch a serious title challenge.

"I don't believe the decision to return was made on the basis of 'let's go and see what happens.' Ott Tänak is known as an athlete who is very clearly goal-oriented. He has set himself a clear objective. Since 2019, when he won his first world title, the goal has naturally remained the same. Things simply haven't gone the way they should have," Kiiver said, adding Tänak may have taken a step back from top-level WRC racing, but has been behind the wheel a lot in other categories and in testing.

"I'm inclined to think that, compared with the drivers who have competed in the World Championship this year, Ott has covered more kilometers this year. All the testing he has done while getting to know the car. At the same time, he has maintained a good physical shape," he noted.

Tänak and Järveoja after clinching the WRC world champion title in Catalunya, back in 2019. Source: Toyota Gazoo Racing Team

Kiiver also believes Tänak has one major advantage over his rivals.

"He has something that many other drivers don't have – a hunger. He hasn't competed for a year, apart from that one rally in the U.S. (in September — ed.). He is hungry to compete, and I think that is one of his plus points."

"Perhaps there is also some indication in the fact that he is not the only one who has tested these new Toyota models. Testing has different objectives, so you cannot make direct comparisons, but you can get some sense of where you stand compared with [reigning champion] Elfyn Evans, Oliver Solberg or Kalle Rovanperä."

"We don't know how much information circulates within the Toyota team, but there is some data on which to base such a decision. Maybe I'm talking complete nonsense here, but I think that is the only way you can get some sense of where you stand compared with the other drivers," Kiiver said.

Given Tänak's influence on Estonian sport, the show's participants found it worthwhile discussing how motorsport has managed during the year now drawing to a close without a man competing at the highest level of the WRC and what should now be done to make the most of the renewed interest for the benefit of the sport. The same questions are relevant to Estonia's premier domestic event, Rally Estonia.

Some relatively new names did emerge this year, Kiiver noted.

"Estonian motorsport did quite well. We added more world titles, with Robert Virves and Jakko Viilo in the WRC2 class. On the other hand, we had Paul Aron, who was very much in the picture in Formula 1, taking part in free practice sessions. Admittedly, he did not get to race," he said.

"Looking at it in that light, it wasn't a bad year overall. Rally Estonia also managed without Ott, although it took a lot of work to get people out to the stages. Quite a lot of spectators actually came to watch the young Estonians compete. Both the media and fans focused a little more this year on our young drivers, who had inevitably been in the shadow of Ott Tänak and Martin Järveoja before," Kiiver added.

Outside of their home country, how eagerly was Tänak and Järveoja's return anticipated in the wider rally world?

Kiiver said very much, adding: "I believe it was very eagerly anticipated. The WRC is going through a period of transition. It has a new promoter, whose biggest efforts will start to bear fruit next season, and a colorful character like Tänak certainly adds a lot to the championship."

"I would venture to state that Ott Tänak is an even bigger name around the world than we can conceive of. He is highly respected among rally fans worldwide," the expert went on, noting that while Tänak may be a man of few words, those comments he does make are always on point.

"The WRC is getting back a very serious and highly goal-oriented professional," Kiiver concluded.

Background:

Tänak is joining a veritable stable of drivers at Toyota – not only will new world champion Elfyn Evans (Wales) be his teammate, but so too will be Takamoto Katsuta, from Japan, Toyota's home country, Norwegian-Swedish driver Oliver Solberg and Finn Sami Pajari. The team will continue to run the Yaris, but will also be entering the all-new GR Celica Rally1 next season.

The first race as per tradition is the Monte Carlo rally in January 2027.

World.title: Analyst: Isamaa's lethargy downright baffling
World.content:
While Isamaa or Center would win the elections today, SDE is gaining ground and much could change before voters head to the polls in March, political analyst Tarmo Jüristo said.

"Not that I'm particularly distressed about it, but I've still been quite astonished to watch what Isamaa is doing right now, as everyone is overtaking them at full speed," political analyst and head of the SALK think tank Tarmo Jüristo told Vikerraadio Wednesday.

SALK provides its polling results and analyses to liberal parties and, to some extent, the Center Party, but not to EKRE or Isamaa.

"Isamaa has been on a gradual decline since the beginning of the year," Jüristo said, referring to how the Center Party has overtaken Isamaa in polls conducted by both the Institute for Societal Studies and SALK.

"When [Isamaa board member] Riina Solman and a few others, including [Isamaa Chairman Urmas] Reinsalu, I believe, have said that Isamaa is timing its peak performance for the elections, I wonder how what they're doing now — dealing with the management crisis at Tallinn Zoo and all sorts of other things, [Kristiine district elder] Ahti Kallikorm publishing strange articles comparing the European Union to the Soviet Union and so on — fits into their campaign strategy," Jüristo said.

"When I look at the numbers, it seems to me that Isamaa should have realized long ago that it needs to get moving and do something about these issues. But the fact that they're holding back their peak performance right now has been a bit surprising to me, because there really isn't that much time left for them to keep putting things off. But maybe next week," he said.

Discussing how other parties are preparing for the elections, Jüristo highlighted how the Reform Party has placed a strong emphasis on pensions, promising not to cut them, alongside its usual focus on security and the economy.

This puts the Reform Party at odds with Parempoolsed (Right-Wingers), which has promised to freeze pensions. According to Jüristo, Parempoolsed is trying to outflank the prime minister's party on the right by adopting an even more economically liberal stance than the Reform Party.

He also pointed out that, contrary to popular belief, pensioners do not overwhelmingly vote for the Center Party. In the last election, their votes were split primarily between the Center Party and the Reform Party.

"Your voting preferences largely stay with you throughout your life and those who were economically successful 30-year-olds in the 1990s are now starting to reach retirement age. That means it makes perfect sense for the Reform Party to adapt to the changing priorities of its core voters and pensions are an important issue for people approaching retirement," he explained.

Meanwhile, the Social Democrats need to tailor their campaign messages to reflect the higher proportion of young people among their supporters, the analyst noted.

"Social Democratic voters are very young and the party's support among young people is very high compared with other age groups. That, in turn, determines which issues the Social Democrats want to focus on during the campaign — issues that tend to be more relevant to younger voters."

The program also included an extended discussion about compiling candidate lists and the criteria used to decide which electoral districts candidates should run in.

Isamaa would still win today

Asked who he predicts will win the March 7 elections, Jüristo stressed that it is still too early to say, but that if the elections were held this Sunday, either Isamaa or the Center Party would win.

"At this point, I'd still lean slightly toward Isamaa, simply because the Center Party's support is somewhat softer. Russian-speaking voters are less likely to turn out, which makes it a little harder for the Center Party to translate its support into actual votes than it is for Isamaa," he explained.

"But that's a slightly different question from who will win the elections on March 7. And realistically, it's impossible to say anything about that right now," he noted.

Jüristo highlighted the rise of the Social Democrats, whose support has grown to around 17 percent, putting them further ahead of EKRE and the Reform Party.

"They've now made it roughly halfway to where they need to be, around 21-22 percent, where Isamaa and the Center Party currently stand. Four or five percentage points might not sound like much, but gaining that much support actually takes a lot of work. They seem to have good momentum right now, especially since Isamaa still appears to be in a state of lethargic slumber. But I'm fairly certain that won't last, that the campaigns will pick up steam and a lot could change," he said.

"Just think back to the last elections, for example, and what happened in the final six months before election day and how much those developments changed the outcome. What you can predict six months in advance isn't really a prediction. It's a hypothetical snapshot of where everyone stands on the starting blocks today. But how fast each party runs and which path it takes will have a much greater impact on the result than where things stand today," he said, summing up the situation.

World.title: Viljandi city government quietly 'waives' downtown parking fines
World.content:
The South Estonian town of Viljandi has had no parking enforcement officer since June, leaving it tens of thousands of euros short of budgeted fine revenue, Sakala reported .

Viljandi's budget is €40,000 less than expected fine revenue as it has had no parking enforcement officer since June, when the long-serving municipal officer left only for their successor to quit after a couple of months in the post.

The city, population around 17,000, had hoped to take in €48,000 in fines this year from its central paid parking zone, but has taken just €8,100 — €33,000 less than last year.

Mayor Jaak Pihlak (Isamaa) says the shortfall won't throw the budget out of balance, adding that issuing fines was never an objective in itself — the intention is free parking for the town center.

Parking sign (picture is illustrative). Source: Siim Lõvi /ERR

A year ago both governing parties, Isamaa and EKRE, promised to abolish paid parking entirely, their coalition agreement pledging to "restore free parking in central Viljandi." Deputy Mayor Silvia Takkel (EKRE) says that is now infeasible, as the hospital has started charging staff to use its underground garage, meaning nearby free lots would fill with hospital staff vehicles and others taking advantage.

The City Government has proposed keeping the Turu parkla lot, near to the hospital, as paid; the traffic committee must take a position before the Council decides at the end of November.

Ticket revenue has held steady at about €3,000 a month, suggesting drivers haven't taken advantage of the missing enforcement, though the city has lost violation charges that once brought in more than €1,700 in some months — no €40 fines issued for nearly six months against 1,500 a year previously.

Parking has been charged at the market lot and surrounding streets since summer 2025, with enforcement launched in 2022 — more than 70 warnings in the first week alone — and the introduction of fines reportedly restored order fairly quickly.

World.title: Port of Tallinn eyes 2028 start for modern terminal A construction
World.content:
Plans for a new Terminal A building at the Port of Tallinn are moving ahead, with the structure set to be built on the current parking lot in front of the existing terminal.

The terminal A currently serves Viking Line and Eckerö Line ferries traveling to Finland. The old terminal would be demolished after the new one is completed.

Riho Joala, head of development at the Port of Tallinn, said the detailed plan is currently being processed by the city. That process could be completed within a couple of months, after which the port would apply for a building permit. Construction could begin in 2028.

"The start of the development depends on when the terminal A detailed plan is approved," Joala said. "After that, the management board and supervisory board of the Port of Tallinn must make the investment decision."

"Vihur," the winning design of the Port of Tallinn's A-terminal architecture competition. Source: Port of Tallinn/Molumba OÜ

The large-scale project is intended to transform the port area into a modern urban environment and open up more views of the sea. Joala said it is also important that both passengers and ferry operators receive equal treatment at the A and D terminals.

"Since the terminal D and its surrounding area have already been modernized, it is only natural that the terminal A and its surrounding urban space should also be updated and transformed into a more people-friendly area with a more modern architectural character," Joala added.

Delfi reported last summer that the port was also considering demolishing the Port Market building next to the terminal A. The building currently houses the Sadamaturg grocery store, including its SuperAlko section, the Kai café and facilities for the marina. The building was formerly the terminal C.

The Port of Tallinn's Terminal A, Old City Harbor. Source: Siim Lõvi /ERR

Joala said the future of that particular building remains undecided. No demolition or renovation work is planned in the coming years. He added that redevelopment of the site will be addressed through a separate detailed plan from the terminal A project, and preparing that plan will take longer.

"For the time being, the building will remain as it is," Joala said. "From a planning perspective, it forms part of the area surrounding Admiralty Basin. When that area eventually undergoes redevelopment, the entire immediate surroundings of Admiralty Basin will receive a new design solution. At that point, that building will also be renewed."

World.title: Estonian guard Stefan Vaaks' Illinois suffer first loss at Texas Tech
World.content:
Estonian basketball player Stefan Vaaks and his Illinois Fighting Illini teammates suffered their first NCAA Division loss of the season Tuesday night, falling 84-78 at No. 16 Texas Tech in Lubbock.

Vaaks, a 21-year-old Estonian guard in his first season with the Fighting Illini, who are competing in the Big Ten Conference, played 22 minutes and scored 10 points on 1-of-2 shooting from two-point range and 2-of-10 from three, adding three rebounds and one block . Illinois, ranked No. 3 nationally, trailed 49-29 at halftime before cutting the deficit to one point with 5:37 remaining, but could not complete the comeback .

The 6-foot-7 Vaaks joined Illinois this season as a transfer from Providence, where he averaged 15.8 points and 3.2 assists as a freshman and earned Big East All-Freshman Team honors . A native of Tabasalu, Estonia, he played professionally in the Latvia-Estonia Basketball League before moving to the United States .

Illinois (2-1) returns home to host Sam Houston on Friday . The Illini opened the season with wins over Fairleigh Dickinson (120-45) and Pennsylvania (112-70) before Tuesday's loss.

World.title: Estonia's new apartment buildings' renovation plan meeting resistance
World.content:
Technical consultants and apartment associations oppose the government's plan to allocate €160 million in renovation subsidies over the next two years exclusively to prefabricated apartment building renovations.

The government has finalized a plan to allocate €160 million in funding under the latest support program exclusively to the prefabricated renovation of apartment buildings, leaving conventional renovation projects ineligible for state support. The program will cover 2027 and 2028.

According to the Association of Technical Consultants (TKL), the government's plan could leave many apartment associations without the financial support they need, cause a slowdown in the conventional construction sector and result in a significant portion of the funding going unused.

TKL added that concentrating support on a single construction method could reduce orders for conventional construction companies and weaken competition.

"The aim of apartment building renovation subsidies must remain to modernize the housing stock, not to prioritize the development of one particular industry," TKL said.

In practice, prefabricated renovation involves manufacturing exterior wall panels and sometimes roof elements in a factory, complete with insulation, windows, ventilation ducts and finished facades. The panels are then transported to the site and attached to the building. The main difference from conventional, on-site renovation is that the facade work is carried out in a factory, leaving only installation to be completed on-site.

One reason the government has begun favoring prefabricated renovation, which is considered faster, is that Estonia needs to renovate 14,000 apartment buildings over the next 20 years.

Minister of Infrastructure Kuldar Leis also told ERR that speed was partly behind the decision. "Prefabricated renovation allows apartment buildings to be renovated faster and to a higher standard. Much of the work is carried out in controlled factory conditions and the construction period on-site is shorter, meaning less disruption for residents," he said.

"Estonia has many apartment buildings constructed to the same design, making this an excellent solution for renovating them. Estonian companies also export prefabricated renovation solutions and their export potential is growing," he added.

Minister: All state subsidies must return to the state budget through tax revenue

However, according to TKL, only a handful of manufacturers of prefabricated facade elements in Estonia have experience with this type of renovation. A survey conducted by the association also indicates that interest in a subsidy covering just 20 percent of prefabricated renovation costs could be extremely low.

TKL therefore recommends that the government cover 30 percent of the cost of prefabricated renovation and provide subsidies of at least 20 percent for conventional and phased renovation projects.

The Estonian Union of Co-operative Housing Associations also emphasized, in an appeal to the government and the Ministry of Climate, that apartment associations must retain the freedom to choose a renovation method suited to their building, location and financial circumstances. The union recommends increasing the subsidy for prefabricated renovation to 35 percent and extending the 20 percent renovation subsidy to apartment buildings undergoing conventional renovation.

However, the Ministry of Climate has no plans to change the current support program. Leis said the reason the government does not want to increase its contribution beyond 20 percent is that all the funding comes from the state budget and is expected to return to it in full through tax revenue.

"The renovation subsidies for the current EU funding period, which is coming to an end, have already been allocated, but we will have to wait several more years for the next funding period. To avoid a multiyear gap in renovation support, we requested funding from the state budget this time. The allocation came with two important conditions. First, the measure must be budget-neutral, meaning a 20 percent subsidy that provides meaningful support for renovation while ensuring that taxpayers' money returns to the state budget through tax revenue," he said.

Prefabricated renovation. Source: Airika Harrik/ERR

"The second condition was that the measure must contribute to increasing Estonia's export capacity. Prefabricated renovation provides work for Estonian prefabricated building manufacturers and engineers and helps develop an industry with higher added value and export potential," he added.

According to Leis, there is no reason to fear a shortage of contractors. He said Estonia has a strong prefabricated building industry and that experience with prefabricated renovation is growing. In addition, the €160 million is to be distributed in two rounds, giving companies time to expand their production capacity.

TKL, however, noted that prefabricated renovation is not necessarily faster or better in quality.

"Installing factory-made facade elements that also incorporate ventilation ducts is only one part of a building's comprehensive renovation. The remaining construction work does not differ significantly from the work carried out during conventional renovation," TKL said, adding that potentially faster facade installation does not automatically translate into a faster or higher-quality renovation project overall.

Regular renovations to be supported using EU funds

Leis, however, is confident that directing all the funding toward prefabricated renovation is the right decision and that the entire €160 million will eventually be allocated.

"Consultations with market participants give us confidence that there are apartment associations willing to undertake renovation projects under these conditions. The plan is to direct the entire €160 million allocated from the state budget toward prefabricated renovation," he said.

Leis added that support for conventional renovation will continue under the EU's next funding period.

"At the same time, it is quite likely that subsidy rates will remain lower than in previous years, as demand for support is several times greater than the available budget. This will allow the state to help more apartment associations," he said.

The government also plans to expand the range of apartment buildings eligible for support. Previously, subsidies were available only for apartment buildings that had been put into use before 2000, but the new round will have no such restriction.

Leis acknowledged that prefabricated renovation is not suitable for all apartment buildings. However, he said that since the previous funding round had primarily supported smaller-than-average buildings, it is now only fair to balance this out by directing support toward medium-sized and large apartment buildings constructed to standardized designs, which are well suited to prefabricated renovation.

On-site renovation of an old apartment building in Sillamäe. Source: Dmitri Fedotkin/ERR

World.title: 11 human smuggling suspects caught in Estonia in October
World.content:
Police detained 11 people suspected of illegally transporting people across the Estonian border in October. One suspect has already been convicted and begun serving a sentence, while 10 remain in custody.

Thousands of migrants have crossed the Belarusian-Latvian border this year into the European Union in what officials say is a "hybrid attack" orchestrated by the regime in Minsk.

The migrants, mostly from Africa and the Middle East, then travel on to other countries in western or northern Europe, using Estonia as a transit country.

However, more than 400 people have been caught in Estonia this year after Poland and Germany boosted security checks on their borders, and smugglers changed their routes.

A statement from the Police and Border Guard Board (PPA) and Prosecutor's Office on Wednesday said 11 people have been detained this year for suspected people smuggling. This includes a Lithuanian, a Latvian, a Bulgarian, a German, Ukrainians and Pakistanis.

"Despite their different backgrounds, the same patterns recur in their stories: a desire to make money quickly and a willingness to take significant risks. In most cases, offers to transport migrants were received through social media. The PPA has had more than 100 social media accounts shut down for sharing information related to human smuggling and recruiting drivers," the joint statement added.

'Continuous flow' of migrants

Veiko Kommusaar. Source: Siim Lõvi / ERR

Veiko Kommusaar, deputy director general of the PPA for border management, said migration pressure originates at the Belarusian-Latvian border.

"We are not talking about dozens of migrants who have lost their way, but a continuous flow emerging at the Belarusian border, which the authorities there deliberately allow through. An entire shadow economy has rapidly grown around this, where the movement of people has become a commodity and an opportunity for smugglers to make money. The network connecting customers, drivers and routes extends across Europe," Kommusaar said.

He added that the situation has not ended and Estonia will continue to enhance internal border checks and help Latvia on the Belarusian border.

Senior prosecutor Toomas Koitmäe said those transporting migrants are taking on the risks associated with international organized crime.

"Human smuggling organizers give the impression that this is a simple transport job and a way to make quick money. In reality, the journey can end in prison. The courts have already sentenced several recent drivers to prison. Proceedings are continuing in the remaining cases, and the suspects are being held in custody," Koitmäe said.

11 suspects

The PPA and Prosecutor's Office provided details about the 11 cases, which ERR News is republishing below.

On October 1, at around noon, the PPA stopped a vehicle with Latvian license plates on Viljandi maantee in Harju County. Six foreigners were found in its cargo compartment. According to the men traveling in the cargo compartment, they were from Morocco and Somalia, and none had identity documents. The 54-year-old Latvian citizen driving the Fiat van was detained on suspicion of illegally transporting foreigners across the border.

On October 3, at around 5 p.m., police stopped a Volvo with Latvian license plates in Tori Municipality, Pärnu County, driven by a 62-year-old German citizen. Seven men were found in the passenger compartment and trunk of the vehicle. They said they were from Morocco and Somalia and had no legal basis for staying in Estonia.

On October 4, border guards discovered three foreigners staying in Estonia illegally hidden under a blanket in the trunk of an Audi bound for Sweden at Paldiski North Port. The men said they were from Eritrea and Ethiopia. The 20-year-old Ukrainian citizen driving the vehicle had a Swedish residence permit, but the driver's license he presented turned out to be forged. Another Ukrainian citizen was also in the car. The two Ukrainian citizens were detained as suspects, while the other foreigners were placed in a detention center.

In the early morning of October 5, at around 4 a.m., police stopped a Toyota with Lithuanian license plates in Häädemeeste Municipality, Pärnu County. The vehicle was driven by a 22-year-old Pakistani citizen with a Lithuanian residence permit. Also in the car were another Pakistani citizen with a Lithuanian residence permit and two Somali citizens who had no identity documents. The group was taken to Pärnu police station to check the circumstances of their arrival in Estonia and their right to stay in the country. The Pakistani citizens were detained as criminal suspects.

A suspected people smuggler. Source: PPA

On October 6, at around 1 a.m., police stopped a Kia Sportage with Latvian license plates at kilometer 85 of the Tallinn-Tartu-Luhamaa Highway. The vehicle was driven by a 63-year-old Bulgarian citizen.

There were seven men from third countries in the car who had entered Estonia illegally. The migrants were taken to Tartu police station, while the Bulgarian was detained as a suspect.

The court sentenced the Bulgarian citizen to one year and ten months in prison, of which he must serve three months immediately. If he commits another crime, the court can order him to serve the entire sentence. After serving his sentence, the man will be expelled from Estonia and subject to a five-year entry ban.

On October 12, at 11:20 a.m., police detained a 31-year-old man at Tallinn Airport who had arrived from Düsseldorf and forgotten his shoulder bag on the plane. The bag contained Swedish identity cards belonging to other people. According to the suspicion, the man, who lives in Germany, had come to Estonia to provide foreigners staying in the country illegally with other people's documents to enable them to cross the Schengen border illegally.

On the same day, at around 5 p.m., a 51-year-old Ukrainian citizen was detained in central Tallinn. Two Iraqi and two Somali citizens were found in the cargo compartment of his Ford Transit, none of whom had a legal basis for staying in Estonia. According to the suspicion, the Ukrainian planned to transport the foreigners staying in Estonia illegally onward to Finland.

On October 23, at around 6:30 p.m., a 48-year-old Lithuanian citizen was detained in Pärnu on suspicion of repeatedly transporting illegal migrants across the state border. According to the suspicion, the man transported at least 25 foreigners from countries in North Africa and the Horn of Africa across the Estonian border during October. The migrants were discovered in Tallinn's Mustamäe and Nõmme districts and the port area.

On October 28, at 9:30 p.m., three Pakistani citizens heading for a flight to Barcelona were detained in the Schengen area of Tallinn Airport. They claimed to reside in Spain. Police checked with the Spanish authorities whether the men had the legal right to stay there. The response confirmed that the Pakistani citizens had no legal basis for staying in Spain. One 56-year-old man with dual Belgian and Pakistani citizenship is suspected of migrant smuggling.

World.title: Estonian politicians still oppose food VAT cut even after prices fall in Latvia
World.content:
Latvia's experiment of slashing VAT on food has lowered prices and boosted sales, while Estonian politicians remain divided over a similar move.

Latvia's decision to reduce value-added tax (VAT) on selected food products has led to lower prices and increased sales, Rimi Latvija CEO Valdis Turlais told a conference organized by the Estonian Traders Association, Postimees writes.

Since July 1, Latvia has applied a reduced VAT rate of 12 percent to bread and baked goods, milk, eggs and fresh chicken as part of a pilot project running until June 30, 2027. While the tax cut was theoretically expected to reduce retail prices by 7.44 percent, Latvia's Competition Council found that prices across the four categories had fallen by an average of 8.32 percent by September. Turlais said Rimi's sales volumes in the affected categories were 12 to 20 percent higher in October than a year earlier, with some suppliers struggling to meet increased demand.

However, Reform Party politician Aivar Sõerd opposed a similar measure in Estonia, citing an International Monetary Fund assessment that described reducing food VAT as fundamentally misguided. Sõerd argued that cutting VAT on basic food products to 13 percent would cost the state €100 million to €120 million annually, while wealthier households would benefit more in absolute terms.

Parempoolsed leader Lavly Perling also opposed a separate reduced VAT rate for food, instead advocating a general VAT reduction that would benefit consumers across all purchases.

Meanwhile, Isamaa leader Urmas Reinsalu pledged to reduce VAT on basic food products by July 1, 2027, if his party wins a mandate in the next election. Representatives of three other parties — EKRE's Siim Pohlak, Social Democratic Party leader Lauri Läänemets and Center Party chairman Mihhail Kõlvart — have also supported lowering VAT on food, the newspaper reports.

Estonia sports a near-universal 24 percent VAT rate, with accommodation (13 percent) and books and medicines (9 percent) the only current exceptions.
