World.title: [OPINION] Why ‘Trump Out’?
World.content:
It's not because we hate America. It's because we don’t want to be its military outpost anymore, its source of cheap labor and resources, or its faraway battlefield.

When US President Donald Trump arrives in Manila next week for the 49th ASEAN Summit, he will be greeted not only by the red carpet rolled but by the Philippine government but by the red flags and banners of thousands of Filipinos protesting his visit.

Under the slogan “Trump Out,” various activist groups, people’s organizations and social movements have declared 12 days of protest from November 4 until Trump’s arrival on Monday, November 16.

Why protest the visit of the leader of a country that our government considers its closest and most important ally?

Trump is arguably the most racist, misogynistic, arrogant, and self-serving president in modern US history. And that’s from the point of view of many Americans themselves as shown by the result of the recent US midterm elections.

His political career has been built on demonizing immigrants, vilifying Muslims, degrading women, attacking minorities, and cultivating fear and hatred on those he considers enemies.

His administration’s brutal crackdown on undocumented immigrants has torn families apart, militarized communities, and subjected suspected people of color to arbitrary detention and deportation. His attacks on diversity, equity, and inclusion, particularly surrounding gender, race, religion, and reproductive rights have emboldened right wing forces who want to reverse decades of social progress.

Trump’s misogyny is not merely a matter of offensive language. His repeated degradation of women and attacks on their rights, plus membership in the so-called Epstein class, reveal a worldview that upholds male domination and privilege.

Nor is his corruption simply a matter of rhetoric. He was convicted of 34 counts of falsifying business records. He makes no qualms about mixing public office, private business interests, and personal political loyalty, raising serious conflict of interest issues and questions about his abuse of power.

Most alarming is Trump’s authoritarianism.

He has repeatedly attacked the press, demonized political opponents, undermined democratic institutions, and encouraged the politics of intimidation. His refusal to accept defeat in the 2020 elections caused the January 6, 2021 assault on the US Capitol.

Trump’s rule bear the hallmarks of a fascistic political project: extreme nationalism, racism, a strongman cult, contempt for democratic accountability, and the use of state power to silence dissent. Surely, Filipinos who endured the Marcos dictatorship recognize the danger and reject such kind of politics.

A warmonger and threat to world peace

Trump claims to be a peacemaker. But his actions show the opposite.

In total disregard of his promise to end America’s forever wars and in flagrant violation of international law, he has pursued a policy of military aggression, coercive sanctions, and intervention against countries that refuse to submit to Washington’s dictates.

From the genocide in Gaza to the senseless war on Iran, from the economic strangulation of Cuba to the hostage of Venezuela and other Caribbean countries, from his “Donroe Doctrine” to his cold war with China, Trump’s foreign policy shows the willingness of the world’s most advanced and powerful military to impose US interests through force.

His support for Israel exposes the US’s hypocrisy as a champion of human rights and international law. Same for the continued use of economic sanctions against Iran, Cuba and Venezuela that punish entire populations while claiming to promote freedom and democracy.

Far from promoting peace, Trump is accelerating a global arms race, demanding increased military spending from allies, and treating international relations as a contest of military and economic domination.

As usual, the US military-industrial complex, giant energy corporations, big tech, financial institutions, and other powerful interests stand to profit from it all while ordinary people — workers, farmers, women, children, and entire communities whose lives and livelihoods are destroyed by bombs, blockades, sanctions, and forced displacement — suffer.

As Filipinos, we have every reason to oppose Trump’s wars. We have a painful history of American colonial conquest, military intervention, and support for dictatorships. How can we possibly welcome an American president whose foreign policies are a throwback to the colonial era?

Plunder and war in the guise of security

The most compelling reason for us to protest Trump’s visit is what he intends to do to our country vis a vis China. Under the Marcos regime, the Philippines has become a crucial platform for America’s strategic competition with our most powerful neighbor.

The expansion of US access to nine of our military bases under the Enhanced Defense Cooperation Agreement (EDCA), expanded and neverending joint military exercises, deployment of advanced missile systems and drone facilities, establishment of military warehouse and logistics hubs, and growing integration of our armed forces into the US Pacific Command have pushed our country to the frontlines of the escalating US-China rivalry.

This is especially dangerous given the unresolved territorial and maritime disputes in the West Philippine Sea. Our legitimate maritime concerns are being used to justify an increasingly militarized confrontation with China, with our fisherfolk, coast guard and navy bearing the consequences of a conflict between the two major powers.

The US is not strengthening and expanding its military presence in our islands out of an altruistic concern for our fisherfolk or our sovereignty. It’s strategic objective is to contain China’s rise as a superpower, preserve US military dominance in Asia, and secure access to the region’s vital sea lanes, markets, resources, and infrastructure.

Then there’s Trump’s weaponization of our industrial development.

The proposed Pax Silica Economic Security Zone in Tarlac aims to integrate the Philippines into US-controlled supply chains for critical minerals, semiconductors, and other ingredients for the new arms race involving artificial intelligence.

It remains to be seen whether Pax Silica will lead to the development of genuine Filipino industries or create decent and sustainable jobs. What is more likely is that our land, labor, energy, water, and natural resources will be used as cheap inputs for US big tech and military-industrial partners.

What will happen to the indigenous peoples, farming communities and the environment affected by Pax Silica? Who will control these AI hubs, their resources and technologies? Will these dual-use facilities serve as military targets in a future US-China war?

The “Trump Out” protests target Trump and his unhinged regime. Rather than an expression of hostility, it is an act of solidarity with the American people who just last week voted overwhelmingly to reject Trump’s authoritarianism, racism, and wars.

Real friendship with the US requires resisting its imperialist agenda, which hurt both Americans and Filipinos and other peoples of the world.

Trump, of course, is only the tip of the iceberg. US foreign policy transcends administrations and political parties. But we have to start somewhere and fight the battles that come our way any which way we can.

Trump’s visit is a chance to assert our dignity as a sovereign nation. We say “Trump Out” not because we hate America, but because we don’t want to be its military outpost anymore, its source of cheap labor and resources, or its faraway battlefield. – Rappler.com



Teddy Casiño served as Bayan Muna’s partylist representative from 2004-2013 and was a former commissioner of the EDSA People Power Commission. He is the current chairperson of Bagong Alyansang Makabayan, a alliance of nationalist and democratic peoples’ organizations and movements in the Philippines.

World.title: COP31 leaders try out new sales pitch for climate action: Do it for the economy
World.content:
FAMILY PHOTO. Australia's Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, Simon Stiell, executive secretary of the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres, Turkish President Tayyip Erdogan, Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev pose for a family photo with other leaders during the UN Climate Change Conference (COP31) in Antalya, Turkey, on November 11, 2026.

(1st UPDATE) John Kerry, a former US secretary of state who has been advocating for climate action for decades, says he likes the reframing of the issue

ANTALYA, Turkey – Leaders at the COP31 summit in Turkey are trying out a new sales pitch for climate action that is tailored to the times: do it to bolster the economy and bring down the cost of living.

The message, being repeated in the hallways and on the plenary stage of the annual UN conference, reflects efforts by organizers to capture the attention of governments wrestling with crises that have pushed global warming down the list of priorities.

Among those is rampant inflation driven in part by disruptions to Middle East crude oil shipments since the onset of the Iran war. Consumer price pressures from fuel to food were a major driver in the US midterm elections that handed control of Congress to Democrats, and are an important vulnerability for leaders across Europe, Asia and elsewhere.

“Three-quarters of humanity live in countries that import fossil fuels, hostage to price shocks they did not create and cannot control,” UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres told world leaders attending the summit on Wednesday, November 11.

“Recent conflicts make clear that this is a recipe for chronic insecurity and a cost-of-living meltdown,” he added, saying the clear solution is a shift to renewable energy.

Simon Stiell, head of the UN’s climate office, made the same point. “Today, chaos in global energy markets and climate disasters are supercharging inflation, slamming government budgets, pushing household bills up and living standards down,” he told the conference.

“The political costs of fossil fuel dependency are unforgiving. Climate action can help relieve the pressures.”

John Kerry, a former US secretary of state who has been advocating for climate action for decades, said he liked the reframing of the issue.

Climate change has become a massively divisive political issue in recent years, including in the US, where President Donald Trump last year withdrew the world’s top historical greenhouse gas emitter from international climate cooperation after calling warming a hoax.

“I think everybody who is working on climate needs to change the way they talk about it,” Kerry told reporters on the sidelines of the summit.

“I think that grouping of security, health, jobs, stability of communities and food supply are all very real and very much on people’s minds when I talk to them.”

To be sure, speakers at COP31 tended to agree the primary motivation for climate action should center on the overwhelming scientific evidence that warming is human-driven and dangerous.

“It is our responsibility to turn scientific evidence into political action and ensure that our decisions are guided by fact, not short-term political interests,” Slovenian President Natasa Pirc Musar said in a speech to the summit on Wednesday.

But European energy commissioner Dan Jorgensen said emphasizing the other benefits of cutting emissions could help build a consensus for action that could even include climate sceptics.

“Because even if you don’t believe in climate change, which I obviously do, we should be able to agree that moving away from a dependency on fossils is extremely smart for security reasons,” he said. – Rappler.com

World.title: DSWD: More than 1,400 vendors affected by ASEAN Summit
World.content:
AYUDA. Vendors in Pasay City affected by the ASEAN Summit receive P10,000 from the Department of Social Welfare and Development on November 11, 2026.

(1st UPDATE) The vendors whose livelihoods have been disrupted are receiving cash aid and family food packs from the Department of Social Welfare and Development

MANILA, Philippines – There are more than 1,400 vendors whose livelihoods have been affected by the Philippines’ hosting of the 49th Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Summit and Related Summits, according to the Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD).

The DSWD said in a statement on Thursday, November 12, that it provided 1,462 vendors from Baclaran with P10,000 each from the Assistance to Individuals in Crisis Situations program, as well as family food packs, during aid distribution in Parañaque City on Wednesday, November 11.

Social Welfare Secretary Rex Gatchalian told reporters on Wednesday that the Parañaque City government forwarded to the DSWD a list of vendors affected in Baclaran, a bustling market area, amid security measures implemented for the ASEAN hosting.

The city government said street vendors are “temporarily prohibited” from operating along Roxas Boulevard and its service roads, from Redemptorist Road to Quirino Avenue, as well as the road beneath the Light Rail Transit until November 20.

Since Baclaran is near Pasay City as well, the DSWD is also coordinating with the local government to identify more affected vendors in the area.

“Bagamat humihingi kami ng paumanhin sa mga naantala ang hanapbuhay dahil sa napipintong ASEAN Summit, ang direktiba ng ating Pangulo ay masigurado na mabigyan sila ng tulong pinansiyal kasi alam natin na wala silang kikitain sa mga araw na ‘yon,” Gatchalian said on the sidelines of the aid distribution.

(We apologize to those whose livelihoods were put on hold because of the upcoming ASEAN Summit, but the directive of the President is to ensure that they will be given financial support because we know they will not have earnings during those days.)

Play Video

In Pasay City, around 50 ambulant vendors and eatery workers also received P10,000 and family food packs on Wednesday.

It was the second batch following the aid distribution to some 30 individuals on Sunday, November 8.

Most of the beneficiaries were located along Diokno Boulevard.

“Malaking tulong na rin naman po kahit papaano…. Pagkakasyahin hangga’t walang trabaho (This is still a great help somehow. We’ll make do with it while we have no work),” said Anabel de Luna, 34. The eatery where she works temporarily closed on Monday, November 9, and may resume operations on November 20 or 21.

But others like Rizal Villaula, a 40-year-old pares cart owner, had to stop selling on October 22 amid road clearing operations. He has since entered into multiple gigs, like towing services.

Maria Joanna Cristina Samarro, a 46-year-old ambulant vendor, has been selling cigarettes for the past weeks to earn just enough for some meals.

But she took the chance to set up her table in front of the Senate building, also along Diokno Boulevard, to sell various items such as bread, coffee, and soft drinks, as protesters gathered there on Wednesday morning.

When there are no road restrictions, she can earn up to P500 a day.

Gatchalian said remaining affected vendors in Parañaque City will receive their cash aid and food packs by Thursday.

Malacañang earlier declared November 16 to 18 as special non-working days in Metro Manila to make way for the ASEAN Summit. – Rappler.com

World.title: Sara Duterte’s ‘loose investments’ in Gencorp earn her P2.1-M ‘return of capital’
World.content:
OATH. Gencorp Industries Inc. and Metro City Chow Foods Corporation in-house counsel Suzette Punay takes the witness stand on Day 42 of the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte on November 11, 2026.

An article of incorporation presented by the prosecution during the impeachment trial shows the Vice President paid P46,000 in capital stock

MANILA, Philippines – An in-house corporate counsel of Gencorp Industries Inc. denied that Vice President Sara Duterte has business interests in the company, despite it being listed in her sworn Statements of Assets, Liabilities, and Net Worth (SALNs).

On Day 42 of the impeachment trial on Wednesday, November 11, Suzette Balucanag-Punay refuted a portion of the forensic financial report of lawyer Alexander Cabrera, which indicated that Duterte owns a 20% stake in Gencorp and has paid-up capital in the company amounting to P250,000.

Play Video

Balucanag-Punay also said Duterte is not a stockholder of Gencorp and does not participate in any stockholders’ meetings. She said the Vice President also has no involvement in the board of directors, management, as well as in the decision-making of the company.

“She is not a beneficial owner of Gencorp,” the corporate counsel told the impeachment court.

Balucanag-Punay, however, said Duterte received more than P2.1 million in “return of capital” from Gencorp between 2022 and 2025 from what she described as “loose investment.”

Duterte received return of capital amounting to P337,500 from Gencorp in 2022; P555,750 from May to December 2023; P612,419 in 2024; and P636,700 in 2025.

She, however, did not receive any return of capital from January to April 2023.

“I termed it as a loose investment, your honor. It’s coming from the contributions that the Vice President made for Davao Bounty Times before the actual commencement of the operations of Jollibee Times Square,” said Balucanag-Punay.

According to the witness, Duterte initially invested in Davao Bounty Foods Corporation, a company that attempted to acquire the franchise of a Jollibee branch in Davao. The franchise, however, was not granted, and Duterte’s investments were carried over to the companies that operated the Jollibee Times Square branch, including Gencorp.

Gencorp now operates five Jollibee branches in Davao: Centerpoint Plaza, Davao Gaisano Mall, Abreeza Mall, Times Square Plaza Center, and Bolton.

Balucanag-Punay said Duterte’s investments only covered the Jollibee Times Square branch and not Gencorp. She also said she is unaware of the nature of the investments and their exact amount.

An article of incorporation presented by the prosecution showed Duterte paid capital stock to Davao Bounty amounting to P46,000.

Prosecution counsel Lorna Kapunan pressed Balucanag-Punay on Duterte’s possible other investments in Gencorp, citing the ballooning of her investment from P46,000 to P2.14 million.

“I am unaware if there’s any because I cannot verify it from other records,” Balucanag-Punay said, adding she could not confirm how the returns of capital were calculated and if the Vice President still receives income from Gencorp.

Article XII, Section VII of the 1987 Constitution prohibits the president, vice president, and members of the Cabinet from holding any other office or employment during their tenure. They are also barred from “directly or indirectly, practice any other profession, participate in any business, or be financially interested in any contract with, or in any franchise, or special privilege granted by the Government or any subdivision, agency, or instrumentality thereof, including government-owned or controlled corporations or their subsidiaries.”

Balucanag-Punay’s responses did not sit well with some senator-judges, including Senator-judge Raffy Tulfo, who questioned her credibility.

“You know that you will testify here, so you should have researched. Now, you cannot even present any document that would back up your claims that it was return of investment,” Tulfo said.

Duterte is facing impeachment proceedings under Article II of the articles of impeachment, which involves allegations of unexplained wealth, including allegedly undeclared assets and properties.

As part of the impeachment article, the prosecution challenged Duterte’s inclusion of stock ownership in Gencorp in her 2024-2025 SALN, despite her name’s absence on the company’s corporate records.

Defense drops witnesses

In a related development, the defense dropped some of its witnesses, announcing they were dispensing with the testimonies of subpoenaed bank officials — except representatives from Bank of the Philippine Islands (BPI) — to expedite the proceedings.

“We don’t think there’s a need to waste the time of the court in presenting all of the bank representatives, so we tightened the list and left only the BPI official. It’s in the interest of expediting the proceedings,” defense lawyer Michael Poa said. – Rappler.com

PAGADIAN CITY, Zamboanga del Sur — Police seized around P16 million worth of suspected shabu and arrested a high-value target in a buy-bust operation early Wednesday in Ipil, Zamboanga Sibugay.

Lt. Joy Necesario, Zamboanga Sibugay Police Provincial Office information officer, said the suspect was a 32-year-old male resident of Barangay Tenan, Ipil.

The operation was conducted at 3:20 a.m. on Nov. 11 at Purok San Francisco in Barangay Poblacion. It was led by the Ipil Municipal Police Station, alongside other local law enforcement units.

Article continues after this

Operatives confiscated nine heat-sealed transparent plastic sachets containing a white crystalline substance believed to be shabu (methamphetamine hydrochloride), weighing approximately 2.33 kilograms and valued at P15,844,000.

The confiscated drug evidence will be turned over to the Zamboanga Sibugay Forensic Unit for quantitative and qualitative examination.

LINGAYEN, Pangasinan — It’s a special non-working day on Friday, Nov. 13, in Pangasinan as the province commemorates the 130th birth anniversary of former House Speaker Eugenio Perez.

Pangasinan Governor Ramon Guico III issued Executive Order 0131-2026 on Nov. 9, enjoining Pangasinenses to observe the occasion and participate in activities honoring Perez’s life and contributions to the province and the country.

The declaration is pursuant to Republic Act No. 6741, enacted on March 20, 1989, which designates Nov. 13 of every year as a special public holiday in Pangasinan in honor of the late lawmaker.

Article continues after this 

READ: Outstanding son: Pangasinan honors forgotten Speaker

Perez was born in Obong, a former sitio of San Carlos City that is now a barangay of Basista town. He represented the second district of Pangasinan from 1946 to 1957, which then included San Carlos, and also served in the National Assembly during the Commonwealth period.

He became the first Pangasinan official to serve as Speaker of the House of Representatives, heading the chamber during the First Congress under the Philippine Third Republic.

Perez was also credited with authoring Republic Act No. 170, which paved the way for Dagupan’s conversion into a city in 1947.

Among his other legislative contributions were the passage of the Bell Trade Act and the Parity Rights Amendment to the Constitution, which shaped the country’s postwar economic and political relations with the United States.

The Speaker Eugenio Perez National Agricultural School was also established in recognition of his legacy and advocacy for the development of Pangasinan. /mcm

World.title: This BINI’s content may be ‘Pantropiko’ – but not ‘pantrapiko’
World.content:
DISTRACTED DRIVING Screenshot from Mikha Lim’s video that earned the BINI member a show cause order.

MANILA, Philippines — A member of the pop girl group BINI became the latest content creator to be penalized by the Land Transportation Office (LTO) for distracted driving.

Mikha Lim, whose group is behind hits such as “Pantropiko,” was issued a show cause order (SCO) on Wednesday after she was seen in a now-viral video recording herself while driving.

Article continues after this 

The video showed her holding a phone, which later fell off her hand. But instead of pulling over for safety, she continued driving and was seen reaching down to retrieve the device.

A memorandum issued by the Land Transportation Franchising and Regulatory Board (LTFRB) in July warned content creators of the risks of taking videos while driving.

READ: LTFRB tells PUV drivers: Don’t vlog and drive

Lim’s video, which was reportedly uploaded on Weverse, prompted calls for an investigation by the LTO.

The agency later issued her an SCO for possible violation of Republic Act No. 10913, or the Anti-Distracted Driving Act; for reckless driving; and for being “an improper person to operate a motor vehicle.”

Article continues after this 

‘Very apologetic’

RA 10913 prohibits motorists from using mobile communication devices while driving, including for calls, text messages and other distracting activities.

The LTO gave Lim until Nov. 20 to submit an explanation, but she already appeared at the agency’s Quezon City office on Wednesday.

Article continues after this 

She “was very apologetic and acknowledged her mistake,” according to Assistant Secretary Markus Lacanilao.

Later on Wednesday night, Lim issued a statement saying “I take full responsibility for what happened,’’ and vowed to be mindful of the rules after learning a “big lesson.”

“Road safety rules exist to protect everyone, something we need to take seriously,” she said.

Lim’s license to drive was suspended for 90 days, the LTO said, as it reiterated its warning against cell phone use while behind the wheel.

LTFRB memo

“It is our duty to ensure that the law is enforced fairly and without bias, regardless of a person’s status or popularity,” Lacanilao said. “Whether famous or not, everyone is expected to abide by traffic laws. If found to have violated them, the LTO will impose the appropriate penalties.”

In July, the LTO also suspended the license of some drivers and vehicle owners involved in a social media content showing an intentional car collision.

“Others may find this amusing, but for the LTO, no content is funny if it endangers lives and the safety of motorists,” Lacanilao then said.

The violations were committed even after the LTFRB’s issuance of Memorandum Circular No. 2026-050 reiterating the enforcement of the Anti-Distracted Driving Act.

World.title: El Niño damage to crops nears P10 billion – DA
World.content:
“Very strong” El Nino is now active in tropical Pacific, says Pagasa. —Photo Courtesy of OMH-Hilongos, Leyte

MANILA, Philippines — The El Niño phenomenon has wiped out nearly P10 billion in farm produce, according to the Department of Agriculture’s (DA) latest tally.

In an advisory on Wednesday, the DA said the prolonged drought has caused P9.99 billion in damage, up 16.6 percent from the P8.57-billion recorded on Oct. 21.

The latest recorded damage has reached almost half of the P20 billion in losses earlier projected by the DA.

Article continues after this 

So far, El Niño has affected 324,327 farmers in various regions, namely Cordillera, Ilocos Region, Cagayan Valley, Central Luzon, Calabarzon, Mimaropa, Bicol, Western Visayas, Negros Island Region, Central Visayas, Eastern Visayas, Zamboanga Peninsula, Northern Mindanao, Davao, Soccsksargen and Caraga.

READ: Declaring PH-wide ‘El Niño’ state of calamity ruled out

The volume of production losses stood at 288,424 metric tons (MT), spanning 323,419 hectares (ha) of agricultural areas.

Corn and rice comprised more than 92 percent of the total damage.

READ: Manila Water South Luzon steps up El Niño preparations

Article continues after this 

Among commodities, corn sustained P5.63 billion in losses, equivalent to 56.43 percent of the total. Damage to rice, on the other hand, was at P3.65 billion, accounting for 36.54 percent of the total.

Losses were also recorded in cassava, high-value crops and livestock and poultry.

Article continues after this 

The DA has set aside P18.64 billion worth of interventions to mitigate the adverse effects of El Niño, which is expected to reach its peak by year-end and persist until the first half of 2027.

These include P10.82 billion in farm inputs and P6.26 billion in financial assistance through the Presidential Assistance for Farmers and Fisherfolk Program, benefiting 2.69 million individuals.
