World.title: Police reviewing 'shocking' tasering of woman at Canberra bus stop
World.content:
Warning: This story contains footage that some readers may find distressing.

ACT Policing is reviewing a case in which officers tasered an Aboriginal woman with an intellectual impairment at a Canberra bus stop.

The woman is suing police over the interaction at Deakin in January, which was sparked by a report from a member of the public that she had a knife.

Body-worn camera footage, released to the ABC this week, shows her pleading with officers not to taser her and telling them she had not done anything wrong.

The woman was pulled to the ground, tasered in the back, handcuffed and put headfirst into the back of a police van.

In September, Special Magistrate Sean Richter criticised the conduct of police as "unwarranted and heavy-handed".

"I find it amazing that in this day and age the police reacted in the way that they did," he said.

A subsequent search of the woman's bag revealed she had two pairs of scissors, not a knife.

Deputy Chief Police Officer Richard Chin told 666 ABC Radio Canberra a review of the case was now underway.

"The comments of the magistrate certainly brought that to light for us to have a look at that issue," he said.

He said the officers involved were still on duty.

"I think we need to look into the circumstances in detail and look at the context as well, and we'll determine what happens from there," he said.

The woman is suing police over the arrest at Deakin. (ABC News: Ian Cutmore)

The incident has been condemned by First Nations leaders, with the Aboriginal Legal Service describing the footage as "shocking, but … something the public needs to see".

Assistant Commissioner Chin acknowledged the body-worn camera footage could be concerning for viewers.

"Policing … can result in difficult and confronting environments, and all kinds of incidents that we deal with can be quite difficult to watch and see and experience," he said.

"We want the best possible relations we can have with our First Nations community here in the ACT.

"We note the comments of the Special Magistrate ... weren't particularly positive in that regard.

"We'll certainly take that on board and have a look at how that fits into the context of the circumstances."

'It wasn't about race': AFP Association president

Australian Federal Police Association president Alex Caruana has defended the officers' conduct.

"To me it was very clear that she struck out at police officers first," Mr Caruana said.

"It wasn't about race, it wasn't about gender or anything like that.

"The information was that this person was carrying a knife, so police had to act decisively to make sure that the community was safe."

By the time the woman was sentenced in September, all but one of the charges against her — possessing a knife without a reasonable excuse — had been withdrawn.

Her subsequent lawsuit accuses police of assault and battery, breaching her human rights, and misfeasance in public office.

Police have not yet been required to file a defence.

World.title: Marrickville Golf Club says Anthony Albanese's membership worth $1,100
World.content:
Marrickville Golf Club's management says the honorary membership it gifted Prime Minister Anthony Albanese granted full access, putting its worth over $1,000, far more than the $5 social membership Mr Albanese claimed he was conferred.

The club's management also admitted the $6.05 million grant it was awarded by Mr Albanese was never intended to fund sewerage fixes, which are being done under a separate NSW grant.

Earlier this month, Mr Albanese conceded he was wrong when he told the House of Representatives that the grant he had promised the Marrickville Golf Club at the 2025 election was to stop septic tank sewage flooding into the river.

"When it floods in Marrickville, raw sewage flows into the Cooks River. That is what the funding is for," Mr Albanese told the House of Representatives in September.

General manager Mathew Ward, however, said sewerage upgrades were never part of the federal grant.

"I think that's basically correct … we were very optimistic about the prospects of the [NSW] grant. Certainly that was one of the leading issues we brought to [Mr Albanese's] electorate office," he said.

"It was not ultimately part of what was funded with the $6.05 million."

Anthony Albanese promised the Marrickville Golf Club $6.05 million at the 2025 federal election. (Supplied)

Mr Ward said the grant had come about after the club had approached Mr Albanese's electorate office with proposed fixes, and was invited in return to put forward other upgrade ideas it might have.

Mr Ward returned with a "bundle of ideas" in November 2024, which, beyond a $1 million stormwater harvesting upgrade, he said he had costed at $6.05 million based on "a bit of an educated guesstimate".

"[It was] purely my estimates based on a combination of my experience of renovations at golf clubs," Mr Ward said.

The general manager noted after the club had been invited to apply for that funding, it commissioned "very detailed" professional costings.

Club reveals honorary membership worth $1,100

Mr Albanese made the claims in the chamber that the grant was for sewerage fixes under scrutiny over his undisclosed honorary membership, revealed by the ABC.

The prime minister said that same day the membership was worth just $5 for two years.

"If anyone wants to join what is affectionately known as Royal Marrickville, what they need for two years' membership is $5," Mr Albanese told the House of Representatives.

"I don't have a card, I don't go in there, I haven't been in there for years."

The club's management said it had three membership types: a social membership worth $5 for two years, golfing membership worth $1,100 a year and honorary membership, which grants all the rights of a golfing member.

The conferral of Mr Albanese's honorary membership also led to the creation of a golfing account for him in national handicapping service GOLF Link, now Golf Australia CONNECT.

The club's management said Mr Albanese's membership had been entered into its database without accompanying public notification or acknowledgement by the board at the time.

"Conventionally you only give it to people who never use it," Mr Ward joked.

The prime minister has received golfing lessons from the Marrickville Golf Club's head professional, but the club confirmed there were no entries under his honorary membership since it was granted in 2012.

Mr Albanese wrote to the golf club to formally decline his membership following the ABC's report.

World.title: How Blues star has created unimpeachable legacy ahead of historic feat
World.content:
A player capable of doing extraordinary things on the football field, Darcy Vescio has never shied away from standing up for what they believe in off it.

And Vescio feels their football experience is richer for doing so.

The inaugural AFLW player will become the first Carlton star to reach 100 games in Saturday night's semifinal against Hawthorn at Princes Park.

Want to win an AFLW flag? Club culture matters, data shows AFL Players Association CEO James Gallagher says the gap between AFLW clubs getting workplace culture right is widening and the results can be seen on the field.

Vescio remains one of the league's most skilful and intelligent forwards and is highly respected by teammates and opponents.

The 33-year-old, who came out as non-binary in 2021, has proudly represented the LGBTIQ+ community and takes pride in their Chinese and Italian heritage.

Vescio has also played a pivotal role in the AFLW collective bargaining agreement negotiations over the years, helping drive the league's pay, conditions and professionalism forward.

"That adds, not weight, but it makes the footy experience a lot more rich," Vescio said.

"I love the game and every challenge that that brings, physically and mentally.

"But when you can extrapolate further and see the way you can shape things and push the game into a better space and I guess impact different communities who might not have always seen themselves in footy, for me, that adds to my experience of being a human playing footy.

Darcy Vescio sees their role as more than just a football player despite 100 AFLW games. (Getty: Kelly Defina)

"From the outside, it can be tempting to just want footy players to just focus on footy. But the reality is when you step out onto the field, you're a fully formed human with a brain and with things going on in your life.

"So if you're able to, I guess, service all areas of yourself whilst playing footy, it just makes it feel like a lot more worthwhile experience."

Vescio overcame calf issues earlier in the season in time to reach the 100-game milestone this year.

"It's not a milestone I ever imagined I'd be able to celebrate. So it feels really special," Vescio said.

Vescio, who has just re-signed for 2027, hopes the game continues to grow and credits their longevity to an eagerness to adapt to the AFLW's ever-improving and evolving standards.

Darcy Vescio is the first Carlton player to reach 100 AFLW games. (Getty Images: Michael Willson)

"It's been something that's kept me really engaged with playing footy, the fact that you have to keep evolving with the game," Vescio said.

"Every few years we see a real step up in the way the game's played, and it is constantly shifting.

"I enjoy the challenge of trying to keep up with the game, and it gets better and better to be part of."

Carlton lost its qualifying final to North Melbourne but will be looking to reclaim its home-ground advantage against Hawthorn.

"You want [opposition] people to not feel welcome when they come here," Vescio said.

"Even heading into last week's game … [North Melbourne star Ashleigh] Riddell was very public in saying she loves playing at Ikon Park because they've built great memories here and they're really home here.

"So that's something we do want to wrestle back."

AAP

World.title: 'I had to have it': Boag's worker wins auction for last Tasmanian brew
World.content:
The final Tasmanian-brewed James Boag beer has sold for $1,300, as the brewery that predates electricity in the state closes its doors.

Former brewery electrician Sam Cox, who spent 14 years working at the Launceston institution, has become the proud owner of the final can and case of locally brewed Boag's Red.

"I've always been a fairly strong believer in Boag's Red, love the brand, great drop," he told ABC Northern Tasmania.

" Being the last carton, I had to have it. "

The case has the message 'last Tassie carton' printed on its side. (ABC News: Georgia Hogge)

A case of Boag's Red retails for about $70.

In 2024, parent company Lion shifted production of James Boag to the mainland, but Tasmania's supply continued to be brewed locally.

In June, it announced the Launceston brewery would close, due to a long-term decline in Australia's beer market, forcing it to operate at about one-fifth of its capacity, and making operations unviable.

The James Boag Brewery was established in 1881. (Facebook: James Boag Brewery Experience)

After 145 years, the brewery bottled its final beers in Launceston last month, and shut last week.

Mr Cox bought the prized "Ruby Tubes" or "Red Tins" at a Boag's Alumni Day, coming out on top in a bidding war with the band performing at the event.

"When I heard that they were going to put their whole set's worth of money on the carton, I walked up to them and I said: 'Going to have to have deep pockets, boys,'" he said.

Sam Cox outbid the band playing at the alumni day for the last case. (ABC News: Georgia Hogge)

Sentimental purchase, no plans to sell

Despite his appreciation for the beer, Mr Cox said he would not be drinking it, instead putting the memorabilia on prime display.

"It'll be in my house, in the lounge room," he said.

"I've got good security cameras, so watch out."

Sam Cox's 'Final Pour' shirt commemorates the closure of Boag's Brewery. (ABC News: Georgia Hogge)

The Tasmanian history comes with a signed certificate of authenticity from the brewery's director, Michael Stylianou.

Mr Cox believed his purchase had already gone up in value, and would continue to, but said its value to him was sentimental.

The last carton came with a certificate of authenticity. (ABC News: Georgia Hogge)

"I won't be getting rid of it," he said.

" It would have to be a ridiculous amount of money ... it'd have to be over $10,000. "

New tattoo to go with auction win

Sam Cox got a tattoo to commemorate the end of the brewery. (Supplied)

Mr Cox said it felt "awesome" to be one of the final workers, and has paid tribute to "the final 44" through a tattoo of the James Boag logo against a Cradle Mountain backdrop, with the years of operation.

He said it had "been going pretty viral" online.

"We're like a little family," he said.

"I'm hopefully that the mainland breweries can replicate what we used to make.

World.title: AFP officers forced to flee Türkiye over crime boss threats
World.content:
Two Australian Federal Police (AFP) officers had to be relocated from their posts in Türkiye over safety concerns after targeting a high-profile Australian crime boss.

The former fugitive, who cannot be named, was considered one of the nation's most-wanted men and a major global crime figure when he was eventually captured in 2022.

According to a statement tendered in an unrelated case, two officers posted to Ankara had to be temporarily relocated after working to capture the underworld identity.

Superintendent Marie Andersson (right). (Supplied: Australian Federal Police)

"AFP has received information raising concerns around safety and security of AFP members at Ankara Post," Superintendent Marie Andersson said in a statement.

"An assessment of further information led to the decision to relocate two AFP members … and their families out of Türkiye until a security assessment and implementation of recommended security measures could be conducted."

The AFP officers spent six weeks in another country before it was deemed safe for them to return to their overseas post in Türkiye.

The officers who helped capture the crime boss spent weeks in hiding over safety concerns. (Supplied: Australian Federal Police)

The nature of the threats they faced after the crime figure was deported to Australia was not elaborated on.

The operation to return the crime figure back to Australia came at the height of the AFP's focus on an offshore crime group dubbed the "Aussie Cartel".

The group had set up shop in Istanbul and spent the better part of a decade on the run from Australian authorities.

Police suspect the "cartel" is responsible for large-scale drug shipments into Australia and operates a network of contacts from Asia to Europe.

Documents reveal cartel's Istanbul hideout

Mr Zakaria argues the AFP broke the law in having him deported to Sydney in 2023. (ABC News)

The statement and its details emerged as part of accused Sydney gangster Masood Zakaria's attempt to have two gangland murder charges thrown out of court.

Mr Zakaria wants his case dismissed over claims he was illegally deported to Australia when the AFP paid Skytraders and Hart International $1 million to return him in 2023.

Superintendent Andersson was called to give evidence by Mr Zakaria last week over her role in his deportation and denied any wrongdoing in the operation to return him in 2023.

Her statement, tendered to court this week, has provided a glimpse into the milieu of Australian fugitives who called Istanbul home at the time.

At the head of the criminal conglomerate, Superintendent Andersson said, was former Sydney bikie Hakan Ayik, who is facing the prospect of spending 262 years in a Turkish jail after his arrest there.

Alleged drug lord Ayik, dubbed the 'Facebook gangster' over his social media antics while on the run. (Facebook)

The ABC previously revealed Ayik and his cousin Hakan Arif led the global crime syndicate, which was worth billions, while in hiding from police in Istanbul.

Superintendent Andersson's statement claimed that, at the time, the pair were among several "high value targets" for the AFP in Türkiye.

"We suspect most of these organised crime targets were associates of or had been provided contact points to the Hakan Ayik and Hakan Arif network in Istanbul," the statement said.

The Istanbul hideout: Secret files expose Australia's underworld empire offshore Istanbul was once the hideout of choice for Australian crooks. Now a Sydney gangster's legal challenge has revealed how it all unravelled for the "Aussie Cartel".

Lawyers for the AFP initially fought to keep the details about the pair secret, but on Thursday they abandoned their request for a non-publication order.

Hakan Ayik's criminal empire eventually came crashing down in 2021 when he was revealed to have unwittingly passed on AFP-bugged phones to associates.

The operation, dubbed the AN0M sting, was followed by his arrest by Turkish police on drug and money laundering offences.

World.title: What is in Usman Khawaja's book Sabr and what did he actually say about Sandpapergate?
World.content:
Usman Khawaja's revelations about the sandpaper scandal have reopened a massive rift in Australian cricket: who knew what? Who's lying? Who's telling the truth.

Much of the problem lies in the ambiguity of language that Khawaja has used in his interviews and moreover in his newly release autobiography, Sabr, which he is now publicising.

When Khawaja told the Nine newspapers that "It was all of us. Not the batters, not the bowlers, not the staff. All of us," what exactly did he mean?

Was he inferring that the entire team knew about the plot to sandpaper a cricket ball during the third Test in Cape Town in 2018?

Cameron Bancroft was banned for nine months and Steve Smith for a year for their roles in the sandpaper scandal. (Photo by Ashley Vlotman/Gallo Images/Getty Images) (Getty Images: Ashley Vlotman)

That clearly is how most of Australia understood that statement.

Or was he saying that everyone in the Australian set-up needed to take responsibility?

We don't know and that is because of Khawaja's deliberate attempts to not name names as he told Sarah Ferguson on 730 this week, "it's never been for me about pointing fingers."

"This is my story," he wrote in his book.

Loading...

But what is clearly inferred from the book is that even if he wasn't pointing fingers at individuals, the knowledge of the ball tampering was widespread and discussed within the team and on the field.

So, what exactly is in Khawaja's book?

The sandpaper chapter is dedicated to three players who were banned for their involvement in the incident, then captain, Steve Smith, Cameron Bancroft and "my childhood friend David Warner".

"The truth will set you free," he wrote.

The set-up happened before the first test in Durban when he alleges a member of the coaching staff told the team: "I don't care what you have to do, or how, but we need to get it moving in the air."

The Australians celebrate the final wicket of the first Test in Durban in 2018. (Getty Images: Lee Warren/Gallo Images)

"It was so much harder to bat when the ball was moving in the air, particularly when it was reverse swinging. "We had to keep doing what all of us had been doing for years in domestic and international cricket: finding a way to make it go reverse. "We were all complicit. "Reverse swing on those older, flatter Test wickets was how you won matches, come day four and five."

The first reference to sandpaper in the chapter comes in reference to the size of the change rooms during the South Africa series.

"Of course I bloody knew what was happening with the sandpaper. "There wasn't much in those small change-rooms that got past me. It was a room full of banter and it was very hard to hide anything. Let alone when you used sandpaper on the ball and it would leave these huge swirl marks on it."

Sandpaper, he explains, is readily available in cricket change rooms, because batters use it to clean up their bats.

On day two of the second test at Port Elizabeth (now Gqeberha), he described an experiment to use sandpaper on a cricket ball.

Steve Smith and David Warner appeal for a wicket during the second Test of the series. (Getty Images: Ashley Vlotman/Gallo Images)

"What we saw was unbelievable. The ball was completely dry and extremely scuffed on the side we'd sandpapered. There was no way it wouldn't reverse if we bowled with it. Everyone had a look at the ball and was laughing their heads off."

He wrote that a plan was hatched to sandpaper the ball in the Test immediately after breaks in play when the umpire would drop the ball on the boundary before the players went onto the field.

Cameron Bancroft offered to do the deed, because David Warner was conscious that the TV cameras were focused on him.

Khawaja recounted Bancroft saying: "No worries — it'll be easy."

"At this stage, Steve Smith put his hands up and said, 'I don't want to know about anything about this,' and walked out of the room."

Smith used almost the exact same words to describe his actions in a press conference during his subsequent one-year ban.

Nevertheless, the plan went ahead as Khawaja described in his book.

Australia cut through the South African batters after Cameron Bancroft had taken to the ball with sandpaper. (Getty Images: Ashley Vlotman/Gallo Images)

"The next session, we absolutely went through the South Africans. Bangers (Bancroft) had walked on the field after the break, picked up the ball that the umpires had left on the field, and given it a few twists and turns. The ball came up a treat. The shiny side was shiny and the buffed and, thanks to the sandpaper, the reverse side was really rough and dry. "Every time during that session the ball was passed to me at gully, I'd take a look and think, wow, even I could reverse swing this ball. It was ridiculous. The bowlers went to work and bowled beautifully. Reversing it around corners. We got four wickets for 28 runs. "It was moving so much that, at one point, one of the bowlers said in the huddle after a wicket, 'Guys, it's going heaps now. Just don't do anything else to it, because it's silly how much it's going'.

Khawaja doesn't name the bowlers who took the four wicket in the book, but the scoreboard shows Mitchell Marsh took two, while Josh Hazlewood and Mitchell Starc took one each.

Even so, Australia lost the test. Khawaja claimed that the South African bowlers were reverse swinging the ball "everywhere", starting after about 21 overs.

"We didn't know what they were doing with the ball — all we knew was that they were better than us at getting it go reverse. And we were using sandpaper!"

Come the third test at Cape Town, drizzle was making the ball wet and hard to swing.

Khawaja described a member of the coaching staff approaching Bancroft who he was sitting next to.

"Bangers, whatever you're doing, we need more of it. It's wet out there — we just need more of it," Khawaja says the coach said.

Khawaja wrote the sandpaper helped take the wet surface layer off the ball, making it dry and more conducive to reverse swing.

It was the next session when the infamous shots of Bancroft trousering a small yellow sliver of sandpaper were broadcast on the big screen at Newlands.

Bancroft, he wrote, was "catatonic".

Cameron Bancroft was called over by the umpires after being caught with the sandpaper. (Gallo Images via Getty: Ashley Vlotman)

"Every one of the boys on the field was shitting themselves."

Khawaja wrote it was after the game he had a conversation with the team manager, Gavin Dovey.

"We need to cop this as a team. We did it as a team, so we cop it as a team. "[Dovey] said I was right but that two guys in the team disagreed."

During a subsequent team meeting, Khawaja wrote he expressed the same view that the entire team should accept responsibility.

"There was silence when I said that. Most of the guys agreed, but Painey (Steve Smith's replacement as captain, Tim Paine) knew not everyone felt that way. And so, my idea fell flat."

Khawaja concludes the chapter saying: "I can only speak for myself, and it's very clear I knew what was going on."

Khawaja wants the rest of us to draw our own conclusions.

World.title: Disability funding changes labelled 'a win for every dodgy provider'
World.content:
As people with disability adjust to the biggest-ever cuts to the National Disability Insurance Scheme (NDIS), longstanding advocacy organisations supporting them through the change are now facing their own funding reductions.

The end of this month will see the decades-old government program that funds disability advocacy organisations replaced with a new one.

Several longstanding organisations across multiple states have been told by the Department of Health they will not be part of the new funding process.

What is a disability advocacy organisation? Read more Read more Disability advocates help people navigate systems such as the NDIS, health, guardianship and housing.

They also help people understand and challenge decisions that affect them, including cuts to NDIS plans.

They are generally non-profit organisations and are separate to service providers, which deliver services in exchange for money.

One of those organisations, Villamanta Disability Rights Legal Service in regional Victoria, said it was now losing 30 per cent of its total funding, with the "immediate and significant" impact to result in job losses and a dramatic reduction in the support available to people with disability.

CEO Annie Nash said it meant Villamanta could no longer accept new clients at a time of unprecedented demand made worse in recent months by widespread cuts to the NDIS.

"This is a win for every dodgy provider unlawfully evicting an NDIS participant from their home," she said.

"It is a win for every person using guardianship or administration powers to commit family violence against a person with disability.

"It is a win for every disability service that has caused a loss to an NDIS participant or is pursuing them for an unlawful debt."

Disability advocates help people fight a range of things including cuts to NDIS plans and guardianship determinations. (ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke)

Ms Nash said the decision was difficult to understand given a review carried out by the Department of Health in March recognised Villamanta as a leader in the sector that provided an "invaluable service".

"So many of our supporters have come out in the last 24 hours … We're getting inundated because we're trusted, we're respected and we provide high-quality support," she said.

Disability Advocacy Network Australia acting CEO, Cherry Baylosis, said the changes were "out of touch" with what people with disability needed right now and many advocates were already unable to keep up with demand.

She said many advocates were a lifeline for people, assisting them through difficult times such as hospital visits and finding emergency accommodation.

"Advocates are the person who will stand in somebody's corner … without that we can expect to see people navigating a crisis without appropriate support," Ms Baylosis said.

"It means people are potentially going to be left on their own … or responsibility will be placed on families and carers who are often already overrun".

The Department of Health did not directly answer questions about how many advocates had lost funding or whether the reallocation of funds was made strategically to prevent people with disability from seeking support.

In a statement, a spokesperson said the new funding model was in response to disability royal commission recommendations.

"Up to $184 million (GST exclusive) was available over six financial years (2026–27 to 2031–32)," they said.

"The open competitive grant opportunity allowed both existing and new advocacy organisations to demonstrate the capabilities required to deliver the new program."

The spokesperson said organisations with funding under the current model would continue to receive it until February 2027 to support the transition to the new program.

The advocacy sector says many organisations have been unable to meet the demand for their services for a long time. (ABC News: Billy Cooper)

The Albanese government's overhaul of the now more-than $50 billion NDIS is expected to see 240,000 participants removed from the scheme over the next four years, saving more than $38 billion.

Cuts to a category of funding allowing participants to pay for therapies and another for support workers to take them to appointments, work and social activities, began on October 1.

The NDIS, which now supports more than 782,000 participants, has been growing at 10.5 per cent per year.

That is about half the rate it was when Labor was elected in 2022, but the Albanese government hopes its changes will help slow the scheme's growth to its target of 2 or 3 per cent per year.

World.title: Beau Lamarre-Condon trial live updates: Accused double murderer, former NSW Police officer returns to witness box after judge sends jury home due to ‘unexpected issue’
World.content:
Warning: Graphic content

Hello and welcome to our live coverage of Beau Lamarre-Condon’s double murder trial in the NSW Supreme Court in Sydney.

Yesterday’s hearing was cut short after Justice Natalie Adams told the 15-person jury about 12.30pm that “an issue has arisen unexpectedly”. They were told to return at 10am today and there was a short delay before the hearing resumed.

A court sketch of Beau Lamarre-Condon during his testimony last week. Rocco Fazzari

“These things happen in trials all the time, as you’ve probably learnt by now,” the judge said yesterday.

The accused returns to the witness box today for further cross-examination by Crown prosecutor Brett Hatfield, SC.

The former NSW police officer has pleaded not guilty to two counts of murder over the deaths of Jesse Baird, 26, a former TV presenter, and Luke Davies, 29, a Qantas flight attendant. There is no dispute that the men died of gunshot wounds from his police-issued pistol on February 19, 2024, and that the accused disposed of the bodies on February 22, 2024.

The Crown alleges that Lamarre-Condon planned to kill Baird after developing an obsessive and jealous infatuation with him and that he killed Davies, Baird’s boyfriend, to eliminate a witness to his crime.

The defence case is that Lamarre-Condon acted in self-defence after entering Baird’s Paddington share house dressed as an Uber Eats rider to collect some of his possessions after Baird ended their non-exclusive relationship in November 2023. He said he struck upon the idea for the disguise that morning as a way to ensure Baird did not accuse him of harassment, and he thought nobody was home.

Lamarre-Condon said he shot Baird once to disarm him after Baird lunged at him with a knife and a second shot through his head was accidental. He says that Davies accidentally shot himself after grabbing the gun.

The 31-year-old accused has told the court he had his police pistol with him because he had contemplated taking his own life the previous night over work-related trauma.

He has given the following evidence over three days of cross-examination:

Lamarre-Condon has denied executing Baird and said he stood by his decision to fire the first shot. He said he was responsible for Baird’s death but did not intend to kill him.

He has also denied stalking Baird before his death, including when he saw the then TV presenter having sex with another man while standing outside his bedroom window after the men broke up for the first time in April 2023. He said he was there to collect some belongings.

The men had met in Sydney in October 2022, the court has heard, and their relationship was not exclusive, but the accused said they started going on “romantic dates” in December that year. The men resumed contact briefly around August or September 2023, after their first break-up, before Baird ended the relationship permanently in November 2023.

Lamarre-Condon rejected a suggestion by the prosecution that he was obsessed with Baird “right from the start”. “Smitten, yes. Obsessed, no,” the accused said.

The accused admitted he invaded Baird’s privacy and went through his phone on two occasions, in March and April 2023.

He denied breaking into Baird’s home on August 17, 2023. The court has heard he messaged one friend in the aftermath of the alleged incident that Baird had “a home invasion”. He said that he panicked and ran out of Baird’s home with the TV presenter’s phone and wallet after Baird woke up while he was attempting to take the phone outside to go through his messages.

The accused told the court he entered the home using a key that Baird left out for him that night, but put a bobby pin in the lock of the door to give the impression someone else had been in the house in case Baird woke up while he was looking through the phone outside. The Crown case is that he used a key he had stolen or had copied, an allegation he denied.

After being shown a screenshot of a text message he sent Baird on the day of the alleged break-in, in which he wrote, “Haha I’ll take that as a no to doing the catch up then”, Lamarre-Condon said he communicated with Baird on other platforms including FaceTime and social media.

He agreed that a friend had called him “Bobby P” in a joke referring to him putting the bobby pin in the door.

He rejected Hatfield’s suggestion that it appealed to him that Baird was a TV presenter. “Jesse Baird could have been a garbage cleaner,” he said. “We actually never really talked much about his work. I wasn’t really interested in that, to be honest.”

He also denied that he had misrepresented the nature of his relationship with Baird in a video he made of them on a farm stay holiday in March 2023.

Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic Family Violence Counselling Service at 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732), the Men’s Referral Service on 1300 766 491, and Lifeline on 13 11 14.

Another industrial relations manager at major contractor John Holland has told the Big Build royal commission the company believed it needed to show an ability to work with the CFMEU in Victoria more so than any other jurisdiction thanks to the union’s close relationship with the state Labor government.

Trent Smith, the second witness to appear today, said the CFMEU was “more militant” in Victoria and Queensland but the company felt it needed to maintain a good relationship with the union pushed into the civil construction sector.

Commissioner Chris Kourkais asked: “Was it a view linked to a particular government that is party politically linked?”

Smith replied: “It was more so in Victoria that we thought we needed to demonstrate an ability to work with the CFMEU, absolutely. But it did play out in Queensland as well.”

The commission has now adjourned for lunch and will return just after 2pm.

World.title: ‘He’s grounded for life’: Teen survives six days in bush on chips and water
World.content:
Breaking NationalVictoriaMissing person ‘He’s grounded for life’: Teen survives six days in bush on chips and water Hannah Hammoud November 12, 2026 — 1:05pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

A missing Morwell teenager has been found alive after an incredible six-day ordeal in the bush, surviving on little more than a packet of chips and water after falling down a cliff and becoming trapped. Seventeen-year-old William, known as Will, was rescued following a six-day search, with his relieved mother revealing he escaped with just sunburn and a few scratches – but could now face a lifetime grounding. William hugs his mother after being rescued by police helicopter. Victoria Police His mother, Elizabeth Barkley, said her son was in “good health and good spirits” despite spending almost a week stranded in the bush. “He fell off a bit of a cliff and couldn’t move. So he just stayed there and waited,” she said.



Will was last seen near Stoney Creek Road, close to T2 Track, at about 4pm on Friday, November 6, while camping with another teenager for the weekend. Police said he had walked a short distance to another part of the campsite. When he failed to return, his friend searched the surrounding area but was unable to find him. Police said the air wing were conducting an aerial search of the Cowwarr area on Thursday when they spotted a tackle box in bushland about two kilometres east of Stoney Creek. Zooming in on the tackle box, they found William lying down close by in a creek. “Flight officers winched down and retrieved Will before bringing him back to the command post to reunite with his mum,” police said in a statement.



“Amazingly, William is in good spirits and for the most part, in good health. He was taken to hospital for monitoring.” Barkley, who lives about 40 minutes from the search area in Morwell, said she was waiting as emergency services prepared their next search area when she received the news her son had been found alive. The 17-year-old was last seen near Stoney Creek Road on November 6. Victoria Police “They came in and told me and I waited outside until the helicopter landed, and I saw him wave as he came out,” she said. “I never gave up hope, I knew in my heart he was still alive, and I just prayed to God for a miracle, and a miracle happened. So as soon as that helicopter landed, and they got him off I gave him the biggest hug.”



While Barkley was still unsure exactly how far her son had fallen, she understood he had remained in the same spot, unable to move, until rescuers finally reached him. Will was taken to hospital for further checks, with his mother making it clear that while she was overjoyed to have him home safe, his camping adventures might be on hold for quite some time. “He is now going to the hospital to get checked out, and after that, he’s grounded for life. Never leaving my sight again,” she said. Be the first to know when major news happens.

World.title: Dalaroo fires up diamond drill hunt for African gold riches
World.content:

Dalaroo Metals is about to fire up the diamond rigs at its Bondoukou Gold Ridge project in Côte d’Ivoire, chasing up a substantial high-grade gold discovery made at the project last month. The company says an initial five-hole, 1750-metre program will test the down-dip and along-strike extensions of mineralisation at its Wilfred target, where fresh results have since reinforced the maiden discovery and confirmed its high-grade hits as no flash in the pan. Core yard pad under construction at Dalaroo Metals’ Bondoukou Gold Ridge project in Côte d’Ivoire. The initial discovery came from two opposing maiden holes drilled to more than 200m. One returned a standout 18m at 7.31 grams per tonne (g/t) gold from 63m, including a second zone of 16m at 1.46g/t, while the other delivered a solid 23m at 2.14g/t gold from surface. The new diamond holes will test for mineralisation down to 350m, pushing well beyond the depths reached by earlier reverse-circulation (RC) drilling.



Adding to the excitement, Dalaroo has also hit a second, significant shallow zone of mineralisation 1.25km north of the original Wilfred discovery, pointing to the potential for a much bigger system emerging at Bondoukou. The company says it is planning a staged approach to the new round of exploration, with initial step-out holes staged in 80m strike extensions from known mineralisation. If a step-out hole is successful, another will be drilled 80m further out to define the limits of the gold-bearing structure. A second diamond rig is expected on site by the end of this month to begin follow-up drilling at the northern discovery zone, with Dalaroo hopeful it can connect the two discoveries across a major structural ridge. The company says after completing its current RC orientation program, it will use diamond rigs for all subsequent drilling. Core from diamond drilling will then provide crucial structural information on the geometry and orientation of its mineralisation to guide all future drilling. Dalaroo has linked up with experienced drilling contractor Easy Drill for an estimated 20,000m of diamond drilling and two rigs at a time when rig availability in the booming West African nation is at a premium. In a move to preserve its cash, Dalaroo has structured the deal to pay for the drilling with 50 per cent cash and 50 per cent shares, although it can elect to pay a greater portion in cash.



Dalaroo appears well-funded for the campaign, with roughly $2 million in the bank and a massive 263 million in-the-money options outstanding, potentially tipping a further $13.54 million into its coffers if exercised. The timing of the company’s drilling campaign looks impeccable, set against a booming gold industry backdrop and government support in Côte d’Ivoire. The nation’s gold production has skyrocketed from 13 tonnes in 2012 to a forecast 62 tonnes this year, with the government positioning to become Africa’s biggest gold producer by 2035. This has fuelled a rush of exploration investment, which surged 82 per cent last year to US$186 million (A$272 million). With a high-grade discovery in the bag and a second zone 1.25km away, Dalaroo’s Bondoukou Gold Ridge project has the makings of something big. If Wilfred can connect up along strike and keep going at depth, things could heat up very quickly. Is your ASX-listed company doing something interesting? Contact: mattbirney@bullsnbears.com.au

World.title: Downfall of world’s chipmaker-in-chief a potential headache for Beijing as well as US
World.content:
Analysis WorldAsiaChina relations Downfall of world’s chipmaker-in-chief a potential headache for Beijing as well as US Lisa Visentin November 12, 2026 — 12:51pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Beijing: We will probably never know if Jensen Huang’s swagger, connections and status as the world’s chipmaker-in-chief would have been enough to save him from the blast radius of an affair with an alleged spy. The emergence of a second extramarital affair looks poised to sink the Nvidia boss. The company is reportedly preparing to cut him loose. It would be an act of almost self-decapitation. Huang built Nvidia from the ground up over three decades into one of the world’s most valuable companies, through which he commanded enormous influence over the unfolding tech revolution and frenzied race between the US and China. Inside Nvidia, he concentrated power in his leadership with 60 executives reporting directly to him. There is no succession plan.



The emergence of a second extramarital affair looks poised to sink Nvidia boss Jensen Huang. Bloomberg His apparent downfall leaves a question mark not just over Nvidia’s future direction, but US chip policy more broadly. In Washington, Huang has been a forceful lobbyist for giving China access to some less-advanced Nvidia chips, arguing that keeping Beijing hooked on US technology would slow the development of its own high-powered domestic chip industry. Related Article Inside China Trump may have just helped turbocharge China’s military National security hawks loathed the deal he cut with US President Donald Trump last year to sell Nvidia’s powerful H200 chips to China in exchange for the US government taking a 25 per cent cut. They would toast his defenestration.



In Beijing, too, some would rue the departure of a tech titan whose corporate interests in making the world dependent on Nvidia aligned with their own. “Although we compete against China, they are not our enemies,” Huang told Bloomberg in a recent interview where he criticised US chip restrictions. Would Nvidia’s next chief executive take the same line? Either way, ousting Huang will not stem the tide of scrutiny coming Nvidia’s way. The company faces multiple investigations into whether its chief’s affair has exposed it to a foreign intelligence plot, and whether Nvidia did enough to stop its chips from allegedly being smuggled into China. The spy scandal



For a spy scandal in the digital age, the plot is strikingly analogue. In this photo, posted to Weibo, Jensen Huang and Alice Huang dine at a Shanghai restaurant. A powerful tech billionaire with a direct line to the president has apparently been compromised, not by a sophisticated cyberespionage operation or a malevolent team of AI super-agents, but by the age-old trope of sleeping with the enemy. Related Article Updated

Technology & democracy ‘I was unfaithful to my wife’: Nvidia boss admits to affair with suspected Chinese spy For all the salacious speculation of a Beijing-orchestrated honeypot scandal, there are many missing details about the woman at the centre of it, Chinese data company executive Alice Huang (no relation).



The New York Times, which broke the initial story, reported that US agencies suspected she was recruited by China’s Ministry of State Security (MSS) and used her affair with Huang to funnel information back to Beijing. Anonymous sources cited in media reports have not leaked what evidence the US gathered or the nature of Huang’s suspected ties to the MSS, and neither Nvidia nor its founder appear to have been told about them. But there were enough red flags in Alice Huang’s background for both to be more curious. Do US authorities believe she was an MSS operative carrying out a calculated intelligence-gathering agenda, or a savvy businesswoman whose genuine closeness to Huang the agency sought to exploit? Several China analysts think the latter is more likely. Jensen Huang has had easy and regular access to US President Donald Trump. Bloomberg



More importantly, what did China potentially gain? It’s hard to overstate Nvidia’s role as the American company at the apex of US-China tech rivalry, and the role of Jensen Huang as its founder in influencing artificial intelligence policy. Nvidia’s advanced chips, which China cannot yet match, are key to the US maintaining its lead in AI and its edge across a range of fields, including high-tech weapons systems. Related Article Technology & democracy Who is Alice Huang? The suspected Chinese spy at the centre of the Nvidia scandal Needless to say, it is a huge coup for the MSS if it has cultivated an agent who was in close contact with the Nvidia chief.



“This is a counter-intelligence nightmare,” says Ryan Fedasiuk, a former US State Department official, now at the Foundation for American Innovation. Two parts of Alice Huang’s role are under scrutiny. First, her business dealings as a former top executive at Megaspeed, a little-known Singapore-based data centre company that somehow amassed funds to buy $US4.8 billion ($7 billion) of Nvidia equipment, purportedly for its data centres in South-East Asia. These third-country transfers are not illegal under US chip export controls, but US investigators are examining whether Megaspeed exploited them to smuggle restricted AI chips into China. Related Article Analysis

China relations Beijing gets ready to welcome Putin and ‘lame duck’ Trump Fedasiuk says the affair has overshadowed what should be a focus on the actions Nvidia may have taken on behalf of Megaspeed, after it emerged that Nvidia’s general counsel sought to intervene in a US government probe into the Chinese company.



“This was the CEO of the largest company in the world having a covert relationship with his customer, and not only producing a potential conflict of interest in that, but actually using the conflict of interest in terms favourable to the customer,” Fedasiuk says. “And unfortunately, that customer is alleged to be a Chinese intelligence asset on top of it all.” As China analyst Bill Bishop speculated, a good relationship with Jensen Huang “likely meant more chips for the Megaspeed front company and the entities back in the PRC to which those chips flowed,” he posted on X. Second, what kind of sensitive information could Alice Huang have been privy to, including via so-called “pillow talk”, that may now be in the hands of Chinese intelligence? ‘He’s China’s lifeline when it comes to artificial intelligence; Nvidia chips are really indispensable for China’s AI development.’ Alex Joske, managing director at Garnaut Global, a China-focused risk advisory firm.



Jensen Huang has had easy and frequent access to Trump. This continued after Trump was briefed about the suspected spy scandal twice, most recently in May while en route to his Beijing summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping. The Nvidia boss joined him on that summit. Did Alice Huang seek to influence his lobbying efforts, or pass updates to Chinese intelligence? Did he confide in her confidential information about Nvidia’s corporate plans or even his conversations with Trump? Some of these details may be shaken out in upcoming investigations, including when Jensen Huang is called before Congress to answer questions at a closed-door meeting later this month. The FBI is also investigating, while Nvidia has launched its own internal probe. Jensen Huang admitted the affair in an email memo to Nvidia staff. NYT Under Xi, the MSS has risen in status, resourcing, and prowess and has prioritised artificial intelligence operations as it seeks to close in on the US’s lead, says Alex Joske, an analyst who specialises in Chinese influence operations.



“Jensen Huang ticks every box from the perspective of Chinese intelligence services,” says Joske, who is managing director at risk advisory firm Garnaut Global. “He’s got top-level political access, and his company is at the heart of the most important technological feud in US-China competition. “He’s China’s lifeline when it comes to artificial intelligence; Nvidia chips are really indispensable for China’s AI development.” The Nvidia boss maintains he was unaware his lover was an alleged spy. We know this because he told Trump this week, who relayed it to reporters, proving the scandal hasn’t ended his direct access to the president. The Chinese Foreign Ministry has dismissed the allegations as “totally unfounded” smears.



Beijing had been hoping it could ride out the remaining two years of Trump’s presidency on the uneasy detente both sides had secured. But this explosion is poised to unite Democrats and Republicans angry at Nvidia’s influence and Trump’s softening on China in a campaign to further strangle Beijing’s access to backdoor chips. It adds to swirling atmospherics at next week’s APEC summit, when Trump and Xi will meet for the third time this year. This time, though, don’t expect Jensen Huang to secure a seat on Air Force One. World.title: Adidas to open first Australian airport store in Brisbane
World.content:
Exclusive NationalQueenslandBrisbane Airport Adidas to open first Australian airport store in Brisbane Cameron Atfield November 12, 2026 — 12:43pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Global sportswear giant Adidas will open its first Australian airport store at Brisbane Airport – one of more than a dozen new and refurbished retailers at both terminals as part of the $5 billion Future BNE project. Brisbane Airport commercial executive manager Scott Norris said the businesses would complement the overhaul of the terminals’ dining offering. “Passengers travelling through Brisbane Airport will soon enjoy an upgraded shopping experience, with a mix of convenience stores, big-name brands and travel essentials coming to our terminals as part of our ongoing transformation,” he said. The new Relay store at Brisbane International opened this week. Brisbane Airport “The addition of these outlets will boost the retail offering at Brisbane Airport, giving a record number of passengers more choice and greater convenience at every step of their journey.”



Speaking at a business breakfast at the airport on Thursday, Brisbane Airport chief executive Gert-Jan de Graaf said passengers could expect to see retail construction for “another year or so” for this round of improvement, but he expected more up to and beyond the 2032 Olympic and Paralympic Games. “An airport is always ready, but never completed,” he said. “...[It will be a] fantastic new experience for all travellers. “There’s work in progress – there’s still a lot of hoarding up – but in the next couple of weeks, you will see quite a lot of it coming down.”



New outlets planned for Terminal 1, the international terminal, include Rip Curl, Sunglass Hut, an UGG store and souvenir outlet Discover Australia, which opened its doors this week, and premium fashion and luggage boutique The Edit. A new Adidas store is on the way for Brisbane Airport’s domestic terminal. Bloomberg Three of five new Relay stores, selling travel essentials, have already opened at the international terminal and the existing Lotte Duty Free footprint was set to double in size. To cater for arriving international passengers, Telsim and Optus will offer telecommunications services in the arrivals hall, while Prosegur Change Currency Exchange has opened its permanent shopfront after operating pop-up kiosks since late last year. Over at the domestic Terminal 2, the Adidas shop was expected to open early next year.



Related Article Brisbane Airport New Brisbane Airport flightpath plan offers noise breaks for 482,000 Joining the German sportswear giant would be chocolatier Koko Black, Hairhouse and another UGG store. All new retail outlets, apart from The Edit, were being progressively delivered through to 2027. The Edit and the Lotte Duty Free expansion planned to be progressively delivered until 2029. World.title: The Devil Wears Prada had Miranda Priestly. I Love Boosters goes one better
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

There has to be a hellzapoppin’ party going on inside Boots Riley’s head, right? Anyone who saw the filmmaker-cum-rapper’s anti-capitalist satire, Sorry to Bother You, is probably still dazed by its hotchpotch of barbs about telemarketing, the horny version of Siri dirty-talking everyone in the telemarketers’ executive lift and a climactic rebellion led by people with the heads of horses. But Boots wasn’t finished: hell, no. So here he is again with I Love Boosters, in which a vibrant girl gang of career shoplifters joins forces with Chinese sweatshop workers via a teleporter in the shape of a toilet seat. Demi Moore, having been so gloriously reborn in The Substance, plays a fashion maven called Christie Smith so mean she makes Miranda Priestly look like Maria von Trapp. And if you fancy a lovelorn demon who sucks out women’s souls during oral sex, he’s here in the comely person of LaKeith Stanfield. A ton of stuff is going on. Demi Moore as Christie Smith in I Love Boosters. Maslow Films Oakland, the culturally diverse city north of San Francisco where Boots Riley has lived all his 55 years, has always had its boosters: people who steal from downtown stores and resell the goods in the neighbourhood. They are both recognised and, he says, respected. “Somebody had the hook-up and they’d have, you know, an apartment full of stuff,” he says. He went for the clothes. “Being a broke rapper for a long time and needing to look fly as part of the job requirement, you needed to know some boosters.” Although, he says, his best-ever booster buy was a laptop. In I Love Boosters, his three heroines – sassy leader Corvette (Keke Palmer), Sade (Naomi Ackie) and Mariah (Taylour Paige) – know how to avoid security guards and stuff their sweatpants with clubbing gear, but they barely scrape together a living. Corvette, the leader of the so-called Velvet Gang, is squatting in an abandoned fried chicken shop that still stinks of old oil and is literally running away from debt; her unpaid bills have rolled themselves into a gigantic ball that chases her down the street. Stuff like that happens all the time. Boots Riley at the Rome Film Festival in October. AP Photo/Andrew Medichini The three of them dream of designing clothes themselves, but nobody on their side of the tracks gets to be a Christie Smith. Riley certainly isn’t down on fashion; he dresses with a pronounced sense of showmanship. “For some people, that ends up becoming their only chance to show their creativity, right?” he says. “You know, to express themselves to a certain extent. Because the movie ultimately is about loneliness and how we try to get connection through various ways: through art, through success, through love.”



Ackie, who sounds 100-per-cent Oakland in the film but in fact comes from London, was photographed at a Schiaparelli show not long before the film screened at the London Film Festival. “That’s quite meta, isn’t it?” she says, laughing. As the daughter of a seamstress, she grew up loving the craft behind clothes. “With this film, I think it takes that love and then it goes really deep into the good and bad sides of it,” she says. “I guess, to me, the film is about whether we can do two things at the same time: create a beautiful world, where we have access to express ourselves the way we want to through film, music, fashion, art, but also a world where the people who are behind the scenes and who are creating it aren’t exploited.” Loading Riley describes himself as a communist, which is a bold and unusual position to take in the United States. “Well, it’s interesting,” he says. “Because like 40 something per cent of the population, even in right-wing polls, are saying that they’d rather see us in a socialist society. They might say, ‘I don’t think that’s going to be able to happen’, but they also say, ‘That’d be great if it could.’” (The subsequent midterm results would suggest he’s onto something.) From left: Naomi Ackie, Taylour Paige and Keke Palmer steal clothing but would prefer to be designing their own in I Love Boosters. Maslow Films For him, boosterism is an integral part of the consumer culture, and despite sporadic campaigns to make the sins of the poor an issue, nobody really cares about shoplifting.

“Boosters are not outside of capitalism, even though what they’re doing is illegal. They’re part of the distribution of the commodity.” Fakes and copies are also part of the system. “It only mentions a little bit in the film, but they know it’s happening, and it’s the way that their products get advertised, right? Because the cool people are now wearing the stuff. They kind of talk about it in the Gucci movie [House of Gucci, 2021]: that they let bootlegs happen because then people see other people with their handbags and that’s who they want to be.” All he does, he says, is take that into the realm of the fantastical.



Related Article Streaming Male critics hated it, Gen Z loves it. How Marie Antoinette got the last laugh Riley has notebooks in which he writes things down that occur to him. “Sometimes it’ll be a lyric. Sometimes it’s more of an album concept,” he says. “But a lot of times it’s like problem-solving. Like: where would Christie Smith live?” Answer: she lives in a condo in an achingly fashionable high-rise that is falling over, so that her floor is about a one-in-three gradient. “It’s a fact,” says Riley, “that there is a building that’s sinking like two inches in San Francisco called the Millennium Tower. You’re not going to notice that, but people are like rolling marbles to show you that it is. So it’s like leaning on that a little bit. How do I take it to another level? How do I heighten those contradictions?” Naomi Ackie and Boots Riley at the London Film Festival in October. Getty Images for BFI “[Riley] creates this really specific world,” says Ackie, who has always loved reading fantasy for the same reason. “But then you get on set and he’s like, ‘OK, do whatever you want.’ There’s a lot of trust and a lot of letting go, which I think is a beautiful, creative space to be in. It reminded me of when I used to do devised theatre at school, where there are no rules; it’s like you’re in a toy box.” What made the mind of Boots Riley fizz this way? He went to film school, he says, but what really inspired him was seeing Spike Lee making movies that people wanted to see. Until then, alongside his musical career, he had been involved with a community theatre where 40 people would cram into a room to see plays about the workers’ struggle. “And I was like, OK, we’re going to have to make a lot of plays to help make the revolution this way. “Then Spike Lee made Do the Right Thing. And I was like, ‘Oh, OK. Even though we have different politics, I see he’s doing something.’” Riley thought if he turned economic analysis into something wild, he could make the audience feel it. “But I would say that politics is what gives me the aesthetic of the movie. So much art is only considered artful when it’s nihilistic. This is not nihilistic. Because I have an optimistic viewpoint. I think that we can change things.” Imagination – for Boots Riley, at least – has no limits.

World.title: Beau Lamarre-Condon trial live updates: Accused double murderer, former NSW Police officer returns to witness box after judge sends jury home due to ‘unexpected issue’
World.content:
Warning: Graphic content

Hello and welcome to our live coverage of Beau Lamarre-Condon’s double murder trial in the NSW Supreme Court in Sydney.

Yesterday’s hearing was cut short after Justice Natalie Adams told the 15-person jury about 12.30pm that “an issue has arisen unexpectedly”. They were told to return at 10am today and there was a short delay before the hearing resumed.

A court sketch of Beau Lamarre-Condon during his testimony last week. Rocco Fazzari

“These things happen in trials all the time, as you’ve probably learnt by now,” the judge said yesterday.

The accused returns to the witness box today for further cross-examination by Crown prosecutor Brett Hatfield, SC.

The former NSW police officer has pleaded not guilty to two counts of murder over the deaths of Jesse Baird, 26, a former TV presenter, and Luke Davies, 29, a Qantas flight attendant. There is no dispute that the men died of gunshot wounds from his police-issued pistol on February 19, 2024, and that the accused disposed of the bodies on February 22, 2024.

The Crown alleges that Lamarre-Condon planned to kill Baird after developing an obsessive and jealous infatuation with him and that he killed Davies, Baird’s boyfriend, to eliminate a witness to his crime.

The defence case is that Lamarre-Condon acted in self-defence after entering Baird’s Paddington share house dressed as an Uber Eats rider to collect some of his possessions after Baird ended their non-exclusive relationship in November 2023. He said he struck upon the idea for the disguise that morning as a way to ensure Baird did not accuse him of harassment, and he thought nobody was home.

Lamarre-Condon said he shot Baird once to disarm him after Baird lunged at him with a knife and a second shot through his head was accidental. He says that Davies accidentally shot himself after grabbing the gun.

The 31-year-old accused has told the court he had his police pistol with him because he had contemplated taking his own life the previous night over work-related trauma.

He has given the following evidence over three days of cross-examination:

Lamarre-Condon has denied executing Baird and said he stood by his decision to fire the first shot. He said he was responsible for Baird’s death but did not intend to kill him.

He has also denied stalking Baird before his death, including when he saw the then TV presenter having sex with another man while standing outside his bedroom window after the men broke up for the first time in April 2023. He said he was there to collect some belongings.

The men had met in Sydney in October 2022, the court has heard, and their relationship was not exclusive, but the accused said they started going on “romantic dates” in December that year. The men resumed contact briefly around August or September 2023, after their first break-up, before Baird ended the relationship permanently in November 2023.

Lamarre-Condon rejected a suggestion by the prosecution that he was obsessed with Baird “right from the start”. “Smitten, yes. Obsessed, no,” the accused said.

The accused admitted he invaded Baird’s privacy and went through his phone on two occasions, in March and April 2023.

He denied breaking into Baird’s home on August 17, 2023. The court has heard he messaged one friend in the aftermath of the alleged incident that Baird had “a home invasion”. He said that he panicked and ran out of Baird’s home with the TV presenter’s phone and wallet after Baird woke up while he was attempting to take the phone outside to go through his messages.

The accused told the court he entered the home using a key that Baird left out for him that night, but put a bobby pin in the lock of the door to give the impression someone else had been in the house in case Baird woke up while he was looking through the phone outside. The Crown case is that he used a key he had stolen or had copied, an allegation he denied.

After being shown a screenshot of a text message he sent Baird on the day of the alleged break-in, in which he wrote, “Haha I’ll take that as a no to doing the catch up then”, Lamarre-Condon said he communicated with Baird on other platforms including FaceTime and social media.

He agreed that a friend had called him “Bobby P” in a joke referring to him putting the bobby pin in the door.

He rejected Hatfield’s suggestion that it appealed to him that Baird was a TV presenter. “Jesse Baird could have been a garbage cleaner,” he said. “We actually never really talked much about his work. I wasn’t really interested in that, to be honest.”

He also denied that he had misrepresented the nature of his relationship with Baird in a video he made of them on a farm stay holiday in March 2023.

Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic Family Violence Counselling Service at 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732), the Men’s Referral Service on 1300 766 491, and Lifeline on 13 11 14.

World.title: Big Build royal commission LIVE updates: Big Build royal commission LIVE updates: Claims Setka described former Andrews adviser as a ‘good asset to the union’ as Gap Road probe continues
World.content:
Another industrial relations manager at major contractor John Holland has told the Big Build royal commission the company believed it needed to show an ability to work with the CFMEU in Victoria more so than any other jurisdiction thanks to the union’s close relationship with the state Labor government.

Trent Smith, the second witness to appear today, said the CFMEU was “more militant” in Victoria and Queensland but the company felt it needed to maintain a good relationship with the union pushed into the civil construction sector.

Commissioner Chris Kourkais asked: “Was it a view linked to a particular government that is party politically linked?”

Smith replied: “It was more so in Victoria that we thought we needed to demonstrate an ability to work with the CFMEU, absolutely. But it did play out in Queensland as well.”

The commission has now adjourned for lunch and will return just after 2pm.

World.title: ‘He’s grounded for life’: Teen survives six days in bush on chips and water
World.content:
Breaking NationalVictoriaMissing person ‘He’s grounded for life’: Teen survives six days in bush on chips and water Hannah Hammoud November 12, 2026 — 1:05pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

A missing Morwell teenager has been found alive after an incredible six-day ordeal in the bush, surviving on little more than a packet of chips and water after falling down a cliff and becoming trapped. Seventeen-year-old William, known as Will, was rescued following a six-day search, with his relieved mother revealing he escaped with just sunburn and a few scratches – but could now face a lifetime grounding. William hugs his mother after being rescued by police helicopter. Victoria Police His mother, Elizabeth Barkley, said her son was in “good health and good spirits” despite spending almost a week stranded in the bush. “He fell off a bit of a cliff and couldn’t move. So he just stayed there and waited,” she said.



Will was last seen near Stoney Creek Road, close to T2 Track, at about 4pm on Friday, November 6, while camping with another teenager for the weekend. Police said he had walked a short distance to another part of the campsite. When he failed to return, his friend searched the surrounding area but was unable to find him. Police said the air wing were conducting an aerial search of the Cowwarr area on Thursday when they spotted a tackle box in bushland about two kilometres east of Stoney Creek. Zooming in on the tackle box, they found William lying down close by in a creek. “Flight officers winched down and retrieved Will before bringing him back to the command post to reunite with his mum,” police said in a statement.



“Amazingly, William is in good spirits and for the most part, in good health. He was taken to hospital for monitoring.” Barkley, who lives about 40 minutes from the search area in Morwell, said she was waiting as emergency services prepared their next search area when she received the news her son had been found alive. The 17-year-old was last seen near Stoney Creek Road on November 6. Victoria Police “They came in and told me and I waited outside until the helicopter landed, and I saw him wave as he came out,” she said. “I never gave up hope, I knew in my heart he was still alive, and I just prayed to God for a miracle, and a miracle happened. So as soon as that helicopter landed, and they got him off I gave him the biggest hug.”



While Barkley was still unsure exactly how far her son had fallen, she understood he had remained in the same spot, unable to move, until rescuers finally reached him. Will was taken to hospital for further checks, with his mother making it clear that while she was overjoyed to have him home safe, his camping adventures might be on hold for quite some time. “He is now going to the hospital to get checked out, and after that, he’s grounded for life. Never leaving my sight again,” she said. Be the first to know when major news happens.

World.title: Dalaroo fires up diamond drill hunt for African gold riches
World.content:
Sponsored BusinessCompaniesBulls N' Bears Dalaroo fires up diamond drill hunt for African gold riches Brought to you by BULLS N’ BEARS Andrew Todd November 12, 2026 — 1:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Dalaroo Metals is about to fire up the diamond rigs at its Bondoukou Gold Ridge project in Côte d’Ivoire, chasing up a substantial high-grade gold discovery made at the project last month. The company says an initial five-hole, 1750-metre program will test the down-dip and along-strike extensions of mineralisation at its Wilfred target, where fresh results have since reinforced the maiden discovery and confirmed its high-grade hits as no flash in the pan. Core yard pad under construction at Dalaroo Metals’ Bondoukou Gold Ridge project in Côte d’Ivoire. The initial discovery came from two opposing maiden holes drilled to more than 200m. One returned a standout 18m at 7.31 grams per tonne (g/t) gold from 63m, including a second zone of 16m at 1.46g/t, while the other delivered a solid 23m at 2.14g/t gold from surface. The new diamond holes will test for mineralisation down to 350m, pushing well beyond the depths reached by earlier reverse-circulation (RC) drilling.



Adding to the excitement, Dalaroo has also hit a second, significant shallow zone of mineralisation 1.25km north of the original Wilfred discovery, pointing to the potential for a much bigger system emerging at Bondoukou. The company says it is planning a staged approach to the new round of exploration, with initial step-out holes staged in 80m strike extensions from known mineralisation. If a step-out hole is successful, another will be drilled 80m further out to define the limits of the gold-bearing structure. A second diamond rig is expected on site by the end of this month to begin follow-up drilling at the northern discovery zone, with Dalaroo hopeful it can connect the two discoveries across a major structural ridge. The company says after completing its current RC orientation program, it will use diamond rigs for all subsequent drilling. Core from diamond drilling will then provide crucial structural information on the geometry and orientation of its mineralisation to guide all future drilling. Dalaroo has linked up with experienced drilling contractor Easy Drill for an estimated 20,000m of diamond drilling and two rigs at a time when rig availability in the booming West African nation is at a premium. In a move to preserve its cash, Dalaroo has structured the deal to pay for the drilling with 50 per cent cash and 50 per cent shares, although it can elect to pay a greater portion in cash.



Dalaroo appears well-funded for the campaign, with roughly $2 million in the bank and a massive 263 million in-the-money options outstanding, potentially tipping a further $13.54 million into its coffers if exercised. The timing of the company’s drilling campaign looks impeccable, set against a booming gold industry backdrop and government support in Côte d’Ivoire. The nation’s gold production has skyrocketed from 13 tonnes in 2012 to a forecast 62 tonnes this year, with the government positioning to become Africa’s biggest gold producer by 2035. This has fuelled a rush of exploration investment, which surged 82 per cent last year to US$186 million (A$272 million). With a high-grade discovery in the bag and a second zone 1.25km away, Dalaroo’s Bondoukou Gold Ridge project has the makings of something big. If Wilfred can connect up along strike and keep going at depth, things could heat up very quickly. Is your ASX-listed company doing something interesting? Contact: mattbirney@bullsnbears.com.au
