World.title: Downfall of world’s chipmaker-in-chief a potential headache for Beijing as well as US
World.content:
Analysis WorldAsiaChina relations Downfall of world’s chipmaker-in-chief a potential headache for Beijing as well as US Lisa Visentin November 12, 2026 — 12:51pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Beijing: We will probably never know if Jensen Huang’s swagger, connections and status as the world’s chipmaker-in-chief would have been enough to save him from the blast radius of an affair with an alleged spy. The emergence of a second extramarital affair looks poised to sink the Nvidia boss. The company is reportedly preparing to cut him loose. It would be an act of almost self-decapitation. Huang built Nvidia from the ground up over three decades into one of the world’s most valuable companies, through which he commanded enormous influence over the unfolding tech revolution and frenzied race between the US and China. Inside Nvidia, he concentrated power in his leadership with 60 executives reporting directly to him. There is no succession plan.



The emergence of a second extramarital affair looks poised to sink Nvidia boss Jensen Huang. Bloomberg His apparent downfall leaves a question mark not just over Nvidia’s future direction, but US chip policy more broadly. In Washington, Huang has been a forceful lobbyist for giving China access to some less-advanced Nvidia chips, arguing that keeping Beijing hooked on US technology would slow the development of its own high-powered domestic chip industry. Related Article Inside China Trump may have just helped turbocharge China’s military National security hawks loathed the deal he cut with US President Donald Trump last year to sell Nvidia’s powerful H200 chips to China in exchange for the US government taking a 25 per cent cut. They would toast his defenestration.



In Beijing, too, some would rue the departure of a tech titan whose corporate interests in making the world dependent on Nvidia aligned with their own. “Although we compete against China, they are not our enemies,” Huang told Bloomberg in a recent interview where he criticised US chip restrictions. Would Nvidia’s next chief executive take the same line? Either way, ousting Huang will not stem the tide of scrutiny coming Nvidia’s way. The company faces multiple investigations into whether its chief’s affair has exposed it to a foreign intelligence plot, and whether Nvidia did enough to stop its chips from allegedly being smuggled into China. The spy scandal



For a spy scandal in the digital age, the plot is strikingly analogue. In this photo, posted to Weibo, Jensen Huang and Alice Huang dine at a Shanghai restaurant. A powerful tech billionaire with a direct line to the president has apparently been compromised, not by a sophisticated cyberespionage operation or a malevolent team of AI super-agents, but by the age-old trope of sleeping with the enemy. Related Article Updated

Technology & democracy ‘I was unfaithful to my wife’: Nvidia boss admits to affair with suspected Chinese spy For all the salacious speculation of a Beijing-orchestrated honeypot scandal, there are many missing details about the woman at the centre of it, Chinese data company executive Alice Huang (no relation).



The New York Times, which broke the initial story, reported that US agencies suspected she was recruited by China’s Ministry of State Security (MSS) and used her affair with Huang to funnel information back to Beijing. Anonymous sources cited in media reports have not leaked what evidence the US gathered or the nature of Huang’s suspected ties to the MSS, and neither Nvidia nor its founder appear to have been told about them. But there were enough red flags in Alice Huang’s background for both to be more curious. Do US authorities believe she was an MSS operative carrying out a calculated intelligence-gathering agenda, or a savvy businesswoman whose genuine closeness to Huang the agency sought to exploit? Several China analysts think the latter is more likely. Jensen Huang has had easy and regular access to US President Donald Trump. Bloomberg



More importantly, what did China potentially gain? It’s hard to overstate Nvidia’s role as the American company at the apex of US-China tech rivalry, and the role of Jensen Huang as its founder in influencing artificial intelligence policy. Nvidia’s advanced chips, which China cannot yet match, are key to the US maintaining its lead in AI and its edge across a range of fields, including high-tech weapons systems. Related Article Technology & democracy Who is Alice Huang? The suspected Chinese spy at the centre of the Nvidia scandal Needless to say, it is a huge coup for the MSS if it has cultivated an agent who was in close contact with the Nvidia chief.



“This is a counter-intelligence nightmare,” says Ryan Fedasiuk, a former US State Department official, now at the Foundation for American Innovation. Two parts of Alice Huang’s role are under scrutiny. First, her business dealings as a former top executive at Megaspeed, a little-known Singapore-based data centre company that somehow amassed funds to buy $US4.8 billion ($7 billion) of Nvidia equipment, purportedly for its data centres in South-East Asia. These third-country transfers are not illegal under US chip export controls, but US investigators are examining whether Megaspeed exploited them to smuggle restricted AI chips into China. Related Article Analysis

China relations Beijing gets ready to welcome Putin and ‘lame duck’ Trump Fedasiuk says the affair has overshadowed what should be a focus on the actions Nvidia may have taken on behalf of Megaspeed, after it emerged that Nvidia’s general counsel sought to intervene in a US government probe into the Chinese company.



“This was the CEO of the largest company in the world having a covert relationship with his customer, and not only producing a potential conflict of interest in that, but actually using the conflict of interest in terms favourable to the customer,” Fedasiuk says. “And unfortunately, that customer is alleged to be a Chinese intelligence asset on top of it all.” As China analyst Bill Bishop speculated, a good relationship with Jensen Huang “likely meant more chips for the Megaspeed front company and the entities back in the PRC to which those chips flowed,” he posted on X. Second, what kind of sensitive information could Alice Huang have been privy to, including via so-called “pillow talk”, that may now be in the hands of Chinese intelligence? ‘He’s China’s lifeline when it comes to artificial intelligence; Nvidia chips are really indispensable for China’s AI development.’ Alex Joske, managing director at Garnaut Global, a China-focused risk advisory firm.



Jensen Huang has had easy and frequent access to Trump. This continued after Trump was briefed about the suspected spy scandal twice, most recently in May while en route to his Beijing summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping. The Nvidia boss joined him on that summit. Did Alice Huang seek to influence his lobbying efforts, or pass updates to Chinese intelligence? Did he confide in her confidential information about Nvidia’s corporate plans or even his conversations with Trump? Some of these details may be shaken out in upcoming investigations, including when Jensen Huang is called before Congress to answer questions at a closed-door meeting later this month. The FBI is also investigating, while Nvidia has launched its own internal probe. Jensen Huang admitted the affair in an email memo to Nvidia staff. NYT Under Xi, the MSS has risen in status, resourcing, and prowess and has prioritised artificial intelligence operations as it seeks to close in on the US’s lead, says Alex Joske, an analyst who specialises in Chinese influence operations.



“Jensen Huang ticks every box from the perspective of Chinese intelligence services,” says Joske, who is managing director at risk advisory firm Garnaut Global. “He’s got top-level political access, and his company is at the heart of the most important technological feud in US-China competition. “He’s China’s lifeline when it comes to artificial intelligence; Nvidia chips are really indispensable for China’s AI development.” The Nvidia boss maintains he was unaware his lover was an alleged spy. We know this because he told Trump this week, who relayed it to reporters, proving the scandal hasn’t ended his direct access to the president. The Chinese Foreign Ministry has dismissed the allegations as “totally unfounded” smears.



Beijing had been hoping it could ride out the remaining two years of Trump’s presidency on the uneasy detente both sides had secured. But this explosion is poised to unite Democrats and Republicans angry at Nvidia’s influence and Trump’s softening on China in a campaign to further strangle Beijing’s access to backdoor chips. It adds to swirling atmospherics at next week’s APEC summit, when Trump and Xi will meet for the third time this year. This time, though, don’t expect Jensen Huang to secure a seat on Air Force One. World.title: Adidas to open first Australian airport store in Brisbane
World.content:
Exclusive NationalQueenslandBrisbane Airport Adidas to open first Australian airport store in Brisbane Cameron Atfield November 12, 2026 — 12:43pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Global sportswear giant Adidas will open its first Australian airport store at Brisbane Airport – one of more than a dozen new and refurbished retailers at both terminals as part of the $5 billion Future BNE project. Brisbane Airport commercial executive manager Scott Norris said the businesses would complement the overhaul of the terminals’ dining offering. “Passengers travelling through Brisbane Airport will soon enjoy an upgraded shopping experience, with a mix of convenience stores, big-name brands and travel essentials coming to our terminals as part of our ongoing transformation,” he said. The new Relay store at Brisbane International opened this week. Brisbane Airport “The addition of these outlets will boost the retail offering at Brisbane Airport, giving a record number of passengers more choice and greater convenience at every step of their journey.”



Speaking at a business breakfast at the airport on Thursday, Brisbane Airport chief executive Gert-Jan de Graaf said passengers could expect to see retail construction for “another year or so” for this round of improvement, but he expected more up to and beyond the 2032 Olympic and Paralympic Games. “An airport is always ready, but never completed,” he said. “...[It will be a] fantastic new experience for all travellers. “There’s work in progress – there’s still a lot of hoarding up – but in the next couple of weeks, you will see quite a lot of it coming down.”



New outlets planned for Terminal 1, the international terminal, include Rip Curl, Sunglass Hut, an UGG store and souvenir outlet Discover Australia, which opened its doors this week, and premium fashion and luggage boutique The Edit. A new Adidas store is on the way for Brisbane Airport’s domestic terminal. Bloomberg Three of five new Relay stores, selling travel essentials, have already opened at the international terminal and the existing Lotte Duty Free footprint was set to double in size. To cater for arriving international passengers, Telsim and Optus will offer telecommunications services in the arrivals hall, while Prosegur Change Currency Exchange has opened its permanent shopfront after operating pop-up kiosks since late last year. Over at the domestic Terminal 2, the Adidas shop was expected to open early next year.



Related Article Brisbane Airport New Brisbane Airport flightpath plan offers noise breaks for 482,000 Joining the German sportswear giant would be chocolatier Koko Black, Hairhouse and another UGG store. All new retail outlets, apart from The Edit, were being progressively delivered through to 2027. The Edit and the Lotte Duty Free expansion planned to be progressively delivered until 2029. World.title: The Devil Wears Prada had Miranda Priestly. I Love Boosters goes one better
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

There has to be a hellzapoppin’ party going on inside Boots Riley’s head, right? Anyone who saw the filmmaker-cum-rapper’s anti-capitalist satire, Sorry to Bother You, is probably still dazed by its hotchpotch of barbs about telemarketing, the horny version of Siri dirty-talking everyone in the telemarketers’ executive lift and a climactic rebellion led by people with the heads of horses. But Boots wasn’t finished: hell, no. So here he is again with I Love Boosters, in which a vibrant girl gang of career shoplifters joins forces with Chinese sweatshop workers via a teleporter in the shape of a toilet seat. Demi Moore, having been so gloriously reborn in The Substance, plays a fashion maven called Christie Smith so mean she makes Miranda Priestly look like Maria von Trapp. And if you fancy a lovelorn demon who sucks out women’s souls during oral sex, he’s here in the comely person of LaKeith Stanfield. A ton of stuff is going on. Demi Moore as Christie Smith in I Love Boosters. Maslow Films Oakland, the culturally diverse city north of San Francisco where Boots Riley has lived all his 55 years, has always had its boosters: people who steal from downtown stores and resell the goods in the neighbourhood. They are both recognised and, he says, respected. “Somebody had the hook-up and they’d have, you know, an apartment full of stuff,” he says. He went for the clothes. “Being a broke rapper for a long time and needing to look fly as part of the job requirement, you needed to know some boosters.” Although, he says, his best-ever booster buy was a laptop. In I Love Boosters, his three heroines – sassy leader Corvette (Keke Palmer), Sade (Naomi Ackie) and Mariah (Taylour Paige) – know how to avoid security guards and stuff their sweatpants with clubbing gear, but they barely scrape together a living. Corvette, the leader of the so-called Velvet Gang, is squatting in an abandoned fried chicken shop that still stinks of old oil and is literally running away from debt; her unpaid bills have rolled themselves into a gigantic ball that chases her down the street. Stuff like that happens all the time. Boots Riley at the Rome Film Festival in October. AP Photo/Andrew Medichini The three of them dream of designing clothes themselves, but nobody on their side of the tracks gets to be a Christie Smith. Riley certainly isn’t down on fashion; he dresses with a pronounced sense of showmanship. “For some people, that ends up becoming their only chance to show their creativity, right?” he says. “You know, to express themselves to a certain extent. Because the movie ultimately is about loneliness and how we try to get connection through various ways: through art, through success, through love.”



Ackie, who sounds 100-per-cent Oakland in the film but in fact comes from London, was photographed at a Schiaparelli show not long before the film screened at the London Film Festival. “That’s quite meta, isn’t it?” she says, laughing. As the daughter of a seamstress, she grew up loving the craft behind clothes. “With this film, I think it takes that love and then it goes really deep into the good and bad sides of it,” she says. “I guess, to me, the film is about whether we can do two things at the same time: create a beautiful world, where we have access to express ourselves the way we want to through film, music, fashion, art, but also a world where the people who are behind the scenes and who are creating it aren’t exploited.” Loading Riley describes himself as a communist, which is a bold and unusual position to take in the United States. “Well, it’s interesting,” he says. “Because like 40 something per cent of the population, even in right-wing polls, are saying that they’d rather see us in a socialist society. They might say, ‘I don’t think that’s going to be able to happen’, but they also say, ‘That’d be great if it could.’” (The subsequent midterm results would suggest he’s onto something.) From left: Naomi Ackie, Taylour Paige and Keke Palmer steal clothing but would prefer to be designing their own in I Love Boosters. Maslow Films For him, boosterism is an integral part of the consumer culture, and despite sporadic campaigns to make the sins of the poor an issue, nobody really cares about shoplifting.

“Boosters are not outside of capitalism, even though what they’re doing is illegal. They’re part of the distribution of the commodity.” Fakes and copies are also part of the system. “It only mentions a little bit in the film, but they know it’s happening, and it’s the way that their products get advertised, right? Because the cool people are now wearing the stuff. They kind of talk about it in the Gucci movie [House of Gucci, 2021]: that they let bootlegs happen because then people see other people with their handbags and that’s who they want to be.” All he does, he says, is take that into the realm of the fantastical.



Related Article Streaming Male critics hated it, Gen Z loves it. How Marie Antoinette got the last laugh Riley has notebooks in which he writes things down that occur to him. “Sometimes it’ll be a lyric. Sometimes it’s more of an album concept,” he says. “But a lot of times it’s like problem-solving. Like: where would Christie Smith live?” Answer: she lives in a condo in an achingly fashionable high-rise that is falling over, so that her floor is about a one-in-three gradient. “It’s a fact,” says Riley, “that there is a building that’s sinking like two inches in San Francisco called the Millennium Tower. You’re not going to notice that, but people are like rolling marbles to show you that it is. So it’s like leaning on that a little bit. How do I take it to another level? How do I heighten those contradictions?” Naomi Ackie and Boots Riley at the London Film Festival in October. Getty Images for BFI “[Riley] creates this really specific world,” says Ackie, who has always loved reading fantasy for the same reason. “But then you get on set and he’s like, ‘OK, do whatever you want.’ There’s a lot of trust and a lot of letting go, which I think is a beautiful, creative space to be in. It reminded me of when I used to do devised theatre at school, where there are no rules; it’s like you’re in a toy box.” What made the mind of Boots Riley fizz this way? He went to film school, he says, but what really inspired him was seeing Spike Lee making movies that people wanted to see. Until then, alongside his musical career, he had been involved with a community theatre where 40 people would cram into a room to see plays about the workers’ struggle. “And I was like, OK, we’re going to have to make a lot of plays to help make the revolution this way. “Then Spike Lee made Do the Right Thing. And I was like, ‘Oh, OK. Even though we have different politics, I see he’s doing something.’” Riley thought if he turned economic analysis into something wild, he could make the audience feel it. “But I would say that politics is what gives me the aesthetic of the movie. So much art is only considered artful when it’s nihilistic. This is not nihilistic. Because I have an optimistic viewpoint. I think that we can change things.” Imagination – for Boots Riley, at least – has no limits.

World.title: Lyall Bay group looks to toilet humour in wake of Moa Point failure
World.content:
A resident of Lyall Bay, on Wellington's south coast, says some well-placed toilet humour could be an antidote to tough times in the community.

Informal community group, The High Tide Club is seeking backers to raise $7000 to build a more than four-metre-tall inflatable poo emoji to float out in the surf of the bay.

Club member Johnny Carpenter said after a year blighted by the catastrophic failure of the nearby Moa Point waste water plant and severe storm damage, the community deserved to make their own statement.

"Hopefully it just gives people a laugh and, maybe around the council table, it will get people talking and getting more motivated to get this problem fixed.

"If a few people decide to get their wallet out for a laugh and a conversation then I think it's money well spent," Carpenter said.

Carpenter, who works as a real-estate agent in the area, said The High Tide Club had sprung from a handful of locals who used debris strewn on the beach after recent storms to build a driftwood Tiki Bar on the shorefront at the beginning of the year.

"Most people in Wellington, whether you're a business owner or someone who's just lost a job or lost an income, that combined with the environmental disaster that's on our doorstep… We've joked that the club's become a bastion of hope in the community, which might be a bit rich but probably rings true in some respects," Carpenter said.

Johnny Carpenter, his son as well as fellow High Tide Club member, restauranteur Lorenzo Bresolin and friends enjoy some down time at the Lyall Bay tiki bar. Supplied

Carpenter said a PledgeMe campaign was awaiting approval and should go up on-line shortly.

Co-owner of the Maranui Café in Lyall Bay, Katie Richardson said she appreciated the humour but she was unsure if the poo emoji was something she wanted to tie the community's identity to.

"I do think it's quite funny. When I saw it, I laughed I thought 'Oh my god that's hilarious'. [Making] light of a serious situation, because it's not a great situation, but it's going to get fixed soon hopefully anyway," Richardson said.

Owner and principal manufacturer of Verdure Surfboards, Jack Candlish was less impressed.

He said since the failure of the wastewater plant he'd lost 40 percent of his business.

"I don't know if it's a good idea. I think it's already embarrassing enough, the situation as it is and I don't know if adding that will be constructive," Candlish said.

Informal Lyall bay group The High Tide Club are seeking backers to help build a large poo emoji to float off shore from the bay. Supplied

He said the massive amount of sewage which had flooded into the sea, so close to the airport of New Zealand's capital city, made a mockery of the country's clean green image.

"It's been the hardest financial year for me personally it's hard for me to find a humorous aspect to it.

"All the businesses around here have been really struggling. We had a meeting with the council and one of the business owners broke down in tears. That's how devastating it's been for us.

"If they want to do it, that's totally cool, but I don't think the business owners will be contributing to the fundraiser," Candlish said.

Candlish said he was considering relocating his business further north but, after a "rollercoaster" year, he wasn't sure how he could even afford to do that.

World.title: ‘Our island no longer exists’: Solomon Islands climate documentary heads to COP31
World.content:
A documentary captured in virtual reality is telling the story of Solomon Islanders forced to abandon their homes as sea levels rise.

Solwata which means "salt water" in Solomon Islands pidgin premiered at the Venice Film Festival and is now heading to Türkiye for COP31.

Narrated by Hollywood actor and climate activist Mark Ruffalo, Solwata brings audiences face to face to the realities of climate displacement through virtual reality.

Video player removed for printing https://players.brightcove.net/6093072280001/default_default/index.html?videoId=6408006988112

The 25-minute documentary follows the communities of Walande, Ngongosila and Kwai in Solomon Islands' Malaita Province, where the climate crisis has forced families to confront the possibility of leaving their homes behind.

And for the people of Walande, this is not a distant threat, but a reality as the island they once called home has already been swallowed by the sea.

Human Rights Watch climate displacement researcher Erica Bower said this documentary will put global audiences in the shoes of Solomon Islanders.

"Today, their island no longer exists," she said. "It is submerged beneath the waves. When you stand on their mainland in their new site and you look back to where the island used to be, all you see are posts sticking up above the waves."

Walande, a community of approximately 800 people, was forced to relocate from its small offshore island after decades of battling rising seas, king tides and increasingly severe storms.

The community largely organised and financed the move itself, with support from its diaspora and some outside assistance.

But even after relocating to the mainland, residents continue to face threats from flooding and limited access to land.

Created by NowHere Media and coproduced by Human Rights Watch and Agog - The Immersive Media Institute, the documentary combines virtual reality, spatial audio, physical interaction and firsthand testimonies.

Participants wearing virtual reality headsets can move between physical and digital environments, reaching into water and interacting with culturally significant objects as they experience the stories of Solomon Islanders.

By June 2024, all buildings have disappeared, and no part of Walande is above sea level at hide tide. In the relocation site, houses are progressively filling all the flat and open areas available. Satellite Image © 2025 Airbus. Google Earth. Analysis and Graphics © 2025 Human Rights Watch Satellite Image © 2025 Airbus. Google Earth. Analysis and Graphics © 2025 Human Rights Watch

Bower said the technology helps audiences to understand the crisis beyond statistics and scientific climate projections.

"This is really a project about how climate change is a deeply human story.

"We often see climate change discussed through data and policy and projections, but Salwata is really focusing on the human experience, what it means when people lose their homes and their communities and their cultural identities because of rising seas."

While relocation is often discussed as a practical response to rising seas, Bower says it is more complex.

The loss of ancestral land can also mean losing connections to cultural traditions, family histories and places of spiritual significance.

For Walande, preserving such connections has been particularly difficult. Bower says the emotional toll remains more than a decade after the community began relocating.

"There is a lot of trauma. There is a lot of tears that are still shed because of because of this process, and it's been over a decade."

Academy Award-nominated actor Mark Ruffalo, known for his role as the Hulk in Marvel's Avengers films, joined the project as narrator and executive producer.

Mark Ruffalo records the narration of Solwata. © 2026 Human Rights Watch © 2026 Human Rights Watch

A longstanding advocate for environmental justice and human rights, Ruffalo said the documentary moved him because of the personal stories of families whose lives have been uprooted by the climate crisis.

"Well, this is a global issue, and we don't know how it's impacting the communities that are on the front lines. They're usually remote, and they're usually outside of our media and storytelling."

He said the immersive experience offers audiences an opportunity to connect with people whose struggles might otherwise remain unseen.

One story in particular, left a lasting impression on him.

"There's a story about a girl who keeps going back there to the submerged island to. her canoe there, and she spends hours and hours there, kind of mourning her her the loss of it, you know."

For Ruffalo, the documentary is also a reminder of the strength of communities facing such extraordinary challenges.

"We have to act together. When the going gets tough, they don't go into self-survival mode. They actually come together."

Bower said Ruffalo's involvement has helped draw international attention to the project, but the voices of Solomon Islanders remain at its centre.

The documentary builds on Human Rights Watch's 2025 report, There's Just No More Land: Community-Led Planned Relocation as Last Resort Adaptation in Solomon Islands, which examined the community's experience and the human rights implications of climate displacement.

Children sit on oil drums in Solomon Islands. © 2025 NowHere Media/Human Rights Watch

Bower said the findings reinforce the need for governments and international donors to provide meaningful support for communities facing relocation.

That includes ensuring communities themselves have a say in how funding is used, where they move and how their cultural identities are protected.

"Fundamentally, it's about really protecting the right to self-determination to make sure that especially indigenous communities can make adaptation decisions on their own terms and on their own timelines in a dignified way."

'Time to learn lessons'

With COP31 taking place in Antalya, Türkiye, from 9 to 20 November, Solwata will bring the experiences of Solomon Islanders into the world's biggest climate conference.

Bower hoped the documentary will encourage governments to recognise that climate displacement is not simply an environmental issue, but one that directly affects fundamental human rights.

She saids countries must develop stronger policies to support communities facing relocation, with adequate funding, community consultation and safeguards for cultural heritage.

"So really, now is the time to learn lessons from the past, from communities like Wolande, make sure their voices are heard, and really get implementation right to make sure that there's adequate financial and technical support for communities like Wallande in the future."

World.title: Insurer told traveller not to disclose medical condition
World.content:
Audio player for " What's the biggest risk to our economy right now? " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v0.KrRTFtoPsaA8nSDloPZ4KejQJr59ANQpD9ULgGwzaM0/business/2556529%2Finsurer-told-traveller-not-to-disclose-medical-condition

A travel insurer has been told to pay a woman $5000 plus the cost of her business class flights, after she became seriously ill in Bali.

The woman complained to the Insurance and Financial Services Ombudsman scheme about the way the insurer handled her claim.

She became so unwell that she could not return to New Zealand as planned. Doctors told her she needed a travel companion to make the trip and Air New Zealand's medical team said she would need a nurse or doctor as a medical escort.

A representative for the insurer told her she would not be covered for medical escort costs and she was fit to travel without one. It suggested she book a different airline and not tell it about her medical conditions.

She had originally booked an Air New Zealand Economy Skycouch so she could lie flat. The insurer said business class with another airline was a suitable alternative and gave her details of a flight it could book, but said it would cover only her seat, not a travel companion's.

She asked a friend, a former paramedic, to travel to Bali and help her get home, and booked a cheaper business-class flight for them both.

She suffered a medical emergency on the flight to Sydney and was admitted to hospital there. She had to book new flights home to New Zealand for herself and her friend.

She made a claim to the insurer for her additional travel, accommodation and medical costs, including her travel companion's flights.

The insurer only partially accepted the claim. It paid her an amount equivalent to an Economy Skycouch seat but declined the full cost of her business-class flights and all her travel companion's flights. It also only paid half the expenses it considered shared, and didn't pay for the rebooked flights from Sydney.

The Insurance and Financial Services Ombudsman scheme investigated and found the evidence supported her need for a companion.

It also found business class was reasonable because she had booked Skycouch so she could lie flat.

Because her travel companion needed to stay with her and assist her, the insurer also had to cover her business-class fare. The insurer was also required to pay for the new flights from Sydney to Christchurch after she was admitted to hospital.

Karen Stevens, Insurance and Financial Services Ombudsman, said the case highlighted the importance of insurers properly considering the evidence when handling claims.

"When someone is seriously ill overseas, they need clear information and practical support from their insurer. In this case, the medical evidence supported [the traveller's] need for a travel companion. We were seriously concerned that after Air New Zealand said [she] needed a medical escort, the insurer suggested she use another airline without telling it about her medical conditions. This directly risked [her] health in order to reduce costs," Stevens said.

She said it showed that what was reasonable depended on the circumstances.

"Business class might sound unusual in a travel insurance claim, but [she] had originally booked a Skycouch that allowed her to lie flat, and the insurer itself had identified business class as the suitable alternative. Her travel companion needed to stay with her to provide assistance, so that fare was also part of getting [her] home safely."

The scheme said the insurer's conduct went beyond failing to treat her fairly and supported a finding that it had acted in bad faith. It also found the insurer had materially breached its fair conduct obligations under the Financial Markets Conduct Act 2013 and failed to provide its service with reasonable care and skill under the Consumer Guarantees Act 1993.

The insurer was required to pay the travel companion and business class travel costs, as well as $5000 for the special inconvenience caused by its handling of the claim.

Travel insurance claims quite often cause headaches.

In another case dealt with by one of the other external dispute resolution schemes, FSCL, a man complained after his insurer turned down a claim to cover the costs of missed flight because he had lost his passport.

He was meant to travel home to New Zealand in December last year but could not find his passport the morning of his flight. He had to stay for two extra days while it was replaced.

The insurer covered the cost of the new passport but not the expenses incurred in the two additional days. The insurer said that the insurance cover for travel disruption was for situations when flights are delayed, cancelled, or where a person could not board due to overbooking.

FSCL said the insurer had assessed his claim correctly and there was no cover for expenses due to lost travel documents.

In another case last year, a woman was found to have no cover because she had not bought a return ticket before she left the country, so did not meet the requirements of her credit card insurance cover.

World.title: NorthTec a step closer to city centre campus
World.content:
Northland's biggest tertiary education provider is a step closer to relocating to Whangārei city centre after the Government confirmed funding of almost $35 million for the move.

The plan would see NorthTec shift from its current campus in Raumanga, about 3km from the CBD, to the former council headquarters at Forum North. NorthTec operations lead Derek Slatter said a central city location would bring students closer to public transport, businesses and community services. It would also make vocational education more visible and connected to the rest of the city, he said. If all went to plan the new campus would open in 2029.

Tertiary Education Minister Penny Simmonds said nurse training would be a key part of the new campus, with dedicated teaching spaces and simulation facilities designed to help ākonga [learners] hone their clinical skills and gain confidence in realistic settings.

She said approval of the business case, and confirmation of the $34.7m investment, were major steps towards making sure Northlanders had access to modern vocational education and training facilities.

The funding was announced in principle in April, provided the business case was successful. RNZ understands NorthTec was notified on Monday the business case had been approved.

Meanwhile, Slatter said the future of NorthTec land on Raumanga Valley Road would be decided through a separate process. Any land disposal would be subject to legal requirements, including the Public Works Act.

NorthTec's marae, Te Puna o Te Mātauranga, would also be moved to the city centre. That would require close engagement with hapū and iwi, and would be approached with care and respect, Slatter said.

Concept image of the proposed NorthTec campus at Forum North in Whangārei. Supplied / NorthTec

The previous Labour Government absorbed NorthTec into a single, nationwide mega-polytechnic called Te Pūkenga.

That was reversed by the coalition Government, which brought back standalone regional institutes - but NorthTec was one of a handful around the country put on notice that it would be closed down if it did not become financially viable.

Since then NorthTec has undergone significant restructuring and staff cuts. It is due to be re-established as a standalone polytechnic on 1 January.

The Whangārei District Council moved out of Forum North into its newly built Te Iwitahi headquarters in mid-2023. The council offices have been vacant since then, though other parts of the Forum North complex, including the exhibition hall and Capitaine Bougainville Theatre, are still in use.

A decision on the future of NorthTec satellite campuses in Kerikeri and Ngāwhā (pictured), near Kaikohe, is expected later this year. Peter de Graaf

Slatter said the hall and theatre would remain accessible to the public after NorthTec's move.

Ken Couper. Supplied / LDR

Whangārei Mayor Ken Couper said a strong NorthTec in the centre of Whangārei would bring major benefits for learners, employers, businesses and the wider community.

"Education is one of the strongest levers we have to unlock Northland's potential. Our aspirations are to connect learning with local jobs, local industries and local outcomes, giving our young people more reason to stay, train and build their futures here."

The proposal also aligned with the council's long-term vision for a vibrant CBD, he said.

"A thriving city centre needs people, energy and purpose. Bringing education into Forum North would support exactly the kind of active, connected civic heart this council has been working towards."

NorthTec currently has a student headcount of 3393, or 1599 in full-time-equivalents.

World.title: Mississippi electing Scott Colom as senator may be one of the biggest shocks of 2026
World.content:
First Person - There have been many shocks in American politics the past few weeks, but there's nothing that quite compares to the election of Senator Scott Colom in Mississippi.

Colom, a Democrat and Black district attorney, stunned poll watchers by narrowly defeating the white Republican sitting US Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith.

The final vote, which took more than a week to confirm, shows Colom winning by a narrow 4000 or so votes - a result pretty much nobody outside of Mississippi saw coming even in the face of a mighty "blue wave" for Democrats nationwide.

The Associated Press and CNN projected Colom as the winner on Thursday (NZ time).

Embedded content removed for printing https://twitter.com/Phil_Lewis_/status/2120640219871384044

It is impossible to fully describe the magnitude of a Black Democrat winning a Senate seat in Mississippi, a state that's been deeply Republican for decades and has a long, sordid history of oppression of Black voters.

Colom will be the first Black senator in Mississippi since 1881 - and that man was born enslaved.

He's also the first Democrat elected there since 1982. The campaign of Colom, 43, seemed filled with energy, compared to the lethargic efforts by Hyde-Smith, 67.

Sixty, seventy years ago, he could have been killed for even trying to vote in Mississippi, where the Ku Klux Klan and others fought any attempt by Black people to vote well in the 1960s.

District Attorney and U.S. Senate candidate for Mississippi Scott Colom speaks as he gives an update on state of Senate race against Cindy Hyde-Smith November 4, 2026 in Jackson, Mississippi. ROGELIO V. SOLIS / AFP / Getty Images

Mississippi is a word which feels haunted, slippery with meaning. There's no more evocative American state name, with all that entails.

The roots of my family run deep there. My mother was raised there, my grandparents and great-grandparents are buried there, in a quiet cemetery beneath the trees, tucked away down shadowy side roads.

I lived there myself from the ages of 18 to 25, from a freshman at the University of Mississippi to a fumbling young working journalist.

A mural in Oxford, Mississippi celebrating local cultural figures, August 2026. RNZ / Nik Dirga

In August, I visited friends and family in Mississippi for the first time in years. The political campaign signs were only starting to come out, but nobody was talking about Scott Colom winning the Senate race. It didn't seem possible.

Every place on Earth has a tragic past if you dig far enough, but Mississippi is unique in its stains and glories. I can think of nowhere else I've lived where the absolute worst and the shining best of a place are so deeply intertwined, where one seemingly cannot exist without the other.

The horrors that were visited on the Black population there in the 20th century still turn my stomach, the suppression, cruelty and casual dehumanisation. The story of Emmett Till - a 14-year-old boy tortured and murdered by white racists in 1955 for allegedly daring to whistle at a white woman - is as good as any to illustrate how horrible things could get.

My mother was just about the same age as Till and grew up an hour or two away from where his blood was spilled. But she knew nothing about it at the time, until many years later when the story began to seep out into the wider culture. The South endlessly romanticises itself, which can create both great stories and cover up hard truths.

Emmett Till was 14 years old when he was tortured and killed in Mississippi in 1955 for allegedly whistling at a white woman in a local store. File photo

A place can have a terrible past and yet still have things to admire and love; in our everything-is-good-or-evil digital world, it can be hard to explain a place that is full of troubles and still working hard to be better, and yet can be full of kindness and talent. Mississippi is complicated.

The Mississippi I visited in August felt like it was inching forward still with reconciling that past - the university campus of what's known as 'Ole Miss' was now dotted with prominent signs about the historic racial outrages and terror, and the looming county courthouse, as Southern as it gets, now also features a large memorial about lynchings held there.

Democratic Mississippi Senate candidate Scott Colom is joined by his daughters after speaking to voters during a midterm campaign rally on October 30, 2026 in Tupelo, Mississippi. BRAD VEST / AFP / Getty Images

A monument to James Meredith, who became the first Black student at Ole Miss despite bloody, fatal protests in 1962, now stands proudly beside the campus library. Courage, a sign proclaims.

Bad things still happen in Mississippi all the time, like just this past week when two white female university students made global news for racist gestures toward Black students. Yet one hopes those foolish students are the exception of their generation - youth aged 18 to 29 overwhelmingly voted for Colom in Mississippi, by a 30-point margin.

Video player removed for printing https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Nga2Q207-58

Colom marked his campaign with viral and witty ads (if you haven't heard about "pick another protein", watch it above), but he chose to end his run with a deeply serious ad filmed at the home of Medgar Evers, a civil rights activist shot dead in his driveway in 1963 while his wife and children waited inside.

"It's a powerful reminder of the sacrifice to gain the ballot, and nobody sacrificed more than Medgar Evers and his family," Colom told the media Friday.

Video player removed for printing https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ny3jT9yDUuE

"What was important to me about that ad is we didn't ask people to vote for me. We just talked about the sacrifice, talked about the story. We just wanted that to be the closing ad because I wanted that to be the last message that the people of Mississippi heard."

Colom's victory is not a rejection of the past. It's steeped in the past, and hopes for a future that eases Mississippi's massive inequalities.

Mississippi's William Faulkner famously said "The past is never dead. It's not even past," and that's still as Mississippi a thought as you can get.

I lived in Mississippi, loved a lot about it, grimaced at some things, and learned so very much about stories, writing and myself in my time there.

One election win doesn't fix America, of course, and Scott Colom may turn out to be just another politician. But even he can't stop what he symbolises today, in the often troubled country I came from that can still sometimes manage to surprise me.

World.title: Retail NZ hit by email scam
World.content:
Audio player for " What's the biggest risk to our economy right now? " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v0.KrRTFtoPsaA8nSDloPZ4KejQJr59ANQpD9ULgGwzaM0/business/2556405%2Fretail-nz-hit-by-email-scam

Retail NZ has been the victim of scammers who sent emails purporting to be from one of its accounts.

On Wednesday, some people in its contacts list received an email claiming to be from its membership email address, saying that a protected document had been shared and recipients should click a link to access it.

The organisation sent another email later in the day saying that its office accounts had been compromised.

Retail NZ chief executive Carolyn Young. Supplied

"We have got our IT provider to run through the necessary checks and they have locked down the affected account. They have advised us that no other Retail NZ accounts have been compromised.

"Our IT provider is still investigating the issue, but they have assured us that it was only the membership account that has been affected and that you are safe to interact with all other email addresses from Retail NZ."

Last year, NBR was subject of a similar scam. People received emails claiming to be from journalist Mike McRoberts.

The National Cyber Security Centre said attackers would send spoof emails to collect personal information about recipients. Spoof emails were those that were made to appear as though they came from your account, when the scammers did not actually have access.

A business email compromise, on the other hand, happened when an attacker managed to get access to an organisation's email and could then use contact lists to try to get money or personal details.

World.title: Nvidia reportedly preparing to fire CEO Jensen Huang, amid of second affair
World.content:
Media reports out of the United States suggest chip giant Nvidia's board is preparing to oust Chief Executive Jensen Huang, following claims of a second extramarital affair.

The Wall Street Journal says the NVDA.O board is preparing to meet as soon as later today.

It follows reports in the New York Times that Huang had an extramarital affair with a company executive who reported to him.

Earlier this week, Huang apologised for having an affair with a Chinese businesswoman who US officials reportedly believe was a Chinese spy.

Nvidia is looking into whether Huang had been targeted by a foreign intelligence operation.

Reuters say Nvidia has not responded to a request for comment on the latest reports.

World.title: No opposition left in Naoero after all MPs join government
World.content:
Naoero, formerly Nauru, no longer has an opposition after its handful of opposition members of parliament joined President David Adeang's administration to form a "united government".

The Micronesian island nation, which is one of the world's smallest republics with a population of around 12,000, made the announcement via a government statement on Tuesday, calling the move a "truly historic moment".

Adeang described that all 19 MPs coming together - the first time since independence in 1968 - to support one government as "a moment of unity, stability and shared purpose".

Naoero does not have any political parties, and its MPs are elected as independent candidates to four-year terms from across eight multi-member constituencies. During the previous two parliaments (2019 and 2022), there were six opposition MPs.

Adeang, 56, was re-elected as president unopposed during the 25th Parliament in October 2025.

He is expected to run the island nation without formal parliamentary opposition until the next election, due in 2029.

The government since its inception had been willing to take different paths, explore new opportunities and lead with boldness, Adeang said.

"Our future decisions must continue to strengthen essential services, protect our national resources and create a sustainable future that does not leave the next generation carrying the burdens of today," he said.

Nauru President David Adeang ABC News / Ian Cutmore

Earlier this year, Adeang's administration changed the country's name without holding a referendum - as was initially expected under the country's parliamentary procedures - as a sign of "national pride and patriotism".

World.title: Warner hits out as batting coach calls Khawaja claims 'absolutely false'
World.content:
The fallout from Usman Khawaja's 2018 South African tour ball-tampering allegations shows no sign of abating after Australia's former batting coach Graeme Hick weighed in to insist they were "absolutely false".

Hick's strong denial of Khawaja's assertion that the whole team knew of the plan to use sandpaper to alter the state of the ball in the series eight years ago also dragged David Warner back to social media as he launched further barbs at Cricket Australia.

In his new book, former Test batting luminary Khawaja's revelations about the infamous "sandpapergate" tour have received both strong support and vehement denials.

The latest rebuttal of his claims has come from former Zimbabwe-born England batting star Graeme Hick, who joined paceman Mitchell Starc and former head coach Darren Lehmann.

Sandpapergate continues to wound Australia Usman Khawaja and David Warner's Sandpapergate revelations may have set the scene for civil war in Australian cricket as the 2018 ball-tampering scandal continues to captivate and damage.

Hick, who worked with the Australian team from 2016 to 2020, told the Sydney Morning Herald: "I have seen the various statements around the coaches and I'm very disappointed with the broad nature of them.

"Khawaja puts it simply: 'It was all of us. Not the batters, not the bowlers, not the staff. All of us.' To me, what Khawaja is implying here is absolutely false.

"In regard to any discussions around the ball-tampering in Port Elizabeth or Cape Town, I will say in true honesty that I did not hear or know anything.

"My first knowledge of all this was, like many, when it appeared on the big screen in Cape Town as I was sat on the outside balcony at the time."

Khawaja's fellow opener Warner, who was one of three players who took the blame for the 2018 sandpaper scandal at Cape Town along with captain Steve Smith and batter Cameron Bancroft, has backed Khawaja's stance and thanked him, saying: "It's 100 per cent accurate what you've said. Now everyone knows the truth."

After reading Hick's comments, Warner returned to social media with another post that seemed to imply the English Test player was hardly at the heart of the team as Cricket Australia's appointment after the popular Michael Di Venuto resigned.

"Let's get the facts straight," Warner wrote. "Graeme Hick was only appointed because Cricket Australia was unwilling to pay Michael Di Venuto what he deserved.

"As players, we valued Michael so highly that we even offered to contribute from our own salaries to retain him.

"These discussions were taking place during the New Zealand tour. That alone speaks volumes about how highly we regarded him and how determined we were to keep him involved. Adds to why Graeme has spoken!!"

AAP

World.title: The Wallabies-Scotland rivalry born in a Melbourne backyard
World.content:
Sione Tuipulotu used to smash Isaac Kailea in their Melbourne backyard battles, but Wallabies prop Kailea hopes to get revenge when his "lippy" cousin leads out Scotland at Murrayfield.

Tuipulotu is another who got away from Australian rugby, a centre who forged his own path before using his ancestry to become Scotland's Aussie braveheart, an inspirational captain who led them to victory over the Wallabies two years ago.

None of which surprises his old mate Kailea, who as a kid always looked up to the guy he saw as a role model in their close-knit Tongan community in Melbourne.

It is also why Sunday's (Monday AEDT) international also means so much to 26-year-old Kailea, who came off the bench in that 2024 clash when Tuipulotu scored a try in the Scots' 27-13 victory.

"If I get the chance again, I'd love to get a win over him," Waratahs loosehead Kailea said, reflecting on the close bond between his family and the Tuipulotu brothers, Sione and younger rugby-playing siblings Sese and Tavi.

Tuipulotu toured Australia with the British and Irish Lions last year. (Getty Images: Chris Hyde)

"Sione's probably one of the most competitive people I know, so when he puts on that Scottish jersey, he's going to give it 100 per cent.

"Whether he goes extra hard because we're Australia, I couldn't say. I just know he's always putting in that effort, especially now he's their captain.

"I know him quite well. I grew up with him and his younger brothers, we pretty much just call each other cousins. Our dads, both of Tongan heritage, met in Melbourne, and there's a couple of other Tongan families there we all grew up with.

"So a lot of boys, a lot of pretty rough games in the backyard, but Sione was always the leader among the kids, as the oldest. We played a couple of times in the backyard. He used to run amok — he'd smash us to bits.

"The younger kids just followed his lead, and the leadership he showed there is something I can see him doing now with Scotland. Even the way he talks, it's still the same. It's pretty cool to see."

Kailea said the rest of the younger boys saw saw Tuipulotu as a role model, especially once he played for the Melbourne Rebels.

Kailea has joined his "cousin" on the international stage. (AAP Image: Joel Carrett)

"It was a bit tough for him in Australia, he went on his own little journey, through Japan, and now he's ended up in Scotland, and his brothers are over here as well, chasing the dream," Kailea said.

Hooker Tavi plays alongside Tuipulotu at Glasgow Warriors and centre Sese is at Edinburgh Rugby.

"It's pretty crazy to be honest," Kailea said.

In that 2024 clash, Tuipulotu played like a man with something to prove.

"He can be pretty lippy on the field, just like he is off it, so he was throwing a bit of chat, but nothing too crazy. I don't think he'd get too disrespectful," smiled Kailea, recalling how Tuipulotu collected the match trophy off his Scottish gran, Jaqueline Thomson.

He also got flattened by a thunderous tackle from Joseph Aukuso-Suaalii in that match which actually caused an arm injury to the Australian and left Tuipulotu reflecting: "I've never been hit like that in my career."

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.

AAP

World.title: The women's RLWC final is a fight against fate
World.content:
The women's Rugby League World Cup has ended up exactly where it was fated to be, with Australia to face New Zealand in the final for the third tournament in a row.

Barring the kind of upset that sends bookies broke, this was the only way it could be given the Jillaroos and Kiwi Ferns have romped their way through with a near contemptuous ease.

Only Fiji, a delightful surprise packet in their maiden tournament who lost to New Zealand by six in the group stage and Australia by 16 in the semi-final, managed to run either of them close. The former is the only game of the World Cup to be decided by one score or fewer.

Australia names teams for World Cup finals Australia has named its men's and women's sides for this Sunday's Rugby League World Cup finals against New Zealand.

Even counting the valiant efforts of the Bulikula, Australia and New Zealand have outscored their opponents by a combined 272-20 and 182-24 respectively.

Fiji's emergence and Papua New Guinea and Samoa's continued development are positives but if the journey truly matters more than the destination this one has been a trudge.

It has felt inevitable from the start and perhaps it was. There could have been improvements to the draw — Australia had no business playing a team like Wales — but none that would have changed this outcome.

A tournament like this and a final like this, where Australia are deserved 20-point favourites given they've only lost to New Zealand once in the past ten years, is the wrong end of the double-edged sword women's rugby league is trying to wield.

The Jillaroos are the game's lone superpower, without peer or rival, because they are the end-product of almost a decade of transformation via the NRLW.

Australia have done it easy through much of this World Cup. (Getty Images: Janelle St Pierre)

They play the same sport as developing nations, but they're in a different game to nations like Wales, France and Papua New Guinea.

There's a value in having a team that stands so tall because they're a gold standard to aspire to for some and a target to aim at for others.

They are proof of what is possible for women's rugby league with investment from the bottom up and the top down, as well as giving it the patience for that investment to rise to the top.

It makes the Jillaroos an incredible creation and victory on Sunday would confirm what most already know — that this is the greatest collection of talent in the history of women's rugby league.

Lopsided women's rugby league The rise of Pasifika rugby league teams in the international men's game contrasts with a widening gulf in the women's game.

Just as the 2017 final, the last before the start of the NRLW, signalled the beginning of a new kind of history so would a Jillaroos win here be the capstone on Australia remaking the game in their own image.

It would mark their fourth World Cup final win in a row, pulling them past New Zealand who currently have three with the last coming back in 2008.

Their dominance is a by-product of the game's progress but it's also so complete and smothering it's become a problem. The things that have made them great have worked too well.

Australia have moved so far and so fast not only is there nothing left for them to overtake, they can barely see New Zealand over their shoulders. They must keep looking though, because there is nobody else to see.

New Zealand are the only team to come close to Australia in recent years. (Getty Images: Chris Hyde)

They are Everest and New Zealand are the only other team who have even been able to try to climb a mountain before. Everybody else is stuck at base camp.

As talented as their opponents are — and with Raecene McGregor at halfback, Mele Hufanga and Stacey Waaka in the centres and inspirational captain Georgia Hale leading a forward pack who could skin a crocodile their talent is considerable — just playing well is not enough for New Zealand to win.

They'll need an off night by the Australians, a few bounces of the ball, perhaps a referee call or two falling their way, just to bring them into the contest.

A win is possible, but it would be the greatest upset of this era and when the second-best team in the world needs a fair bit of luck to take it to the best, things have gotten way too top heavy.

Australia's World Cup record breaker helps nobody Australia ran up the biggest win in women's international rugby league history with its World Cup victory over Wales but it was the kind of result that served little purpose other than stuffing the stats sheet.

Australia have taken giant strides while everyone else is trying to catch up with smaller steps.

The great-grandparent rule might help in the short-term if it allows more elite talent to filter through to other nations.

Any potential NRL investment in Super League would surely include a women's component and that would give the game in the northern hemisphere a boost it sorely needs.

Both moves would build on the progress of this World Cup, which has mainly come through in excellent television ratings even if the contests haven't been close.

But further development is required before there's any thought of a standalone World Cup, which will likely be tabled until 2034 at the earliest because it cannot happen until this game is for more than one player.

There are glories that lie outside ultimate victory and those can be easier to find once teams like Fiji, Samoa and Papua New Guinea have more time to develop but when it comes to Australia that's a hard thing to remember.

They are the best by such a margin the rest are barely in sight, a grim fate they can confirm with glory on Sunday.

World.title: Swimming embraces short and sharp with new Swim GP competition
World.content:
No sport is immune from a fight for relevance in a jam-packed sporting marketplace.

And Swim GP is Swimming Australia's latest attempt to blend sporting entertainment, just 12 months on from its last foray into the genre, Australia vs The World in Brisbane.

This year, the nation is keeping things in-house with a slightly tweaked format involving teams of domestic swimmers.

"I think it's a really exciting opportunity," three-time Commonwealth Games champion Jenna Forrester told ABC Sport.

"I wasn't actually at Aus vs The World last year, so this is going to be my first time doing an event like this.

"But I got to watch some of it on TV and I thought that it was a really cool concept."

Swimming's revolution begins with pumping night at The Valley Swimming stepped out of its tried and trusted format in a novelty, multi-event competition in Brisbane on Friday night.

A cool concept but not an unfamiliar one.

Swimming has toyed with events like this for more than 30 years, since the Qantas Skins events in the mid-1990s.

Before COVID, the International Swimming League (ISL) came in to shake up the perceived monotony of conventional competition and act as a vehicle to keep interest in the sport high between Olympics.

The league has not been seen since 2021, partially as a result of COVID, partially due to the Russia-Ukraine war. The ISL's principal backer is Ukrainian businessman Konstantin Grigorishin.

However, later this year, the ISL will return with a one-off All-Star Match at the London Aquatics Centre on December 19.

The International Swimming League (ISL) took place before COVID. (Getty Images: Catherine Ivill)

That is despite there being legal issues between World Aquatics and the ISL: World Aquatics settled with a group of 263 swimmers in September 2025, who said they were denied a chance to compete, and therefore earn money, in ISL competitions.

World Aquatics paid those swimmers a combined $US4.6 million, and allowed them to participate in independent competitions such as the ISL without losing their ability to compete in the Olympics.

There is also a separate, ongoing lawsuit between the ISL and World Aquatics.

The ISL also played a role in forming the College Swimming League (CSL) in the USA, which had its first competitions in September.

The league brings together 12 programs from three of the biggest NCAA conferences: the SEC, ACC and Big Ten.

The ISL aimed to give international swimmers more visibility, and hopes to do the same for college swimmers with the CSL. (Getty Images: Catherine Ivill)

The league featured multiples, four-team competitions, with 30 events at each competition. That includes Skins events and a "jackpot" scoring rule.

Chief executive Rob Kent told Reuters the league was designed for a TV audience and for each meet to last a TV-friendly two and a half hours.

TV-friendly is exactly what Swim GP is going for too.

"I think it's just going to be a year-by-year thing that will just keep getting better and better as the event progresses," Forrester said.

"It is really exciting and it definitely is a bit different to what we're used to."

Skins matches, multi-round elimination races, play a big role in Swim GP, as do mystery relays and power plays, much in the same way they did in Brisbane last year.

It will also provide high-intensity race prep for swimmers outside of the major championships.

"It's a really exciting opportunity, and short course as well, so it'll be short and fast," Forrester said.

Jenna Forrester's versatility was instrumental in her early selection. (Supplied: Swimming Australia/Delly Carr)

"It'll be good race practice and good race practice in coming together as a team, because that's something that's really important in swimming.

"It is an individual sport, but when we go away on the Australian team we really focus on the culture and bringing that Australian spirit.

"I think this will be kind of a good practice into turning swimming into more of a team sport."

At Swim GP, Australia's best and brightest able-bodied and para swimmers have been split into four teams: Team Kraken, Wahoo, KingTide and Tsunami.

Each team has platinum athletes as their headliners: KingTide has Flynn Southam and Lani Pallister; Kraken selected Kyle Chalmers and Mollie O’Callaghan; Wahoo had Meg Harris and Sam Short; Tsunami went with Kaylee McKeown and William Petric.

The first overall pick went to Wahoo, who selected sprint specialist Ben Armbruster.

Ben Armbruster is a versatile sprinter. (Supplied: Swimming Australia/Delly Carr)

Armbruster is as versatile a sprinter as they come.

The 24-year-old won Commonwealth and Pan Pac gold in the 50-metres butterfly, having reached the semifinals of the 50m freestyle at the Paris Olympics and the final of the 50m backstroke at the 2022 Commonwealth Games in Birmingham.

Mel Marshall used her first pick, second overall, to select Forrester for KingTide.

"To be second pick, that was kind of crazy to be honest," Forrester said.

"I'm curious to see what events they have because I feel like a lot of it will be kind of sprint events. I'm interested to see how I go trying to do some of those.

"It really just shows that I've had a pretty good year, I guess.

"Maybe that hasn't really settled in for me yet, maybe some other people are seeing it before I am."

World.title: Want to win an AFLW flag? Club culture matters, data shows
World.content:
AFLW sides are more likely to finish down the bottom of the ladder when their players rate their workplace culture low, the players' association says.

Data collected from the union around the middle of the season suggests a strong correlation between workplace culture and on-field performance.

"If we look at AFLW, what we're seeing is there is a bit of a widening gap between the best of our workplace culture data and that which is more at the bottom," AFL Players Association chief executive James Gallagher told ABC Sport.

"We're seeing some of the highest scores ever reported at the top end, so that's fantastic. That's what we want to see, but we are seeing a gap between the best and the bottom end."

Collingwood's woeful AFLW season Former AFLW player and coach Lauren Arnell has criticised the standard of Collingwood, while emphasising the responsibility of coaches to "put on a show" to grow the game.

This year, four teams were assessed as having the best workplace culture on record and four teams the worst.

This was evaluated according to club care, mental breaks, off-field expectations, relationships, schedule flexibility and study/work support.

Five of this year's finals teams were in the top seven for "overall workplace culture". Non-finalist teams overwhelmingly rated on the lower end for workplace culture scores.

It comes after widespread media scrutiny on struggling clubs, particularly Collingwood.

James Gallagher says there is a correlation between successful AFLW sides and workplace culture ratings. (Getty: James Wiltshire/AFL Photos)

The Magpies, along with St Kilda, finished with one win each this season, while GWS and Essendon had just two victories out of their 12 games.

Of those four bottom-ladder clubs, all but the Giants parted ways with their head coaches.

The Magpies and Saints are now set to undertake external reviews of their women's programs,. Essendon has opted to conduct an expanded internal review.

North Melbourne, Geelong, Melbourne, Carlton, Gold Coast, Sydney, Western Bulldogs and Hawthorn finished in the top eight this year.

Sydney and the Western Bulldogs featured in the finals series this year. (Getty: Darrian Traynor)

The Kangaroos have lost one game in three years and the Demons have regularly finished in the finals.

The data also showed some players as having rated respect for the men's AFL club head of performance and head coach as low to extremely low.

Furthermore, men's players being embroiled in off-field news, such as the Sydney Swans saga involving allegations of sexual assault or GWS' "controversial couples" night leading to player sanctions, can impact the women's programs.

"There's no doubt they are extraordinarily challenging for all to navigate. I mean, do they have an impact on AFLW playing groups? In some cases, they do for sure," Mr Gallagher said.

"Making sure there's an opportunity for those players' views to be heard and considered is a really important part of how footy clubs in 2026 now operate."

Pies launch AFLW review As a tough season nears its end, Collingwood announces a strategic review into the struggling AFLW program, with the club's president admitting the Pies had not "got it right".

Crucially, with the seasons overlapping more every year, men's and women's programs require access to the same facilities, including the gym and communal areas.

Just half of all players said they felt their men's and women's programs were aligned.

"Those clubs that report the strongest workplace environments are much more likely to be successful, and that's reflected in the final series in front of us," Mr Gallagher said.

"The game is a high-performance game and to enable that to be successful you do need people who are fronting up, comfortable, confident, feeling like they're really well supported, and we're seeing that reflected in the wins and losses column now, for sure."

Women's teams with strong workplace culture are more likely to make the finals, according to the AFLPA. (Getty: Kelly Defina)

Workplace culture includes club support for players outside football commitments, including work and study.

While players have seen huge strides in increased contact hours since season one, more than half of all players still work outside football.

Sixty-four per cent engage in casual work, 32 per cent work part-time and 4 per cent full-time. None of the 45 Irish players can work due to their visas.

The players' association expects next year's AFLW season to accommodate more double-headers. The start date is yet to be announced.

World.title: The rebuild is on as Labuschagne makes shaky return to Shield cricket
World.content:
Marnus Labuschagne's return to first-class cricket following his axing from the Test team lasted 36 balls for Queensland in the Sheffield Shield on Wednesday.

Labuschagne made 12 runs before nicking off to Tasmania's Jake Doran off the bowling of Riley Meredith.

The 32-year-old's dismissal looked similar to so many of his recent failings at Test level, prodding on fourth stump without a hint of foot movement.

Ordinarily Sheffield Shield games retain some semblance of importance for Test players searching for form ahead of The Summer of Cricket.

Uniquely for Queensland's captain, this match means nothing — at least in the short-term.

He's already been flung on the Test scrap heap, a dire run of form eventually hastening his demise from an Australian Test team that crushed England in last year's Ashes, but has won just two of its last five Tests against Bangladesh and South Africa, without claiming a series victory.

Spectators didn't mind that though, and more than a handful had turned out to show support to their beleaguered skipper.

Those who arrived on time had to wait an hour and 20 minutes before Labuschagne came to the crease after Angus Lovell (18 off 60 balls) edged Beau Webster into the slips. The opener furiously smacked his bat after doing so much of the hard work on a pitch that offered plenty of zip.

Labuschagne's arrival was greeted with warm applause, the clapping briefly drowning out the incessant jackhammering of the building sites around the Gabba.

"Come on Marnus," one punter among the hundred or so faithful called out as he took his mark.

Marnus Labuschagne lasted 36 balls in his first return to the crease since South Africa. (Getty Images: Bradley Kanaris)

Labuschagne wasted no time in getting into the thick of the action, crushing a square drive for four off the very first ball he faced from former Test teammate Webster.

A streaky edge past third slip off the bowling of Jackson Bird though, reiterated that Labuschagne's rebuild could be a process as drawn out as the redevelopment around the ground.

As good as his opening salvo was, the idiosyncrasies that all too often verged towards idiocies during his faltering stays in the middle during Test matches, were still there.

There was a wave of his hands here, a period of shadow-batting there that were as prevalent at the Gabba as they were in Gqeberha, where he scored 14 and 39 in Australia's innings defeat.

As Bell got closer to the off-stump, Labuschagne's leaves became ever more flamboyant, a batting matador daring the bull to crash into his stumps.

He lasted until lunch, walking off with eight runs to his name.

His demise came soon after the break when edged a delivery he didn't need to play at into the gloves of the keeper.

Labuschagne waited a moment at the crease, miffed at his dismissal, before trudging off.

Fortunately for him, it was far from a bumper day of scores around the country.

Sam Konstas scored 24 and Kurtis Patterson a duck for New South Wales as they were bundled out for 204 against South Australia, while Marcus Harris managed just 15 on an MCG pitch that looked good for batting, given Peter Handscomb's century for Victoria.

It is far too soon after his return from South Africa to rectify any wrongs in his technique or banish the demons residing within his head.

As much as the hammering taking place outside the Gabba, the work to build Labuschagne back into a principle Test batter will take time.

World.title: How a small scrap of sandpaper shed light on cricket's so-called dark arts
World.content:
Eight years after then-prime minister Malcolm Turnbull felt the need to weigh in on Australia's ball tampering in the Cape Town Test, sandpaper and cricket are back in the headlines together.

Usman Khawaja's book, featuring revelations, allusions and confirmations of what most everyone already believed, has reignited conversations about the Australian team's conduct during that 2018 tour of South Africa.

But whatever the team did, who did it and who knew about it, one thing is for sure: they weren't the first to fiddle with the ball.

So why did they do it and why was the reaction so extreme?

'A beautiful art'

Reverse swing can make even the best batters look silly. (Getty Images: Tom Shaw)

In the wake of Khawaja's exclusive interview with Nine Newspapers on the weekend, outspoken former Australia fast bowler Geoff Lawson added to the conversation with a brilliantly headlined article.

" I don't know a bowler who hasn't licked, flicked, scratched or slobbered on a cricket ball. "

Thanks for those mental images, Geoff.

Evocative wording or not, the 46-Test veteran is right. But why?

Explaining the mysteries of swing bowling It is one of the most devastating weapons a fast bowler can own — but the art of swing is steeped in mystery and myths that only science can explain.

The science of conventionally swinging a cricket ball through the air is relatively simple and adheres to some basic rules of drag, air pressure and laminar flow (a lot of the same stuff that keeps an aeroplane in the air).

When a cricket ball is new, its stitched seam is standing at its tallest, allowing a bowler to angle that seam towards or away from the batter and the air will get caught on the seam, dragging the ball in that direction.

But the proud seam on a dark red ball is clearly visible to a batter, and the best ones can see what's happening and account for it.

Reverse swing is a little more complicated and prized due to it being more difficult to deliver, predict and face.

Conventional swing (left) vs reverse swing (right). (ABC News: Gabrielle Flood and Nina Maile Gordon)

"As a batter it's the hardest thing to face. It's a beautiful art," former Proteas captain Faf du Plessis told The Grade Cricketer podcast on the eve of Australia's return to Cape Town last month.

The ball swings towards the side of the ball that looks smoother due to small abrasions on that "shiny" side of the ball, more of which is facing the batter and therefore offering more surface area and turbulent airflow, this time dragging the ball in the opposite direction to the way the seam is facing.

It also happens later in the ball's flight, often too late for the batter to react.

It only comes after the ball has been bowled for a few dozen overs and whacked around the field a bit; once the seam has flattened out, and the leather has been, crucially, roughed up and dried out.

Weather conditions have to be perfect, the bowlers have to be incredibly skilled and the care for the ball has to be spot-on, to the point that former England captain Alastair Cook was prized as a ball shiner because he barely sweats.

Of course, there are other ways to help this along.

Spit, sunscreen and swing

There are plenty of legal ways to shine the ball. (Getty Images: Paul Kane)

Once a cricket pitch has flattened out from the start of a game, the new ball has lost its shine and proud seam, and before it becomes a spinner's paradise on days four and five (although this is becoming more and more rare), reverse swing is one of the few tools in fast bowler's arsenal.

For decades, cricket teams have worked on the ball feverishly to try to work on conventional and reverse swing.
