Tech.title: A Startup Wants to Fight AI Bioweapons With AI
Tech.content:
Frontier AI labs have warned that their technology could help develop dangerous bioweapons.

Now, a startup says it has developed a defense. On Wednesday, Radical Numerics announced that it has developed a new edge model called Omnii Defense that is designed to flag natural and AI-engineered pathogens using a laptop and a USB gene sequencer. It can also run without an internet connection, allowing researchers in the field with spotty connections to use it. Though many scientists say AI-made bioweapons are a low-likelihood threat, Radical Numerics hopes its technology will help researchers and public health officials identify emerging biological threats.

Eric Nguyen, cofounder and CEO of Radical Numerics, says he sees a coming arms race in biodefense similar to what’s playing out in cybersecurity, where threat actors and security defenders are leveraging AI in an attempt to gain an edge.

“We felt that the biosecurity space was far behind on the defense side,” he says.

Nguyen and his cofounders were part of the research team behind Evo and Evo-2, open-source DNA foundation models they worked on during their doctoral research at Stanford University. They founded Radical Numerics in 2025.

Tech.title: The AO3 Shutdown Is Pitting Fanfic Readers Against Authors
Tech.content:
Avery has been writing fan fiction for about six years, now mainly focused on the gay hockey romance Heated Rivalry. Until last month, it all lived in one place—Archive of Our Own. Then, on October 29 the fan fiction behemoth went dark due to a “security incident.” Within days, Avery was alarmed to find her works on mirror sites she hadn’t posted them to.

“To me it’s a security risk,” Avery, who did not want her real name used due to fears of backlash on social media, tells WIRED via DM. “One bad actor could put malware in that drive.”

She emailed the sites—Squidgeworld and AO3.Life—and the stories were removed, though she’ll never know if she has found every copy online. (AO3.Life has since been taken down, and Walter Hopgood, president of Squidge.org, which hosts Squidgeworld, told WIRED it removes works that are posted without an author’s permission.)

Avery’s problem is one shared with many fanfic authors since the team behind AO3 announced the site will remain offline for up to four weeks.

Hosting more than 18.8 million fan works across hundreds of thousands of fandoms, AO3 is among the most visited websites in the world. When it went down, some fans started freaking out over the “AO3 apocalypse.” Within days, readers who had saved stories on their own device placed them onto shared libraries on Google Drives. But finding alternatives has caused friction in the community, as some authors are unhappy with the way their works are being distributed without their permission, breaking fanfic norms and exacerbating fears about AI scraping.

One of the many drives to pop up was the Archive Salvation Google Drive project, a collective of fan fiction downloaded from AO3. It faced criticism after launching, though a spokesperson tells WIRED it offered ways for authors to ask for their work to be removed. But it’s since been hacked and is no longer accessible, according to a November 3 statement on a moderator’s TikTok, though the group behind it is still sharing fanfics in a closed Discord server.

“We continue to acknowledge the controversies of such drives but also want to acknowledge the joy this has brought readers and the authors who submitted their fics to us,” the statement said, adding, “our drive was controversial and very public, so the hacker is most likely someone who stands against drives like this in general.”

Avery doesn’t mind her work circulating in private drives or being asked for copies of their work for fans to read—her concern is with her work being uploaded to giant drive libraries.

Tech.title: China’s Nvidia Honeypot Isn’t Surprising. Jensen Huang Fell for It Anyway
Tech.content:
There’s a specific mantra drilled into government workers, military officers, and intelligence personnel during counterintelligence briefings: “If she’s a 10 and you’re a 5, she’s a spy!” Or, as the US Army’s Counterintelligence Command posted on Valentine’s Day: “It doesn’t take a mathematician to figure out ‘10 + 5 = honeytrap.’” The very beautiful woman who is suddenly interested in your very ordinary existence probably has ulterior motives, is the message.

Jensen Huang surely doesn’t live a typical life—he’s a centibillionaire, the swashbuckling CEO of Nvidia, one of the hottest and most geopolitically consequential companies of the 21st century. Surely he’s aware of the possibility that he’d cross paths with intelligence assets. In fact, it’s hard to think of many companies in the world that would be a higher priority target for foreign intelligence agencies.

All of that makes the stock-shaking news this week all the more surprising. How did Huang get embroiled in a spy scandal that mixes infidelity, international espionage, the Trump administration, and the economic behemoth of the multitrillion-dollar AI industry?

The story kicked off just before Halloween, with a six-byline story in The New York Times reporting that Huang was the target of a Chinese spy plot. Starting somewhere between 2024 and 2025, Huang allegedly had an affair with Alice Huang (no relation), a one-time executive at a Singapore-based cloud provider known as Megaspeed. US intelligence agencies warned top US officials that they believed she was a Chinese intelligence asset. So far, Nvidia’s board, which has launched its own investigation, says it has “no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised,” but that’s far from the only concern.

As one would expect, China has denied any nefarious plot centered on Jensen Huang. A Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson on Monday said, “The narrative about so-called Chinese spies is entirely based on groundless speculation—it’s nothing more than slander and smearing.”

But according to reporting by The New York Times and the Financial Times, US intelligence officials also claim that Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, was reporting to China’s Ministry of State Security intelligence agency. On Monday, Megaspeed said on LinkedIn that US authorities found “no evidence of any violations concerning the illicit transfer of chips or any illegal activities." (There’s no indication so far that Alice Huang, a one-time Chinese state journalist, is an employee or “officer” of Chinese intelligence; she’s believed to be an “asset,” an outsider who aids an intelligence agency, sometimes for pay, sometimes not.)

China, though, has elevated economic espionage to a core pillar of its economic and military development, stealing the designs for everything from US fighter jets to solar panels and commercial paint recipes. “Honeypots” or “honey traps”—positioning an alluring operative to seduce or develop a relationship with a key target—are one of intelligence’s most infamous and well-established strategies. French officials have warned specifically about Chinese honeypots since at least 2011, when intelligence reports cited a pharmaceutical researcher who was seduced and then blackmailed by a Chinese spy operation.

Tech.title: Duolingo, Strava, and Ticketmaster Are All Caught Up in EU’s New Digital Fairness Rules
Tech.content:
The European Commission announced a sweeping set of updates to consumer law on Wednesday to protect European Union citizens from “harmful digital practices”—whether while online shopping, browsing social media, or doing their Duolingo lesson.

Within the package, the Commission unveiled its Digital Fairness Act to address harmful practices online. Proposed rules include banning dark patterns—practices that manipulate consumers into making decisions they would not otherwise make, such as falsely claiming a product is running low. They will also curb dynamic pricing by ticket retailers, like Ticketmaster; force influencers to disclose when they are being paid to promote a product; outrule personalized advertising and pricing targeting minors or taking advantage of sensitive data; make digital subscriptions easier to cancel; and give consumers a right to interact with human customer service.

The package “represents the most significant reform of EU consumer protection rules in more than 20 years” according to Michael McGrath, the EC Consumer Protection Commissioner, noting that existing consumer rules were developed before ecommerce, the attention economy, and use of personal data for marketing took off. “The digital fairness act will make sure the digital economy works for consumers and not against them,” he said at a press conference.

The bill will also enable all consumers to turn off addictive design features on digital services, such as autoplay of videos and streaks—including on apps like Strava and Duolingo.

Some of these patterns the EU has already restricted for children through its Kids Act, which in addition to banning under-13s from accessing social media and chatbots, targets addictive designs in those services. Some European rights groups have called for those protections to be extended to all consumers and, teasing the Digital Fairness Act in September’s State of the Union address, President Ursula von der Leyen said: “But it is not only minors who are at risk. Addictive design, for example, is harming everyone. That is why we need a wider framework.”

Some of the risks are also already regulated by the EU Digital Services Act. On Friday, the European Commission said ByteDance’s TikTok had breached those rules with the “rabbit hole effect” of its “For You” feed algorithm which personalizes content recommended to users. The tech regulator had previously found TikTok’s “addictive design” broke the rules by including features such as infinite scroll, autoplay, and push notifications, in addition to the algorithm. In July, it found Meta to be in breach of the act due to similar features on Instagram and Facebook. If confirmed, both companies may now face fines of up to 6 percent of worldwide annual turnover.

The new regulation is designed to fill the gaps between this, the Digital Markets Act, and August’s AI Act, says executive vice president Henna Virkkunen, “not duplicate this.” The package should simplify consumer protection rules across the bloc’s 27 members and be a “strong safety net in the digital world,” she adds.

The Commission aims to accelerate cross-border cooperation through strengthened enforcement rules. These would also give the regulator direct powers to investigate large-scale impact and fine firms up to 6 percent of their worldwide annual turnover. Non-EU companies would be required to appoint a local legal representative to cooperate with authorities.

Tech.title: Best Indoor Garden Systems I’ve Been Testing for Years (2026)
Tech.content:
Others Tested

Click & Grow Smart Garden 9 Photograph: Kat Merck

Click and Grow Smart Garden for $102: Click & Grow Smart Garden's seed pods come in a Nespresso-evoking plastic three-pack with a tear-off cover. (A three-pack of pods starts at around $15.) Put a nutrient-packed “smart soil” seed pod in one of the Click & Grow’s cups with the wicking bottom, fill the reservoir, and that’s it. It was one of the simplest watering systems I tried: a wick at the bottom of the cup brings water up to the pods, and the roots stay in the cups. A little bobber on one end tells you when the water level is low and needs a top-off, simply by floating lower than the growing surface. It's also small, so you can plop it on a shelf or countertop. (Note that the 9, pictured above, is currently out of stock, but you can sign up to be notified when it's available.) At the same time, this was also one of the slowest-growing gardens I tested—it took weeks to get even one lettuce leaf. One of my lettuce pods didn’t even sprout at all. Still, this isn't a terrible option for busy people who are interested in growing something like flowers, where yields aren't a concern.

North Spore Automated Monotub Kit for $165: If you already know how to DIY your own mushroom-cultivating monotub setup, this is not for you. Nor is it for those who want something fully plug-and-play. It's a bare-bones kit—a tub with a lid, filters, a hygrometer, a humidifier, and a fan to maintain airflow—for growing either fruiting blocks or substrate-based mushroom species. My kit came with no paper instructions, so I had to figure out how to use it completely via YouTube and trial and error. That said, when you figure it out, it works. I've run it through multiple harvests now, producing more oyster and lion's mane mushrooms than I knew what to do with. However, note that you will need to replace the filters after a couple of runs; mine got blocked and grew mold.

Rise Garden 3 for $1,499: The three-level Rise has far and away the biggest capacity of any non-DIY indoor garden I’ve seen, along with a pretty traditional form factor. In fact, I'm pretty sure I saw one of these in the corner of my college biology class. Since it's so large, assembly was a bit tricky, and vague instructions weren't helpful. I also didn't find out until after I had already set it up that the peat pods need to germinate first in plastic-lidded “nurseries.” My test unit didn't come with enough nurseries, so I had to improvise with shallow plastic containers, with the pods weighted to keep them upright in water. After a few days, I noticed the containers—all of them, including the provided nurseries—had begun to grow algae, and the black-plastic surface of the Rise trays was noticeably warm. I brought out my infrared temperature gun to test the temperature and found that the 195-watt LEDs paired with the black plastic had brought the surface up to 95 degrees Fahrenheit. For reference, all of the other indoor gardening systems were room temperature, in the mid-70s. Over time, I noticed herbs and lettuce bolted faster in the Rise 3 than in other gardens, likely due to this heat, which also puts plants at risk for cases of root rot. I'm still a big fan of the Rise's form factor and its capacity, though, and I think it would be a first choice for heat-tolerant crops, like tomatoes and peppers.

Modern Sprout Garden Jars for $20: These cute Mason jars are as simple as it gets: Rinse the included gravel, then add seeds and water. They're guaranteed to sprout in five to 10 days and make a fun hostess gift with a tea towel and/or a bottle of olive oil. However, they are definitely more for looks than harvests—I have had the basil, cilantro, and rosemary versions on my windowsill for a little over a year, and I’ve only seen a few usable leaves.

Lettuce Grow Counterstand Photograph: Kat Merck

Lettuce Grow Counterstand Set for $149: New from the makers of the flashy Lettuce Grow Farmstand (8/10 WIRED Recommends), this simple, no-pump setup consists of three amber beakers that look straight out of a high school chemistry lab, plus an 18-inch-tall LED lamp that runs on a 16- or 18-hour timer. It relies on the Kratky method of hydroponics, invented by horticulturist Dr. Bernard Kratky, where the plant sits in a cup above a nutrient-enriched water source. In the Counterstand's case, a wick draws water up to the seedling until its roots can grow into the water. Included with your order are three credits for live seedlings of your choice—I picked parsley, basil, and butter lettuce. This setup is stylish, but consider the counter space it requires, the yields are tiny—maybe a small handful of leaves a week.

Vego EZ Microgreens Planter (2-pack) for $60: This system for growing nutrient-packed microgreens for salads, smoothies, and sandwiches isn't smart, but it is nifty enough to warrant a mention. Just fill each half-gallon reservoir (made of food-safe plastic) with water, and then cover it with the optional humidity dome. From there, bamboo-fiber capillary grow mats on top will absorb water to germinate your microgreen seeds (not included). Set it near a sunny window, use a grow light, or add Vego's 10 x 20 dome with a built-in grow light ($80), which fits over both planters. I placed my planters on a Ferry-Morse pop-up plant stand with a grow light from LetPot and had consistent success across multiple grows.

Not Recommended

Photograph: Lisa Wood Shapiro

Plantaform Smart Indoor Garden for $800: Plantaform is “the world's first smart indoor garden that uses fog to grow plants,” according to the company's press release, and it has definitely garnered attention, winning an Innovation Award at the 2025 Consumer Electronics Show (CES). The “fogponics" technology, ostensibly building on NASA-developed aeroponics, delivers water and nutrients to plants' roots via an ultrafine mist. The futuristic look of the egg-shaped planter certainly captivated us at WIRED, but when contributor Lisa Wood Shapiro tested it to grow lettuce, she found that you can't combine different types of plants (i.e., you can only grow lettuce at one time, or tomatoes, or herbs). The machine also degraded her indoor air quality, as tested with an air quality monitor. Users must add an included fertilizer mix to the water, with the resulting concoction being what's aerosolized in the container; Wood Shapiro found this was not airtight. She suggests limiting the Plantaform's use to a basement or another space where air quality isn't as much of a concern, but it's probably best to hold off on this one until Plantaform can work out some more kinks.

LetPot Smart Seed Starter for $84: There are many grow-light–enabled seed starters on the market, but LetPot's Smart Seed Starter has more features than most, including a sensor for soil temperature and EC and a 24-watt heating pad underneath. A plastic lid with adjustable vents on either end sits on top. I love the concept, but sadly, quality control is lacking. On my test unit, the power adapter makes a high-pitched sound when the lights are on, the EC sensor only works intermittently, and auto-mode erases whenever it's unplugged. After about six months of regular use, the light stopped staying on, and to get the unit to cooperate, I had to unplug and replug it repeatedly.

AeroGarden Harvest Lite for $93: Formerly my top pick for Most Giftable, I loved the simplicity of this system, which requires no app—push or hold a single embossed AeroGarden logo on the top to run through all of the controls and settings. However, it doesn't include sponges, baskets, or pods, which is a bit of a miss at this price point, and the pump failed after only a year of use. AeroGarden offers no replacement parts to fix this issue, which online reviews suggest isn't uncommon, so faulty units end up in the landfill.

FAQs What Is Hydroponics? AccordionItemContainerButton LargeChevron In the simplest terms, hydroponic gardening means growing plants without roots in soil. Sometimes plants are suspended in water, like in the Rise or Gardyn; sometimes they're in pods attached to a wick, like in the Click & Grow; and sometimes water is sprayed or misted onto their roots, like in the Lettuce Grow. Usually, this process works alongside an artificial light source, either indoors or in an outdoor enclosure. What Are the Benefits of Hydroponics? AccordionItemContainerButton LargeChevron In addition to the obvious plus of cleaner produce without mud, dirt, or synthetic pesticides, hydroponic systems use much less water than conventional growing methods, since all the water used is either recirculated or taken up by the plants. Some farmers also say they get higher yields from hydroponic systems, as the variables of weather, light, and nutrients are far easier to control. And, because of these variables, farmers are also able to grow varieties of plants in just about any season or region. And there are no weeds! What Kinds of Things Can I Grow in a Hydroponic Garden? AccordionItemContainerButton LargeChevron Just about anything you can think of! I asked FX Rouxel, creator of Gardyn, if there was anything you couldn't grow in these systems, other than ground-dwelling plants like peanuts or potatoes. “All the things that have big roots,” he said—like carrots, parsnips, and so on. “Otherwise, mostly things that are too big, like apples or lemons.” So, there you have it: No long roots, no trees. But anything else is fair game to try. What Are the Downsides of Hydroponic Systems? AccordionItemContainerButton LargeChevron First of all, it's no secret hydroponic systems cost more than just planting some seeds outside in the dirt. Then you've got to worry about power outages, pump maintenance, algae, and just general maintenance. And if you're not careful, water can harbor some nasty stuff, even if that's just fertilizer, as WIRED contributor Lisa Wood Shapiro found when she reviewed the Plantaform. Some also claim that hydroponically grown herbs, greens, and vegetables have less flavor than their soil-grown counterparts, but I personally have not noticed a difference; I've grown perfectly flavorful snap peas, cauliflower, shell beans, salad greens, and even strawberries in nutrient-infused water. In fact, one of the best cucumbers I've ever had in my life came from my Gardyn Studio, of all places. Will I Save Money by Growing My Own Vegetables? AccordionItemContainerButton LargeChevron In short, no. The ready-made systems simply remove a great deal of hassle and guesswork from the process, and they usually look pretty cool in the process. It's also nice to have warranty and tech support in the event something goes wrong. As is often the case with anything filled with water, when something does go wrong, it goes really wrong. (Speaking of, be sure to check out our guide to the Best Water Leak Detectors.) How Much Can I Really Grow in These Things? AccordionItemContainerButton LargeChevron It largely depends on what you're growing and how many individual plants can fit in your system. My yields have ranged from a handful of lettuce leaves in the Click & Grow to huge bagfuls of salad greens per day in the Rise—more than my family could possibly eat. As a rule, lettuces and other greens tend to grow faster, while fruiting plants like tomatoes and peppers grow slower and sometimes need pollination to produce. (For instance, with strawberries I have to use a small paintbrush to brush the flowers each morning.) Where Can I Put Them in My House? AccordionItemContainerButton LargeChevron Most of these systems take up only a square foot or two, so space isn't as much of a consideration as lights and pump noise. Lights for these gardens typically need to be on around 16 hours a day, and they are bright, so if this schedule would be disruptive, you may want to place them away from a bedroom or any other room where darkness is necessary. On a related note, many of these gardens, like the Lettuce Grow and Gardyn, have loud pump cycles, while Rise's pump runs continuously. I wouldn't recommend placing a garden with a noisy pump cycle near a TV or office, where the noise could be a disturbance during certain times of the day. If any amount of noise is a concern (perhaps you live on the top floor of an apartment), you may want to consider a totally silent garden like the Auk or Click & Grow. How Much Do They Cost to Keep Going? AccordionItemContainerButton LargeChevron Gardens with subscriptions and/or proprietary pods, like Gardyn and Click & Grow, are obviously going to be more expensive over the long run than a truly DIY system like the LetPot. On the one hand, with proprietary pods, you won't have to source seeds or sponges; you can be assured the seeds are appropriate for that system and hydroponics in general, and if something doesn't germinate, you will be able to get a replacement or a refund. But on the other hand, this is a recurring cost that will reduce any savings you gain from growing your own food or flowers. As for power, systems with a continuously running pump, like Rise, are going to cost more than ones with no pump, like the Auk. However, I haven't noticed a significant bump in my electricity bill while testing these gardens, except for one period where I had seven (yes, seven) going at one time. How I Tested AccordionItemContainerButton LargeChevron I unboxed, assembled, and set up each garden exactly as described in the provided instructions, using the seeds, pods, or seedlings that came with the garden. I paid attention to ease of setup, ease of use, maintenance needs, how much space each system required, and how well (or not well) the plants did and why. I noted what was or was not included with each system, and allowed all of the plants to grow to the harvest stage, paying attention to bolting, yields, and general health. I'm a full-time working parent, so I also paid attention to maintenance needs, light schedules, and any general hassles that came up and annoyed me. How I Chose Which Gardens to Test AccordionItemContainerButton LargeChevron I am genuinely passionate about indoor gardening and have an eye on what’s going on in the landscape: what’s new, what’s hot, what’s working for people, what’s not working. I’m always on the lookout for interesting new devices that I find cool and that I believe WIRED readers would like to know about. Affiliate status does not factor into my decision about what to test and write about. If you have a unique, tech-forward indoor garden you like that I haven’t featured, please let me know in the comments. How Do I Acquire Gardens to Review? AccordionItemContainerButton LargeChevron Most of the gardens I receive to test are samples provided by the companies, with no guarantee of coverage or expectation of what that coverage will look like. Some of the gardens are kept by WIRED in order to perform extended testing, while others are donated locally.

Tech.content:
AMD is working on a software update to fix a driver issue that causes excessive, continuous data writes to solid-state drives across its Radeon GPU lineup.

First reported on sites including Tom’s Hardware and Neowin, the bug has been traced to two pieces of software: AMD External Events Client Module and Utility, known as atieclxx.exe or atiesrxx.exe under Windows processes. The background service handles monitoring functions, but as some users have noticed, it’s also writing a large amount of data to SSDs, as much as 432GB in 24 hours, according to Neowin.

This excessive data writing is a concern because it can accelerate the wear and tear on an SSD, potentially shortening its lifespan. According to PC Gamer, that could mean losing 1% of the drive’s health in just a month. As one Reddit poster pointed out, this is not a new bug and in one case may have caused SSD degradation for nearly a year and a half.

More from CNET

In an email to CNET, an AMD spokesperson said the company didn’t have additional details but pointed to a help article that mentions its Adrenalin Edition driver software, which includes the External Events software as a background process. Contrary to reports online that a variety of AMD GPU models could be affected, the help article suggests only Radeon RX 7000 and 9000 series products are affected.

Details are scant on the page, which describes the issue as “excessive SSD write activity” that occurs when systems are idle. It says that AMD is actively working toward a fix and that its knowledge base article will be updated once there’s a resolution. Company staffers have also been posting on Reddit that a fix is coming, potentially as early as the next Adrenalin Edition release, 26.11.1.

The cost of SSDs has spiked dramatically in the last couple of years, so it could be an expensive problem to fix if it causes significant wear on a drive.

How to check for the bug

The same Reddit users who helped uncover the bug and spread the word have a few ideas on how to keep this from happening. First, check the Windows Resource Monitor (you can access it by pressing Windows key + R and typing “resmon”) and look in the Disk tab to see if you’re experiencing excessive writing to your SSD from either atieclxx.exe or atiesrxx.exe processes.

Some who are seeing this are disabling the External Events software entirely. You can do that in Windows by typing Windows key + R and entering “services.msc.” Once there, you can look for the AMD External Events Utility, open its Properties and set Startup Type to Disabled. That will keep it from starting up automatically when you reboot. You can also stop the process while you’re there for the current session. You’ll want to restart your computer after this change.

Keep in mind that disabling the software could affect some display functions and game performance. Others have tried disabling a Resizable Bar, or ReBAR, a PCI Express process for accessing video card memory. Some have switched to alternative AMD drivers that are only compatible with AMD chipsets, not those with Intel or other chipset motherboards.

Using any of those methods carries the risk of breaking other functions on your machine, so make sure your system has a recent restore point.

Tech.title: Logitech Gives Its Employees a Day Off for Grand Theft Auto 6 Launch
Tech.content:
It’s going to be tough to ignore the Nov. 19 release of Grand Theft Auto 6. A PCMag survey reports that roughly 12.5 million US workers are likely to take time off when the game comes out, resulting in over $1 billion in lost productivity. Technology company Logitech is deciding not to fight this, giving the entire company the option to take GTA6 launch day off.

Logitech calls this impromptu company holiday Logi Game Day, and it allows all employees to call off work for a day to play whatever game they want. The company is obviously expecting quite a few people to use the day to play GTA6, but employees who don’t can take a different day off if they choose. This invitation to spend time gaming extends from the upper ranks of Logitech all the way down to the interns.

“It’s time to retire the stereotype that gaming is a waste of time,” Logitech CEO Hanneke Farber said in a statement. “As a company designing products for work and play, we see every day how engagement in one sphere supports performance in the other.”

More from CNET

In addition to giving everyone the day off, the company is also hosting a streaming event on Nov. 19, hosted by Robin Piispanen, general manager of Logitech’s gaming brand, Logitech G.

“We see firsthand how Logitech employees who sharpen their skills in-game translate directly back to work and problem-solving,” Piispanen said in a statement.

The few, the proud, the gamer-friendly companies

Logitech even made a graphic depicting a fake doctor’s note dated Nov. 19 for the big launch. Logitech

Logitech is the largest company to announce company-wide permission to take a day off to play Grand Theft Auto 6, but it’s not the only one. At least three other organizations are granting official paid time off so employees can play the game.

The first such organization to announce free time off for the launch was the US Army’s 9th Brigade Engineer Battalion of the 3rd Infantry Division at Fort Stewart, Georgia, which gave soldiers a four-day leave to play the game if they reenlisted. That leave runs from Nov. 20-23, effectively giving soldiers a four-day weekend.

The SoCal-based company Burger Motorsports announced on its Instagram that it would pause operations for the day on Nov. 19 to give employees time to play the game. Canada’s Edison Motors gave up asking employees to come in on Nov. 19 and 20, granting the company a four-day weekend to play the game.

Why this is a good idea

Companies that take the initiative and give employees days off are ahead of the curve. Rather than penalizing anticipated absences, these employers are leaning into the launch — a move that could yield unexpected workplace benefits.

Logitech cited two such studies in its press release, including one that found that 81% of gamers believe that playing games increases confidence, reduces anxiety and stress, and is directly correlated with stronger day-to-day work performance. The other study showed that 98.8% of enterprise IT decision-makers reported that gaming skills directly translated into work performance.

Psychiatrist Douglas McWilliams told Psychology Today that taking time off to play games can also help reduce burnout, which is one of the leading causes of high turnover, absenteeism, lost productivity, and mental and physical health struggles among employees.

“Being able to mentally detach from work is generally accomplished through taking time off,” McWilliams told the magazine. “For recovery to occur, the time off needs to result in mental disengagement from work; it must involve some sort of activation energy; it must be relaxing; and it must be a decision within an individual’s control.”

McWilliams goes on to say that major video game launches such as Grand Theft Auto 6 and The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time — due out Nov. 21 — can meet these conditions and may positively affect the mental health of employees who take time off to play them.

Tech.title: Amazon Has a New Meal Delivery Partner Ahead of Black Friday
Tech.content:
If you’ve been on the fence about adding an Amazon Prime membership to your list of subscriptions, the new perk might win you over. And it’s just in time for Black Friday and holiday shopping from your couch.

Two words: Uber Eats.

On Thursday, Amazon announced that Prime members in the US will get free delivery on Uber Eats orders made directly through Amazon’s app or website. And you’ll get $20 off the first two Uber Eats eligible orders of $25 or more for the first 14 days, plus Amazon-exclusive offers. That adds up to $40 in savings on Uber Eats orders. And if you have a Prime Visa credit card, you’ll earn 5% back on all Uber Eats orders until Dec. 5, with a Prime membership.

More from CNET

It’s another perk that may make Amazon Prime membership worthwhile, in addition to Black Friday deals that are weeks away. And it may be worthwhile if you already use Uber Eats often or want a cheaper meal delivery option.

How to get the Uber Eats discount on Amazon Prime

In order to get free delivery and $20 off your order, go to the Uber Eats tab at the top of your Amazon app or Uber Eats on Amazon’s website. Place your order as usual with a participating restaurant but make sure the $20 discount applies at checkout.

I tried the new perk and promo out for Saturday’s dinner. However, I will say the tip, a nearly $10 service fee, tax and the delivery fee all added up to the cost of another meal — which is worth paying attention to when you order.

What happened to the Amazon and GrubHub partnership?

But you may wonder what that means for the GrubHub partnership that both Amazon and GrubHub touted for years — dating back to 2022. Before now, your Prime subscription included a GrubHub Plus membership at no additional cost. GrubHub Plus included no delivery fees, lower service fees and 5% back on pickup orders.

The new partnership launched the same day that Lyft and DoorDash announced that they’re teaming up for a new subscription, Lyft Go. An Amazon spokesperson said in an email to CNET that the GrubHub and Amazon partnership ended on Thursday. There’s no telling how long Amazon will partner with Uber Eats.

“We continuously evaluate our third-party offers to ensure they provide the best possible value for Prime members,” the spokesperson said. “As part of that ongoing evaluation, we identified an opportunity to deliver an even better restaurant delivery experience.”

However, a GrubHub spokesperson said in an email to CNET that if you have a Prime membership and activated GrubHub Plus, you’ll have the membership until Dec. 31, 2027.

GrubHub shared a joint statement from Amazon and GrubHub in an email to CNET:

On Nov. 5, Grubhub and Amazon have decided to end the Prime-exclusive Grubhub Plus offer, and Amazon customers will no longer be able to place Grubhub orders through Amazon.com or the Amazon Shopping app. Amazon and Grubhub are proud of the partnership and the value provided to Prime members over the years. As the agreement concludes, both companies remain committed to serving our customers and delivering a great customer experience.

The new Uber Eats perk is now available to all Prime members, including those with Prime Access and Prime for Young Adults. And if you’re looking for another dining option, your Amazon Prime membership still offers free same-day delivery on perishable grocery orders over $25 when you order from Amazon Grocery.

Tech.title: Which Foldable Phone Has the Best Battery Life? We Put Them to the Test
Tech.content:
For years, foldable phones haven’t exactly been praised for their battery life. However, that’s starting to change.

Because of their unique design, foldables have traditionally struggled to match the battery life of conventional slab phones. Their massive displays, space-consuming hinge mechanisms and limited room for heat dissipation all present challenges. But battery technology has improved in recent years, with some of the newest foldables benefiting from higher-energy-density silicon-carbon batteries and more power-efficient processors. Even slim phones like the Galaxy Z Fold 8 can last all day, showing that you don’t have to sacrifice practicality for a sleek, innovative design.

Still, foldable phones remain a niche category, even with a major player like Apple entering the market with the iPhone Duo. But they offer an appealing alternative for anyone looking to break away from the sameness of more traditional slab phones. And with battery life being a key consideration when choosing a new device, it’s important to know which phone can keep up with all your scrolling, streaming and snapping without constantly reaching for a charger.

We’ve dug into CNET’s extensive smartphone lab data to find out which foldable phone in 2026 delivers the best battery life. Because book-style and flip phones differ in design and screen size, we’re separating the results to provide a more accurate comparison.

Here’s how devices from Samsung, Apple, Google and Motorola stack up.

Which book-style foldable has the best battery life?

This year, CNET has reviewed and tested five book-style foldable phones: the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8, Z Fold 8 Ultra, Motorola Razr Fold, Google Pixel 11 Pro Fold and the Apple iPhone Duo. These devices are phone-tablet hybrids, with designs ranging from taller, narrower builds to squatter, passport-style designs. (We didn’t include Samsung’s Galaxy Z TriFold because of its unique design.)

Apple’s $1,999 iPhone Duo may be late to the foldable game, arriving seven years after Samsung’s first Galaxy Fold ushered in the modern era of foldable phones. Still, given Apple’s strong brand loyalty and mainstream appeal, the Duo has generated considerable buzz.

And there’s another reason Apple’s first foldable deserves attention: its battery. The iPhone Duo achieved the highest average score in CNET’s testing among book-style phones. It’s a testament to its dual-cell battery design, which is standard in foldables, and the efficiency of the A20 Pro chip powering the device.

To test a phone’s battery, CNET runs a 3-hour streaming video test and a 45-minute endurance test that includes watching videos, scrolling through social media, playing a game and joining a video call. Both tests take place on the foldable phone’s inner screen, starting with a full charge and while connected to Wi-Fi.

The iPhone Duo had the highest remaining charge after the 45-minute endurance test, finishing with 99%. It ended the 3-hour streaming test with 84%, placing it just below the Razr Fold, Galaxy Z Fold 8 and Z Fold 8 Ultra in that category. That average gives the Duo, which has a 4,883-mAh battery, the number-one place in our foldable battery tests.

Not far behind is the Razr Fold, Motorola’s first book-style foldable. This phone has a whopping 6,000-mAh silicon-carbon battery, which helped it earn one of the top spots in our battery testing.

Samsung’s Galaxy Z Fold 8, which is the company’s first palm-size foldable phone, just barely tops the more standard-size Z Fold 8 Ultra. Both phones are the thinnest in this ranking, which makes their results even more impressive. The Galaxy Z Fold 8 measures 4.5mm thick when unfolded and 9.7mm when folded, and has a 4,800-mAh silicon-carbon battery. The Z Fold 8 Ultra is 4.1mm thick when open and 8.9mm when closed, and it has a 5,000-mAh silicon-carbon battery.

Close behind the competition is Google’s Pixel 11 Pro Fold, which has a 4,806-mAh battery. Like the other phones, including the iPhone Duo, it performed relatively better in the endurance test than in the streaming test. That suggests these devices handle shorter bursts of use well but can take a more noticeable battery hit during prolonged activities like video streaming. Even so, they should easily power through a full day of mixed use, whether you’re watching movies, scrolling through social media or taking photos.

Overall, every book-style foldable we tested demonstrated strong battery results. Beyond the numbers, our hands-on experience suggests you can get through most days without constantly worrying about your phone’s battery level. Be sure to check out CNET’s in-depth reviews for more on the everyday experience using each of these phones.

Which clamshell foldable has the best battery life?

Some people may prefer the more nostalgic design of a flip phone. Motorola revived its iconic Razr brand for the smartphone era, and now has a handful of devices at varying price points to choose from. Samsung’s Galaxy Z Flip 8 is another pocket-friendly choice.

These clamshell devices have less space for a battery than larger foldable and slab phones. Still, Motorola’s and Samsung’s battery specs are nothing to sniff at.

This year’s $800 Motorola Razr has a 4,800-mAh battery, the $1,100 Razr Plus has a 4,500-mAh battery and the $1,500 Razr Ultra has a 5,000-mAh battery. Meanwhile, the $1,200 Z Flip 8 has a 4,300-mAh battery. Every one of these phones uses a silicon-carbon battery to squeeze more power into a smaller design.

Impressively, the baseline Motorola Razr got the best average score in our battery testing of clamshell phones. It also had the highest result in CNET’s 3-hour streaming test among its peers and tied with the much pricier Razr Ultra in our battery endurance test. The Razr Ultra, Galaxy Z Flip 8 and Razr Plus are in close succession.

Interestingly, the flip phones aren’t that far behind their book-style counterparts in our testing. One key advantage is that their smaller cover and inner displays require less power, helping them keep pace with larger foldables.

The results are also a testament to how battery technology is progressing, with the mobile industry increasingly shifting toward high-density silicon-carbon batteries, which can pack more capacity into tighter dimensions. This means that regardless of whether you choose a book-style or clamshell foldable, you can be assured that your battery won’t leave you in the lurch as you go about your day.

Final thoughts: How good is the battery life on foldable phones?

From the newest foldables like the iPhone Duo and Pixel 11 Pro Fold to flip phones from Motorola and Samsung, you no longer have to sacrifice battery life for a more versatile mobile design. Today’s devices can comfortably get you through a full day of swiping, scrolling and snapping photos, even with larger screens to power.

In fact, when ranked among all the phones CNET tested this year, including non-folding options, the iPhone Duo sits among the top five performers, with the iPhone 18 Pro Max taking the top overall spot.

That’s especially important given that a major part of a foldable phone’s appeal is the ability to switch between two displays. You can quickly send a text on a smaller screen, then move to a larger one to watch a movie, for example. That versatility requires a battery capable of handling more intensive tasks like streaming and gaming, as well as extended activities like browsing and working across multiple displays.

And while the iPhone Duo and Motorola Razr topped CNET’s foldable battery tests, the other phones we evaluated weren’t far behind, highlighting just how competitive battery life has become across the leading brands. Ultimately, choosing the right foldable will come down to other factors, including camera performance, design and price.

Our testing data, combined with real-world experiences shared in our in-depth reviews, illustrates just how far foldable phones have evolved. They’re no longer just a novelty; they’ve become increasingly practical devices in their own right.

Tech.title: Your Air Fryer Can Make Perfect Hard-Boiled Eggs
Tech.content:
Hard-boiled eggs should be one of the simplest things you cook, but in practice, the stovetop method requires a multistep production involving boiling water, careful timing and an ice bath. But there’s a better way to cook up those eggs, and it’s been sitting on your counter this whole time. The air fryer makes hard-boiled eggs that are just as good, consistently easier to peel and completely hands-off from start to finish.

The rapid air cooks them with perfect consistency, freeing you up to do anything else while they’re in the air fryer basket, which makes changing methods a no-brainer. You get eggs that are easy to peel and cooked exactly how you want them, without any of the babysitting. It’s time to retire the pot and let the machine take over.

The Best Air Fryers Out of Dozens We Tested See at CNET

Air fryer hard-boiled eggs come out consistently cooked and dramatically easier to peel than the stovetop version. Pamela Vachon/CNET

Why you should make hard-boiled eggs in the air fryer

A better question is, why shouldn’t you make hard-boiled (or soft-boiled, or any cooked-in-shell) eggs in the air fryer? It’s not like boiling water is adding any flavor, as it would with salted pasta water. Like most tasks you might put the air fryer to, cooking eggs this way yields more consistent results with fewer variables, in less time and with less cleanup involved. I basically gave it a quick wipe out with a paper towel once I was finished with the egg cooking experiment.

More from CNET

The case is basically closed, but if you need more reasons, your eggs have a decreased risk of cracking during cooking, which can be caused by being jostled around during a rolling boil. Even the smallest air fryers can manage at least a half-dozen eggs or more. Plus, it’s another tick on the list of reasons to leave the air fryer out on the counter, letting it handle as many kitchen tasks as possible for you.



Best practices for making boiled eggs in the air fryer

High heat in the air fryer produces uneven cooking and makes them harder to peel. Pamela Vachon/CNET

From yolks between runny to jammy to hard-cooked, the air fryer can handle it. No waiting for water to boil, no forgetting to set a timer at the key moment. There’s a lot of internet voodoo about dos and don’ts when it comes to boiled eggs in the air fryer, but in my experience, you can disregard most of it. You don’t need to bring eggs to room temperature first. You don’t need a layer of foil as a nest for your eggs. You don’t really even need to preheat the air fryer. (Who started the rumor that air fryers need to preheat anyway? They’re not ovens.)

Here’s what you should do for the best air fryer boiled eggs

Test with a single egg first to determine the best temperature and timing for your air fryer model. (While I wholeheartedly stand by this method, I wouldn’t go in with a dozen all at once without having tried it out first.)

Use a low-temperature setting between 270 and 300 degrees Fahrenheit.

Arrange eggs in a single layer.

Set the air fryer timer based on the kind of yolk you want (see times below).

Plunge cooked eggs in cold water, removing them from the air fryer to stop residual heat from taking the yolk any further and to ensure easy peeling.

Submerge eggs in cold water after cooking. Pamel Vachon/CNET

Cooking times for air fryer boiled eggs

Runny yolk : 7-8 minutes

: 7-8 minutes Soft yolk : 9-10 minutes

: 9-10 minutes Jammy yolk : 12-13 minutes

: 12-13 minutes Hard-cooked yolk: 15-17 minutes

Nine minutes in the air fryer produces a perfectly soft-boiled egg. Pamela Vachon/CNET

Mistakes to avoid for air-fryer boiled eggs

Don’t fall into the trap of thinking that cranking the heat on the air fryer will allow you to shave a significant number of minutes off the cooking time. While air fryer-boiled eggs take a little less time, as they don’t require waiting for water to boil, they aren’t designed to complete the task quickly. In my experience, a higher temperature in the convection environment of the air fryer caused the eggs to cook unevenly. (Consider that boiling water is only 212 degrees Fahrenheit.)

I read a handful of comments about air-fried boiled eggs that suggested they were harder to peel. I didn’t find that to be the case at all when using a lower temperature setting. However, I did find that to be true for the one egg I cooked at about 400 degrees. It also produced an “eggier” smell while the egg was cooking.

Tech.title: From Green Screen to Gray Box: AI Is Stepping Onto the Hollywood Sound Stage
Tech.content:
On screen, a woman runs toward a cliff and peers anxiously over the edge, teetering as she looks down at a perilous mountain dotted with boulders, her hair flying in the wind.

She’s not, though. I can see her from where I’m standing in the middle of a Disney sound stage in Los Angeles. She’s standing in a “gray box,” a small, walled-off space on the studio floor, neutral-colored walls speckled with small cross marks for positioning. She’s next to a stack of blue-carpeted boxes that serve as a stand-in for whatever large prop that post-production decides to add in digitally later.

A camera is pointing at her, following her every move. And an almost instant rendering on a screen has placed her on that cliff, perfectly lit, wind tousling her hair, thanks in part to AI.

More from CNET

Green screens and blue screens have been used for more than half a century in TV and filmmaking, allowing post-production crews to insert visual effects and backgrounds behind the actors. But the bright hue can reflect onto objects and skin, and constant adjustments to the backdrop are needed when the director wants to switch to a new angle of the shot.

Filming in a gray box like the one I’m standing next to offers more flexible shots. And combining that with AI-generated or assisted backgrounds speeds up post-production, according to entertainment studio Promise Advanced Imagination, which showcased its filming product during the Disney Accelerator Demo Day last week.

Even the lighting changes instantly to match the sets being generated or assisted by AI. Disney/Screenshots by CNET

Setting up shots takes less time in gray boxes than it does with a green screen background, Promise co-founder and chief creative officer Dave Clark told me, giving crews more time to be creative because “they’re not bogged down by having to take 2 to 3 hours to change the setup.”

“You’re able to still capture the right performance and the right blocking … this allows me to just focus on the story, focus on the creative and not worry,” Clark said. “You can get multiple takes because you can get them faster, you don’t have to worry about moving the crew, you don’t have to worry about changing lights, everything stays consistent so I can just focus on the story.”

Crews can save time while filming by using these gray boxes. More time (and cost) is saved during post-production by using AI tools to help fill in the backgrounds and replace lighting and objects.

While some environments are wholly AI-created, most are made by human 3D renderers and visual effects artists working with AI as one of their tools. Using AI to help fill in backgrounds lowers the cost of production but still ensures it has the size and scale of high-quality productions, Clark says, with production companies needing a lot less capital to produce pilots.

Clark, who’s also a director, insists that everything still “goes through the hands of human artists,” however.

“Much like Disney or Pixar, the process begins with the script, then it goes into storyboard and then (filming),” Clark said. “I think that traditional mindset and that traditional skill set that you only learn over decades of experience is really what amplifies this technology and lets it work for your creative capabilities.”

As filmmaking and animation studios increasingly explore the use of AI tools in streamlining productions, there have been concerns that human jobs will be removed, including across actors, animators, writers, set designers and more.

David Min, vice president of Disney Innovation, told me this system just fills in the background of movies, which is already done with other technologies, such as green screens. This just makes it easier and faster, since lighting changes can even be done in post-production. It means the people on set can focus just on the performances and direction. There will always be directors, writers and actors, he said.

Disney CEO Josh D’Amaro agrees, saying “technology itself is not the goal.”

“We’re being very aggressive about exploring emerging technologies,” D’Amaro said at the event. “It’s to put it in the hands of our creators … to create these incredible and immersive stories.”

Corinne Reichert/CNET

During the demo day at Walt Disney Studios in Burbank, California, Promise CEO George Strompoulis explained to the media that the company — which bills itself as a generative AI studio developing movies, series and visual effects to “support human artistry” — is made up of four major components: Promise Studios can help produce “studio-quality features at a fraction of the cost and timeline”; then there’s the Muse AI technology platform workflow software; the Curious Refuge AI Filmmaking academy, to serve as “a pipeline of the best artists in the world” and to “upscale” existing film industry workers; and The Generation Company, which is Promise’s AI visual effects business.

Promise has done some testing with the Disney teams, and has a series pilot in production with another studio.

“I think it’s easy for people to have the misconception that there’s an AI button that could just make a movie,” said Rob Bredow, senior vice president of creative innovation at Disney. “That is not the approach that Disney’s taking; it’s not the approach that Promise is taking, which is why this has been a good collaboration.”

I watch the screens as the same woman from the cliff edge now appears to be crouching fearfully next to a blown-out car as explosions rain debris around her.

She’s still right in front of me, squatting next to those blue boxes in the Disney studio sound stage, camera trained on her. I also watch her pick up a screwdriver from the floor. On screen, it transforms into a mysterious scroll out of a Lara Croft-esque adventure movie.

“The ability to do this at cinematic-quality level is something that we’re at the beginning stages of now,” Clark said. “You not only need great filmmakers; you need creative technologists, you need artists who are masters in the AI tools.”

Tech.title: Want Apple Intelligence for Your Home Security Camera? You’ll Need These 4 Things
Tech.content:
Aqara is one of the few camera brands that works well with Apple products. Aqara

In the past months Apple has unveiled a host of new Apple Intelligence and Siri AI features, with more on the way. And some features immediately caught my attention because they can enable security cameras on Apple devices in all-new ways. The most interesting option even adds video descriptions, essentially using AI to “read” your security clips and give you texts about what’s happening in them, so you don’t have to view them yourself.

It’s a nifty trick, one that I’ve seen come to Google Nest, Arlo, Ring, Blink and other home security camera companies in the past year or two. Now it’s Apple’s turn, but enabling this AI feature takes more work this time around. Apple wants to keep users inside its ecosystem, so there are more requirements than usual for smart video descriptions and similar capabilities. Let’s go through exactly what you’ll need.

1. A newer iPhone or iPad, updated to the latest software

The iPhone 18 Pro and the iPhone Duo both can run Apple Intelligence features. Patrick Holland/CNET

Apple Intelligence doesn’t run on just any device. Your first requirement is an iPhone or iPad that can handle it. If you recently downloaded iOS 27 or iPadOS 27 and received an update about Apple Intelligence now being on your device, you should be good to go.

More from CNET

Specifically, you’ll need an iPhone 15 Pro, iPhone 15 Pro Max or iPhone 16 model or later to run these features. If you prefer using an iPad, you’ll need the iPad Mini (A17 Pro or later) or an iPad model with the M1 chip or later.

Before you start using security features with Apple Intelligence, make sure everything is updated – you’ll want the latest iOS if you don’t have it yet.

2. A home hub Apple device

The Mini 2 can’t compete with the large HomePod but otherwise does very well. Tyler Lacoma/CNET

Smart home devices that work with Apple Home typically need a hub to pair with, and security cameras using Apple Intelligence are no exception. That means you’ll need another Apple device that can act as a hub, and you’ve got several choices.

Apple hubs include the second-gen HomePod, the HomePod Mini and Mini 2 or an Apple TV 4K model. Apple briefly gave some iPads the ability to become home hubs but then stopped, so an iPad won’t be sufficient here.

3. A compatible security camera for Apple Home

Apple’s new camera line has 2.5K resolution and works readily with Apple devices. Ajay Kumar/CNET

You’ll need a security camera that works well with Apple Home, but that’s easier said than done. If you can wait, Apple’s own security camera line, made in partnership with LG, should be here by the end of 2026, and should have the best results.

However, those Apple cams will be very expensive, so I understand if you want to look for a more affordable option. Not many security cams currently work with Apple, but one of the best brands is Aqara, like this Aqara G3650 camera hub ($140) I’m testing right now. Aqara models go down to $40, so there’s plenty of room to save here.

Note that, at least for the base subscription, I’ve seen reports that AI features like video descriptions only work with one camera at a time, so getting a whole fleet of cams won’t make much difference here. And speaking of subscriptions, there’s one final piece you’ll want.

4. The right iCloud Plus subscription

Apple Intelligence features may require an advanced iCloud subscription. Apple/Screenshot by CNET

You’ll want an iCloud Plus subscription to enable the full suite of Siri AI capabilities and avoid running into daily limits. But to be clear, even if you don’t use Siri AI, these security Apple Intelligence features will require at least a 2TB plan, which starts at $10 per month. That’s not surprising – video descriptions like this typically come with a subscription requirement, up to $20 per month in some cases.

Now you’ve got everything you need for Apple Intelligence security features. To get started, just go to Apple Home, go to Home Settings and make sure Apple Intelligence is toggled on. Then you should be able to choose an added camera to turn on video descriptions.
